units.la: ETVS verbũ est, illu-strissime Princeps, Patria est vbicumque est bene, Teucro Telamonis filio attributum: multisque seculis coprobatum. nam fortis animi excelsiq; videtur esse, vt cetera incommoda, sic etiam exilium, æquo animo ferre: ingrataéq; patriæ, tanquam nouercæ, iniurias contemnere. Verùm, ego longè esse arbitror secus. nam si parentum mores, atq; adeò asperitatem iniquius ferre, sceleratum, ac prope impium videtur: quanto magis patriæ quam sapientes omnes, una & mente & voce, semper parentibus anteposuerunt. Est quidem hominis securi, & de suis tantùm commodis cogitantis, patriæ caritatem suis opportunitatib. metiri. sed illa tāta securitas, pars quædam eius immanitatis videtur, quæ propria, vel Epicureorum, vel Cynicorum fuit: unde vox illa furialis profecta est, Me mortuo, terra misceatur incēdio. à qua ne illud quidem vetus Tyrannicum abhorret, Pereat amici, dum unà inimici intercidant. Est in mansuetis ingeniis caritas quædam innata patriæ, quæ deleri, nisi cum reliquis humanitatis sensibus, non potest. qualem caritatem Homerus in Vlysse describit, qui patriam Ithacam saxis præruptis & asperis, tanquam nidulum, affixam, omnibus tamen deliciis, atque adeo Regno sibi à Calypsone oblato anteposuit.
units.tr: "Wherever one is well off, there is one's country" is a saying, most illustrious Prince, attributed to Teucer, son of Telamon, and approved through many ages. For it seems the mark of a strong and lofty spirit to bear exile calmly, as it bears other misfortunes, and to scorn the wrongs of an ungrateful country as if it were a stepmother. But I think quite otherwise. For if to bear the manners and harshness of one's parents more unjustly seems wicked and almost impious, how much more so [is it to bear unjustly the wrongs] of one's country, which all wise men, with one mind and one voice, have always placed before parents. Indeed, it belongs to a man who is careless and thinks only of his own advantage to measure love of country by his own convenience. But such carelessness is a part of that savagery which was peculiar to the Epicureans or the Cynics, from which came that frenzied cry: "When I am dead, let the earth be mixed with fire." Not even that old tyrant's saying shrinks from it: "Let friends perish, provided the enemies perish with them." In gentle natures there is a certain love of country implanted, which cannot be destroyed except together with the rest of the feelings of humanity. Homer describes such love in Ulysses, who preferred his country Ithaca, fixed like a little nest upon steep and rough rocks, to all delights, and even to the kingdom offered him by Calypso.

units.la: Nescio qua natale solum dulcedine cunctos Afficit, immemores nec sinit esse sui,
units.tr: I know not by what sweetness the native soil moves all men, and does not let them forget themselves.

units.la: vt vere Poeta vetus cecinit: cùm & cœli, vnde primum spiritum duximus, & soli in quo prima vestigia posuimus, & cognatorum, propinquorum, æqualiúmque nobis in mentem venit. Verumenimuerò, dicet aliquis, delira interdum patria est, mentisque errore afficitur: vt Plato de sua locutus est: interdum etiam furore amens crudeliter bacchatur, atque in sua viscera sæuit. Primùm cautio est, ne alienam culpam innocenti patriæ ascribamus. Multi Romæ, multi aliis in locis Tyranni immanes fuerunt. hi non modò bonos viros, verumetiam benemeritos de patria cives omnibus cruciatibus afficiebant. Continuóne verum fuit, illorũ insânias patriæ acceptas ferre? Memoratur Imperatoris Macrini crudelitas: quem Iulius Capitolinus Macellinum nominatum scribit, propterea quòd domus eius, vt macellum sanguine pecudum, sic illa hominũ sanguine cruentabatur. Complures alij passim ab historicis commemorantur: quorum alius (vt idem Capitolinus scribit) ab eadem crudelitate Cyclops, alius Busiris, alius Siron, alius Typhon, alius Gyges nominatus est: cum illi sic animum induxissent, regna & imperia nisi crudelitate retineri non posse. Idcircone cura omnis & solicitudo patriæ, ciuibus bonis abiiciendâ fuit? imo verò tanquam oppressæ & miseræ & natorum opem imploranti succurrendum: remediaque modis omnibus coquirenda. quamquam, ô for-
units.tr: As the old poet truly sang, when there come into our minds both the sky from which we first drew breath, and the soil on which we first set our feet, and our kinsmen, relations, and companions, all the tortures afflicted them. But someone will say: "Sometimes the fatherland is mad and is affected by a derangement of mind, as Plato said of his own; sometimes too, raving with fury, it rages cruelly and turns against its own vitals." First of all, we must take care not to ascribe another's guilt to an innocent country. Many cruel tyrants have existed at Rome and in other places. These not only subjected good men, and citizens who had deserved well of their country, to every kind of torment. Is it true, then, that the madness of these men must be borne as the fault of the fatherland? The cruelty of the Emperor Macrinus is recorded, whom Julius Capitolinus writes was named Macellinus, because his house was stained with human blood as the meat-market is with the blood of cattle. Several others are mentioned here and there by historians: of whom one (as the same Capitolinus writes) was called a Cyclops for the same cruelty, another Busiris, another Siron, another Typhon, another Gyges, since they had made up their minds that kingdoms and empires could not be kept except by cruelty. Is therefore all care and concern for the fatherland to be cast off by good citizens? On the contrary, one must come to the aid of one's country as of someone oppressed, wretched, and imploring the help of its children, and remedies must be sought by every means. Although, alas,

units.la: ô fortunatas bonis & mansuetis Principibus regiones: ô beatos cives, quibus Principum suorum benignitate, tranquillè licet in patriis avitísque sedibus, cum coniugibus & liberis consenescere. nam plerunque certè vsuuenit, vt remedia malis ipsis, quibus ea quæruntur, deteriora sint. Anni sunt, vt opinor, sexdecim, Princeps illustrissime, ex quo Deus optimus maximus partem Germaniæ Rhenanæ nō exiguam fidei ac potestati C.T. commendauit. vix dici potest, quantam ex eo tempore tranquillitatem, & tanquam in pacato mari malaciam toto Palatinatu videre licuerit: quàm pacata semper sedataque omnia, quàm piè, sanctè, & religiosè constituta. Macte igitur ista mansuetudine esto, clementissime Princeps: quod ego, quantum & animi & corporis viribus contendere possum, iterum exclamo: Macte ista virtute esto, placida & mansueta: nō quemadmodum Seneca memoriæ prodidit, moris apud Romanos fuisse, vt sanguinolentis & ex acie redeuntibus, Macellinis deniq; cruore madentibus diceretur, Macte virtute esto. Sed macte ista mansuetudine animi, clementia, pietate, iustitia, facilitate, & imperij ac ditionis tuæ tranquillitate.
units.tr: O regions fortunate in good and gentle princes! O citizens blessed, who under the kindness of their princes may grow old quietly, with their wives and children, in their ancestral homes. For it very often happens that the remedies turn out worse than the evils they were sought to cure. It is, I think, sixteen years, most illustrious Prince, since God, best and greatest, entrusted a not small part of the Rhenish Germany to the faith and power of Your Highness. It can hardly be said how much tranquillity has been seen since that time, and how, as on a calm sea, there has been a dead calm throughout the whole Palatinate: how peaceful and settled everything has always been, how piously, holily and religiously it has been ordered. Therefore, blessed be you in that gentleness, most merciful Prince; and I, with all the strength of mind and body I can muster, cry out again: blessed be you in that virtue, calm and gentle. Not as Seneca records, that it was the custom among the Romans to say to those returning bloodied from the battle line, and at last to Macellinus drenched in gore, "Blessed be you in your virtue." But blessed be you in that gentleness of spirit, in clemency, piety, justice, affability, and in the tranquillity of your rule and dominion.

units.la: Atque hic cùm fere sit vestræ Germaniæ status, quemadmodum qui nauigationem instituunt, freta turbulenta, & tumultuosa deuitant, sedatos ac tranquillos cursus quærunt: similiter quamplurimi hodie regiones latrociniis infestas fugiunt, tranquillas & pacatas quærunt. Ac fuit tempus, cùm in Francogallia nostram undique ex omnibus terrarum oris, sese studiosi adole-
units.tr: And since the state of your Germany is nearly of this kind, just as those who undertake a voyage avoid turbulent and tempestuous straits and seek calm and tranquil courses, so very many today flee regions infested with brigandage and seek tranquil and peaceful ones. And there was a time when from every quarter of the earth, young scholars betook themselves to our France from all directions.

units.la: olescentes effunderent, & ad nostras Academias, tanquam ad bonarum artium mercaturam conferrent. nūc illas quasi maria piratis infesta horrent, neque secus quàm Cyclopicam barbariem execrantur. Cuius rei meū pectus memoria exulcerat: cùm cogito miseram & infortunatam patriam duodecim iam feré annorum spatio incendiis ciuilibus exarsisse. Sed multo me acerbior excruciat dolor, cum considero non modò tam multos esse otiosos incendiorum spectatores, (qualem olim Neronem Romæ conflagrantis fuisse memorant) verumetiam flammas illas impiorum quorundam vocibus ac libellis, tanquam flabellis, excitari: ad eas autē extinguendas perpaucos ac feré nullos accurrere. Mea quidem quam sit tenuis, quamq; humilis conditio non sum ignarus. sed ta-
units.tr: ...young men poured in from every corner of the earth and flocked to our Academies as to a market for the liberal arts. Now they shudder at them as at seas infested by pirates, and they curse them no less than they would a Cyclopean barbarism. My heart is sore with the memory of this. When I think that our unhappy and ill-fated country has for almost twelve years now been set ablaze by civil fires, I am tormented by a grief far more bitter, because I see that there are not only so many idle spectators of these burnings (like Nero, as they say, once watching Rome in flames), but that those flames are also being fanned by the voices and pamphlets of certain impious men, as if with fans, while hardly anyone, or almost no one, runs to put them out. I am not unaware of how slight and humble my own position is. But ta-

units.la: men ut in communi incendio si quis quantumuis abiecta fortuna sitellam aquæ deferat, studium credo eius nemo repudiet: ita spero neminem patriæ communis amantem meam hanc in quærendis remediis operam aspernaturum. Superioribus quidem mentibus in tantarum calamitatum cogitatione defixus, veteres Francogalliæ nostræ historicos & Gallos & Germanos euolui: summamque ex eorum scriptis confeci eius status, quem annos amplius mille in Republicano-stra viguisse testantur: ex qua incredibile dictu est quantam maiorum nostrorum in constituenda Republica nostra sapientiam cognoscere liceat. ut mihi quidem nequaquam dubium esse videatur, quin ab illa certissimum tantorum malorum remedium peteнdum sit. Nam mihi attentius in ista-rum rum calamitatum caussam inquirenti, sic videbatur: sicuti corpora nostra vel externo impulsu atq; ictu, vel intestinis humorum vitiis, vel senio intereunt: ita Rerumpublicarum alias hostili impetu, alias domesticis dissensionibus, alias vetustate confici. nostræ autem Reipublicæ incommoda etsi vulgò ex intestinis dissidiis nata existimantur, tamen hanc non caussam, sed principium malorum esse animaduerti: quod principium à caussa plurimum discrepare, grauis auctor inprimis Polybius demonstrat. Caussam autem confirmo esse plagam quam annis abhinc circiter centum ab illo accepit, quem constat primum omnium præclara maiorum nostrorum instituta labefactasse. Quemadmodum autē corpora nostra externo aliquo ictu luxata sanari, nisi mēbris suum quibus-
units.tr: Still, just as in a general fire, if someone of however lowly fortune carries a little bucket of water, I believe no one would reject his zeal, so I hope that no one who loves our common country will scorn this effort of mine in seeking remedies. Earlier, while my mind was fixed on the thought of such great calamities, I went through the old historians of our France, both Gallic and German, and from their writings I drew up a summary of the constitution which, they testify, flourished in our Republic for more than a thousand years. From it one can learn, incredible to say, how great was the wisdom of our ancestors in establishing our Republic. So it seems to me beyond doubt that the most certain remedy for such great evils must be sought from that constitution. For when I inquired more carefully into the cause of these calamities, this is how it appeared to me: just as our bodies perish either from an external blow or impact, or from internal corruption of the humours, or from old age, so commonwealths are destroyed, some by hostile attack, some by domestic dissensions, and some by age. Although the troubles of our Republic are commonly thought to arise from internal dissensions, I have observed that these are not the cause but the beginning of the evils; and that the beginning differs greatly from the cause is shown above all by the weighty author Polybius. I maintain, however, that the cause is the blow which our Republic received about a hundred years ago from the man who is known to have been the first to undermine the excellent institutions of our ancestors. But just as our bodies, dislocated by some external blow, are not restored unless each of their members is set back in its own

units.la: que in locum & naturalem sedem restitutis, non possunt: ita Rempublicam nostram tum denique sanatam iri confidimus, cùm in suum antiquum & tanquam naturalem statum diuino aliquo beneficio restituetur. Et quia C. T. patriæ nostræ semper se amicissimam præbuit, optimum factu iudicaui, summam hanc historiæ nostræ illustrissimo tuo nomini inscribere, quasique consecrare: ut eius patrocinio atque auctoritate tutior in hominum manus peruenire possit. Vale Illustrissime Princeps, & Salue. Deũ opt. max. oro, ut illustrissimum genus vestrum perpetuò beatissimum ac florentissimum esse patiatur. XII. Kalendas Septemb. MDLXXIII. Illustriss. C.T. obsequentissimus Franc. Hotomanus.
units.tr: and cannot be healed unless they are restored to their proper place and natural seat. In the same way, I trust that our commonwealth will at last be made whole when, by some divine blessing, it is restored to its old and, as it were, natural condition. Because C. T. has always shown the greatest goodwill toward our fatherland, I judged it best to inscribe this summary of our history to your most illustrious name, and so, as it were, to consecrate it, so that under your patronage and authority it may come more safely into people's hands. Farewell, most illustrious Prince, and be well. I pray God, best and greatest, to allow your most illustrious house to remain forever most blessed and flourishing. Twelve days before the Kalends of September, 1573. Your most illustrious C. T.'s most obedient servant, Franciscus Hotomanus.

units.la: De statu Galliæ priusquam à Romanis in prouinciam redigeretur. CAP. I.
units.tr: On the condition of Gaul before it was reduced by the Romans into a province. CHAP. I.

units.la: OGITANTI mihi de Francogalliæ nostræ institutis, quantum ad vsum Reipub. nostræ, & horum temporum opportunitate satis esse videbitur, conscribere: principiò exponendum videtur, qui Galliæ status fuerit, antequam à Romanis in Prouinciæ formam redigeretur. Nam quæ de gentis origine & antiquitate, de bellicis laudibus, eloquétię studio, regionis situ & natura, priuatorumque moribus apud Cæsarem, Polybium, Strabonem, Ammianum & reliquos scripta extant, nota sunt omnibus, mediocriter quidem eruditis. Pleraque Gallia (inquibat M. ille Cato Censorius in Originibus) duas res industriosissime persequitur: rem militarem, & argutissime loqui. Intelligendum est igitur, eo tum statu Galliam fuisse, vt neq; vniuersa vnius
units.tr: Pondering what I should set down about the institutions of our France, as far as they bear on the government of our commonwealth and on what suits the present times, it seems right first to explain what the condition of Gaul was before it was reduced by the Romans into the form of a province. For what has been written about the origin and antiquity of the people, their military glory, their devotion to eloquence, the situation and nature of the region, and the private customs of its inhabitants, in Caesar, Polybius, Strabo, Ammianus and the others, is known to everyone at least moderately learned. Most of Gaul, said that famous Cato the Censor in his Origins, pursues two things most diligently: warfare, and speaking very keenly. It must therefore be understood that Gaul was then in such a state that it was neither ruled in its entirety by a single power, nor was each of its states under the power of the people or of the nobles;

units.la: A imperio regeretur: neque singulæ ciuitates vel in populi, vel in Optimatū potestate esset: sed ita diuisam in Ciuitates Galliā vniuersam fuisse, vt plereq; Optimatū consilio regeretur, quę Libere dicebātur: ceteræ Reges habepět: omnes qui de hoc institutū tenerent, vt certo anni tempore publicū gentis conciliū agerent: quo in cōcilio quæ ad summā Reipub. pertinere videbantur, cōstituerent. Ciuitates autem quatuor & sexaginta Corn. Tacitus numerat lib.3. hoc est, vt ex Cæsare intelligitur, Regiones, quæ non modò lingua, moribus, & institutis, verùm etiam ijsdē magistratibus vtebantur: quales ipse multis locis Æduorum, Aruernorum, & Rhemorum ciuitates præcipuè commemorat. Itaque cùm Æduum Dumnorigem Cæsar interficiendum curaret, resistere, inquit, ac se manu defendere, suorumque fidem implorare cœpit: sæpe clamitans, liberum se, liberæq; ciuitatis esse. libro quinto, cap. 3. Quapropter in eandem sententiam Strabo lib. 4. ita scribit: ἀεὶ συχραπικὰ δ' ἥσαν ἀπλεῖους τῶν πολιτειῶν ἕνα δ' ἡγεμόνα ἡρῶντο κατ' ἐναντίον παλαιὸν ὡς δ' αὔτως εἰς πόλεμον εἰς ὑπὸ τῶν πολλῶν ἀπδεικνυῶς σπαρτός. Pleraq;, inquit, ciuitates Optimatum consilijs regebantur: vnum aūt magistratum olim quotannis deligebant: sicut & ad bellum gerendū vnus à populo imperator creabatur. Eodē pertinet ḡ Cæsar lib.6. ca.4. his scribit verbis: Quæ ciuitates commodius suam Rēp. administrare existimantur, habent legib. sanctū, si qs quid de Reipub. à finitimis rumore aut fama acceperit, vt ad Magistratū deferat, néve cũ quo alio cómunicet: Magistratus quæ vila sunt, occultant: quæq; esse ex vlu iudicauerint, multitudini produnt. De Rep. nisi per conciliũ loqui nõ conceditur. De communi vero totius Gentis cõcilio pauca hæc ex Cæsare testimonia proferemus. Petierunt, (inquit, lib. 1 .c.12.) vt sibi concilium totius Galliæ in diem certâ indicere, idq; Cæsaris voluntate facere liceret. Item lib.7. c. 12. Totius Galliæ concilium Bibracte indicitur. eodem conueniunt vndiq; frequētes multitudines. Et lib. 6. cap. 1. Cæsar concilio Gallię primo vere (vt instituerat) indicto, cùm reliqui præter Senones, Carnutes, Treuirosque venirent, concilium Lutetiam Parifiorum transfert. Et lib.7.cap.6. Quæ ab reliquis Gallijs ciuitates dissentiebant, has sua diligentia (de Vercingentorige loquitur) adiunctûrũ, atq; vnum concilium totius Galliæ effecturũ, cui cõcilio ne orbis quidem terrarũ possit obstare. Iam verò de regibus, qui ciuitatib. quibusdā præerant, loca sunt apud eundem auctorem propè innumera: ex quib. illud memoria dignũ intelligitur, moris fuisse Romanis, vt quos Regulos ad suas rationes accommodatos, id est, ad res nouas, conturbádasq; ciuitates & inimicitias cũ alijs exercendas idoneos iudicabant, eos sibi amicitia & societate adiungerent: summiq; honoris ac beneficij loco, socios atq; amicos suos honorificētissimis decretis appellarent: eumq; verborum honorem reges exteri complures magnis largitionib. à ciuitatis Romanæ principibus comparabant. Reges autem vel Regulos potius, Galli eos nominabant, qui non ad tempus, vt ciuitatum magistratus: sed in perpetuum, regium imperium quantumuis exiguis finibus obtinebant: quos immutata temporum consuetudo, Duces, Comites, Marchiones appellauit. Earum porrò ciuitatum aliæ alijs potentiores erant: quarum se in fidem & clientelam, quæ minus per se poterant, studiosè conferebant. Has Cæsar superiorum stipendiarias, vectigales, & earum imperio subiectas appellat. Plerunque tamen in fide aliarum esse scribit. Regnante Romæ Prisco Tarquinio (inquit Liuius lib.5.) Celtarum penes Biturigas summa imperij fuit: ij Regem Celtis dabant. Aduentu Cæsaris in Galliâ, (qui fuit annus ab vrbe condita DCXCV.) Galliæ totius factiones erant duæ. Harum alterius principatum tenebant Ædui: alterius, Aruerni: multosque annos de potentatu inter se contenderant. Sed illa contentio ea re magnopere augebatur, quòd Biturigæ Aruernorum finitimi, in fide & imperio Æduorum erant. Sequani contrà, Æduorum finitimi, in Aruernorum fide. lib.1.cap.12. lib.6.cap.4. Cùm has Gallorum contentiones Romani ad suas rationes, id est, ad suam potentiam amplificandam aptissimas iudicarent, studiosè illas alebant. Itaque Æduos in societatem asciuerunt, eosque exquisito verborum honore Fratres consanguineosque suos appellarunt. In Æduorum fide & clientela reperio fuisse primùm Senones, quibus cum Parisij paulò ante suam ciuitatem fœdere & societate coniunxerant.lib.6.cap. 1.tum Bellouacos, quorum tamen erat ciuitas magna, & plurimum inter Belgas & virtute, & auctoritate, & hominum multitudine valebat, lib. 2. cap. 4. & lib. 7.cap. 7. Sub imperio Neruiorum Cæsar numerat Centrones, Grudios, Læuacos, Pleumosios, Gordunos. lib. 5. cap.11. Treuirorum clientes idem numerat Eburones,& Condrusos.lib.4.cap. 1. Venetorum autem ciuitatis (hi sunt in Armorica) lõgè amplissimam auctoritatem idem fuisse scribit omnium oræ maritimæ regionum earum, omnesque ferè qui eo mari uti consueuerant, illius fuisse vectigales. lib.3.cap. 2. Aruernorum autem tanta erat amplitudo, ut non modò se Æduis adæquarent, verumetiam paulò ante Cęsaris aduentum magnam clientum partem ab illis ad se traduxissent.lib.6.cap. 4. lib. 7.cap. 10. Itaq; Strabo lib. 4. scribit, eos quadringentis hominum millibus duce Vercingetorige bellum aduersus Cæsarem gessisse. Hi ab regio imperio abhorrebant. Itaque cùm Celtillus Vercingentorigis pater summę potentiæ atque auctoritatis esset, eoque totius Galliæ principatum obtineret, ob eam causam quòd Regnum appetebat, ab ciuitate interfectus fuerat. lib.7.c. 1. Sequani cõtrà Catamantaledé Regem habebat, quem Romani amicũ ac fociũ appellarant. lib. 1.c. 2. Suessiones quoq; qui latissimos feracissimósque agros possidebant,oppidáque habebant numero xii, & armatorū ⁊.millia cōficere poterant, Diuitiacum totius Galliæ potentissimum Regem paulo ante habuerant: qui non tantū magnæ partis Belgarum, verumetiam Britanniæ imperiū obtinuerat. Cæsaris aduentu Regem Galbam habebant. lib. 2. cap. 1. In Aquitania Pisonis cuiusdam Aquitani auus regnū obtinuerat, & à Romanis amicus appellatus fuerat. libro 4. cap. 5. Senones quoque, quæ fuit ciuitas in primis firma, & magnæ inter Gallos auctoritatis, quod tempore Moritasgum regem habuerant, cuius etiam maiores regnum in eadem ciuitate obtinuerant. lib. 5. cap. 13. Item Nitiobriges Olloniconem Regem habuerat, Amicum à Senatu Romano appellatum. libro 7. cap. 6. In illis porro regnis illud obseruatione dignum, neq; leuiter prætereundum videtur: primùm quòd hæreditaria non erant, sed à populo propter iustitiæ opinionem deferebantur: deinde quòd Reges non infinitum, solutum & effrenatum imperium habebant: sed certis legibus ita circunscriptum, vt non minus ipsi in populi, quàm populus in ipsorum ditione ac potestate esset: vt ferè illa regna nihil aliud, nisi magistratus perpetui viderentur. Nam multos Cæsar nominat priuatos, quorum tamen parentes ac maiores regnum obtinuerant: in his Casticū Catamantaledis filium, cuius pater in Sequanis multos annos regnum obtinuerat. lib. 1. cap. 2. Item Pisonem Aquitanum libro 4. capite 3. Item Tasgetium, cuius maiores in Carnutum ciuitate cum Regio imperio fuerant.lib. s.ca.8. De imperij verò & potestatis modo, Ambiorix rex Eburonum apud eundem auctorem ita loquitur, (lib.s.cap.8.) Sua esse eiusmodi imperia, vt non minus haberet in se iuris multitudo, quā ipse in multitudinem. Quam optimam ac præstantissimam Reipub. formam esse, propterea Plato & Aristoteles,& Polybius,& Cicero iudicarunt,quòd regalis dominatus,si sine freno,vt ait Plato, relinquatur, vbi in tantam omniū rerum potestatem, tanquam in lubricum locum, venerit, facillimè in tyrannidem delabitur.qua de caussa, inquit, Optimatum & delectorum auctoritate, quibus eam potestatem populus permittit,tanquam freno coercendus est.
units.tr: but the whole of Gaul was so divided into states that most of them were governed by the counsel of the nobles, and these were called free; the rest had kings. All of them were bound by custom to hold a public council of the nation at a fixed time of the year, in which they settled whatever seemed to pertain to the supreme interest of the commonwealth. Cornelius Tacitus counts sixty-four states in book 3. These, as is understood from Caesar, were regions which used not only the same language, customs and institutions but also the same magistrates; such as he himself mentions particularly in many places as the states of the Aedui, the Arverni and the Remi. So when Caesar was arranging to have the Aeduan Dumnorix killed, Dumnorix, says Caesar, began to resist and to defend himself with his hands, and to implore the good faith of his own people, often crying out that he was free and belonged to a free state (book 5, chapter 3). To the same effect Strabo, book 4, writes: Most states, he says, were governed by the counsel of the nobles, but they used to choose one magistrate each year, just as one commander was chosen by the people to conduct a war. [ἀεὶ συχραπικὰ δ' ἥσαν ἀπλεῖους τῶν πολιτειῶν ἕνα δ' ἡγεμόνα ἡρῶντο κατ' ἐναντίον παλαιὸν ὡς δ' αὔτως εἰς πόλεμον εἰς ὑπὸ τῶν πολλῶν ἀπδεικνυῶς σπαρτός.] To the same point Caesar writes in book 6, chapter 4, in these words: Those states which are thought to administer their commonwealth more advantageously have it laid down by law that if anyone has heard any rumour or report from neighbouring peoples about the commonwealth, he must bring it to the magistrate and communicate it to no one else. The magistrates conceal what they consider it useless to know, and reveal to the multitude what they judge to be expedient. About the commonwealth it is not permitted to speak except through the council. About the common council of the whole nation we will cite these few testimonies from Caesar. They asked (book 1, chapter 12) that they might be allowed to summon a council of the whole of Gaul on a fixed day, and to do so with Caesar's consent. Likewise (book 7, chapter 12): a council of all Gaul is summoned at Bibracte; to it come crowds from every side. And (book 6, chapter 1): Caesar, when the council of Gaul had been summoned for early spring, as he had arranged, and the rest, except the Senones, Carnutes and Treviri, had come, transferred the council to Lutetia of the Parisii. And (book 7, chapter 6): those states which dissented from the rest of Gaul, he (speaking of Vercingetorix) would bring over by his diligence, and would make one council of the whole of Gaul, which not even the whole world could withstand. Indeed, as to the kings who presided over certain states, there are almost countless passages in the same author; from these it is worth noting that it was the custom of the Romans to bind to themselves by friendship and alliance those petty kings whom they judged suitable to their purposes, that is, for stirring up new affairs, disturbing states and carrying on feuds with others; and to call their allies and friends, as an honour and a benefit of the highest kind, by the most honourable decrees; and foreign kings in great numbers purchased this empty title of honour from the leaders of the Roman citizenry with large gifts. The Gauls called these kings, or rather petty kings, those who held royal power not for a time, as the magistrates of the states did, but for life, even over very small territories; and the later custom of the times called them dukes, counts and marquises. Moreover, some of these states were more powerful than others, and those which were weaker eagerly placed themselves under the protection and clientship of the stronger. Caesar calls these, as subject to the others, tributary and dependent, and subject to their power. Yet he writes that they were for the most part under the protection of others. When Priscus Tarquinius was reigning at Rome, says Livy (book 5), the supreme power of the Celts lay with the Bituriges; they gave a king to the Celts. At the coming of Caesar into Gaul (which was the year 695 from the founding of the city), Gaul as a whole had two factions. The leadership of one of these was held by the Aedui, of the other by the Arverni; and for many years they had contended with each other for supremacy. But that contention was greatly increased by this fact: the Bituriges, neighbours of the Arverni, were under the faith and power of the Aedui, while the Sequani, on the contrary, neighbours of the Aedui, were under the faith of the Arverni (book 1, chapter 12; book 6, chapter 4). When the Romans judged these disputes among the Gauls most suitable for their own ends, that is, for enlarging their own power, they eagerly fostered them. And so they took the Aedui into alliance, and called them, with a chosen honour of words, their brothers and kinsmen. I find that the Senones were the first under the faith and clientship of the Aedui, with whom the Parisii had shortly before joined their state by treaty and alliance (book 6, chapter 1); then the Bellovaci, whose state was indeed large, and who among the Belgae were most powerful in courage, authority and multitude of men (book 2, chapter 4; book 7, chapter 7). Under the power of the Nervii Caesar counts the Centrones, Grudii, Levaci, Pleumoxii and Gordunni (book 5, chapter 11). The same author counts the Eburones and Condrusi as clients of the Treviri (book 4, chapter 1). He writes that the state of the Veneti (these are in Armorica) had by far the greatest authority over all the coastal regions and nearly all who were accustomed to use that sea, and that all of them were tributary to it (book 3, chapter 2). The Arverni, however, were of such greatness that they not only matched the Aedui but, shortly before Caesar's arrival, had drawn a large part of their clients from them over to themselves (book 6, chapter 4; book 7, chapter 10). And so Strabo, book 4, writes that they waged war against Caesar under the leadership of Vercingetorix with four hundred thousand men. These men shrank from royal rule. Thus, although Celtillus, father of Vercingetorix, was of the highest power and authority, and held the leadership of all Gaul, he was killed by his own state for this reason, that he aspired to kingship (book 7, chapter 1). The Sequani, on the other hand, had as king Catamantaloedis, whom the Romans had called friend and ally (book 1, chapter 2). The Suessiones also, who possessed the widest and most fertile fields and had twelve towns, and could raise an army of 50,000 armed men, had shortly before had as king Diviciacus, the most powerful king of all Gaul, who held rule not only over a great part of the Belgae but also over Britain. At Caesar's arrival they had King Galba (book 2, chapter 1). In Aquitaine the grandfather of a certain Piso of Aquitaine had held the kingship and had been called a friend of the Romans (book 4, chapter 5). The Senones too, a state which was among the firmest and of great authority among the Gauls, had as king Moritasgus, whose ancestors had also held the kingship in the same state (book 5, chapter 13). Likewise the Nitiobriges had as king Ollonicus, who was called a friend by the Roman Senate (book 7, chapter 6). Furthermore, in those kingdoms this point seems worthy of observation, and not to be passed over lightly: first, that they were not hereditary, but were conferred by the people on account of their reputation for justice; then, that the kings did not have an unlimited, absolute and unbridled power, but were so limited by fixed laws that they were no less under the authority of the people than the people were under their rule; so that those kingdoms seem for the most part to have been nothing other than lifelong magistracies. For Caesar names many men as private persons, although their parents and ancestors had held the kingship; among these Casticus, son of Catamantaloedis, whose father had held the kingship among the Sequani for many years (book 1, chapter 2); likewise Piso of Aquitaine (book 4, chapter 3); likewise Tasgetius, whose ancestors had held royal power in the state of the Carnutes (book 5, chapter 8). As to the measure of power and authority, Ambiorix, king of the Eburones, speaks thus in the same author (book 5, chapter 8): Their rule is of such a kind that the multitude has no less right over him than he has over the multitude. This is the best and most excellent form of commonwealth, which is why Plato, Aristotle, Polybius and Cicero judged it so: because royal rule, if it is left without a bridle, as Plato says, when it comes into such great power over all things, as into a slippery place, very easily slides into tyranny. For this reason, says Plato, it must be curbed like a horse by the authority of the best men and the chosen, to whom the people entrusts that power.

units.la: Quæ priscis temporibus Gallorum lingua fuisse videatur. CAP. II.
units.tr: What language the Gauls seem to have spoken in ancient times. CHAP. II.

units.la: HOcloco non prætermittenda quæstio videtur, multorum eruditorum hominum tractata disputationibus: qui nam, priscis illis temporibus Gallorum sermo fuerit. Nam quę ad religiones,& priuatorum mores, ceteraque instituta pertinent, Cæsar (vt ante diximus) copiosè exposuit. Primùm autem meminisse oportet, quod idem auctor initio Commentariorum scribit, cùm Gallorum alij Belgæ alij Aquitani,alij Celtæ essent,omnes nó modo institutis,verùetiá lingua inter se disc epasse. Quod aperte Stra. li.4. testatur,vbi ait eos ὁμογλώσσως nō fuisse, ἀλλ' ἐνίως μικρὸν παραλλάττοντας τὰς γλώττας. Idemque Ammianus Marcell. lib. 15. confirmat.
units.tr: Here a question seems not to be passed over, one that many learned men have discussed: what language the Gauls spoke in those early times. Caesar (as we said before) set out fully their religious practices, private customs and other institutions. But first we must remember what the same author writes at the beginning of his Commentaries: although the Gauls were divided into Belgians, Aquitanians and Celts, they differed from one another not only in institutions but also in language. Strabo clearly attests this in book 4, where he says they were not of one language [ὁμογλώσσως], but differed slightly in their tongues [ἀλλ' ἐνίως μικρὸν παραλλάττοντας τὰς γλώττας]. Ammianus Marcellinus in book 15 confirms the same.

units.la: Quod vero doctissimi complures, ac praesertim nostri populares, disputant, Gallos Graeca lingua vsos fuisse, vel ex eo solo refelli potest, quod Caesar lib. 5. cap. 12. commemorat, cum Q. Cicero à Gallis obsessus suis in castris teneretur, epistolam ei se Graecis literis scriptam misisse, ne, si interciperetur, sua consilia à Gallis cognosceretur. Item lib. 1. cap. 4. Vbi scribit, se cum Diuitiaco Dūnorigis fratre, per C. Valerium Troacillum, principem Galliae prouinciae, familiarem suum, remotis quotidianis interpretibus, locutum esse. Nam Troacillus ciuis R. factus & Latinae & Gallicae linguae vsum habebat. Quod si Diuitiacus Graecae linguae notitiam habuisset, quid Caesari ad colloquium cum eo instituendum interprete opus fuisset? Eodem etiam illud Ciceronis pertinet in Orat. pro Fonteio: Vbi de Gallis loquens: Hi vagantur, inquit, laeti atque erecti, passim toto foro, cum quibusdam minis, & barbaro atque immani terrore verborum. Nam Graecam linguam Ciceroni barbaram atque immanem fuisse, nemo, opinor, existimarit.
units.tr: As for the claim, made by very many learned men and especially by our own countrymen, that the Gauls used the Greek language, this can be refuted by that fact alone which Caesar reports in book 5, chapter 12: when Quintus Cicero was held under siege by the Gauls in his camp, he sent him a letter written in Greek characters, so that if it were intercepted his plans would not be known to the Gauls. Likewise in book 1, chapter 4, where he writes that he spoke with Diviciacus, brother of Dumnorix, through Gaius Valerius Troucillus, a chief man of the province of Gaul and his close friend, with the daily interpreters dismissed. For Troucillus, a Roman citizen, had the use of both the Latin and the Gallic language. But if Diviciacus had known Greek, what need would Caesar have had of an interpreter to hold a conversation with him? That passage of Cicero in the speech for Fonteius also bears on this, where he speaks of the Gauls: "They wander," he says, "cheerful and elated, here and there all over the forum, with certain threats and a barbarous and monstrous terror of words." For I suppose no one would think Greek was barbarous and monstrous to Cicero.

units.la: Vlpianus in l. Fideicommissa, 11. D. de Legat. 3. Fideicommissa quocunq; sermone relinqui possunt: non solum Latina vel Graeca, sed etiam Punica, vel Gallicana, vel alterius cuiuscunque generis lingua. Sed occurritur ab nonnullis, proferentibus Strabonis locum ex eodem lib. 4. vbi scribit, omnium optimarum artium, ac praepræsertim Græcarum literarum, studia Massiliç viguisse: vsque eò vt Galli eorum exemplo Græcæ linguæ studio caperentur: & iam pacta conuentaque Græcè scriberent. Ҩ φιλέμλωας (inquit) καταςκευάσαι ​​τὰς Γθάτας, ὥστε καὶ τὰ συμβόλαια ἑλλωι- νὶ γεάφειν. Verùm huic obiectioni facilis & expedita responsio est. Primum enim si Galli Massilienfium exemplo Græcam linguam discebât, an non perspicuum est, vernaculam illam eorũ linguam non fuisse? Deinde Strabo eodem loco non obscurè ostendit, morem illum pacta & contractus Græcè scribendi, suo demum tempore initium cepisse, cùm iam vniuersa Gallia Romanis parere didicisset. Præterea de iis tantum præcisè loquitur, qui Massilien-sibus erant finitimi: quibus in locis non modò priuati complures, verumetiam ciuitates, inquit, doctos viros Massilia publico consilio propositis honorarijs ad iuuentutem suam instituendam euocabant. Cum tamen alijs plerisque in Galliæ locis Academiæ florerent, in quibus sermone Gallico artes ac disciplinæ iuuentuti tradebantur, quod Hieronymus ad Rusticum scribens his ostendit verbis: Mater post studia Galliarum quæ florentissima sunt, misit te Romam, vt vbertatem, nitoremq; Gallici sermonis grauitas Romana condiret. Superest locus ille apud Cæsarem, vbi ait, Gallos in publicis priuatisq; rationibus Græcis literis vsos fuisse. Sed videamus ne vox Græcis eo loco non modò vt superuacanea, verumetiam vt importuna & adulterina tollēda fit: quippe,cùm ad Cæsaris sententiam exprimędam satis fuissent dixisse, Gallos in sola Druydum disciplina literis & scriptione vsos nō esse: in cæteris omnibus,& priuatis & publicis rationibus,literis vsos esse. Nam Vti literis, pro Scribere,locutio est Latinis auctoribus crebrò vsitata. Fabius lib. 11.cap. 11. Quanquam inuenio apud Platonē,obstare memoriæ vsum literarū. Præterea repugnant, Gallos linguæ Græcæ imperitos fuisse: (quod Cæsar illo superiore loco dixerat) & vulgo tabulas rationesq; suas publicas ac priuatas Græcis literis conscripsisse.Quod autem plerique existimant, Græcas literas eo loco non pro scriptione, sed pro formis literarū vsurpari: nobis ppterea minus probatur,ꝓ locis innumeris(vt modò dicebamus )veteres scriptores Vti literis dixerunt,ꝑ Scribere:at pro, formas literarū ducere, quantum adhuc obseruare licuit, nusquā. Neq;.n. illos adiuuat, quod idem Cōmentario primo scripserat, repertas in Heluetiorum castris tabulas,literis Græcis conscriptas:quasi verò qui Græcis literarū notis scribere didicerat,non idē eadem opera Græco sermone scribere didicisset:aut non esse potuerint in Heluetia vel sacerdotes,vel adolescentes nobiles,qui, vt hodie tam multi sunt qui Latinè didicerunt,ita literas Græcas, quæ tum in honore & pretio erant, perdiscere potuerint. Quā opinionē vel vnica Massilienfis scholæ vicinitas refellit.Itaq; idem Cæsar lib.5. vbi de illa sua ad Ciceronē epistola loquitur: Hanc,inquit,Græcis COM- conscriptam literis mittit: ne intercepta epistola, nostra ab hostibus consilia cognoscantur. Iustin. lib. 20, Facto S.C. nequis postea Carthaginensis aut literas Græcas, aut sermonem studeret, ne aut loqui cum hoste, aut scribere sine interprete posset. Tacitus de moribus Germ. Monumenta & tumulos quosdam Græcis literis inscriptos in confinio Germaniæ Rhetiæque adhuc extare. Livius lib. 9. Vulgò tum Romanos pueros, sicut nunc Græcis, ita Hetruscis literis erudiri solitos. Idem lib. 28. Ibique aram Annibal condidit, dedicavitque cum ingentium rerum ab se gestarum titulo, Punicis Græcisque literis insculpto. Item lib. 40. Literis Latinis Græcisque utraque ara inscripta erat. Vlpianus Iurisc. tit. de instit. tor. act. Proscribere sic accipimus, claris literis, utrum Græcis, an Latinis? Puto secundum loci conditionem: ne quis causari posset ignorantiam literarum. Trebell. Pollio in Æmiliano: Fertur enim apud Memphim in aurea columna Ægyptiis literis scriptum, tunc demum, &c. Denique non ambitror isto sensu dicturum Cæsarem fuisse, Græcis literis scribere: sed potius Græcarum literarum forma, vel figura, vel notis. Velut apud Tacitum lib. 11. Novas literarum formas addidit: comperto Græcam literaturam non simul coeptam absolutamque. Et mox: Et formæ literis Latinis quæ veterrimis Græcorum. Item apud Paulum Iurisc. sub tit. De oblig. & actionibus. Non figura literarum, sed oratione quā exprimunt literæ, obligamur. Item apud
units.tr: Ulpian, in the law Fideicommissa 11, D. de legatis 3: "Trusts may be left in any language: not only Latin or Greek, but also Punic, or Gallic, or any other kind of language." But some object, citing Strabo's passage from the same book 4, where he writes that the study of all the finest arts, and especially of Greek letters, flourished at Massilia, to such an extent that the Gauls, following their example, were captivated by the study of the Greek language and already wrote their agreements and contracts in Greek [φιλέλληνας κατασκευάσαι τοὺς Γάλλους, ὥστε καὶ τὰ συμβόλαια ἑλληνιστὶ γράφειν]. But the answer to this objection is easy and ready. For first, if the Gauls learned Greek on the model of the Massilians, is it not plain that their own language was not Greek? Next, Strabo in the same place clearly shows that this custom of writing agreements and contracts in Greek began only in his own time, when all Gaul had already learned to obey the Romans. Moreover, he speaks only of those who bordered on the Massilians, among whom not only private persons but even cities, he says, summoned learned men by public decision from Massilia, offering rewards to teach their youth. Yet in many other places in Gaul there were also flourishing academies, in which the arts and sciences were taught to the young in the Gallic language, as Jerome shows in his letter to Rusticus with these words: "After the studies of Gaul, which are most flourishing, your mother sent you to Rome, so that Roman gravity might season the richness and polish of the Gallic speech." There remains that passage in Caesar where he says that the Gauls used Greek letters in public and private accounts. But let us see whether the word "Greek" in that place must be removed, not only as superfluous but even as out of place and spurious. Since to express Caesar's meaning it would have been enough to say that the Gauls did not use letters and writing only in the teaching of the Druids, but used letters in all other matters, public and private. For "to use letters" in the sense of "to write" is a phrase often found in Latin authors. Quintilian in book 11, chapter 11: "Although I find in Plato that the use of letters harms memory." Moreover, it is inconsistent that the Gauls were unskilled in the Greek language (which Caesar had said in that earlier passage) and that they commonly wrote their public and private accounts and records in Greek letters. As for the view held by many, that in that place Greek letters are used not for writing but for the forms of the letters, this seems less probable to us, because in countless places (as we just said) the ancient writers used "to use letters" for "to write," but "to lead forms of letters" I have nowhere found, so far as I have been able to observe. Nor does it help them that in the same Commentary, book 1, he wrote that tablets written in Greek letters were found in the camp of the Helvetii: as if one who had learned to write Greek letters had not at the same time learned to write in the Greek language, or as if there could not have been priests or noble young men among the Helvetii who could learn Greek letters, which were then held in honour and esteem, just as today there are so many who have learned Latin. The nearness of the school at Massilia alone refutes this opinion. So too Caesar, in book 5, speaking of that letter of his to Cicero: "He sends it," he says, "written in Greek letters, so that if the letter were intercepted, our plans would not be known to the enemy." Justin, book 20: "When a decree of the senate had been passed that no Carthaginian should afterwards study either Greek letters or the language, so that he could neither speak with the enemy nor write without an interpreter." Tacitus, On the Manners of the Germans: that monuments and certain tombs inscribed with Greek letters still stand on the border of Germany and Raetia. Livy, book 9: "Commonly then Roman boys were accustomed to be taught in Etruscan letters, just as now in Greek." The same, book 28: "And there Hannibal set up an altar and dedicated it, with an inscription of his great deeds, carved in Punic and Greek letters." Likewise book 40: "Each altar had an inscription in Latin and Greek letters." Ulpian, Jurist, title On the Institutory Actions: "We understand 'to post publicly' as in clear letters: in Greek or in Latin? I think according to the condition of the place, so that no one could plead ignorance of the letters." Trebellius Pollio in Aemilianus: "For it is said that at Memphis, on a golden column, inscribed in Egyptian letters, then at last, etc." Finally, I do not think Caesar would have used the phrase "to write in Greek letters" in that sense, but rather "in the form, shape or characters of Greek letters." Just as in Tacitus, book 11: "He added new forms of letters, having discovered that Greek writing had not been begun and completed at once." And soon after: "and forms of letters like the most ancient of the Greeks." Likewise in Paul the Jurist, under the title On Obligations and Actions: "We are bound not by the shape of the letters but by the words the letters express." Likewise in

units.la: Cicero. Tuscull. 1. Aut qui sonos vocis, qui infiniti videbantur, paucis literarum notis terminauit. Ac ne quis nimiopere admiretur vocem GRÆCIS apud Cęsarem irrepsisse, proferam similem casum apud Plinium lib. 8. cap. 57. vbi sic scriptum est: Gentium consensus tacitus primum omnium conspirauit, vt IONVM literis vterentur. Et mox, Sequens gentium consensus in tonsoribus fuit. Et mox: tertius consensus est in horarum obseruatione. Nam vocem IONVM tollendam esse, quis non videt? non tam quia planè superuacanea est: (nam ad Plinij institutum satis fuit dicere, primum Gentium consensum fuisse in scriptione & literatura) quàm quia salsum est, IONVM primas fuisse literas: vt ipse Plin. superiore primo capite docuit, & Tacitus lib. 11. Animaduerti tamen apud Gregorium Turon. lib. 5. & Aimoinum lib. 3. cap. 41. locos duos, quibus significari videtur, Gallos Græcarum literarum notis vsos fuisse. nam vbi de Chilperico Rege loquuntur: Addidit (inquiunt) & literas literis nostris: id est ω,ɥ,ζ,φ. & misit epistolas in vniuersas ciuitates regni sui, vt sic pueri docerentur. Apud Aimoinum autem tres tantum ponuntur χ,θ,φ. Verùm intelligendum est, Francos istos fuisse, non Gallos: vel potius Francogallos: qui Germanica lingua, id est, patria & natiua, non illa veterum Gallorum, quæ Romanorum dominatu obsoleuerat, vtebantur. deinde si Francogalli Græcis literis vsi fuissent, quid ita reliquas omnes, his solis exceptis, vsurpassent? Verùm hæc quidem plus satis. Superest eorum opinio, qui putant Gallos Germanica lingua vsos fuisse: quos vel vnus ille Cæsaris lib. 1 .refellit locus, in quo scribit, Ariouistum propter longinquam in Gallia consuetudinem lingua Gallica vsum esse. Eò accedat Taciti locus ille ex lib. De morib. German. E quib. Marsigni & Burij sermone cultuque Sueuos referunt, Gothinos Gallica, Osos Pannonica lingua coarguit non esse Germanos. Planius autem hoc confirmat Suetonius in Caligula: cõuersus hinc, inquit, ad curam triumphi, præter captiuos & transfugas Barbaros, Galliarum quoque procerissimum quemque, & (vt ipse dicebat) ἀξιοθριάμβευτον, ac nonnullos ex principibus legit, ac sepositi ad pompam, coëgitque non tantum rutilare, & submittere comam, sed & sermonem Germanicũ addiscere, & nomina Barbarica ferre. Vbi planius contrariæ sententiæ testimonium Glareanus, & alij Glareanum secuti protulerint, fidem illis habendã existimabo. Interea duabus de causis mihi eorum probabilis opinio videbitur qui scribunt, veterũ Gallorum linguam propriam, atq; ab aliarũ gentium, præter quàm à Britannorum, sermone dissimilé fuisse: primùm, quia Cæsar scribit moris fuisse, vt qui Druydum disciplinam diligentius cognoscere volebant, plerunque in Britanniam proficiscerentur. Cùm autem libris nullis vterentur, consentaneum est, illos eodem quo in Gallia sermone vsos in docendo fuisse. Deinde quia Corn. Tacitus in Agricolæ vita scribit Britannorum & Gallorū sermonem haud multum diuersum fuisse. Neque mihi Beati Rhenani coniectura displicet, qui sermonem eorum qui hodie Britones Britonantes appellantur, veteris nostræ linguæ reliquias fuisse arbitratur: cum aliis de causis, tum præcipuè quia cōstat Britannos ab Anglis Saxonibus patria pulsos in eam regionem profugisse. Unde illa Eduardi I. Anglorū Regis lex vetus: Britones Armorici, cum venerint in Regno isto, suscipi debent & protegi, sicut probi ciues de corpore regni huius. Exierunt enim quondam de sanguine Britonum regni huius. Atque hæc quidem de prisca Gallorum lingua dicta sint. Nostram autem qua iam utimur, non difficile intellectu est, ex variis variarum gentium sermonibus conflatam esse. Ac, si breuiter dilucideque dicendum est, is quo iam utimur sermo, quadripartito distribuendus est: ac dimidia eius pars Romanis accepto ferenda: quemadmodum Otto Frisingensis testatur lib. Chronic. 4, cap. pen. & quiuis Latinis literis tinctus poterit animaduertere. Nam præterquam quòd ita natura ferebat, ut Galli Romanis subiecti ad eorum se mores & linguam lubenter accommodarēt: satis constat, Romanos ferendi sermonis Latini studiosissimos fuisse: ut per omnes gentes venerabilior diffunderetur: quemadmodum Valerius Maximus testatur: eaque de causa ludos literarios passim instituisse: veluti Augustodu-ni, ni, Vezontione, Lugduni: quod vel ex Tacito & Ausonio cognosci licet. Hierony. ad Ruftic. Ac post studia Galliarum, quę florentissima sunt, misit Roma, vt vbertatem Gallici nitoréq; sermonis grauitate Romana condiret. Itaq; tantum in Gallia Latinæ linguæ consuetudo valuit, vt non modo leges ad summam Regni & Reipublicæ pertinentes Latinis literis conscriberentur: (cuius rei cum vetustissima quæq; monimenta testimonio sunt, tum etiam Regum antiquorum constitutiones, quarum quædam extant in libro inscripto Stilus curiæ parlamenti: verùm etiam Latinè & litigaretur, & sententiæ pronuntiarentur: ac præsertim litigandi rabiosa quadam consuetudine atque arte ex Pontificum Roman. curia in Galliam introducta: potissimum autem vbi de sacerdotijs & eorum opimis vectigalibus litigari cœptum est. quod institutum ad nostram vsque ætatem seruari solitum, Edictum Francisci primi documento est, qui anno 1539 florescentib. bonis in Gallia literis edixit, vt Gallico sermone iudicia exercerentur. Eodem accesserat Religionis disciplina & ratio. nam cum Latinis ab initio literis tradita fuisset, cuius rei veteres ecclesiastici testimonio sunt: Irenæus, episcopus Lugdunensis: Hilarius, Pictauiensis: Sidonius, Bituricensis: Saluianus, Massiliensis: Gregor. Turonensis: postea Rom. ritibus ac ceremonijs in Christianorum ecclesias introductis, multũ ea consuetudo creuit. ac præsertim posteaquam Carolus Magnus
units.tr: Cicero, Tusculan Disputations, book 1: "Or who bounded the sounds of the voice, which seemed infinite, with a few signs of letters." So that no one should be too surprised that the word GREEK has crept into Caesar's text, I will cite a similar case in Pliny, book 8, chapter 57, where it is written: "The silent agreement of the nations first of all agreed to use the letters of the IONES." Soon after: "The next agreement of the nations concerned barbers." And soon: "The third agreement concerns the observance of the hours." Who does not see that the word IONES must be removed? Not so much because it is quite superfluous (for it was enough for Pliny's purpose to say that the first agreement of the nations concerned writing and literature), but because it is absurd that the IONES had the first letters, as Pliny himself taught in the first chapter above, and Tacitus in book 11. Still, I have noticed two passages, in Gregory of Tours, book 5, and Aimoin, book 3, chapter 41, which seem to indicate that the Gauls used the signs of Greek letters. For where they speak of King Chilperic, they say: "He added (they say) letters to our letters, namely [ω, ɥ, ζ, φ], and sent letters to all the cities of his kingdom, so that boys might be taught in this way." In Aimoin, however, only three are given: [χ, θ, φ]. But it must be understood that these were Franks, not Gauls, or rather Franco-Gauls, who used the German language, their native and natural tongue, not that of the ancient Gauls, which had fallen out of use under Roman domination. Next, if the Franco-Gauls had used Greek letters, why would they have employed all the others and taken only these few out? But this is more than enough. There remains the opinion of those who think the Gauls used the German language. One passage of Caesar, book 1, refutes them alone, where he writes that Ariovistus, because of his long habit in Gaul, used the Gallic language. To this add that passage of Tacitus from the book On the Manners of the Germans: he says that by speech and customs the Marsigni and Buri show that they are Suevi, that the Gothini are shown not to be Germans by the Gallic language, and the Osi by the Pannonian language. Suetonius confirms this more plainly in Caligula: "Turning thence," he says, "to the preparations for his triumph, he chose out, besides captives and barbarian deserters, the tallest of the Gauls too, and (as he himself used to say) worthy of the triumph, and some of the chiefs, and set them apart for the procession, and made them not only dye and grow out their hair, but also learn the German language and bear barbarian names." Where Glareanus, and others following Glareanus, have brought forward more plainly the testimony of the contrary opinion, I think their view should be trusted. Meanwhile, for two reasons the opinion of those seems probable to me who write that the language of the ancient Gauls was their own, and differed from that of other peoples except the Britons. First, because Caesar writes that it was the custom for those who wished to learn the discipline of the Druids more thoroughly to set out mostly for Britain. Since they used no books, it is consistent that they used in teaching the same language as in Gaul. Second, because Cornelius Tacitus, in the Life of Agricola, writes that the speech of the Britons and the Gauls was not very different. Nor does the conjecture of Beatus Rhenanus displease me, who thinks that the speech of those who today are called Britons, or Breton speakers, is a remnant of our old language, for other reasons, but chiefly because it is established that the Britons, driven from their homeland by the Anglo-Saxons, fled to that region. Hence that old law of Edward I, king of the English: "The Armorican Britons, when they come into this kingdom, ought to be received and protected, like good citizens of the body of this kingdom, for they once went out from the blood of the Britons of this kingdom." And these things may be said about the ancient Gaulish language. Our present language is not hard to understand as having been compounded from the various speeches of various peoples. And if it must be said briefly and clearly, the language we now use must be divided into four parts, of which half is to be credited to the Romans, as Otto of Freising testifies in book 4 of his Chronicle, last chapter, and anyone steeped in Latin letters can notice. For apart from the fact that it was natural for the Gauls, subject to the Romans, to adapt themselves gladly to their customs and language, it is well established that the Romans were most zealous in spreading the Latin language, so that it might be more venerated among all peoples, as Valerius Maximus testifies; and for this reason they set up schools of letters everywhere, as at Augustodunum, Vesontio and Lugdunum, as can be learned from Tacitus and Ausonius. Jerome to Rusticus. And after the studies of Gaul, which were most flourishing, Rome sent [teachers] to season the richness of the Gallic language with Roman seriousness. So much did the use of the Latin language prevail in Gaul that not only were laws concerning the highest matters of kingdom and commonwealth written in Latin letters (of which the oldest monuments are witnesses, and also the constitutions of the ancient kings, some of which survive in the book entitled The Style of the Court of Parliament), but also lawsuits were conducted and sentences pronounced in Latin. Especially, a certain fierce custom and art of litigation was introduced into Gaul from the court of the Roman Pontiffs, chiefly when lawsuits began to be waged over priesthoods and their rich revenues. That this practice was usually kept up until our own age is shown by the edict of Francis I, who in 1539, when letters flourished in Gaul, ordered that judgments be conducted in the Gallic language. To this had been added the discipline and reason of religion. For since it had been handed down to Christians from the beginning in Latin letters, of which the ancient churchmen are witnesses (Irenaeus, bishop of Lyons; Hilary of Poitiers; Sidonius of Bourges; Salvian of Marseilles; Gregory of Tours), afterwards, when Roman rites and ceremonies were introduced into the churches of Christians, that custom grew greatly. And especially after Charles the Great

units.la: Hieron. ad Rustic. ... (marginal reference, as printed in the text block)

Galliæ regnum Papæ Zachariæ ope consilioque adeptus, in tanti beneficij gratiam edixit, vt Romano more ritus ecclesiæ seruarentur, & cantiones haberentur. quæ lex ipsius cum in Capitulari, tum in legibus Francicis his extat verbis: Vt cantum Romanum pleniter discant: ordinaliter per nocturnalia, vel graduale officium peragatur: secundum quod beatæ memoriæ genitor noster Pipinus Rex decretauit, vt fieret, quando Gallicanum tulit: & ob vnanimitatem Apostolicæ sedis, & sanctæ Dei Ecclesiæ pacificam concordiam. quod idem etiam Sigebertus sub anno 774. memoriæ prodidit. quæ res dici non potest, quantam & Gallicis ecclesijs caliginem offuderit, & pontificibus R. auctoritatem in negotijs religionis tribuerit. qua auctoritate cum illi aduersus Galliæ Reges mirandum in modum abuterentur, repertus est Rex Carolus quintus, cognomento Sapiens, qui circiter annum MCCCLXX. tyrannidi Pontificum insensus sacra Biblia in linguam Gallicam couertenda curauit. quam translationem multis etiā nūc locis in Gallia nostra videre licet, cū hac inscriptione: DE MANDATO ET IVSSV REGIS CAROLI QVINTI. eāq; memini me in Regia bibliotheca Fontanebleæi, anno 1563: iterumque anno 1567. vidisse. Altera vero eius qua nunc vtimur linguę dimidia pars ita distribuenda est, vt partem vnam priscis Gallis attribuamus, alteram Francis, postremam Græcorum literis. Nam Francorum, id est (vt paulò post docedocebimus)Germanorum, innumeras in quotidiano sermone nostro voces occurrere, iam pridem à multis demonstratum est. Ex Græcorum vero lingua complura vocabula ad vsum traducta nostrum fuisse, multi quoque iam dudum eruditi viri ostenderunt. cuius rei causa nō Druydibus (quos Græcè non loquutos docuimus) sed Massiliensium instituţis ac disciplinæ, de qua superius diximus, tribuenda est. Unde sensim ea consuetudo in reliquas Galliæ regiones manauit.
units.tr: Having won the kingdom of Gaul with the help and counsel of Pope Zachary, in gratitude for so great a benefit he decreed that the rites of the Church be observed in the Roman manner, and that chants be sung. This law of his survives both in the Capitulary and in the Frankish laws in these words: that they learn the Roman chant fully, and that the office be carried out in order, by nocturns or the gradual office, just as our father of blessed memory, King Pepin, decreed should be done when he brought in the Gallican [rite], and for the unanimity of the Apostolic See and the peaceful concord of the holy Church of God. Sigebert also recorded the same thing under the year 774. What darkness this matter cast over the Gallican churches, and how much authority it gave the Roman pontiffs in matters of religion, cannot be said. With this authority they abused the kings of Gaul in a remarkable way, until King Charles V, surnamed the Wise, who about the year 1370, hostile to the tyranny of the Pontiffs, took care to have the holy Bibles translated into the French language. Many copies of this translation can still be seen in various places in our Gaul, with this inscription: BY THE COMMAND AND ORDER OF KING CHARLES V; and I remember seeing it in the royal library at Fontainebleau in 1563, and again in 1567. The other half of the language we now use must be divided so that one part is attributed to the ancient Gauls, another to the Franks, and the last to the Greeks. For that countless words of the Franks, that is (as I shall show a little later) of the Germans, occur in our everyday speech, has long since been shown by many. That many words from the Greek language were brought into use among us, learned men have also long shown. The cause of this is to be ascribed not to the Druids (whom I have shown did not speak Greek) but to the institutions and discipline of the Massilians, of which I spoke above. From there that custom gradually spread into the remaining regions of Gaul.

units.la: De statu Galliæ à Romanis in provinciæ formam redacta. CAP. III.
units.tr: On the state of Gaul, reduced by the Romans into the form of a province. CHAPTER III.

units.la: GAlliam à Romanis diu magnis sæpe cladibus tentatā, tandemque à C. Cæsare decenni propè bello, prælijsque compluribus domitam ac subactam fuisse, atque ad extremum in provinciæ formam redactam, eruditis omnibus notum est. Hoc fortissimæ & bellicosissimæ gentis fatum fuit, vt Magnæ Belluæ (quemadmodum in sanctis literis appellatur) tandem aliquando pareret. cum qua tamen ita per annos octingentos (vt Iosephus testatur) de imperio certarat, vt illa nullius alterius nationis armis æque terreretur. Itaque Plutarchus in Marcello & Camillo, Appianus in lib. de civilibus bell. 2. Liuius libro 8. & 10, memoriæ prodiderunt, Gallos Romanis vsque eò formidabiles fuisse,vt lege fancitum haberent,ne vacationes à militia,quæ sacerdotibus & senibus permittebantur,tumultu Gallico valerent.quod idem & Cicero Philippi. 2. commemorat. itaque Sallust. in Iugurth. scribit Romanos omnibus temporibus ita statuisse, alia omnia virtuti suæ prona esse: cum Gallis pro salute, non pro gloria certasse. Quin etiam Cæsar lib. 6. testatur, atque ex eiusdem auctoritate Tacitus in lib. de morib. German. commemorat, fuisse tempus cùm Germanos Galli virtute superarent, & vltrò bella inferrent: ac propter hominum multitudinem trans Rhenum colonias mitterent. Tantæ autem virtutis amissæ iacturam, idem Tacitus amissæ libertati tribuit: in libro de vita Agricolæ: Nam Gallos, inquit, in bellis floruisse accepimus: mox segnitia cum otio intrauit, amissa virtute pariter ac libertate. Et quoniam amori patriæ nonnihil indulgendum est, age, præclarum insuper illud de Gallorum virtute, Iustini testimonium proferamus, ex libro 24. Namque Galli, inquit, abundanti multitudine cùm eos non caperent terræ, quæ genuerant, trecenta millia hominum ad sedes novas quærendas velut peregrinantem miserunt. Ex his portio in Italia consedit, quæ & vrbe Romam captam incendit, & portio Illyricos sinus per strages barbarorum penetrauit, & in Pannonia cóledit: gens aspera, audax, bellicosa, quæ prima post Herculem, cui ea res virtutis admirationem & immortalitatis fidem dedit, Alpium um inuicta iuga, & frigore intractabilia loca transcendit. ibi domitis Pannonijs per multos annos cum finitimis varia bella gesserunt. Hortante deinde successu, diuisis agminib. alij Graeciam, alij Macedoniam, omnia ferro proterentes, petiuere: tatusq; terror Gallici nominis erat, vt etiam Reges non lacessiti, vltro pacem ingenti pecunia mercarentur. Item lib. sequé. Quanquā Gallorum ea tempestate tantæ sœcunditatis iuentus fuit, vt Asiam omnem velut examine aliquo implerent. denique neque Reges Orientis, sine mercenario Gallorum exercitu, vlla bella gesserint: neque pulsi Regno ad alios quàm ad Gallos confugerint. Tantus terror Gallici nominis, siue armorum inuicta felicitas erat, vt aliter neque maiestatem suam tutam, neq; amissam recuperare se posse, sine Gallica virtute, arbitrarentur. Atq; hæc quidem de Gallorum bellicis laudibus & virtute dicta sint: quæ tamen (quemadmodum ex Tacito modò dicebamus) amissa libertate interijt. Nonnullas tamen ciuitates post formam prouinciæ à Romanis constitutam libertati suæ relictas, testis est Plinius libro 4.capite 17. veluti Neruios, Suessiones, Vlbanenses, Leucos: nonnullos etiam fœderatos: in ijs, Lingones, Rhemos, Carnutos, Æduos. quod etiam Tranquillus in Iulio his confirmat verbis: Omnem Galliam quæ saltu Pyrenæo, Alpibusque, & monte Gebenna, fluminibusque Rheno & Rhodano continetur: patetque circuitu ad bis & tricies centena millia passuum: praeter socias ac bene meritas civitates, in provinciae formam redegit: eiq; in singulos annos sestertium quadringenties stipendij nomine imposuit. Quae vero earum civitatum, quae in provinciae formam redactae fuerant, forma & ratio extiterit, facile ex Critognati Aruerni verbis intelligi potest, apud Caesarem lib. 7. Quod si ea, inquit, quae in longinquis nationibus geruntur, ignoratis: respicite finitimam Galliam, quae in provinciam redacta, iure & legib. commutatis, securibus subiecta, perpetua premitur servitute. Itaque Cic. pro Fonteio, Referta, inquit, Gallia negotiatorum est: plena civium R. nemo Gallorum sine cive R. quicquam negotij gerit. numus in Gallia nullus sine civium R. tabulis commovetur. Triplex autem erat servitus: primum ut impofito praesidio firmarentur. quanquam quae pacatae satis & sedatae provinciae videbantur, in eas non magnae copiae mittebantur. Galliam certe Iosephus libro belli Iud. 2 scribit, Imp. Titi tempore mille tantum & ducentorum militum praesidio firmatam fuisse: quanquam, inquit, annos fere octingentos de libertate cum Romanis pugnarint: & pene plures civitates, quam Romanos milites praesidiarios habeant. Alterum servitutis genus fuit, ut Provinciae Romanis stipendiariae ac vectigales essent, eoque nomine publicanos apud se habere cogerentur: id est harpyas & hirudines, quae provincialium sanguinem exugebant. Suetonius autem eo quem modo protulimus loco,itemq; Eutropius lib.6. memoriæ prodiderunt, Cæsarem subactæ Galliæ tributi nomine imperasse in annos singulos HS.quadringenties: hoc est,scutatorum,vt nūc loquimur,decies centena millia. Tertia prouincialium seruitus erat, vt ne legibus suis patrijs vterentur: sed magistratus à populo R. cū imperio & securibus mitterentur, qui apud eos ius dicerent. Hanc triplicem seruitutem cùm omnes ferè prouinciales, tum verò Galli nostri ægerrimè molestissimeque tulerunt. Itaque nō longo post Cæsaris victorias interuallo, imperante Tiberio, Cornel. Tacit. auctor est,Galliæ ciuitates ob continuationem tributorum,sæuitiam fœnoris,& superbiam præsidentium (hæc enim lib. 3.illius verba sunt) rebellionem secisse. pòst etiam Nerone imperante, Suetonius scribit, Gallos illius imperium pertæsos, abipso defecisse. Talem Principem (inquit cap. 40.) paulò minus per xiii. annos perpessus terrarum orbis tandem destituit: initium facientib. Gallis. Quam maiorum nostrorum laudem eximiam satis pro dignitate prædicare nō possumus, quòd primi omnium in orbe terrarum tam potentis Tyranni dominatum à suis ceruicibus amoliri, seseque ex immanis Tyranni seruitute in libertatem vindicare cœperunt. Diuisæ autē sunt à Romanis Galliæ omnes in sexdecim prouincias: Viennensem, Narbonensem primam, Narbonensem secundā: Aquitaniam primam, Aquitaniã fecundã, Nouempopulanam, Alpes maritimas, Belgicã primam, Belgicam fecundã, Germaniam primam, Germaniam fecundam, Lugdunensem 1, Lugdunensem 2, Lugdunésem tertiam, Maximam Sequanorum, & Alpes Græcas, quemadmodum Antoninus in Itinerario, & Sextus Russus tradunt. Subtilius autem singulas enumerat Ammianus Marcellinus lib. 15.
units.tr: It is known to all scholars that Gaul, attacked often by the Romans with great disasters, was at last conquered and subdued by Gaius Caesar in a war of almost ten years and many battles, and finally reduced to the form of a province. This was the fate of that most brave and warlike nation, that at last it should obey the Great Beast (as it is called in the sacred writings). Yet it had contended with that beast for the empire for eight hundred years (as Josephus testifies), so that it was feared by the arms of no other nation as much as by these. Accordingly, Plutarch in his lives of Marcellus and Camillus, Appian in the second book of his Civil Wars, and Livy in books 8 and 10 have recorded that the Gauls were so formidable to the Romans that they had a law that exemptions from military service, which were granted to priests and old men, should not hold good against a Gallic uproar. Cicero also mentions this in the second Philippic. Accordingly Sallust in the Jugurthine War writes that the Romans had always decided that all other things yielded to their courage, but that with the Gauls they had fought for their safety, not for glory. Indeed, Caesar in book 6 bears witness, and Tacitus, on Caesar's authority, mentions in his book on the customs of the Germans, that there was a time when the Gauls surpassed the Germans in courage, and made war on them unprovoked, and sent colonies across the Rhine because of the multitude of their people. Tacitus attributes the loss of this great courage to the loss of liberty, in his book on the life of Agricola: "For we have heard," he says, "that the Gauls flourished in war; then sloth crept in with leisure, and they lost their courage together with their liberty." And since some indulgence must be granted to love of country, come, let us also cite that famous testimony of Justin on the courage of the Gauls, from book 24. "For the Gauls," he says, "when their land, which had produced them, could not hold their abundant multitude, sent three hundred thousand men to seek new settlements, as if on a pilgrimage. Part of these settled in Italy, and burned Rome after capturing it; part penetrated through the slaughter of the barbarians to the Illyrian gulf and settled in Pannonia: a harsh, bold, warlike people, who, first after Hercules, whose exploit gave him admiration for his courage and a belief in his immortality, crossed the unconquered ridges of the Alps and places intractable with cold. There, having subdued the Pannonians, they waged various wars for many years with their neighbours. Then, encouraged by success, they divided their armies, and some made for Greece, others for Macedonia, laying everything waste with the sword; and the terror of the Gallic name was so great that even kings, though not attacked, bought peace from them at a huge price." Likewise in the following book: "Although at that time the youth of the Gauls was so fertile that they filled all Asia as if with a swarm; finally, the kings of the East waged no wars without an army of Gallic mercenaries, and when they were driven from their kingdoms they fled to no one but the Gauls. So great was the terror of the Gallic name, or rather the unconquered good fortune of their arms, that they thought they could neither keep their majesty safe nor recover what they had lost without Gallic courage." These things may be said about the martial glory and courage of the Gauls; yet, as we were just saying from Tacitus, these perished with the loss of liberty. Nevertheless, Pliny in book 4, chapter 17, bears witness that some states were left their liberty after the form of a province had been established by the Romans: for example the Nervii, the Suessiones, the Ulbanenses, the Leuci; and some also as allies: among them the Lingones, the Remi, the Carnutes, and the Aedui. Suetonius also confirms this in his Julius in these words: "He reduced to the form of a province all Gaul, which is bounded by the Pyrenean pass, the Alps, the mountain Cevennes, and the rivers Rhine and Rhone, and which extends in circuit to three hundred and twenty thousand paces, apart from its allied and well-deserving states; and he imposed on it a tribute of four hundred million sesterces every year." What the form and manner of those states was that had been reduced to the form of a province can easily be understood from the words of Critognatus the Arvernian, in Caesar, book 7: "If," he says, "you are ignorant of what is done in distant nations, look at neighbouring Gaul, which, reduced to a province, its laws and rights changed, is subjected to the axes and is held in perpetual servitude." So Cicero in his speech for Fonteius: "Gaul," he says, "is full of traders, full of Roman citizens; no Gaul does any business without a Roman citizen; no coin in Gaul is moved without the account-books of Roman citizens." The servitude was threefold. First, garrisons were placed to secure the provinces; although those that seemed quite peaceful and calm were not sent large forces. Josephus, in book 2 of the Jewish War, certainly writes that Gaul in the time of the Emperor Titus was secured by a garrison of only twelve hundred soldiers: "although," he says, "for almost eight hundred years they fought with the Romans for liberty, and there are almost more states than Roman garrison soldiers." The second kind of servitude was that the provinces were made tributary and subject to tax for the Romans, and on this account were compelled to keep tax-farmers among them, that is, harpies and leeches, who sucked the blood of the provincials. Suetonius, in the passage I have just quoted, and likewise Eutropius in book 6, have recorded that Caesar imposed on conquered Gaul a tribute of four hundred million sesterces a year: that is, as we now say, a hundred thousand scuta. The third servitude of the provincials was that they were not allowed to use their own ancestral laws, but magistrates were sent from the Roman people with imperium and the axes to administer justice among them. Almost all the provincials, but our Gauls above all, bore this threefold servitude with the greatest bitterness and impatience. Accordingly, not long after Caesar's victories, under the reign of Tiberius, Cornelius Tacitus records that the states of Gaul rebelled because of the continual tributes, the cruelty of usury, and the arrogance of the governors (for these are the words of his third book). Later, under Nero, Suetonius writes that the Gauls, weary of his rule, revolted from him. "The world," he says in chapter 40, "having endured such a prince for a little less than thirteen years, at last cast him off, the Gauls making the beginning." We cannot praise this distinguished glory of our ancestors enough as it deserves, that they were the first in the whole world to begin to cast off the dominion of so powerful a tyrant from their necks, and to free themselves from the servitude of a monstrous tyrant. Now all the Gauls were divided by the Romans into sixteen provinces: Viennensis, Narbonensis the first, Narbonensis the second; Aquitania the first, Aquitania the second, Novempopulana, the Maritime Alps, Belgica the first, Belgica the second, Germania the first, Germania the second, Lugdunensis the first, Lugdunensis the second, Lugdunensis the third, Maxima Sequanorum, and the Graian Alps, as Antoninus in his Itinerary and Sextus Rufus record. Ammianus Marcellinus in book 15 enumerates the individual provinces more exactly.

units.la: Nunc, vt ad instítutum reuertamur, incredibile dictu est, quàm indignè atque acerbè Galli Romanorum latrocinia tulerint: quamque crebræ ab ijs defectiones rebelliónesque numerentur. quanquam cùm per se satis virium ad depellendam Romanorum tyrannidem non haberent, vetus institutum tenebant, vt Germanos mercede conductos ad suum auxilium euocarent. Vnde Francicarum coloniarum semina primùm exorta sunt. Nam Germani siue à Romanis victi, siue (quod probabilius videtur) pretio empti, cœpere sensim in Galliæ finibus sedes collocare. Hinc illud Suetonij in Augusto: Germanos vltra Albim fluuium summouit: ex quibus Sueuos & Sicambros dedentes se traduxit in Galliam, atque in proximis Rheno agris collocauit. Idem in Tiberio: Germanico bello quadraginta millia deditiorum traiecit in Galliam, iuxtaque ripam Rheni sedibus assignatis collocauit. Neque verò prætereundum est, quod Flauius Vopiscus de Probi Cæsaris imperio memoriæ prodidit: quo tempore vniuersa propè Gallia, hoc est, sexaginta ciuitates, ab imperio Romano defciuerunt, armaque communi consilio libertatis recuperandæ caussa ceperunt: His gestis, inquit, cum ingenti exercitu Gallias petit, quæ omnes occiso Postumo turbatæ fuerunt, interfecto Aureliano à Germanis possessæ. Tanta autem illic prælia feliciter gessit, vt à Barbaris sexaginta per Gallias nobilissimas reciperet ciuitates. Et cùm iam per omnes Gallias securi vagarentur, cæsis prope quadringentis millibus, qui Romanum occupauerant solum, reliquias vltra Nicrum fluuium & Albim remouit. Quàm crudelis autem & immanis Romanorum dominatus fuerit, quàm acerba latrocinia, quàm tetra, & obscœna vitæ consuetudo, quantoque illa odio atque acerbitati Gallis hominibus, sed præsertim Christianis fuerit, nullius opinor ex scriptis, melius quàm ex Saluiani Massiliensis Episcopi libris de prouidentia, cognosci potest. Itaque incredibile dictu est, quantæ Germanarum gentium copiæ Gallis non modò fauentibus, verum etiam adiuuantibus, sese in Gallias effuderint. Vnde illud Latini Pacati ad Theodosium: Vnde igitur exordiar, nisi à tuis Gallia malis, quæ ex omnibus terris, quas illa pestis insederat, haud iniuria tibi vindicas priuilegium miseriarum? Earum autem Germanicarum gentium partem Francos nostros fuisse, cùm ex Sidonio Apollinari, tum verò præsertim ex illius Saluiani locis complurib. planissimè intelligitur.
