units.tr: Now, to return to our purpose: it is incredible to say how indignantly and bitterly the Gauls bore the robberies of the Romans, and how often they are recorded to have revolted and rebelled against them. Although on their own they did not have enough strength to drive off the tyranny of the Romans, they kept the old custom of calling in Germans hired for pay to their aid. From this the first seeds of the Frankish colonies arose. For the Germans, whether conquered by the Romans or (as seems more probable) bought for money, began gradually to establish settlements within the borders of Gaul. Hence that statement of Suetonius in his Augustus: "He drove the Germans back beyond the river Elbe; of these he brought the Suebi and the Sicambri, who surrendered, over into Gaul, and settled them on fields next to the Rhine." The same author in his Tiberius: "In the German war he transported forty thousand surrendered men into Gaul, and settled them with assigned lands along the bank of the Rhine." Nor must we pass over what Flavius Vopiscus recorded about the rule of the Emperor Probus: at that time almost all Gaul, that is sixty states, revolted from the Roman empire and took up arms by common counsel to recover their liberty. "After these things were done," he says, "he sought Gaul with a huge army; for all of it had been thrown into confusion after Postumus was killed, and after Aurelian was murdered it had been occupied by the Germans. He waged such battles there successfully that he recovered from the barbarians sixty of the most noble states throughout Gaul. And when already the Germans were wandering through all Gaul without fear, after about four hundred thousand of those who had occupied Roman soil had been slain, he drove the remnants beyond the river Nicer and the Elbe." But how cruel and monstrous the Roman domination was, how bitter their robberies, how foul and obscene their way of life, and with what hatred and bitterness it filled the Gauls, but especially the Christians, I think can be learned better from no writings than from the books On the Government of God by Salvian, bishop of Marseilles. Hence it is incredible to say how great were the forces of the German peoples that poured into Gaul, not only with the favour but even with the help of the Gauls. Hence that saying of Latinus Pacatus to Theodosius: "Whence then shall I begin, unless from the evils of your Gaul, which, out of all the lands that that plague had settled, rightly claims for you the privilege of miseries?" That some of these German peoples were our Franks is plainly understood from Sidonius Apollinaris, and especially from several passages of that same Salvian.

units.la: De ortu Francorum, qui Gallia occupata, eius nomen in Franciam vel Franco- galliam mutarunt.
units.tr: On the origin of the Franks, who, after occupying Gaul, changed its name to France or Francogallia.

units.la: QVare instituti nostri ratio postulat, vt hoc loco de Francorum ortu, primisque sedib. & tanquam incunabulis inquiramus. Quain disquisitione illud summè admirandum videtur, quòd cùm Francorum nomen per totam nos magnam totius Europæ partem occuparit, eamque Germaniæ gentem fuisse constet, tamen eorum mentio neque apud Ptolemæum, neque apud Strabonē, aut Plinium, ac ne apud Cornelium quidem Tacitum vlla reperiatur: qui tamen Germanicarum omnium gentium situs & nomina mira diligentia persecutus est. Nam de Francici quidem nominis amplitudine pauca hęc ex multis testimonia proferemus.
units.tr: Our plan therefore requires that in this place we inquire into the origin of the Franks, their first seats, and, as it were, their cradle. In this inquiry the most remarkable point is this: although the name of the Franks has taken possession of a large part of all Europe, and although it is established that they were a German people, no mention of them is found in Ptolemy, Strabo, or Pliny, nor even in Cornelius Tacitus, who nevertheless traced the location and names of all the German peoples with wonderful diligence. Of the wide extent of the Frankish name, we shall offer a few testimonies out of many.

units.la: Primùm ex Hieronym. in vita Hilarionis Heremitę: Namque, inquit, candidatus Constantij Imperatoris, rutila coma, & candore corporis, indicans prouinciā: inter Saxones quippe & Alemannos gens est non tam lęta, quàm valida, apud historicos Germania, nunc verò Francia vocatur. Et paulò pòst: Et qui Francam tàtum & Latinam linguam nouerat. Item ex Iohan. Nauclero, Generat. 27. vbi sic loquitur: Carolus Magnus Rex Francorum dicebatur: quod idem erat ac si nominatus fuisset Rex Germanię & Galliæ. Nam clarum est, quòd eo tempore omnis Gallia Transalpina,& etiā Germania,à montibus Pyrenæis vsque in Pannonias,Francia dicebatur: illa,id est,Germanica,Francia Orientalis :alia, id est, Gallica, Francia Occidentalis, in quo verę historiæ consentiunt omnes. Hæc ille. Itaque Abbas Vrspergensis in Carolo Caluo Franciam Orientalem Ostrofranciam appellat: Occidentalem autem Neustriam appellatam fuisse,quasi Westriam, annotauit Rhenanus. Vnde Sigebert.in Chron. Ebroinum, inquit, maiorem domus Neustriæ. Et mox: Pipinus sibi Neustriam subiugat. Sic etiam Aimoinus lib. 4. cap. 27. & alibi persæpe. Chronicū verò Maioris Monasterij sic habet: Neustria est quicquid à Parisijs & Aurelianis interiacet inter Ligerim & Sequanam inferius vsque ad Oceanum. Sic enim Abbas Vrsperg. Et hac de caussa Otto Frising. duo Francorum regna numerat. Nam lib.4.cap.3. de donatione Constantini sic scribit: Ex hinc Romana Ecclesia Occidentalia regna tanquam sui iuris à Constantino sibi tradita affirmat: in argumentuḿque tributum, exceptis duobus Francorū regnis vsque hodie exigere non dubitat. Eguinarthus in vita Caroli Magni, Carolus,inquit, regnum Francorum quod post patrem Pipinū magnum quidem & forte susceperat, ita nobiliter ampliauit, vt pene duplum illi adiecerit. Nam cum prius nō amplius quam ea pars Galliæ,quę intra Rhenum & Ligerim,Oceanumq; & mare Balearicum iacet, & pars Germaniæ, quæ intra Saxoniam & Danubium, Rhenumque ac Salam fluuium, postea à Francis qui Orientales dicuntur, incolitur, & præter hæc Alemanni atque Baioarij ad regni Francorum potestatem pertinerent, ipse per bella memorata primò Aquitaniam, &c. Otto Frifingen. Chronic. 5. cap. 9. Erat autem Francorum iam terminus (loquitur de Dagoberti Regno) ab Hispania vsque in Pannoniam, duos nobilissimos ducatus, Aquitaniam & Baioariam. Sed multo copiosius postea libro 6. capite 17. eumque imitatus Godefridus Viterb. Chronic. parte 17. sub anno 881. Porrò, inquit, Arnulphus totam Orientalem Franciam, quę hodie Teutonicum regnum vocatur, id est Bauariam, Sueuiam, Saxoniam, Turingiam, Phrigiam, & Lotharingiam rexit. Occidentalem verò Franciam Odo tenuit. Idem sub anno 913. Mihi ex multis scriptorum auctoritatibus patuit, regnum Teutonicorum, quod Imperator Fridericus nostro tempore possidet, partem esse regni Francorū. ibi enim primi Franci fuerunt, cis citraq; Rhenum: quæ hodie Francia Orientalis vsque ad terminos Bauariæ appellatur. Francia verò Occidentalis, est regnum illud, quod est cis citraq; Sequanam & Ligerim fluuios. Et mox: Tempore Caroli Magni regis Francorum, tota Gallia, id est Celtica, Belgica, Lugdunensis, omnisque Germania, quæ est à Rheno vsq; ad Illyricū, vna Francia fuit. quæ omnia ex Ottone, vt dixi, ferè descripta sunt. Vitichindus Saxo lib. 1. Vltimus Carolorum apud Orientales Francos imperantium Lothouicus,&c. Notandum etiam est,quod Regino in Chr. anni DLXXVI ita fcribit:Mortuo Pipino Rege,Ludouicus eius filius, qui ad patris obitum fuerat, & funeris eius obsequia celebrauerat,apud Francofurt,Orientalis regni principalem sedem, residebat. Abbas Vrfperg.Carolus Magnus duas habuit filias, de Fœftrada vxore, quæ de Orientaliū Francorū, scilicet Germanorum gente erat.Idem de orig. Sax. Theodoricus, cùm Auftrafiam accepisset, cuius regni sedes apud Metenfem fuit ciuitate. Liutprandus Ticin. lib. 1.cap.6.Simul vt Wido, quam Romanam dicunt Franciam, Berengarius Italiam obtineret.Et paulò pòst: Cumq; Burgundionum regna transiés, Franciam, quá Romanam dicunt,ingredi vellet, &c. Romanam autem Franciam iccirco appellabant, primùm quia Galliam quæ Romanis paruerat, Franci occuparant. deinde quoniam Romana lingua in ea regione vsitata erat: quemadmodum superiùs diximus: vnde vetus nata locutio, Loqui Romanum, de ijs qui Germanicè fiue Francicè non loquebantur. Indidemqué factum est, vt eadem Gallia Romana diceretur. Regino lib. 2.sub anno 939. Interim Ludouicus Rex Galliæ Romanæ,filius Caroli,consilio inimicorum Regis Alfatiam inuadit. Hinc illud Ottonis Frifing. Chron. 4. cap. pen. Videtur mihi inde Francos,qui in Gallijs morantur, à Romanis linguam eorum, qua vsque hodie vtuntur, accommodasse. Nam alij qui circa Rhenum, ac in Germania remanserunt, Theutonica lingua vtuntur. Et hunc nimium familiariter imitatus multis locis Godfridus Viterb. parte 17. cap.
units.tr: First, from Jerome in the Life of Hilarion the Hermit: "For," he says, "the candidatus of the Emperor Constantius, with his reddish hair and fair complexion, indicating the province: between the Saxons and the Alemanni there is a people not so cheerful as strong; in the historians it is called Germany, but now it is called France." And a little later: "and who knew only the Frankish and Latin tongue." Likewise from Johann Nauclerus, Generation 27, where he speaks thus: "Charles the Great was called King of the Franks; this was the same as if he had been named King of Germany and Gaul. For it is clear that at that time all Transalpine Gaul, and also Germany, from the Pyrenees as far as Pannonia, was called France: the one part, that is, the German, was East France; the other part, that is, the Gallic, was West France; in this all true histories agree." Thus he. Accordingly the Abbot of Ursperg, in his account of Charles the Bald, calls East France "Ostrofrancia"; and Rhenanus has noted that West France was called "Neustria," as if "Westria." Hence Sigebert in his Chronicle: "Ebroin, the mayor of the palace of Neustria." And soon after: "Pepin subjugates Neustria to himself." So too Aimoin, book 4, chapter 27, and very often elsewhere. The Chronicle of the Monastery of Maire, however, says: "Neustria is whatever lies between Paris and Orléans, between the Loire and the Seine, lower down as far as the Ocean." For the Abbot of Ursperg says so as well. And for this reason Otto of Freising also counts two kingdoms of the Franks. For in book 4, chapter 3, on the Donation of Constantine, he writes: "From this the Roman Church asserts that the Western kingdoms were handed over to it by Constantine as its own right, and as a token of this tribute, with the exception of the two kingdoms of the Franks, it does not hesitate to exact even to this day." Eginhard, in the Life of Charles the Great: "Charles," he says, "so nobly enlarged the kingdom of the Franks, which he had received after his father Pepin the Great, and perhaps had received by chance, that he added almost double to it. For whereas before, it extended no further than that part of Gaul which lies between the Rhine and the Loire, the Ocean and the Balearic Sea, and that part of Germany which, between Saxony and the Danube, and the rivers Rhine and Saale, is later inhabited by the Franks who are called Eastern; and besides these, the Alemanni and Bavarians belonged to the power of the kingdom of the Franks: he himself, by the wars mentioned, first conquered Aquitaine, etc." Otto of Freising, Chronicle, book 5, chapter 9: "Now the boundary of the Franks (he speaks of the kingdom of Dagobert) extended from Spain as far as Pannonia, including two most noble duchies, Aquitaine and Bavaria." But more fully afterwards in book 6, chapter 17; and Godfrey of Viterbo, imitating him, in Chronicle part 17, under the year 881: "Moreover," he says, "Arnulf ruled all East France, which today is called the Teutonic kingdom, that is, Bavaria, Swabia, Saxony, Thuringia, Frisia, and Lotharingia. West France, however, Odo held." The same under the year 913. "It has been made clear to me from the authority of many writers that the kingdom of the Teutons, which the Emperor Frederick possesses in our time, is part of the kingdom of the Franks. For there the first Franks lived, on both sides of the Rhine; what is today called East France extends as far as the borders of Bavaria. West France, however, is that kingdom which lies on both sides of the rivers Seine and Loire." And soon after: "In the time of Charles the Great, king of the Franks, the whole of Gaul, that is, Celtic, Belgic, Lugdunensis, and all Germany, which extends from the Rhine as far as Illyricum, was one France." All of these are almost copied from Otto, as I said. Widukind the Saxon, book 1: "The last of the Carolingians ruling among the Eastern Franks was Louis, etc." It must also be noted that Regino, in his Chronicle under the year 876, writes thus: "When King Pepin had died, his son Louis, who had been at his father's death and had celebrated the rites of his funeral, resided at Frankfurt, the principal seat of the Eastern kingdom." The Abbot of Ursperg: "Charles the Great had two daughters by his wife Fastrada, who was of the people of the Eastern Franks, that is, of the Germans." The same, in his work on the origin of the Saxons: "Theodoric, when he had received Austrasia, whose royal seat was at the city of Metz." Liutprand of Cremona, book 1, chapter 6: "At the same time, while Guy, whom they call the Roman France, and Berengar obtained Italy." And a little later: "And when he wished to pass through the kingdoms of the Burgundians and enter France, which they call Roman, etc." Now they called it the Roman France chiefly for this reason: first, because the Franks had occupied Gaul, which had been subject to the Romans; then because the Roman language was in use in that region, as we said above. Hence the old saying, "to speak Roman," said of those who did not speak German or Frankish. And from the same cause it came about that the same Gaul was called Roman. Regino, book 2, under the year 939: "Meanwhile Louis, king of Roman Gaul, son of Charles, on the advice of the king's enemies, invades Alsace." Hence that remark of Otto of Freising, Chronicle, book 4, last chapter: "It seems to me that the Franks who dwell in Gaul adopted from the Romans the language which they use to this day. For the others who remained around the Rhine and in Germany use the Teutonic tongue." And Godfrey of Viterbo, imitating him too closely, in many places, part 17, chapter

units.la: 1. Videntur, inquit, mihi Franci in illis temporibus linguam Romanam, qua vsque hodie vtuntur, ab illis Romanis, qui ibi habitauerant, didicisse. His ex locis perspicuum est, miram Francorum nominis amplitudinem atque auctoritatem fuisse: quippe, cum magnam Europae partem occuparet. Quinetiā videmus Germanos in Neapolitanum & Siculum regnum ab Imp.Frideric. 11. traductos, ibique tanquam colonos presidio collocatos, Francorum nomine appellatos fuisse. Petrus de Vineis libro Epist. 6.cap.25. Viuensiure Francorum, in eo videlicet, quòd maior natu, exclusis minoribus fratribus, in castro ipso succedat. Imp.Fridericus 11. Neapol.const.lib. 2. tit. 32. Ingerentes se casus praesentis materiae circa Francos, qui personarum suarum, plurimarumque rerum suarum omnium fortunam in monomachiam, quę Duellum vulgariter dicitur, reponebant. Et mox: Praedictum igitur probationis modum, quo iure Francorum viuentes vtebantur. Item li.2.tit.33, Quod ius inter omnes tam Francos, quàm Logobardos in causis omnibus volumus esse commune. Haec cùm ita sint, tamen Gregorius Tunon. Episcopus, qui de Francorum ortu octingentis ab hinc annis scripsit, initio historiae suae testatur, se, cùm accuratè de Francorum ortu quaequæsiuissët, nihil tamë certi comperisse: quamuis veterem quendam illorum historicum habuerit Sulpitium Alexandrum: qui neque de primis illorum sedibus, neq; de Regni primordijs quicquam affirmarit. At nos ex ea regione Francos primùm ortos animaduertimus, quæ inter Albim & Rhenum interiecta, Oceano alluitur: vbi ferè Chauci maiores & minores collocantur: populus (vt ait Tacitus) inter Germanos nobilissimus: quíque magnitudine suam iustitia tuetur, & Batauorum regioni finitimus erat. Nam primùm omnium satis constat, Francos in ora maritima sedes habuisse, locis admodum palustribus: reique nauticæ peritissimos, & in bellis maritimis exercitatissimos fuisse. Quarum rerum documenta hæc extant primum apud Claudianum, qui Stiliconi victorias gratulans, ita scribit:
units.tr: 1. "It seems to me," he says, "that in those times the Franks learned the Roman language, which they use to this day, from those Romans who had lived there." From these passages it is plain that the name of the Franks had a wonderful breadth and authority, since it occupied a large part of Europe. Indeed, we see that the Germans who were brought by Emperor Frederick II into the kingdom of Naples and Sicily, and settled there as colonists for protection, were also called by the name of the Franks. Peter de Vinea, book 6 of the Letters, chapter 25: "the living law of the Franks, namely in this, that the eldest son, excluding the younger brothers, succeeds in the castle itself." Emperor Frederick II, Constitutions of Naples, book 2, title 32: "Accidents of the present matter arising concerning the Franks, who staked the fortune of their persons and of most of their possessions on a monomachy, which is commonly called a duel." And soon after: "Therefore the aforesaid mode of proof, by which those living under the law of the Franks used to proceed." Likewise book 2, title 33: "We wish that this law be common to all, both Franks and Lombards, in all causes." Although these things are so, nevertheless Gregory of Tours, bishop, who wrote about the origin of the Franks eight hundred years ago, testifies at the beginning of his history that, although he had inquired carefully into the origin of the Franks, he had found nothing certain, although he had an old historian of theirs, Sulpicius Alexander, who affirmed nothing about their first seats nor about the beginnings of the kingdom. But we observe that the Franks first arose from that region which lies between the Elbe and the Rhine, washed by the Ocean, where the Greater and Lesser Chauci are for the most part located: a people (as Tacitus says) the most noble among the Germans, who maintain their greatness by justice, and who bordered on the region of the Batavians. For first of all it is quite certain that the Franks had their seats on the seacoast, in very marshy places, and that they were most skilled in naval matters and most practised in sea battles. Evidence of these things survives first in Claudian, who, congratulating Stilicho on his victories, writes thus:

units.la: Vt iam transfluuium non indignante Chayco, Pascat Belga pecus mediúque ingressa per Albim Gallica Francorum montes armenta pererrent.
units.tr: So that now, with the Chayci not objecting, the Belgian flock grazes across the river, and the Gallic herds, having crossed the Elbe, roam through the mountains of the Franks.

units.la: Quo loco Chaycos poeticè appellauit, quos Geographi Chaucos nominarunt. De maritima verò illorum regione Panegyricus Constantino Magno dictus, testimonio est, vbi Rhetor ita loquitur: Quid loquar rursus intimas Franciæ nationes, non iam ab his locis quæ olim Romani inuaserunt, sed à proprijs ex origine suis sedibus, atque ab vltimis Barbariæ litoribus auulsas: vt in defertis Galliæ regionibus collocatæ, pacem Romani imperij cultu iuuarent, & arma delectu. Rursus in altero Eumenij rhetoris Panegyrico, vbi sic loquitur: Aut hæc ipsa, quæ modo definit esse barbaria, non magis feritate Francorum, velut hausta desederat, quàm si eam circumfusa flumina & mare alluens operuisset. Eodemq; pertinet Procopij testimonium belli Gothici lib.1.nā vbi eum locum describit, quo Rhenus in Oceanum influit: His, inquit, locis non mediocres sunt paludes: vbi antiquitus Germani habitabāt: natio barbara, nec magnæ tum exi-stimationis homines, qui nunc Franci nominantur. Quem Procopij locum Zonaras in suum Annal. to. 3. retulit; Zosimus autem in Gothici belli librum primum. Eodem etiam pertinet ille Flau. Vopisci locus, in vita Probi Imp. vbi scribit. Fracos à Probo inuijs paludibus profligatos. Testes sunt, inquit, Franci, inuijs strati paludibus. Item illud Sidonij Apollinaris,
units.tr: Here he poetically calls them Chayci, whom the geographers named Chauci. The Panegyric delivered to Constantine the Great bears witness to their maritime region, where the orator speaks thus: "Why should I speak again of the inner nations of the Franks, torn away not from those places which the Romans once invaded, but from their own seats of origin and from the farthest shores of Barbary, so that, settled in the deserted regions of Gaul, they might support the peace of the Roman empire by cultivation and by the levy of arms?" Again, in the other Panegyric, by the rhetor Eumenius, where he speaks thus: "Or this very land, which has only just ceased to be barbarous, did not sink down as if swallowed up by the ferocity of the Franks, but was covered as if by rivers flowing around it and the sea washing over it." To the same point belongs the testimony of Procopius in book 1 of the Gothic War. Where he describes the place where the Rhine flows into the Ocean, he says: "In these places there are no small marshes, where anciently the Germans lived, a barbarous nation, and men not of great reputation at that time, who are now called Franks." Zonaras reported this passage of Procopius in volume 3 of his Annals, and Zosimus in the first book of the Gothic War. To the same point also belongs that passage of Flavius Vopiscus in the Life of the Emperor Probus, where he writes that the Franks were routed by Probus through impassable marshes. "The Franks," he says, "are witnesses, who were laid low in impassable marshes." Likewise that line of Sidonius Apollinaris:
Of the Franks and their most remote marshes

units.la: Intrares venerantibus Sicambris. Iam vero quod de Chaucorum vicinitate diximus, ea planissimè ex collatione locorum, & vtrorumque sedium descriptione perspicitur. Chaucorum quidem apud Plin. lib. 16. cap. 1. Francorum verò, apud illum Rhetorem Panegyristem. Nam Plin. quidem ita loquitur: Sunt in Septentrione vitæ nobis Chaucorum gentes, qui maiores minoresque appellantur, vasto ibi meatu: bis dierum noctiumque singularum intervallis effusus in immensum agitur Oceanus, æteræternam operiens rerum naturæ controuersiam: dubiumque terræ fit, an parte in maris. At Panegyriftes: Quanquam, inquit, illa regio diuinis expeditionibus tuis Cæsar vindicata atque purgata, quam obliquis meatibus callidis (sic legendum, vt in libris vulgatis, non S c a l d i s, vt quidam reposuit) interfluit: quamque diuortio sui Rhenus amplectitur, penè, vt verbi periculo loquar, terra non est. ita penitus aquis permaduit, vt non solùm quæ manifeste palustris est, cedat adnixum, & hauriat pressa vestigium: verumetiam vbi paulò videtur firmior, pedum pulsu tentata quatiatur: & sentire se procul mota pondus testetur. Patefactum igitur arbitramur esse locum, vnde Francorum in Galliam natio propagata est: palustris videlicet ea regio, quæ inter Albim & Rhenum Oceanum attingit. Quod eo etiam argumento confirmari potest, quòd Franci maritimarum rerum vsum maximum habebant, latéque per eam oram vagabuntur.
units.tr: You would enter them while the Sicambri paid reverence. Now indeed, what we have said about the neighbourhood of the Chauci is made perfectly clear by comparing the passages and describing the seats of both peoples: that of the Chauci in Pliny, book 16, chapter 1, and that of the Franks in that rhetor, the panegyrist. For Pliny speaks thus: "In the North there are for us the tribes of the Chauci, who are called Greater and Lesser, living in a vast tract where the Ocean, poured out in immense expanse at intervals of two days and nights each, covers eternally the dispute of nature, so that it is doubtful whether the land is part of the sea." But the panegyrist: "Although," he says, "that region, Caesar, has been claimed and cleansed by your divine campaigns, which the Rhine flows through in winding, devious channels (so it should be read, as in the common editions, not Scaldis, as someone proposed), and which the Rhine embraces in its separation, is almost, to speak with a risk of words, not land at all. It has soaked so deeply with water that it not only yields to one who presses on where it is plainly marshy, and swallows the foot pressed down upon it, but even where it seems somewhat firmer, when it is tested by the stamp of feet it shakes, and testifies that it feels the weight even when it is moved from afar." We therefore judge that the place has been revealed from which the nation of the Franks spread into Gaul: namely that marshy region which, between the Elbe and the Rhine, touches the Ocean. This can also be confirmed by the argument that the Franks had the greatest use of maritime affairs and wandered widely along that coast.

units.la: Nam Eutrop. libro 9. vbi Gallieni Imperatoris historiam percurrit: Post hæc tempora, inquit, Caraufius cum per tractum Belgicæ Armoricæ pacandum mare accepisset, quod Franci & Saxones infestabant. Qua eadem de re Paulus quoque Orofius lib. 7. commemorat. Eodem pertinet alter in illo, quem aliquoties iam protulimus Panegyrico, locus, vbi Rhetor ita loquitur: Franci, inquit, præter cæteros truces quorum vis cùm ad bellum efferuesce-
units.tr: For Eutropius, book 9, where he runs through the history of the Emperor Gallienus, says: "After these times, when Carausius had received the task of pacifying the sea along the tract of Belgic Armorica, which the Franks and Saxons were harassing..." Paulus Orosius also records the same matter in book 7. To the same point belongs another passage in that Panegyric which we have already cited several times, where the rhetor speaks thus: "The Franks," he says, "fiercer than the rest, whose strength, when it was roused to war,

units.la: ret, vltra ipsum Oceanum æstu furoris eueƈta, Hispanorum etiam oras armis infestas habebat. Itaque Iustinianus Imper. li. Codic. 2. vbi Præfeƈti prætorio Africæ officium exponit, mentionem facit Francorum, qui in parte quadã Galliæ finitima Hispaniæ confederant. Memorabile est autem, & ad bellicæ laudis gloriam insigne, quod alio Panegyrici loco narratur, exiguas Francorum copias, quos Imperator Probus bello superatos in Pontum captiuos abduxerat, nauibus aliquot interceptis, vsq; in Græciam & Asiam vagatos esse: Siciliam inuasisse: Syracusas cepisse: post onustos præda & spolijs per fretum Herculeum in Oceanum reuertisse. Recursabat, inquit, in animos, sub diuo Probo, & paucorum ex Francis captiuorum incredibilis audacia, & indigna felicitas: qui à Ponto vsque correptis nauibus, Græciam, Asiamque populati, nec impunè plerisq; Lybiæ littoribus appulsi, ipsas postremò naualibus quondam victorijs nobiles ceperant Syracusas: & immeso itinere permensi Oceanum, qua terras rupit, intrauerant: atque ita euentu temeritatis ostenderant, nihil esse clausum piraticæ desperationi, quò nauigijs pateret accessus. Quam eandem historiam Zosimus sub finem Histor. 1. his verbis commemorat: Cùm Franci ad Imperatorem accessissent, & ab eo sedes obtinuissent, pars eorumquædam defeƈtionem molita, magnamque nauium copiam naƈta, totam Græciam conturbauit. In Siciliam quoq; delata, & vrbem bem Syracusas adorta, magná in ea cædem edidit. Tandem cum & in Africam appulisset, ac reiecta fuisset, adductis Carthagine copijs, nihilominus domum redire, nullum passa detrimentum potuit. Hoc quoque Probo imperáte contigit. Et ad hanc disputationem ea quoque auctorum loca referenda sunt, ex quibus intelligitur, Francorum sedes Batauorum finib. propinquas fuisse. Nam Rhetor ille Maximianum & Constantinum alloquens: Multa, inquit, ille Francorum millia, qui Batauiā aliasque cis Rhenum terras inuaserant, interfecit, depulit, abduxit. Præterea insignis extat locus apud Corn. Tacit. in lib. 20. vbi de Batauiæ & Frisiæ vicinitate commemorans, Caninefates quoque admiscet: quorum eam scribit consuetudinem in Rege creando fuisse, quam posterius verè Francicam fuisse ostendemus. Missi, inquit, ad Caninefates, qui consilia sociarent. Ea gens partem insulæ colit, origine, lingua, virtute par Batauis: numero superantur. Et mox: Brinnio impositus scuto, more gentis, & sustinentium humeris vibratus, dux deligitur. Quæ verba haud exiguĩ esse ad nostram disputationem momēti, posterius, cùm ad eum locum ventum erit, intelligetur. Quæ cùm ita se habeant, satis equidem admirari Adr. Turnebi doctissimi viri iudicium non possum, qui tam multis veterum auctorum locis pro nihilo habitis, scripsit videri sibi Francos ex Scandinauia oriundos: propterea quod apud Ptolemæum in illa insula Phirassi
units.tr: and carried beyond the Ocean itself by the surge of their fury, also kept the shores of Spain under hostile arms." So Justinian, in book 2 of the Code, where he sets out the duty of the Praetorian Prefect of Africa, makes mention of the Franks who had settled in a part of Gaul bordering on Spain. But there is also a memorable passage, notable for the glory of military praise, related in another place of the Panegyric: that the small force of Franks, whom the Emperor Probus had defeated in war and carried off captive to Pontus, after some ships had been seized, wandered as far as Greece and Asia, attacked Sicily, took Syracuse, and afterwards, laden with booty and spoils, returned through the Strait of Hercules into the Ocean. "There came back to mind," he says, "in the time of the deified Probus, the incredible daring and undeserved good fortune of a few captive Franks, who, from Pontus, seizing ships, laid waste Greece and Asia, and, not without impunity, landing on most of the shores of Libya, at last took Syracuse, once famous for its naval victories; and, having traversed an immense journey, they passed into the Ocean where the land is broken through, and thus by the outcome of their rashness showed that nothing is closed to piratical recklessness where ships can make their way." Zosimus records this same story near the end of his first book in these words: "When the Franks had come to the Emperor and had obtained lands from him, part of them, plotting revolt and having got a great number of ships, threw all Greece into confusion. Carried also into Sicily, and attacking the city of Syracuse, they made great slaughter there. At last, when they had also landed in Africa and been driven back, and then, with forces brought from Carthage, they were still able to return home without suffering any loss." This too happened under the rule of Probus. And to this discussion those passages of authors should also be referred, from which it is understood that the seats of the Franks were near the borders of the Batavians. For that rhetor, addressing Maximian and Constantine: "He killed," he says, "destroyed and carried off many thousands of those Franks who had invaded Batavia and other lands on this side of the Rhine." Moreover, a notable passage is found in Cornelius Tacitus, book 20 (sic), where, speaking of the neighbourhood of Batavia and Frisia, he also mentions the Caninefates, whose custom in creating a king he writes was that which we shall later show to have been truly Frankish. "Envoys were sent," he says, "to the Caninefates to join counsels. That people inhabits part of the island, equal to the Batavians in origin, language and courage, but surpassed in numbers." And soon after: "Brinno, placed on a shield in the manner of the people and tossed on the shoulders of those who held it up, was chosen as leader." These words will be seen, when we come to that place, to be of no small weight for our argument. Since these matters stand thus, I certainly cannot but wonder at the judgment of Adrien Turnèbe, a most learned man, who, setting aside so many passages of the ancient authors, wrote that he thought the Franks were of Scandinavian origin, because in Ptolemy, in that island, the name Phirassi

units.la: C collocantur.Quam vocem corruptā,& FRANCI reponendum censet. Neque tamen praeter meram diuinationem vllam huius opinionis suae rationem affert, quae tamen opinio à veterum scriptorum omnium auctoritatibus apertissimè dissidet.De ceteris verò propè omnibus, qui fabulis delectati, Francorum originem ad Troianos,& Francionem nescio quem Priami filium retulerunt, tantum dicimus, Poëtis illos, non historicis scribendi argumentum praebuisse: eoque in numero primum merito locum Guillielmo Bellayo tribuimus: qui cùm omnium optimarum artium doctrina, summaque ingenij laude praestaret, tamen in libello de Galliae & Franciae antiquitatibus, non Francogallicae historiae,sed Amadificarum fabularum institutionem tractationem videtur.
units.tr: C are placed. He thinks this word is corrupt and that FRANCI should be put in its place. Yet he offers no reason for this opinion except mere guesswork, and this opinion is most openly at odds with the authority of all the ancient writers. As for almost all the others, who, delighting in fables, have traced the origin of the Franks back to the Trojans and to a certain Francio, a son of Priam, we only say this: they supplied material for writing to poets, not to historians. Among these we rightly give the first place to Guillaume du Bellay, who, although he excelled in the learning of all the best arts and in the highest praise of talent, yet in his little book on the antiquities of Gaul and France, seems to treat not the history of the Franco-Gallic people but the training of fables in the manner of Amadis.

units.la: De Francorum nomine, variisque excursionibus, & quo tempore regnum sibi in Gallia constituerint. CAP. V.
units.tr: On the name of the Franks, their various wanderings, and when they established a kingdom for themselves in Gaul. CHAP. V.

units.la: SEd ratio postulat, ut de hoc Francorum nomine paulò attentius consideremus: quod nusquam in Germaniae descriptione reperiri superius diximus. Ne diutius teneam, necesse est vel Francorum gentem tenuem obscuramque fuisse, à qua tamen tantarum rerum gerendarum initia nata sunt: quemadmodum in Suitis tenuissimo Heluetiorum pago vsuuenit, à quo cùm recuperandæ libertatis auctores orti primùm fuissent, Suitzerorum nomen in Helvetios omnes propagatum est: vel, quod mihi verisimilius videtur, fictam ex re & occasione appellationem fuisse: cùm ij, qui se libertatis recuperandæ principes atque auctores profitebantur, FRANCOS se nominassent: qua voce liberos, & seruitutis expertes, apud Germanos intelligi, satis inter eruditos & literatos Germanos constare video. indéque Francum popularilingua, pro libero & immuni: & Frácisiam, pro asylo vsurpamus: & Francisare, vel affrácire pro in libertatem asserere. Itaq; rectissime Iohan. Auentinus lib. 4. Francorum nomen, inquit, crebrum est in saltis nostris antiquis: deductū à libertate, quæ Teutonum lingua Freyghait, & Freyghun dicitur. quod cognomen adhuc Franconibus nostris tribui solet. Vocantur enim vulgo, de freyen Francken, hoc est liberi Franci. Item Hieronymus Surita de regib. Aragon. sub anno DCCCXLIV: Carolus Caluus Francorum Rex Barcinonensibus siue Hispani, siue Gothi essent, immunitatem libertatemque elargitur, qua Franci vti assueuerant: permittitque, vt Gothicis legibus iura inter se foraque constituant. Immunitas ea à Francis in Hispania FRANKITAS dicta. Francorum enim nationem Germanicam Carolus Magnus Germanis reliquis & Frisijs commodiore immunitatis conditione antetulerat. Itē sub anno MCX. Iulio mense, vt oppidū frequentissime coleretur, habitareturque, ciuibus Exeanis Frankitatis (id est,ingenuitatis) ornamenta ab Imperatore praestantur. Item Albert. Krantz. lib. 4. metrop. cap. 14. Nam ex Theutonico vocabulo ortum est. Franck enim Germanica lingua liber dicitur, nulli obnoxius seruitutis. Ant. Sabellicus Ennead. x. lib. 11. Francos, inquit, Itali liberos appellant: quippe cum Itali ex Germanorum eluuionibus promanarint. Eius autem rei primum argumentum est, quod Procopius libro Goth. bell. 1. memoriae prodidit, Francos antiquitus generali nomine Germanos appellatos fuisse, post vero quam e finibus suis excesserunt, Francorum nomen obtinuisse. Alterum est, quod Corn. Tacitus lib. 20. vbi de Caninefatibus loquitur (quos Francorum finitimos, vel potius populares, atque adeo Francos ipsos natiuos fuisse ostendimus) eorumque primam aduersus Romanos victoriam describit, his verbis: Clara ea victoria in praesens, in posteru vsui: armaque & naues quibus indigebant adepti, magna per Germanias Galliasque fama, LIBERTATIS AVCTORES celebrabantur. Germaniae statim misere legatos, auxilia offerentes. Valeat igitur omen, ut FRANCI vere proprieque dicantur, qui Tyrannorum seruitute depulsa, honestam, etiam sub regum auctoritate, libertatem sibi retinendam putarunt. Non enim regi parere seruitus est: neque qui regi parent, continuo serui habendi sunt: sed qui Tyranni libidini, qui latroni, qui carnifici, tanquam pecudes lanioni
units.tr: But reason requires that we consider this name of the Franks a little more carefully, since, as I said above, it is nowhere to be found in the description of Germany. To avoid lingering too long, either the Frankish people was a small and obscure nation, from which nonetheless the beginnings of great deeds arose, just as happened among the Swiss in the tiny district of the Helvetii, from which the authors of the recovery of liberty first sprang, and the name Swiss was then spread to all the Helvetii; or, what seems to me more probable, the name was invented from the circumstance and occasion, when those who professed themselves the leaders and authors of recovering liberty called themselves Franks. I see that it is sufficiently agreed among learned and literate Germans that by this word, among the Germans, people free and exempt from servitude are understood. From this we in the vernacular use "Franc" for free and immune, "Frankish" (Fráncisia) for asylum, and "to franchise" or "to affranchise" for to assert into liberty. So Johannes Aventinus rightly says in book 4: "The name of the Franks," he says, "is common in our old woods, derived from liberty, which in the Teutonic tongue is called Freyghait and Freyghun. This surname is still usually given to our Franconians. For they are commonly called de freyen Francken, that is, free Franks." Likewise Jerónimo Zurita, in his work on the kings of Aragon, under the year 844: Charles the Bald, king of the Franks, granted to the people of Barcelona, whether they were Spaniards or Goths, the immunity and liberty which the Franks were accustomed to enjoy, and allowed them to establish among themselves laws and courts according to Gothic law. That immunity was called FRANKITAS by the Franks in Spain. For Charles the Magnus had placed the German nation of the Franks before the other Germans and the Frisians under a more advantageous condition of immunity. Also, under the year 1110, in the month of July, so that the town might be more densely inhabited and settled, the citizens of Exeter were granted by the Emperor the privileges of Frankitas (that is, of freeborn status). Also Albert Krantz, book 4 of the Metropolis, chapter 14: "For it arose from a Teutonic word. Franck in the German language means free, subject to no servitude." Antonio Sabellico, Enneads 10, book 11: "The Italians," he says, "call the Franks free men, since the Italians sprang from the floods of the Germans." The first proof of this is what Procopius, in book 1 of the Gothic War, recorded: that the Franks were anciently called Germans by a general name, but after they had left their own borders they obtained the name of Franks. The second is what Cornelius Tacitus, book 20, says when speaking of the Canninefates (whom we have shown to be neighbours of the Franks, or rather their kinsmen, and indeed the Franks themselves by birth), describing their first victory over the Romans in these words: "That victory was famous for the present and for the future; and having obtained arms and ships, which they lacked, they were celebrated throughout Germany and Gaul as the AUTHORS OF LIBERTY. The Germans at once sent envoys offering auxiliaries." Let the omen stand, then, that those are truly and properly called Franks who, having thrown off the servitude of tyrants, judged that they should keep their liberty honourable, even under the authority of kings. For to obey a king is not servitude; nor are those who obey a king at once to be held as slaves. But those who submit themselves like cattle to the butcher, to the tyrant's lust, to the robber, to the executioner, these at last are to be called by the most abject name of slaves.

units.la: LIBERTATIS AVCTORES lanioni sese subijciunt, ij demum vilissimo seruorum nomine appellandi sunt. Itaque reges semper Franci habuerunt, etiam tum, cùm assertores se ac vindices libertatis profitebantur: & cùm sibi reges constituerunt, non tyrannos, aut carnifices: sed libertatis suæ custodes, præfectos, tutores sibi constituerunt. quemadmodū ex Francogallicæ Reipublicæ forma posteriùs intelligetur. Sic Claudianus lib.3 cecinit, Nusquam libertas gratior vlla est, Quam sub Rege pio. Sic Sallustius, Regem primis temporibus à Romanis habitum scribit, conseruandæ libertatis atque augendæ Reipubl. caussa. Vbi verò suam libertatem labefactari Regum insanijs senserunt, tum ijs pulsis suam sibi tutandam libertatem iudicarunt. Quæ verò Iohannes Turpinus nescio quis, monachus certè stolidus atq; imperitus, qui Caroli Magni, non vitam, sed fabulam conscripsit, de Francorum vocabulo nugatur, vt qui pecuniam ad Dionysianum templum ædificandum contulisset, Francus, id est, liber diceretur: quasi nomen illud Regis illius Caroli tempore demum natum sit: ne memoratu quidem dignum est: non magis quàm reliqua illius omnia, fabulis anilibus ac delirijs referta. Nostram porrò de Francorum nomine coniecturam adiuuat, quòd Gregorius Turon. Ado Viennensis, Sigebertus, Abbas Vrsperg. Godfridus Viterbiensis scribunt, Francos à libertate, & (vt illi ad vocis notionem alludentes loquuntur) à ferocitate nomen inuenisse: propterea quod Valentiniani Imperatoris ftipendarij esse, tributaque aliarum nationum more pendere recusarent. non quò Francorum nominis mentio non multo antiquior sit Valentiniani Imp. ætate: nam (vt superius demonstratum est) amplius centum ante annis sub Gallienis Imp p. vsurpata est. sed quia finitimi populi cùm Francorum exemplum virtutemque imitarentur, seseq; ex Romanorum tyrannide in libertatem vindicarent, eorundem etiam nomen vsurpandum putarunt. Nam quod Hunibaldus ait nominatos à Franco Antharij Sicambrorum Regis filio; idq; factum addit Octaviano Augusto imperante: primum ab omnium Romanorum & Græcorum historijs alienum est, apud quos nulla tam antiquis temporibus Francorum mentio reperitur: vt superius demonstratum est. Deinde cùm illi populi Regē sibi crearent, (sicuti & iam prius dictum est,& postea dicetur) perabsurdum est, existimare populum à Rege potius, quàm Regem à populo denominatum. Multo verò absurdius est, eosdem dicere Francos & Sicambros fuisse: propter hemistichium à diuo Remigio in Clodoveo baptisando vsurpatum: Mitis depone colla Sicamber. Nam alios Francos, alios Sicambros fuisse, versus illi Sido. Apollinaris declarant:
units.tr: The authors of liberty. Therefore the Franks always had kings, even at the time when they professed themselves champions and defenders of liberty; and when they set up kings for themselves, they did not set up tyrants or executioners, but guardians of their liberty, prefects and tutors. This will be understood later from the form of the Frankish-Gallic commonwealth. So Claudian sang in book 3: Nowhere is liberty any more welcome than under a dutiful king. So Sallust writes that in the earliest times the Romans had a king, for the sake of preserving liberty and increasing the commonwealth. But when they felt their liberty undermined by the madness of kings, then, having driven them out, they judged that they must defend their liberty for themselves. As for what a certain John Turpin, a monk assuredly foolish and unskilled, who wrote not the life but the fable of Charles the Great, chatters about the word Franc, namely that whoever had contributed money to build the temple of Dionysius was called Francus, that is, free, as if that name had arisen only in the time of that king Charles: it is not even worth mentioning, no more than all the rest of his writings, which are stuffed with old wives' tales and nonsense. Our conjecture about the name of the Franks is further supported by the fact that Gregory of Tours, Ado of Vienne, Sigebert, the Abbot of Ursperg, and Godfrey of Viterbo write that the Franks got their name from liberty and (as they, alluding to the meaning of the word, put it) from fierceness, because they refused to be paid soldiers of the Emperor Valentinian and to pay tribute like other nations. Not that the mention of the name of the Franks is much older than the age of the Emperor Valentinian, for (as has been shown above) it was in use more than a hundred years earlier, under the Emperor Gallienus. But because neighbouring peoples, when they imitated the example and courage of the Franks, and vindicated themselves from Roman tyranny into liberty, thought that they too should take up the same name. As for Hunibald's claim that they were named after Franco, son of Antharius, king of the Sicambri, and that this happened under the Emperor Octavian Augustus: first, this is foreign to the histories of all the Romans and Greeks, among whom no mention of the Franks is found in such ancient times, as has been shown above. Next, since those peoples set up kings for themselves (as has already been said and will be said again), it is utterly absurd to suppose that the people were named from the king rather than the king from the people. And it is far more absurd to say that the Franks and the Sicambri were the same people, on account of the half-verse which the blessed Remigius used at the baptism of Clovis: "Bow your neck, gentle Sicambrian." For that others were Franks and others Sicambri is declared by those verses of Sidonius Apollinaris:
You would enter even the most remote marshes of the Franks,

units.la: Intrares, venerantibus Sicambris. Item illi Claudiani ad Honorium:
units.tr: with the Sicambri revering you. Likewise those lines of Claudian to Honorius:

units.la: Ante ducem nostrum flauam sparsere Sicambri Cæsariem pauidoq; orantes murmure Franci. Procubuer e solo.
units.tr: Before our leader the Sicambri scattered their yellow hair, and the Franks, trembling and praying with murmurs, fell prostrate on the ground.

units.la: Quare vt illud à Remigio vsurpatum hemistichium concedamus, tamen alludendi potius quàm veri nominis designandi caussa, id factu esse probabile est. Verùm, vt ad institutu redeamus, illud verissimè dici ac prædicari potest, omé Francorum nominis, hoc est (vt Cornelius Tacitus interpretatur) auctorum libertatis ita faustum, felix, fortunatumque fuisse, vt ex eo victoriæ propè innumerabiles consecutæ sint. Nam postea quàm illo consilio Franci è suis finibus excesserunt, non modò Germaniam, patriam communem, verumetiam Galliam, ad extremum etiam Alpes transgressi, partem Italiæ non mediocrem à Romanorum tyrannide liberarunt. Prima autem & antiquissima huius illustrissimi nominis mentio reperitur nō sub Imperatore Decio, vt quosdam nimium confidenter affirmare video: sed sub Imp. Gallieno, hoc est circiter annum Christianæ salutis cclx. Nam Trebellius Pollio in eius vita: Cum ludibrijs, inquit, & helluationi vacaret, neque aliter Rempublicam regeret, quàm cùm pueri singunt per ludibria potestates: Galli, quibus insitum est luxuriosos principes ferre non posse, Postumum ad imperium vocarunt: qui tum Gallieni legatus Galliæ cum imperio præerat. Et paulò post: Contra Postumum igitur Gallienus bellum incepit, & cum multis auxilijs Poftumus iuuaretur, Celticis ac Francicis,in bellum cum Victorino processit. Quibus ex verbis intelligitur, Gallos ad depellendam Gallieni Tyranni seruitutem, Francorum, id est,auctorū libertatis, auxilijs vsos fuisse. Quod idem breuiter Zonaras significans in Gallieni vita,ἐπολέμησε δὲ inquit, Φεσσίρυις &c. Altera eorundem mentio rursus occurrit apud Flau. Vopiscum,in Aureliani vita,his verbis: Apud Moguntiacum Tribunus legionis sextæ Gallicanæ, Francos irruentes, cum vagarentur per totam Galliam, sic afflixit, vt trecentos ex his captos, septingentis interemptis, sub corona vendiderit. Non enim Franci nostri in illo bello, non magis quàm alij in alijs,quantumuis iustis, semper fecundos præliorum euentus habuerunt. Quinetiam à Constantino, qui postea Magnus dictus est,duo ipsorum Reges capti, & bestijs in spectaculo quodam obiecti memorantur. quā historiam Eutrop. lib.9. & Rhetor in Panegyrico,quem superiùs aliquoties protulimus,attingunt.Et quoniam alio loco de bellis in Batauorum finibus gestis idem Rhetor commemorat, quos à nostris non longè abfuisse ostendimus, verba eius subscribemus. Multa, inquit Rhetor, Francorum millia qui Batauiam, aliasque cis Rhenum terras inuaserant,interfecit,depulit, abduxit. Et alio loco: Terram Batauorum sub ipso quondam alumno suo à diuersis Francorum Regum gentibus occupatam omni hoste purgauit,nec contentus vicisse, ipsos in Romanas transtulit nationes: vt non solum arma, sed & feritatem ponere cogerentur. Quo ex loco non obscurè intelligitur, Constantinum Francorum vi atque armis coactum, sedes illis in Romani imperij finibus concessisse. Quinetiam Ammianus lib. 15. scribit,Francos exorto inter Constantinum & Licinium ciuili bello, pro Constantini partibus sæpenumero fortiter decertasse. Sed & alio eiusdem libri loco, imperante Constantino,Constantini filio,Fracos in Regia quam plurimos fuisse memorat: magnaque apud Cæsarem in gratia atq; auctoritate fuisse. Post hæc,inquit,Malarichus subitò nactus, adhibitis Francis, quorum ea tempestate in palatio multitudo florebat. Iam verò imperante Iuliano, qui Apostata dictus est,ijdem Franci coloniam Agrippinam Romanorū seruitute oppressam in libertatem vindicare conati sunt: eamque longa obsidione pressam, deditionem facere coegerunt: quemadmodum idem Ammianus lib.12. commemorat. Cumq; ad flumen Salam aliquot è Francis consedissent, ea re,Salij dicti sunt.de quibus idem Ammianus eodem libro: Quibus paratis, inquit,petit primos omnium Francos, eos videlicet quos consuetudo Salios appellauit: ausos olim in Romano solo,apud Toxiandriam locum, habitacula sibi figere prælicenter. Item Zosimus lib.3.Saliorum nationem, profectam à Francis, & vi Saxonum in hanc insulam(de Batauia loquitur) suis sedibus expulsam, eiecerunt. Hæc infula, prius Romanis in vniuersum subiecta, à Salijs hoc tempore possidebatur.Rursus Ammianus libro 20. Regionem à Francis vltra Rhenum occupatam, & Franciam dictam, commemorat. Rheno,inquit, transmisso, regionem subitò peruasit Francorum, quos Attuarios vocant, inquietorum hominum, licentius etiam tum percursantium extima Galliarum. Et libro 30. vbi de Rege Macriano loquitur,quo cum Valentinianus Imperator ad ripam Rheni,prope Moguntiacum pacem fecerat: Perijt autem, inquit in Francia,postquam dum internecinè vastando perrumpit auidius,oppetijt Mellobaudis bellicosi Regis insidijs circumuentus.Hunc autem Francorum Regem Mellobaudem idem auctor lib. feq. fortem &bellicofum fuisse scribit, & ob virtutem militaré ab Imp. Gratiano comitem domesticorum,& Legatum cum Nannieno factum fuisse,vt exercitum aduersus Lentiates Germanos educeret. Pòst verò imperante Honorio, propter pactam cum illo Imperatore societatem, Galliæ Romanæ fines aduersus Stiliconem tutati sunt. Nam Orofius libro vlt. Excitatæ, inquit,per Stiliconem gentes Alanorum,Sueuorum , Vandalorum, multæque cum his aliæ Francos proterunt, Rhenumque transeunt, Gallias inuadunt. Post Honorij Imperatoris ætatem perexigua de Francorum rebus gestis extat memoria.nam ad illa tempora referendū est,quod D. Ambrosius epistola 29. ad Imper. Theodosium scribit, Francos & in Sicilia & alijs locis compluribus Maximum Romanarum copiarum ducem superasse. Ille igitur,(inquit, de Maximo commemorans) statim à Francis, & à Saxonum gente, in Sicilia, Siciæ, Petauione, vbique denique terrarum victus est. Verùm perante Valentiniano III, hoc est, circiter annum salutis Christianæ CCCCL. illud auctorum omnium consensu constat, Childericum Merouei Francorum Regis filium, post annorum amplius ducentorum contentionem, Galliam è Romanorum seruitute in libertatem vindicasse: primumque in ea Regni sui sedem certam stabilemque constituisse. Nam etsi nonnulli primos Francorum Reges Faramundum & Clodiocrinitum numerant: tamen nemini dubium est, alios antea complures Francorum reges fuisse, qui etiam trāsmisso Rheno in Galliam irruperunt: quorum nemo pacatum in Galliæ finibus imperium obtinuerit. Meroueus autem, quem vulgò tertium numerant, Francorum quidem Rex fuit: sed aduena, & peregrinus, non in Gallia factus, non denique Francogallorum, hoc est, gemellæ & consociatæ gentis iudicio & voluntate creatus. Francorum denique Reges illi omnes fuerunt: non Francogallorum. Primus Childericus, Merouei (vt diximus) filius, à Francis & Gallis, publico gemellæ gentis consilio, rex Francogalliæ creatus est:
units.tr: For this reason, even if we grant that Remigius borrowed that half-line, it is probable that he used it for the sake of allusion rather than to name the people properly. But to return to our subject: it can be said and asserted most truly that the name of the Franks, which means (as Cornelius Tacitus explains) "the defenders of liberty," was so fortunate, happy and blessed that almost countless victories followed from it. For after the Franks, by that resolve, left their own territory, they crossed not only Germany, their common homeland, but also Gaul, and at last even the Alps, and freed no small part of Italy from the tyranny of the Romans. The first and oldest mention of this most famous name is found, not under the emperor Decius, as I see some affirm too confidently, but under the emperor Gallienus, that is, about the year of Christian salvation 260. For Trebellius Pollio, in his life of Gallienus, says: "While he gave himself over to jokes and gluttony, and ruled the commonwealth no differently than boys playing at making officials by pretend games, the Gauls, who are by nature unable to bear luxurious princes, called Postumus to the throne. He was at that time governor of Gaul with authority, as legate of Gallienus." And a little later: "Gallienus therefore began war against Postumus, and since Postumus was helped by many auxiliaries, both Celtic and Frankish, he advanced to war with Victorinus." From these words it is understood that the Gauls, in order to throw off the slavery to the tyrant Gallienus, made use of the aid of the Franks, that is, of the defenders of liberty. Zonaras, expressing the same thing briefly in the life of Gallienus, says: "But he waged war on the Phessyri, etc. [ἐπολέμησε δὲ ... Φεσσίρυις &c.]." Another mention of the same people occurs again in Flavius Vopiscus, in the life of Aurelian, in these words: "At Mainz the tribune of the sixth Gallic legion so crushed the Franks, who were rampaging throughout all of Gaul, that he sold three hundred of them, taken prisoner, with seven hundred killed, under the crown." For our Franks did not have successful outcomes of battles in that war, any more than others always did in their wars, however just. Moreover, two of their kings are recorded to have been captured by Constantine, who was later called the Great, and thrown to the beasts as a spectacle. Eutropius, book 9, and the rhetorician in the Panegyric, which we have cited several times above, mention this story. And since the same rhetorician, in another place, recalls the wars waged in the territory of the Batavians, which we have shown were not far from our own land, we shall set down his words. "He killed, drove off and carried away," says the rhetorician, "many thousands of the Franks who had invaded Batavia and other lands on this side of the Rhine." And in another place: "He cleansed the land of the Batavians, which had once been occupied by various tribes of the Frankish kings under his own former ward, of every enemy; and not content with conquering, he transferred the same people into Roman nations, so that they were compelled to lay down not only their arms but also their savagery." From this passage it is clearly understood that Constantine, compelled by the force and arms of the Franks, granted them dwelling places within the borders of the Roman empire. Moreover, Ammianus, book 15, writes that the Franks, during the civil war that broke out between Constantine and Licinius, often fought bravely on the side of Constantine. But also in another place of the same book, under the rule of Constantine, son of Constantine, he records that there were very many Franks at court, and that they stood high in favour and authority with the Caesar. "After these things," he says, "Malaric suddenly, with Franks added, whose great multitude then flourished in the palace..." Now truly, under the emperor Julian, who was called the Apostate, the same Franks tried to vindicate Cologne (Colonia Agrippina), oppressed by Roman servitude, into liberty, and by a long siege forced it to surrender, as the same Ammianus records in book 12. And when some of the Franks had settled at the river Sala, for that reason they were called Salians. Of them the same Ammianus, in the same book: "With these preparations," he says, "he attacked first of all the Franks, namely those whom custom has called Salians, who once dared to fix their dwellings boldly on Roman soil, at a place called Toxiandria." Likewise Zosimus, book 3, says that the nation of the Salians, having come from the Franks, and driven from its seats by the force of the Saxons, was thrown out of this island (he speaks of Batavia). This island, previously subject in its entirety to the Romans, was at this time possessed by the Salians. Again, Ammianus, book 20, records a region beyond the Rhine occupied by the Franks and called Francia. "Having crossed the Rhine," he says, "he suddenly invaded the territory of the Franks, whom they call Attuarii, restless men, who then roamed more freely over the outlying parts of Gaul." And in book 30, where he speaks of King Macrianus, with whom the emperor Valentinian had made peace on the bank of the Rhine near Mainz: "He perished, however," he says, "in Francia, after rushing forward more eagerly while laying waste with massacre, and was caught and killed by the treachery of Mellobaudes, a warlike king." This same author, in the following book, writes that this Frankish king Mellobaudes was brave and warlike, and that on account of his military valour he was made count of the domestics by the emperor Gratian, and was made legate, together with Nannienus, in order to lead an army against the Lentienses, Germans. Later, under the emperor Honorius, on account of the alliance made with that emperor, the Franks defended the borders of Roman Gaul against Stilicho. For Orosius, in the last book, says: "The peoples of the Alans, Suevi, Vandals, and many others along with them, were roused up by Stilicho; they trampled down the Franks, crossed the Rhine, and invaded the Gauls." After the age of the emperor Honorius there is very little memory extant of the deeds of the Franks. For to those times should be referred what St. Ambrose writes in letter 29 to the emperor Theodosius, that the Franks defeated Maximus, commander of the Roman forces, both in Sicily and in many other places. "Then he" (speaking of Maximus) "was immediately defeated by the Franks and the nation of the Saxons, in Sicily, at Siccia, at Petavio, and finally everywhere on earth." But under the emperor Valentinian III, that is, about the year of Christian salvation 450, it is established by the agreement of all authors that Childeric, son of the Frankish king Merovaeus, after a contest of more than two hundred years, vindicated Gaul from Roman servitude into liberty, and was the first to establish a fixed and stable seat of his kingdom there. For although some count Pharamond and Clodio as the first Frankish kings, nevertheless there is no doubt that many other Frankish kings existed before them, who also crossed the Rhine and burst into Gaul; yet none of them obtained a peaceful rule within the borders of Gaul. Merovaeus, however, whom they commonly number as the third, was indeed king of the Franks, but a newcomer and a foreigner, not made in Gaul, and not chosen by the judgement and will of the Francogauls, that is, of the twin and allied nation. In short, all those were kings of the Franks, not of the Francogauls. The first was Childeric, son of Merovaeus (as we said), who was created king of Francogaul by the public counsel of the twin nation, by the Franks and the Gauls.

units.la: posteaquā Merouēus pater, Attilino prælio interfectus est, imperante Valētiniano III, perdito ac libidinoso principe. Quo tempore Angli & Scoti, Britanniam: Burgundi Sequanorū, Æduorum, & Allobrogum fines: Gothi, Aquitaniam: Wandali Africam atq; Italiam, vrbemque ipsam Romam occupabant. Hunni verò, Attila duce, Galliam cædibus, atque incendijs vastabant. Quam reigerendæ facultatem Merovęus Francorum rex, non aspernatus, magnis coniunctis copijs, Rhenum transmisit, ciuitatibusque compluribus ad eum recuperandæ libertatis causa confugientibus, tandem interiores Celtarum vrbes occupauit. Attila autem cum exercitū haberet hominum circiter quingentorum millium, latè per Galliam, Tholosam vsque vagatus est. Erat tum Galliæ Præses Ætius, qui Attilæ potentiam veritus, Gothos sibi fœdere ac societate adiunxerat. Horum auxilijs instructus, prælium cum Attila commisit, cecidisseque dicuntur eo prælio non minus centum & octoginta hominum millibus. At victor Ætius, cum apud Imperatorem Valentinianum in regni appetendi suspitionem adductus esset, ipsius iussu necatus est. Aliquanto post Imperator ipse quoque opera Maximi, de quo superius mentionem fecimus, est interfectus. Merovęo mortuo, cùm duæ iam Gallorum & Francorum gentes, dispari genere, dissimili lingua, alio atque alio more viuentes in vnam ciuitatē coaluissent, coniunctis animis, Childericum
units.tr: After Merovaeus, their father, was killed in the battle with Attila, under the emperor Valentinian III, a prince who was corrupt and given to pleasure. At that time the Angles and Scots occupied Britain; the Burgundians the territories of the Sequani, Aedui and Allobroges; the Goths Aquitaine; the Vandals Africa and Italy, and the city of Rome itself. The Huns, under Attila as leader, were laying waste Gaul with slaughter and fires. Merovaeus, king of the Franks, did not disdain the opportunity to repel them; with large combined forces he crossed the Rhine, and since many cities had fled to him for the sake of recovering their liberty, he at last took the inner cities of the Celts. Attila, however, having an army of about five hundred thousand men, roamed widely through Gaul as far as Toulouse. At that time Aetius was governor of Gaul; fearing Attila's power, he had joined the Goths to himself by treaty and alliance. Strengthened by their aid, he engaged in battle with Attila, and it is said that not fewer than one hundred and eighty thousand men fell in that battle. But Aetius, the victor, was put to death by the order of the emperor Valentinian, after falling under suspicion before him of seeking the kingdom. Shortly afterwards the emperor himself was also killed, through the contrivance of Maximus, whom we mentioned above. When Merovaeus had died, since the two nations of the Gauls and the Franks, of different origin, with different language and living by different customs, had merged into one community, with united minds they choose Childeric

units.la: Merouei filium regem sibi deligunt: scutoque de more impositum, atq; in humeros sublatū, ter circum comitia deportant: & plausu undiq; excitato, summisque omnium gratulationibus, regem Francogalliæ consalutant. Quarum rerum omnium auctores habemus Sidonium Apollinarem, Paulum Diaconum, Gregorium Turonensem, Otronem Frisingensem, Aimoinum, & ceteros: quorum testimonia, nec ita multò post, vbi de regis inaugurandi more dicenduⁿ erit, proferemus. De vrbium quidem occupatione, Ottonis lib. 4. cap. pen. verba hæc sunt: Franci Rheno transmisso, Romanos qui ibi habitabant, primò fugant. post captis Tornaco & Cameraco, Galliæ vrbibus, ac inde paulatim progredientes, Rhemos, Suessionem, Aurelianum, Agrippinam, Treuerim subiugant.
units.tr: They choose as king Childeric, son of Merovech: placing him on a shield in the customary way and lifting him on their shoulders, they carry him three times around the assembly; and with applause raised on every side and the good wishes of all, they hail him as king of Francogallia. We have as authors for all these matters Sidonius Apollinaris, Paulus Diaconus, Gregory of Tours, Otto of Freising, Aimoin, and others, whose testimonies we will set forth, not much later, when the manner of inaugurating a king is to be discussed. Concerning the occupation of the cities, the words of Otto, book 4, near the end of the chapter, are these: The Franks, having crossed the Rhine, first put to flight the Romans who lived there; afterwards, having taken Tournai and Cambrai, cities of Gaul, and advancing gradually from there, they subdued Reims, Soissons, Orléans, Cologne and Trier.

units.la: Neque verò prætermittendus est insignis Hunibaldi locus, apud quem scriptum ita est: Merouei tempore Franci penè totam Galliam suo regno adiecerunt: Romanorum iam viribus imminutis, ac deficientibus: præsertim post Ætij mortem, quem Valentinianus ex inuidia occiderat. Franci ergo Gallis commixti de ipsorū filiabus sibi acceperunt vxores: genuerunt filios & filias: qui omnes didicerunt linguam eorum, simul & mores: cum quibus sunt deinceps conuersati vsque in præsentem diem. Hæc ille, quib. consentanei sunt ij autorum loci, in quibus per illa tempora Galli & Franci promiscuo nomine appellantur. velut apud Paul. Diaconum, lib. de gest. Langob. 3. cap. 13, Galli autem vehementer afflicti: etsi multi capti, plurimi tamen per fugam elapsi vix ad patriam revertuntur. tantaque strages facta est de Francorum exercitu, quanta nunquam alibi commemoratur. indeque nata vulgaris Francigenarum appellatio est, ijs proprie attributa, qui ex illis Francis suscepti in Gallia fuerant: velut in Syn. Tributicensi, & c.1, ext. De sponsal. De Francia quidam nobilem mulierem de Saxonia duxit, verum quia non ijsdem utuntur legibus Saxones & Francigenae, &c. Atque haec quidem de primo Francogalliae rege, summatim. quibus illud subiungendum est: Cum hoc Francogalliae Regnum annos fere mille ducentos duraret, tres tantum per id omne tempus Regum familias numerari: Merouingiorum, qui orti a Merouaeo stirpem ad annos ducentos octoginta tres propagarunt: Carlouingiorum, qui orti a Carolo Magno, sobolem in annos trecentos triginta septem produxerunt: & Capeuingiorum, qui ab Hugone Capeto prognati, per quingentos iam & octoginta annos Regnum obtinent.
units.tr: Nor must we pass over the notable passage of Hunibald, where it is written thus: In the time of Merovech the Franks conquered almost all of Gaul and added it to their kingdom, the strength of the Romans now being diminished and failing, especially after the death of Aetius, whom Valentinian had killed out of jealousy. The Franks, therefore, mingled with the Gauls, took wives for themselves from their daughters; they begot sons and daughters, who all learned their language and also their customs; and with these they have lived on ever since, down to the present day. Thus he. To these agree the passages of authors in which, during those times, Gauls and Franks are called by a common name, as in Paulus Diaconus, book on the deeds of the Lombards, 3, chapter 13: The Gauls, however, were grievously afflicted; and although many were taken, most nevertheless escaped by flight and scarcely returned to their homeland; and such a slaughter was made of the Frankish army as is never recorded elsewhere. From this arose the common name Francigenae, applied properly to those who, born of those Franks, had settled in Gaul: as in the Synod of Tribur, c. 1, ext. De sponsalibus: A certain man of Francia married a noble woman from Saxony; but because the Saxons and the Francigenae do not use the same laws, etc. And these things, briefly, concerning the first king of Francogallia. To which must be added this: although this Kingdom of Francogallia lasted almost twelve hundred years, only three royal families are to be counted throughout that whole time: the Merovingians, who, descended from Merovech, extended their line to some two hundred and eighty-three years; the Carolingians, who, descended from Charlemagne, produced their offspring over three hundred and thirty-seven years; and the Capetians, who, sprung from Hugh Capet, have held the kingdom now for five hundred and eighty years.

units.la: Regnum Francogalliae utrum hereditate, an suf- fragijs deferretur, & de Regum cre- andorum more.
units.tr: Whether the kingdom of Francogallia was conferred by hereditary succession or by the votes of the people, and concerning the manner of creating kings.

units.la: SEd hoc loco praeclara quaestio exoritur, & ad maiorum sapientiam cognoscendam aptiffima, vtrum Francogalliæ regnum hæreditario iure, an verò populi iudicio & suffragijs deferretur. Germaniæ quidem Reges (quo ex genere Francos nostros fuisse, superius demonstratum est) suffragijs creari solitos, Cornelius Tacitus in libello de moribus Germanorum testatur. Reges, inquit, ex nobilitate, Duces ex virtute sumunt. Quod institutum etiam nunc Germani, & Dani, & Sueui, & Poloni retinent: vt Reges quidem in Concilio gentis eligant: filij tamen demortuorum regum prærogatiuam habeant: & (vt Tacitus memoriæ prodidit) ceteris præferantur. Quo instītuto, haud scio, an quicquam sapientius, aut Reipublicæ salutarius excogitari potuerit. Nam (vt Plutarchus in Sylla luculenter monet) quemadmodum venatores non quod ex generofo cane natum est, sed canem ipsum generosum quærunt: equites non quod ex equo generosissimo natum, sed equum ipsum expetunt: eodem modo qui Rempublicam constituunt, magno errore ducuntur, si, quis Princeps sibi nasciturus sit, potius, quàm qualem habituri sint, exquirant. Eò accedebat, quòd parentes successionis illius spe ad suos filios præclare instituendos adducebantur, ne tanquam paterna successione indigni à populo repudiarentur. Atque hanc maiorum nostrorum in Francogalliæ regno constituendo sapientiam fuisse, documento est, primùm Caroli Magni testamentum, apud Ioann. Nauclerum, & Hen. Mutium editum, in quo clausula hæc extat: Quòd si filius cuilibet horum trium filiorum meorum natus fuerit, quem populus eligere velit, ut patri suo in regni hereditate succedat, volumus ut consentiant patrui ipsius: & regnare permittant filium fratris sui in portione Regni paterni. Quinetiam memorabile est, quod Regino libro Chron. 2. scribit, sub anno DCCCVI, cum Carolus Magnus tres filios haberet, quibus mature in vita sua consulere volebat: Cum primoribus (inquit) & optimatibus Francorum de partitione sui regni inter filios suos placitum habuit. & diuisione facta in tres partes, testamentum de illa fecit, quod per sacramentum interpositum à Francis confirmatum est. Sic Eguinarthus in eiusdem Caroli vita: Euocatum ad se Ludouicum Aquitaniæ regem, qui solus filiorum Hildegardis supererat, congregatis solenniter de toto Francorum regno primoribus, cunctorum consilio confortem sibi totius regni fecit. quem locum totidem verbis scriptor Chronici Belnensis de quo supra commemorauimus, in suum librum transcripsit. Sed superiores videamus. Nam Aimoinus quidem libro 1. cap. 4. de Faramundo, quem vulgò (vt dixi) primum Francorum Regem numerant, ita loquitur: Regem verò ceterarum more nationum Franci sibi eligentes, Faramundum solio sublimant regio. Sed multo copiosius Hunibaldus, scriptor vetustissimus: Anno, inquit, cccccv. omnes Duces, proceres & nobiles Francorum in mense Martio conuenerūt apud Neopagum, pro noui Regis electione facienda. Et mox: Hi omnes cum ceteris vno cõsensu Faramundum de regio genere ortum vnanimiter in Regem elegerunt. Rursus Aimoinus libro 4. capite s 1. Franci autem Danielem quendam clericum cæsarie capitis crescente, in regnum stabiliunt atque Chilpericum nuncupant. Item lib. 4. cap. 67. Mortuo rege Pipino filij eius Carolus & Carolomannus consensu omnium Francorum Reges creati sunt. Et alio loco; Mortuo Pipino, Franci facto solenniter conuentu, ambos sibi eius filios reges constituunt, ea conditione præmissa, vt totum regni corpus ex æquo partirentur. Et rursus post alterius è vita excessum: Carolus autem frater defuncto consensu omnium Francorum Rex constituitur. Atque hæc quidem ex Aimoino. Similia autem apud Gregorium Turonensem testimonia complura extant, è quibus pauca hæc proferemus. Nam lib. 2, cap. 12. Franci, inquit, eiecto Childerico Eudonem sibi vnanimiter Regem asciscunt. Item libro 4. cap. s 1. Tunc Franci, qui quondam ad Childebertum aspexerunt seniorem, ad Sigebertum legationem mittunt: vt ad eos veniens, derelicto Chilperico, ipsum per se Regem stabilirent. Et aliquanto post: Collectus est ad eum omnis exercitus: impositumque super clypeo sibi Regem statuunt. Item alio loco: Sigebertus Francis consentiens, more gentis impositus clypeo, Rex constitutus est, ac Regnū fratris sui Chilperici adeptus. Et nō ita multo post: Burgundiones & Austrasij cum reliquis Francis pace facta, Clothariū in tribus totis Regnis super se Regem leuauerunt. Quod idem Abbas Vrspergensis confirmat: Burgundiones, inquit, & Austrasij facta pace cum Francis, Clotharium in monarchia totius Regni Regem sublimauerunt. Et paulò post: Franci alterum eius fratrem Hildericum, qui Austrasijs iam imperabat, super se Regem constituunt. Nuper etiam incidi in Chronica manuscripta monasterij Befnēsis in Burgūdia, vbi sub an.D CLVIII. hæc reperio: Clotarius Rex immatura præventus morte, regnum sine herede reliquit. (id est, sine filio, more Feudistico) cuius obitum dolētes Frēcorum principes, germanum eius Childericum Regem Austrasiorum, in omni sublimant Francorum regno. Et mox, Childericus ergo Rex paucis annis quibus regnum Francorum obtinuit, defunctus est, & germanus eius Theodoricus in regno fratris loco sublimatus.
units.tr: But here a notable question arises, very apt for learning the wisdom of our ancestors: whether the kingdom of Francogallia was conferred by hereditary right, or rather by the judgment and votes of the people. That the kings of Germany were usually created by votes (and that our Franks belonged to that race, has been shown above) Cornelius Tacitus attests in his little book on the customs of the Germans. "They take kings," he says, "from nobility, leaders from virtue." The Germans, the Danes, the Swedes and the Poles still keep this custom: they elect kings in the assembly of the nation, yet the sons of deceased kings have a prerogative and, as Tacitus recorded, are preferred to others. I do not know whether anything wiser, or more beneficial to the commonwealth, could have been devised than this custom. For (as Plutarch admirably observes in the Life of Sulla) just as hunters seek not a dog born of a noble dog but the noble dog itself, and horsemen seek not a horse born of a most noble horse but the horse itself, so those who establish a commonwealth go badly wrong if they ask who is going to be born as prince to them, rather than what sort of prince they will have. Moreover, parents were drawn by the hope of that succession to bring up their sons excellently, lest they be rejected by the people as unworthy of paternal succession. That this was the wisdom of our ancestors in establishing the kingdom of Francogallia is shown, first, by the will of Charlemagne, published by John Naucler and Henry Mutius, in which this clause stands: "But if any of these my three sons should have a son whom the people wish to choose to succeed his father in the inheritance of the kingdom, we wish that his uncles consent and allow the son of their brother to reign in the portion of the paternal kingdom." Indeed it is worth noting what Regino writes in book 2 of his Chronicle, under the year 806, when Charlemagne had three sons whom he wished to provide for early in his life: "With the chief men and nobles of the Franks," he says, "he held a hearing about the partition of his kingdom among his sons; and, the division having been made into three parts, he made a will concerning it, which, confirmed by an oath taken by the Franks, was ratified." So Eginhard in the Life of the same Charlemagne: "Having summoned to himself Louis, king of Aquitaine, who alone of Hildegard's sons survived, and having solemnly assembled the chief men of the whole Frankish kingdom, by the counsel of all he made him co-sharer of the whole kingdom." The writer of the Chronicle of Belna, of which we spoke above, copied this passage word for word into his book. But let us look at the earlier writers. Aimoin, in book 1 chapter 4, on Pharamond, whom they commonly count (as I said) as the first king of the Franks, speaks thus: "The Franks, choosing for themselves a king as other nations do, raised Pharamond to the royal throne." But Hunibald, a very ancient writer, is much fuller: "In the year 405," he says, "all the dukes, nobles and nobles of the Franks gathered in March at Neopagus to make the election of a new king." And soon after: "All these, together with the rest, unanimously elected Pharamond, born of royal stock, as king." Again Aimoin, book 4 chapter 31: "The Franks established as king a certain clerk, Daniel, when his hair had grown long, and named him Childeric." Likewise book 4 chapter 67: "King Pippin having died, his sons Charles and Carloman were created kings by the consent of all the Franks." And in another place: "Pippin having died, the Franks, holding a solemn assembly, made both his sons kings, on condition that they divide the whole body of the kingdom equally." And again, after the other's departure from life: "Charles, however, on the death of his brother, was made king by the consent of all the Franks." So much from Aimoin. Many similar testimonies are found in Gregory of Tours, of which we shall bring forward a few. For in book 2 chapter 12: "The Franks, having expelled Childeric, unanimously took Eudo as their king." Also book 4 chapter 51: "Then the Franks, who had formerly looked to Childebert the elder, sent an embassy to Sigebert, so that, coming to them and leaving Chilperic, he might establish himself as king over them." And a little later: "The whole army was gathered to him, and, having set him up on a shield, they made him king." Elsewhere again: "Sigebert, agreeing with the Franks, was raised on a shield according to the custom of the nation, and was made king, and obtained the kingdom of his brother Chilperic." And not long after: "The Burgundians and Austrasians, with the rest of the Franks, having made peace, raised Clotaire over themselves as king of all three kingdoms." The Abbot of Ursperg confirms the same: "The Burgundians and Austrasians, having made peace with the Franks, raised Clotaire to be king of the whole monarchy." And shortly after: "The Franks made their other brother Childeric, who was already ruling the Austrasians, king over themselves."
