Lately I also came upon the manuscript chronicles of the monastery of Belna in Burgundy, where under the year 558 I find this: "King Clotaire, forestalled by untimely death, left the kingdom without an heir (that is, without a son, in the feudal manner); and the princes of the Franks, grieving at his death, raised his brother Childeric, king of the Austrasians, to be king over the whole Frankish kingdom." And soon: "King Childeric, then, in the few years in which he held the kingdom of the Franks, died, and his brother Theodoric was raised to the kingdom in his brother's place."

units.la: Item alio loco & multò ante: Dagobertus Metis vrbem veniens cum consilio Pontificum & Procerum, sed & omnibus primatibus regni sui consentientibus Sigebertum filium suum in regnum sublimauit: sedemque Metis ciuitate habere permisit. Itē sub anno D CCLXVIII: Franci facto solemniter generali conuentu, ambos sibi constituunt Reges, ea conditione præmissa, vt totum regni corpus ex æquo partirentur. Eodem pertinet, quod Liutprandus Leuita Ticinensis libro primo capite 6. ita scribit: Cumque Burgundionum regna transiens, Franciam, quam Romanam dicunt, ingredi vellet, Francorum nuntij ei occurrunt, se redire nuntiantes: eo quòd longa expectatione fatigati, cum fine rege diutius esse non possent, Odonem cunctis petentibus elegerunt. Fertur autem hac occasione Francos Widonem sibi regem non assumpsisse, &c. Sed de hoc Odone memorabilis & Reginonis & Sigeberti narratio est, ex qua planius etiam de Regis filio repudiato, & alieno ascito cognoscitur. Nam Regino quidem libro secundo, sic loquitur, sub anno 888. Interea Galliarum populi in vnum congregati, Ottonem Ducem filium Rudperti, cui præ cæteris formæ pulchritudo & proceritas corporis & virium sapientiæque magnitudo inerat, Regem super se pari consilio & voluntate creant. Sed & Annalium Rhemensium scriptor: Quum quotidie, inquit, copijs Roberti crescentibus decrescerent Caroli, clam tandem secedens cum Haganone trans Mosam proficiscitur. Franci Robertum seniorem eligunt, ipsíque se committunt. Itaque Rex Rhemis apud S. Remigium, ab Episcopis & primatibus regni rex constituitur. Rhegino vero sub anno DCCL: Pipinus, inquit, secundum morem Francorum electus in Regem, & vnctus per manum Bonifacij Mogontinensis vrbis Archiepiscopi, & eleuatus est à Francis in regno in Suessionis ciuitate. Sigebertus verò sub anno 890. hoc modo: Franci verò neglecto Carolo Ludouici Balbi puero, vix decenni, regem sibi præficiunt Odonem filium Roberti Ducis, quem à Nortmannis occisum suprà diximus. Item Otto Frifing. Chron. lib. 6. cap. 10. Occidentales, inquit, Franci, Odonem Roberti filium, virum fortem, consensu Arnolphi regem creant. Quæ testimonia eo magis notanda atque obseruanda sunt, quòd perspicuè ac dilucidè demonstrant, summum penes populum ius arbitriumque fuisse, non modò Regum deligendorum, verùm etiam, repulsis ac repudiatis demortuorum Regum filijs, alienorum asciscendorum. quod etiam post Caroli Simplicis mortem vsu venit. Nam Rhegino sub anno DCCCCXXV. Carolus Rex, inquit, in custodia, qua tenebatur, obijt. qui fertur vir hebetis esse ingenij, & minus aptus vtilitatibus regni. Omnes etiam à filio eius deficientes, quendam Rodulphum sibi Regem eligunt. Filium autem Aimoinus Ludouicum appellat: qui minus cōmodè illud narrans, scribit Carolum in custodia præcepisse de Francorum procerum consilio, vt Rudolphus Richardi Burgundionū Ducis filius in regem ordinaretur. Sed Annalium Rhemensium scriptor planius id exponit. Audito, inquit, Franci, quòd Carolus Normannos ad se venire mandasset, ne illi coniungerentur, inter Carolum atque Normannos cum Rodulpho medij resederunt: tumque Carolo trans Mosam refugiente, Rodulphum cuncti Regè eligunt. Item in Appendice Gregor. Turonen. lib. 15. cap. 30. Post Dagoberti decessum, filius suus Clodoueus sub tenera ætate regnum patris asciuit. omnesque leudes (id est, subiecti) eum in Masolano villa sublimant in regnum. Item Sigebert. in Chronic. anno 987. Ludouico Francorum rege mortuo, Francis regnum trasferre volentibus ad Carolum fratrem Lotharij regis, dum ille rem ad concilium defert, regnum Francorum vsurpat Hugo, &c. Multa eiusdem generis apud Adonem testimonia sunt, velut anno 686. Clodoueus rex decessit. Franci Clotarium filium eius regem constituunt. Et mox: Clotarius quatuor annos regnans obijt: cuius loco Franci Theodoricum fratrem eius eligūt. Item anno 669. Franci Danielem quendam clericum post abiectionem tonsurae, in regno stabiliunt, atq; Chilpericum nuncupant. Et mox: Franci Theodericum Dagoberti filium regem super se constituunt. Item apud Ottonem Frisingensem Chron. 6. cap. 13. Ottone, inquit, Francorum rege mortuo, Carolus voluntate omnium rex creatur. Item Appendix Gregor. Turon. lib. 11. cap. 101. Mortuo Theodorico rege, Franci Clodoueum filium eius paruulum elegerunt in regnum. Et cap. 106. Franci verò Chilpericum quendam regem constituerunt. & cap. 107. Quo mortuo Theodoricum regem statuerunt in sedem regni. Item Godfrid. Viterbienf.Chron. parte 17. capit. 4. Pipinus verò per Papam Zachariam ex electione Francorũ factus est Rex Francorum: Hilderico ignauo rege per Francos in monasterium misso. His ex locis, alijsque similibus quamplurimis dilucide patere arbitror, reges Francogalliæ populi potius, hoc est ordinum, &(vt nunc loquimur) statuum iudicio ac studio, quàm hereditario iure constitutos fuisse. cuius rei magno etiam argumento est ritus, quo maiores in regibus inaugurandis vtebantur. Quod enim paulo superiùs diximus, Cornel. Tacitum de Caninefatibus, Francorum popularibus, testari, vt designatum regem scuto imponerent, sublimemque humeris gestarent: idem in regibus nostris vsurpatum animaduertimus. Nam qui populi suffragijs delectus fuerat, hunc scuto impositum subleuabant, humerisque sustentatum ter circum populi comitia, vel, si in castris id acciderat, circum exercitum, plaudentibus atque acclamantibus vniuersis, gestabant. Gregor.libro secundo, vbi de Clodouei Regis electione commemorat: Atilli, inquit, sta audientes, plaudentes tam palmis, quàm vocibus, eum clypeo eueẽtum, super se regem constituunt. Item libro septimo, cap. 10. vbi de Gondebaldo loquitur: Ibique, inquit, parmæ superpositus Rex est leuatus. sed cum tertiò gererent, cecidisse fertur: ita vt vix manibus circumstantium sustentari posset. Qua de re Aimoinus libro tertio, capite 6. ita scribit: Euocatum Gondobaldum more antiquorum Francorum,regem proclamantes esse suum,eleuauerunt eum clypeo. cumque tertiò totum cum eo circuiffent exercitum, repente ruens cum rege vix à terra eleuari potuit. Item Ado Viennensis Ætat. 6. Sigebertus, inquit,Francis consentiens, more gentis impositus clypeo rex constitutus est. Ac nimirum ex eo factum constat,vt Scriptores illi, vbi de rege creato commemorant, plerunq; hanc locutionem vsurpent,vt eum in regem eleuatum dicant.
units.tr: Again, in another place and much earlier: Dagobert, coming to the city of Metz, with the advice of the bishops and nobles, and with the consent of all the chief men of his realm, raised his son Sigebert to the kingdom, and allowed him to have his seat at the city of Metz. Also, under the year 668: the Franks, having held a general assembly with due solemnity, set up two kings for themselves, on condition that the whole body of the kingdom be divided equally between them. To the same point belongs what Liutprand the deacon of Pavia writes in the first book, chapter 6: "When he was passing through the kingdoms of the Burgundians and wished to enter France, which they call Roman, messengers of the Franks met him, announcing that they were returning, because, worn out by long waiting and unable to remain any longer without a king, they had chosen Odo, with everyone asking for him." It is also said that on this occasion the Franks did not take Guy as their king, etc. But there is a memorable account of this Odo in both Regino and Sigebert, from which it is more clearly known that the son of the king was rejected and another taken in his place. For Regino, in the second book, speaks thus under the year 888: "Meanwhile the peoples of Gaul gathered together into one, and with equal counsel and will they made Otto, duke and son of Robert, king over themselves, a man who, above all others, had beauty of form, height of body, and greatness of strength and wisdom." And the writer of the Annals of Reims: "While day by day the forces of Robert grew and those of Charles diminished, he at last withdrew secretly and went across the Meuse with Hagano. The Franks chose the elder Robert and committed themselves to him. Thus at Reims, at the church of St Remigius, he was made king by the bishops and nobles of the realm." But Regino, under the year 750: "Pepin," he says, "was elected king according to the custom of the Franks, and anointed by the hand of Boniface, archbishop of the city of Mainz, and was raised up by the Franks in the kingdom at the city of Soissons." Sigebert, however, under the year 890, in this way: "The Franks, however, having neglected Charles, the boy of Louis the Stammerer, scarcely ten years old, set over themselves as king Odo, son of Duke Robert, whom we said above had been killed by the Northmen." Also Otto of Freising, Chronicle, book 6, chapter 10: "The Western Franks," he says, "with Arnulf's consent, make Odo, son of Robert, a brave man, king." These testimonies must be the more noted and observed, because they show clearly and plainly that the supreme right and power lay with the people, not only of choosing kings but also, when the sons of dead kings had been rejected and set aside, of taking in strangers. This also happened after the death of Charles the Simple. For Regino, under the year 925: "King Charles," he says, "died in the custody in which he was held. He is said to have been a man of dull intellect and less fit for the good of the kingdom. All who had deserted his son also chose for themselves a certain Rudolph as king." Aimoin calls the son Louis, and, telling it less accurately, he writes that Charles, in custody, ordered with the counsel of the nobles of the Franks that Rudolph, son of Richard, duke of the Burgundians, be appointed king. But the writer of the Annals of Reims explains it more plainly: "When the Franks heard that Charles had sent for the Normans to come to him, in order that they should not join him, they sat as mediators between Charles and the Normans with Rudolph; and when Charles fled across the Meuse, they all chose Rudolph as king." Also in the Appendix to Gregory of Tours, book 15, chapter 30: "After the death of Dagobert, his son Clovis, at a tender age, took up his father's kingdom, and all the leudes (that is, subjects) raised him to the kingdom in the village of Masolanum." Also Sigebert in the Chronicle, under the year 987: "When Louis, king of the Franks, had died, while the Franks wished to transfer the kingdom to Charles, brother of King Lothar, and he referred the matter to a council, Hugh seized the kingdom of the Franks, etc." There are many testimonies of this kind in Adso, such as under the year 686: "King Clovis died. The Franks set up his son Clotaire as king." And soon after: "Clotaire, reigning four years, died; in his place the Franks chose his brother Theodoric." Also under the year 669: "The Franks established in the kingdom a certain clerk named Daniel, after he had been shorn of his tonsure, and they called him Chilperic." And soon after: "The Franks set over themselves as king Theodoric, son of Dagobert." Also in Otto of Freising, Chronicle 6, chapter 13: "When Otto, king of the Franks, had died, Charles was created king by the will of all." Also the Appendix to Gregory of Tours, book 11, chapter 101: "When King Theodoric died, the Franks chose his little son Clovis for the kingdom." And chapter 106: "The Franks, however, set up a certain Chilperic as king." And chapter 107: "When he had died, they placed Theodoric on the seat of the kingdom." Also Godfrey of Viterbo, Chronicle, part 17, chapter 4: "Pepin, however, was made king of the Franks by Pope Zacharias, by election of the Franks, Hilderic, a sluggish king, having been sent by the Franks into a monastery." From these places, and from very many similar ones, I think it is clear that the kings of Gaul-France were set up by the judgment and zeal of the people, that is, of the orders, or (as we now say) estates, rather than by hereditary right. A great proof of this is also the rite which our ancestors used in inaugurating their kings. For what we said a little above, that Cornelius Tacitus testifies of the Chatti, the neighbours of the Franks, that they set the designated king on a shield and carried him aloft on their shoulders, we observe was also practised among our own kings. For he who had been chosen by the votes of the people was placed on a shield, raised up, and borne on the shoulders three times around the assembly of the people, or, if this happened in camp, around the army, all applauding and shouting together. Gregory, in book 2, where he records the election of King Clovis: "The Attili," he says, "standing and listening, applauding with their hands as well as their voices, raised him on a shield and made him king over themselves." Also in book 7, chapter 10, where he speaks of Gundobald: "And there, placed upon a shield, the king was raised up. But when they carried him a third time, he is said to have fallen, so that he could scarcely be held up by the hands of those standing around." On this matter Aimoin, in book 3, chapter 6, writes thus: "Gundobald having been summoned, after the manner of the ancient Franks, they proclaimed him their king and raised him on a shield; and when they had carried him three times around the whole army with them, he suddenly fell with the king and could scarcely be lifted from the ground." Also Ado of Vienne, Age 6: "Sigebert, agreeing with the Franks, was set on a shield after the custom of the people and made king." And assuredly from this it is established that those writers, when they record a king being created, commonly use this expression, that he was raised up as king.

units.la: De summa populi potestate in Regibus caussa cognita condemnandis & ab- dicandis. CAP. VII.
units.tr: On the supreme power of the people in condemning and deposing kings, the case proved. CHAPTER VII.

units.la: SEd nunc ad tertium huius disputationis argumentum accedendum est: vt intelligatur, quantum in regibus constituendis, retinendisve, ordinum ac populi ius potestasque fuerit.Siquidem ex omnibus nostris Annalibus constat, regum abdicandorum summam potestatem penes ordinum comitia fuisse. Cuius potestatis insigne documentum is qui primus Francogalliæ rex creatus fuit, nobis præbet:quem cùm populus comperisset flagitijs ac libidini deditum, ætatem in ganeis & scortationibus consumere, publico consilio remouerunt, Galliæque finibus excedere coëgerunt. quod
units.tr: But now we must come to the third topic of this discussion, so that it may be understood how much right and power the orders and the people had in appointing and retaining kings. Indeed, it is clear from all our annals that the supreme power of deposing kings rested with the assemblies of the orders. Our first king of Gaul-France, who was created as such, provides a notable proof of this power. When the people found that he was given over to vices and lust, spending his life in debauchery and whoring, they removed him by public counsel and compelled him to leave the territory of Gaul. Our countrymen attest that this was done in the year 469.

units.la: anno cccclxix. factū nostri testantur. Quinetiam is quem ipsius in locum suffecerunt, Eudo, cùm sua potentia ad superbiam & crudelitatem abuteretur, pari seueritate iudiciorum exauctoratus est. Cuius rei testes sunt Hunibaldus sub anno cccclxvii. Gregor. Turon. lib.2.cap.12. Aimoin.lib.1.cap.7. Godfrid. Viterbiensis parte 17.cap.1. Sigebert. sub anno 461. & 469. Childericus verò (inquit Gregorius) cū esset nimia in luxuria dissolutus, & regnaret super Francorum gentem, coepit filias eorum stuprosè detrahere. Illiique ob hoc indignantes, de regno eum eiiciunt. Comperto autem, quod etiam eum interficere vellent, Thoringiam perijt.
units.tr: Moreover, Eudo, whom they set up in his place, when he abused his power for pride and cruelty, was likewise deposed by the same severity of judgment. The witnesses to this matter are Hunibald under the year 467, Gregory of Tours, book 2, chapter 12, Aimoin, book 1, chapter 7, Godfrey of Viterbo, part 17, chapter 1, and Sigebert under the years 461 and 469. Gregory says: "Childeric, however, being excessively dissolute in luxury, and reigning over the Frankish people, began to debauch their daughters. They, indignant at this, drove him from the kingdom. But when he learned that they meant to kill him as well, he fled to Thuringia."

units.la: Hunibaldus autem: Anno, inquit, regni sui sexto conspirantes contra eum principes & proceres Francorum, propterea quòd impotenter & nimis luxuriosè viuens vxores & filias nobilium plures vitiasset, voluerunt eum occidere. quòd cùm ei innotuisset, cum paucis occultè fugit in Thoringiam. Pòst Franci quendam Ægidium sibi constituerunt in regem: qui regnauit annis octo. quem Franci denuò nimis tyrannisantem, & proceres quosque crudeliter occidentem, tolerare diutius non valentes, eiecerunt. Abbas autem Vrspergensis: Quem (inquit) luxuriosè viuentem, & cum filiabus populi fornicantem, interficere nolentes, abiecerunt. Et Sigebertus: Hildericum (inquit) insolenter & luxuriosè se agentem Franci de regno deturbant: & Ægidium regem sibi praeficiunt. Atque
units.tr: Hunibald writes: "In the sixth year of his reign, the chief men and nobles of the Franks conspired against him, because, living without restraint and in excessive luxury, he had violated many wives and daughters of the nobility; they wished to kill him. When this came to his knowledge, he secretly fled into Thuringia with a few companions. Afterwards the Franks set up for themselves a certain Aegidius as king, who reigned for eight years. When the Franks, unable to endure him any longer because he was again tyrannising and cruelly killing the nobles, cast him out." The abbot of Urspergen says: "Because he lived in luxury and committed fornication with the daughters of the people, they, unwilling to kill him, cast him off." And Sigebert: "The Franks drove Hilderic from the kingdom, as he was acting insolently and luxuriously, and set Aegidius over them as king."

units.la: hoc quidem præclarum ac singulare maiorum nostrorum facinus eo diligentius notandum est, quod in primordijs ac propè incunabulis regni gestum, quasi quædam testificatio fuisse videtur, ac denuntiatio, reges in Francogallia certis legibus creari: non tyrannos, cum imperio soluto, libero, & infinito constitui. Itaque cùm hoc idem institutum posteri retinerent, anno DCLXXIX. Childericum regem vndecimum insolentiùs se in imperio gerentem abdicarunt: cumque nobilem quendam, nomine Bodilonem ad palum alligari, atque indicta caussa virgis cædi iussisset, ab eodem Bodilone paucis post diebus interfectus est: auctoribus Aimoino lib. 4. cap. 44. Adone, Ætate 6. Tritenhemio anno 687. itemque Sigeberto anno 667. Eiusdem modi maiorum nostrorum seueritas aliquanto post extitit aduersus Theodoricum Regē xII. qui cùm iniquo & auaro imperio Regnum administraret, Franci (inquit Aimoinus) super eū insurgunt, ac eum de regno eijciunt, crinesque capitis eius vi abstrahentes incidunt. lib. 4. cap. 44. Ado Ætat. 6. anno 696. Sigebertus autem sub anno 667. magnam illius culpæ partem in præfectū regium Ebroinum cōferunt. Theodoricus, inquit, rex propter insolentiam Ebroini à Francis repudiatur: & frater eius Hildericus à cunctis ad regnum euocatur. Et Ado: Franci, inquit, Theodoricum de regno abijciunt: Ebroinum Lexouio monasterio tondent: Childericum super se regem leuant. Item Appendix
units.tr: This outstanding and singular deed of our ancestors must be noted all the more carefully because it was done at the very beginnings and almost the cradle of the kingdom, and seems to have been a kind of testimony and declaration that in France-Gaul kings are created under fixed laws, and are not established as tyrants, with a power that is unbound, free and unlimited. Accordingly, when their successors kept up the same custom, in the year 679 they deposed King Childeric the Eleventh, who was conducting himself too insolently in his rule. When he had ordered a certain noble named Bodilo to be tied to a stake and beaten with rods without any charge being stated, he was killed a few days later by that same Bodilo. The authorities are Aimoin, book 4, chapter 44, Ado, Age 6, Trithemius under the year 687, and likewise Sigebert under the year 667. A similar severity of our ancestors appeared a little later against King Theodoric the Twelfth. When he was administering the kingdom with an unjust and greedy rule, the Franks (says Aimoin) rose up against him, drove him from the kingdom, and cut off his hair by force. Book 4, chapter 44; Ado, Age 6, year 696. Sigebert, under the year 667, attributes a large part of that fault to the royal prefect Ebroin. "King Theodoric," he says, "is rejected by the Franks on account of the arrogance of Ebroin, and his brother Hilderic is summoned to the kingdom by all." And Ado: "The Franks," he says, "cast Theodoric from the kingdom, shave Ebroin in the monastery of Luxeuil, and raise Childeric as king over themselves." Likewise the Appendix

units.la: Greg.Turon.lib.ii.cap.64. Franci contra Theodoricum insurgunt: eumq; à regno deijciunt, crines capitis eius abscindentes totonderunt: Ebroinumque ipsum tondent. Sed optimè omnium Hunibaldi Appendix:Theodoricus(inquit) otio & inertiæ deditus omnia negotia regni per Comitem Palatij, quem Maiorem domus nuncupabant, disponere cœpit. Huius maior domus fuit Ebruuinus, homo sceleratus & impius, qui multa fecit mala: quibus commoti proceres Francorum, Theodoricum à regno deijciunt,& tam ipsum quàm Ebruuinum, separatos ab inuicem ad duo monasteria intrudunt. Et mox: Hildericus duorum præcedentium frater medius, & Clodouei filius, deiecto à regno Francorum Theodorico fratre iuniore, procerum electione ad regnum de Austrasia vocatus, regnauit annis paucis. qui cum esset moribus asper, & multis nobilibus Francorum odiosus,in venatione occisus est. Eodem accedat Chronologia Idalij nondum in lucem edita sub anno Christi DCCIII. Post Lotharium, inquit, Theodoricus subrogatur in regnum. sed hoc post paucum tempus, cum Ebroino maiore domus expulso, Childericum regem Austrasiorum fratrem eius minorem Franci in toto sublimauerunt regno. Similis eorundem virtus extitit in Chilperico rege XVIII, quem cum propter inertiam tanto imperio indignum censuissent, regno se abdicare coegerunt: atque ad monachatum relegarunt: auctoribus ribus Aimoino libro 4.capite 61. Sigeberto & Tritemio anno 750. & Godfrid.Chron.part. 17.ca.4.Sextum rursus eiusdem seueritatis exemplum extitit in Carolo Crasso rege xxv.qui propter similem ignauiam, & quod Nortmannis Galliæ partem concessisset,regnumque imminui passus esset, ab optimatibus regni (vt Sigebertus loquitur) repudiatus est: anno, vt idé scribit, 890. quod idem Godfridus part. 17. testatur. sed vberius Otto Frising. Chron. 6. cap. 9. vbi memorabile illud adscribit: hūc cùm post Carolum Magnum inter omnes reges Francorum maximæ fuisset auctoritatis, in breui ad tantam tenuitatem venisse, vt panis quoque egens,ab Arnolpho iam rege facto stipendia miserabiliter exigeret: atque ab ipso paucos fiscos gratanter suscipéret. vnde humanarum rerum status miserrimus cognoscitur: quod is qui tam Orientalia, quàm Occidentalia regna cum Romano susceperat Imperio, ad tantam postremò deiectionem venit,vt panis quoque egeret. Septimi etiam exempli memoria extat in Odone rege xxv1. quem cùm Franci, repudiato Ludouici Balbi filio Carolo, regem sibi delegissent, quarto post anno in Aquitaniam amandarunt,ibique considere iusserunt: eiusque in locum Carolum eiusdem Balbi filium suffecerunt. auctoribus Sigeberto sub anno 894.Aimoino lib. 5.c.42.Godfrid. part. 17.Sed & Regino lib. 2. Ottone,inquit, rege in Aquitania commorante, Francorum Principes ex maxima parte ab eo deficiunt: & in Rhemorū ciuitate Carolus filius Ludouici in regnum eleuatur. In eundem quoque numerum ascribitur Carolus rex xxvii. propter stuporem ingenij, Simplex cognomento dictus: qui cùm stultitia sua regnum pessundaret, Lotharingiamque quam prius recuperauerat, amisisset, cap-tus, atque in carcerem coniectus est, eiusque in locum Rodolphus suffectus. auctoribus Aimoino libro 5. cap. 42. Sigebert. anno 926. Et de eodem Annal. Rhemens. auctor, anno 920. Penè omnes, inquit, Franciæ Comites regem suum Carolum Simplicem apud vrbem Suefsionicam, quia Haganonem consiliarium suum, quem de mediocribus potentem fecerat, dimittere nolebat, reliquerunt. Item Rhegino l.2. Chr. an. 838. Ludouicus, inquit, a suis imperio priuatur, regniq; monarchia Lothario filio eius per electionem Francorum datur. Item sub anno 922. Et cum quotidie copijs Roberti crescentibus, decrescerent Caroli, clam tandem secedens cum Haganone trans Mosam proficiscitur. Franci Robertum SENIOREM ELEGERVNT: ipsíque sese committunt. Robertus itaque rex Rhemis apud Remigium ab Episcopis & primatibus regni constituitur. Idem sub anno 923. Auditoque Franci, quòd Carolus Nortmannos ad se venire mandasset, ne illi coniungerentur inter Carolum atque Nortmannos, super Isaram flumen. tumq; Carolo trans Mosam refugiente, Rodolphum cuncti REGEM ELIGVNT. Rodolphus ergo frater Richardi rex apud vrbem Sueffionicam constituitur. Atque hæc quidem post Francogalliæ regnũ constitutum maiorum nostrorum virtus fuit: cuius exemplum ipsi à suis quoque maioribus acceperant. Nam Hunibaldus antiquissimus Francorum historicus, apud Iohannem Tritenhemium de Francis & Heleno ipsorum rege ita scribit: Ann. eius regni xiiii. congregati apud Neopagum Sicambri Helenum regem inerte & inutilem communi omnium sententia deposuerunt à regno: & ad priuatam redire vitā compulerunt: in cuius locum elegerunt fratrē eius minorem. Quæ cum ita se habeant, perspicuum est, Agathium, qui lib. i. scribit, regum Francorum filios à parentibus regnum successione excipere solitos, vel eorum instituti minus peritum fuisse, vtpote Græcum hominem & alienigenam: vel ita intelligendum esse, vt superius diximus: moris fuisse, vt regum filij, regaliter educati atque instituti, prærogatiuam in comitijs haberent. præsertim cum ea spe parentes adducti summum in filijs bene honesteque instituendis studium collocarent. Sed multo imperitius & absurdius est, quod Theo. Nehemius in Nemore vnionis tract. 6. scribit, Carolum Magnum constituisse, vt deinceps Franci ex parentum successione reges haberent: cum superius demonstratum sit, eundem Carolum in suo testamento ius regum constituendorum populo Francico integrum illibatumque reliquisse. Verba Nehemij hæc sunt: Porrò quia ipse Carolus rex Francorum extitit, istud regnū fuit ad eum ex successione devolutum. (Hoc verò quid absurdius dici potuit?) & vides quod ipse factus Imperator, suos hæredes dignitate propria, scilicet regno Francorum penitus denudasset (Et hoc quoque perabsurde scriptum apparet) statuit, ut Francigenæ cum quadam regni Francorum portione regem haberent de regali semine, iure hereditario successorem: qui in temporalibus superiorem non recognosceret: videlicet ut Imp. potestati ad homagium, vel aliquod obsequium teneretur. Hæc ille: quæ, ut vera essent, tamen illud confirmarent, vtq; ad Carolum Magnum Francogalliæ regnum non hæreditate, sed populi arbitrio delatum fuisse. Sed hæc à Nehemio scripta esse apparet, ad tollendam quorundam veterum Iuris Doctorum disputationem, his verbis conceptam, An Rex Gallia Imperatorem aut alium superiorem recognosceret. de qua tractatur à Decretalistis in c. per venerabilem, Qui fil. sint legit. Bald. in confil. 49. vol.
units.tr: to Gregory of Tours, book 2, chapter 64: "The Franks rose up against Theodoric, drove him from the kingdom, cut off and shaved his hair, and shaved Ebroin himself." But best of all is the Appendix of Hunibald: "Theodoric," he says, "given over to ease and idleness, began to leave all the business of the kingdom to the Count of the Palace, whom they called the mayor of the palace. The mayor of this sort was Ebruin, a wicked and impious man, who did much evil. Roused by these things, the chief men of the Franks deposed Theodoric from the kingdom, and thrust both him and Ebruin, separated from each other, into two monasteries." And soon after: "Hilderic, the middle brother of the two preceding kings and son of Clovis, Theodoric his younger brother having been deposed from the kingdom of the Franks, was called from Austrasia to the kingdom by the choice of the nobles, and reigned for a few years. Since he was harsh in character and hateful to many of the Frankish nobles, he was killed in hunting." To this may be added the Chronology of Idalius, not yet published, under the year of Christ 703: "After Lothair, Theodoric is put in place as king. But after a short time, when Ebroin the mayor of the palace had been expelled, the Franks raised his brother Childeric, king of the Austrasians, to the throne of the whole kingdom." A similar virtue of the same people appeared in King Chilperic the Eighteenth, whom, because of his sloth, they judged unworthy of so great a rule, and forced to abdicate the kingdom and sent away to a monastic life. The authorities are Aimoin, book 4, chapter 61, Sigebert and Trithemius under the year 750, and Godfrey, Chronicle part 17, chapter 4. A sixth example of the same severity is King Charles the Fat, the twenty-fifth, who, on account of similar sloth, and because he had allowed part of Gaul to be granted to the Normans and let the kingdom be diminished, was rejected by the nobles of the realm (as Sigebert puts it) in the year 890, as the same writer also records, and Godfrey, part 17, bears witness to the same. But Otto of Freising, Chronicle book 6, chapter 9, gives a fuller account, where he records this memorable fact: that although after Charlemagne he had been of the greatest authority among all the kings of the Franks, he quickly came to such poverty that, lacking even bread, he miserably demanded a pension from Arnulf, already made king, and gratefully accepted from him a few coins. Whence the most wretched condition of human affairs is recognised: that he who had held both the Eastern and the Western kingdoms together with the Roman Empire finally fell to such a low state that he lacked even bread. A seventh example is found in King Odo, the twenty-sixth, whom the Franks, having rejected Charles, son of Louis the Stammerer, chose as their king; four years later they sent him away into Aquitaine and ordered him to remain there, and in his place they set up Charles, son of the same Stammerer. The authorities are Sigebert under the year 894, Aimoin, book 5, chapter 42, and Godfrey, part 17. But Regino also, book 2: "While King Odo was staying in Aquitaine, the princes of the Franks for the most part deserted him, and at the city of Reims Charles, son of Louis, was raised to the kingdom." To the same number is also assigned King Charles the Twenty-seventh, called the Simple on account of the dullness of his wit, who, when he was ruining the kingdom by his folly, and had lost Lorraine, which he had earlier recovered, was captured and thrown into prison, and Rudolf was put in his place. The authorities are Aimoin, book 5, chapter 42, Sigebert under the year 926, and the author of the Annals of Reims concerning the same, under the year 920: "Almost all the counts of France abandoned their king Charles the Simple at the city of Soissons, because he was unwilling to dismiss Haganon, his councillor, whom he had made powerful from humble station." Likewise Regino, book 2 of the Chronicle, under the year 838: "Louis," he says, "is deprived of power by his own men, and the monarchy of the kingdom is given to his son Lothair by the election of the Franks." Likewise under the year 922: "And while daily the forces of Robert grew and those of Charles diminished, at last Charles, withdrawing secretly, set out with Haganon across the Meuse. The Franks elected Robert the Elder, and committed themselves to him. Thus King Robert was set up at Reims, at the church of Remigius, by the bishops and chief men of the kingdom." The same under the year 923: "And when the Franks heard that Charles had summoned the Normans to come to him, lest they should join forces between Charles and the Normans, they gathered beyond the river Oise. And when Charles fled across the Meuse, they all ELECTED RODULF KING. Rodulf, brother of Richard, was therefore set up as king at the city of Soissons." These, then, were the virtues of our ancestors after the kingdom of Gaul-France was established; and they had received the example of it from their own forebears. For Hunibald, the most ancient historian of the Franks, writes thus about the Franks and their king Helenus, as reported by Johannes Trithemius: "In the fourteenth year of his reign, the Sicambrians assembled at Neopagum and, by the common judgment of all, deposed King Helenus from the kingdom, as sluggish and useless, and compelled him to return to private life; in his place they chose his younger brother." Since these things stand thus, it is plain that Agathias, who in book 1 writes that the sons of the Frankish kings were accustomed to receive the kingdom by succession from their parents, was either less skilled in their institutions, as a Greek and a foreigner, or else must be understood as we have said above: that it was the custom for the sons of kings, reared and educated in royal fashion, to have a prerogative in the assemblies, especially since parents, led by that hope, applied the greatest zeal to bringing up and educating their sons well and honourably. But it is far more ignorant and absurd what Theodore Nehemias writes in Nemus Unionis, tract. 6, that Charlemagne established that the Franks should thereafter have kings by succession from their parents; for it has been shown above that this same Charlemagne, in his testament, left to the Frankish people the right of creating kings entire and unimpaired. Nehemias's words are these: "Moreover, because Charles himself was king of the Franks, that kingdom came to him by succession. (But what could be said more absurdly?) And you see that when he himself became emperor, he had stripped his heirs of their own dignity, namely of the kingdom of the Franks altogether (and this too appears to be written most absurdly), and decreed that the Franks should have a king of royal seed, a successor by hereditary right, with a portion of the kingdom of the Franks, who in temporal matters would acknowledge no superior, namely that he should be bound to the imperial power by homage or some other service." Thus he; which, even if true, would still confirm this, namely that the kingdom of Gaul-France came to Charlemagne not by inheritance but by the choice of the people. But it appears that these things were written by Nehemias to overthrow the dispute of certain ancient jurists, framed in these words: Whether the King of France acknowledged an emperor or some other superior. This is treated by the Decretalists in the chapter "Per venerabilem," on the legitimacy of children, and by Baldus in consilium 49, vol.

units.la: Pluribus exstantibus regis demortui liberis, quid iuris in hereditate observaretur. CAP. VIII.
units.tr: When several children of a deceased king are living, what law governs the inheritance. CHAPTER VIII.

units.la: HÆc autem omnia eò pertinent, vt doceamus, regnum Francogalliæ antiquitus nõ hereditatis iure, vt priuata patrimonia: sed ordinũ ac populi iudicio & suffragijs deferri solitum fuisse. quo minus illi relictum quæstioni videtur loci, Si plures regis demortui liberi extarent, quænam in cuiusque iure constituendo ratio teneretur. Nam cùm penes populi Comitia, & publicum Gentis concilium non modò deferendi, verumetiam adimendi regni summa potestas esset, illud necessario consequitur, in eiusdem arbitrio fuisse, vtrum omnibus æqualiter, an vni tantum regni successionem deferret. Quanquam hoc loco quæstio exoritur, si populus filio repudiato alium eligeret, ecquid tamen illi ad suam dignitatem ruendam relinqueretur. Quare intelligendum est, iure quidem Romano earum rerum, quæ in Principis imperio ac ditione sunt, quatuor tantum esse species. aliæ namque ipsius Principis patrimoniales sunt: aliæ Fiscales: aliæ publicæ: aliæ priuatæ. Patrimoniales posteriorum Imperat. Romanorum ætate appellatæ sunt, quæ propriæ ipsius Principis erant, non Principatus, sed patrimonij iure: quæ iccirco de propria Principis substantia esse dicuntur: L.3, §.1. C. de quad. præscriptione. veluti, si cui è proceribus Imperium à populo delatum esset, certũ est, ea bona quæ ante delatum illũ honore propria ipsius erant, in ipsius dominio mansisse. non qua Imperator erat, sed qua Valés, aut Honorius, aut Theodosius. idque in libris nostris Sacrum patrimonium passim appellatur: L. vlt. C. de vectig. L. 1, C. de indiction. pari ergo ratione, si Dagoberto, puta, vel Lothario Francogalliæ regnum ab ordinibus regni delatum erat, quod ante adeptam illam dignitatem in bonis habuerat, pleno iure ipsius manebat. Fiscus autem, sive Fiscalia bona dicuntur, quæ Principi ad tuendam dignitatem suam populi voluntate attributa sunt: sive ea in pecunia numerata, sive in prædijs, sive in iure consistant. quamuis enim Fisci nomen stricte proprieque ad thesauros pertineat: d. L. 3, C. de quadr. præscript. (quod etiam origo appellationis ostendit) tamen etiam ad fundos & prædia productum est, quæ in fisci patrimonio esse dicuntur. L. 2, §. 2, D. ne quid in loc. pub. L. 49. D. locat. L. 38.§. 1, D.ad munic[?]. quin etiam iura vectigalia, mulctę pecuniarię, priuilegiaq; omnia Principi cōcessa, eo nomine cōtinentur, vti patet ex rot.tit. D. & C. de iur. fisc. Magna igitur inter Patrimonium Principis & Fiscum differentia est: multisque locis inter se distinguuntur. veluti d.L. 3, §. 1, C. de quadr. præscript. L. 6. & L. vlt. C. de vectigal. d. L. 49, D. locat. L. 6, D. de iur. fisc. L. vlt. D. qui pot. in pign. hab.
units.tr: However, all these points are meant to show that the kingdom of France was in antiquity customarily conferred not by hereditary right, as private estates are, but by the judgment and votes of the orders and the people. For this reason the question seems to have no place here: if several children of a deceased king are living, what principle ought to govern the right of each one? For since supreme power to confer and also to take away the kingdom lay with the popular assemblies and the public council of the nation, it necessarily follows that it was in their discretion whether to grant the succession to all equally or to one alone. Yet a question arises here: if the people rejected a son and chose another, would anything still be left to him to keep him from losing his dignity? Therefore it must be understood that under Roman law there are only four kinds of things that fall under the power and dominion of the Prince. Some are the Prince's own patrimonial property; others are fiscal; others are public; others are private. Patrimonial property was so called in the age of the later Roman emperors: it belonged to the Prince himself, not by virtue of his rule but by right of patrimony, and for this reason it is said to be part of the Prince's own substance (L. 3, §. 1, C. de quadr. præscript.). For example, if one of the nobles was raised to the imperial office by the people, it is certain that the goods which were his own before he received that honour remained his property, not as emperor but as Valens, or Honorius, or Theodosius. In our books this is commonly called the sacred patrimony (L. ult. C. de vectig.; L. 1, C. de indict.). By the same reasoning, if the kingdom of France was conferred on Dagobert, say, or on Lothair by the orders of the realm, whatever he had held as his own goods before attaining that dignity remained fully his. Fiscal goods, or the fisc, are those assigned to the Prince by the will of the people to support his dignity, whether they consist in money, in estates, or in rights. For although the name fiscus strictly and properly refers to treasuries (d. L. 3, C. de quadr. præscript., as the origin of the word also shows), it has nevertheless been extended to lands and estates, which are said to belong to the fiscal patrimony (L. 2, §. 2, D. ne quid in loc. pub.; L. 49, D. locat.; L. 38, §. 1, D. ad munic.). Indeed, tolls, fines, and all privileges granted to the Prince are included under this name, as is clear from the title D. and C. de iur. fisc. There is therefore a great difference between the Prince's patrimony and the fisc, and they are distinguished from each other in many places (d. L. 3, §. 1, C. de quadr. præscript.; L. 6 and L. ult. C. de vectig.; d. L. 49, D. locat.; L. 6, D. de iur. fisc.; L. ult. D. qui pot. in pign. hab.).

units.la: Nam rerum patrimonialium commercium non est, nisi voluntate Principis. L. cùm seruus, 39.§.vlt.D.de legat.1. Fiscalium autē vsitatum ac legitimum commercium est. L. si procurator, 5, D. §,d. iur.Fisc. L. pacta, 72, §.vlt. D.de cont.empt· ille ad Principis heredes transmittebantur: quàuis imperij successores nō essent. L. quod principi, 56, D.de legat.2. hæc verò quia magis Principatus sunt, quàm Principis, ad eum solum, cui principatus defertur, vna cum principatu transferuntur. qua de caussa Vlp. dixit, res Fiscales, quasi proprias & priuatas ipsius Cæsaris esse. d. L.2, §.2, Ne quid in loc. publie. id est, non vere, proprie ac pleno iure, quamuis interdum illud quasi, omittatur. vt in L. 3, D. de his quæ pro non scripthough hab.
units.tr: For there is a trade in patrimonial things only by the Prince's will: L. cum servus, 39, §ult., D. de legatis 1. Fiscal property, however, has a customary and lawful trade: L. si procurator, 5, D. §d. iur. Fisc.; L. pacta, 72, §ult., D. de contrahenda emptione. The former passed to the Prince's heirs, even though they were not successors in the empire: L. quod principi, 56, D. de legatis 2. But fiscal goods, because they belong more to the principate than to the Prince, pass together with the principate to the one on whom the principate is conferred. For this reason Ulpian said that fiscal things are, as it were, the proper and private property of Caesar himself: d. L. 2, §2, ne quid in loco publico. That is, they are not so in truth, properly, and with full right, although the words as it were are sometimes omitted, as in L. 3, D. de his quae pro non scriptis habentur.

units.la: Publicas autem res appellamus, quæ ciuitatis cuiusque & proprietate & vsu communes sunt: quales sunt, curiæ, fora, arcæ communes, agri publici, veluti compascua & syluę communes. L. 1, §.1. Quod cuiusque vniuers.item,(vt ex ætatis nostræ statu exemplum sumamus) tormenta muralia, vnde illa controuersia, quam And.Tiraquellus quodam loco commemorat, cùm ciuitas quædam Galliæ Regi sua tormenta muralia certum ad vsum commodasseт, ille autem inter homines esse desijsset, ciuitas ab ipsius successore sua tormenta repetebat. Cui assentatores aulici stolidissime respondebant, nouum Regem ex sui decessoris contractibus & obligationibus non teneri. quod absurdissimum esse constat, neque in Francogallia vsurpatum vt Paponius testatur lib. 20, tit. de testa. art. 14. vbi Oldradi consilium 94. in suam sententiam commemorat. Verum est igitur, ciuitates
units.tr: We call public things those which belong in both ownership and use in common to each city: such are the courts, the marketplaces, the common chests, public fields, such as common pasture and woods: L. 1, §1, Quod cuiuscumque universitatis. (To take an example from the condition of our own age:) siege artillery. From this comes the controversy which Andreas Tiraquellus mentions in a certain passage: when a city of France had lent its siege artillery to the King for a fixed use, and the King then died, the city demanded its artillery back from his successor. To this the courtiers replied most stupidly that a new king is not bound by the contracts and obligations of his predecessor. This is known to be most absurd, and it is not the practice in France, as Papon attests in book 20, title on testaments, art. 14, where he cites the consilium 94 of Oldradus in support of his view. It is true, therefore, that cities

units.la: E quamplurimas res proprias habere, à Fiscalibus reb. planè alienas l.2. §. publicæ, Ne quid in loc. publ. L. 2, vbi omnes Doctores late hoc tractât. C. de diuerf. præd. vrb. L. ciuitatibus, 122, D. de legat. 1. L. 1, C. de vend. reb. ciuit. L. 14. §. vlt. D. de feruitut. L. 72, §. vlt. D. de cōt. ēpt.
units.tr: also possess very many things of their own, quite distinct from fiscal things: L. 2, §publicae, ne quid in loco publico; L. 2, where all the doctors treat this widely, C. de diversis praediis urbanis; L. civitatibus, 122, D. de legatis 1; L. 1, C. de vendendis rebus civitatum; L. 14, §ult., D. de servitutibus; L. 72, §ult., D. de contrahenda emptione.

units.la: Priuatæ autem res dicuntur, quæ in cuiusque patrisfa. fortunis ac facultatibus censentur: L.1, D. De ret. diuif. cum similib. quæ latiore interpretatione, æquè vt res publicæ, Principis esse dicuntur, sed, (vt ex Seneca in Quest. Illustrib. docuimus) imperio, non dominio: ditione, non proprietate: vniuerse, non singulatim: sola iuris fictione, non possessione & vsu. Itaq; vendi, donari, legari à priuatis res suas videmus Principi, aut Imper. aut Regi: quæ si antea ipsius propriæ fuissent, iterum ipsius fieri non possent.
units.tr: Private things are those which are reckoned among the property and means of each head of a household: L. 1, D. de rerum divisione, with similar passages. In a wider sense these, like public things, are said to belong to the Prince, but (as we have shown from Seneca in the Quaestiones Illustres) by command, not by ownership; by sovereignty, not by proprietorship; collectively, not individually; by legal fiction alone, not by possession and use. Accordingly we see private persons selling, giving, and bequeathing their own goods to the Prince, whether emperor or king; and if these had previously been his own proper goods, they could not again become his.

units.la: NVnc vt ad institutum, & quæstionem propositam reuertamur, sciendum est antiquitus institutum fuisse, vt Francorum Regib. nō modo Fiscalia illa iura, qualia Romanis Imperatorib. cōcesla erat verūetiam certa quædā fruenda prædia ad regiam suā dignitatem tuendam assignarentur, quæ barbaro vocabulo DEMANIVM Regium appellantur: plerumq; autē DOMANIVM. Est enim Domanium regium quasi dos regni, quomodo veteres dicebant Vatē prædij, siue (vt planius loquamur) quasi quidā vsusfructus certarum possessionum, Regi ad tuendum dignitatis suæ splendorem attributus. Dixi QVASI vsusfructus: propterea quod earum possessionum proprietas penes populum manet: neque vlla eius pars alienari à Rege potest, sine populo auctore: hoc est sine Ordinum & publici Concilij consensu, quemadmodum posterius commodiore loco docebimus. ius tantum vtendi fruendi ei conceditur. Addidi autem particulam, QVASI: quia permultis in rebus ius illud ab vsufructu discrepat. veluti, vt cautio de fruendo boni viri arbitrio praestetur: vt ne forma & species praediorum mutetur, & quae sunt in eodem genere. Vtcunq; fit, magnam ex illa definitione patet esse differentiam inter Patrimonium & Domanium Regale. Nam Patrimonium, ipsius Regis proprium est: Domanii vero, Regni, atq; (vt vulgus loquitur) ipsius Coronæ. Illud pleno iure, Regis est: atq; ideo plena & summa ipsius pro sua voluntate alienandi potestate habet. Huius nuda proprietas est penes vniuersitatem populi, siue Rép. vsusfructus aut penes Regem. qua de causa nulla, vt iā dixim, illius alienandi potestate habet. ac plane verissima est Doctorum hac de re sententia: Par idèq; esse ius Regis in suum domanium: quod est viri, in dote suæ vxoris. quemadmodum præter cæteros tradunt Lucas de Penn. in L. qcunq;. C. de ann. agr. defert. Paris de put. de syndicat. sub Rub. de exceffib. Imper. And. Ifern. in tit. Feud. quæ sunt regal. Inter Domanium aut & Fisco hoc interest, quod illud ad vsum ipsi Regis, h. e. ad annonā, & victū cultūq; Maiest. Regiæ cōsentaneū institutū est: hic, ad statū Regni & Reipub. tuendum atque conseruandum: qui si forte propter bellorum & aliarum eiusmodi necessitatum rationem sufficere non videatur, tum demum in subsidium tributa de communi ordinum sententia in publico Concilio vniuersæ genti indicuntur. Præterea domanij commercium nullum est. Rerum Fiscaliū vsitatum ac legitimum: vt paulo ante demonstrauimus. Illud certum ac definitum est: harū modus incertus, atq; infinitus, quia Fisci nomine non modò ea omnia quæ vulgo præcisè Regalia: plenè autem Iura regalia vocantur, verùm etiam alia innumera quę Regiæ Maiestati ad Rempublicam tuendam concessa sunt, complectitur.
units.tr: Now let us return to our undertaking and the question proposed. It must be understood that it was an ancient custom for the kings of the Franks to be assigned not only those fiscal rights which were granted to the Roman emperors, but also certain estates to be enjoyed in order to maintain their royal dignity. In the barbarous language these are called the royal DEMANIUM, but more commonly DOMANIUM. For the royal domain is, as it were, the dowry of the kingdom, just as the ancients spoke of the dowry of a landed estate. Or, to speak more plainly, it is a kind of usufruct of certain possessions, granted to the king to uphold the splendour of his dignity. I say "as it were" a usufruct, because the ownership of these possessions remains with the people, and no part of them can be alienated by the king without the people's authority, that is, without the consent of the estates and of the public council, as we shall show later in a more suitable place. He is granted only the right to use and enjoy them. I have added the particle "as it were", because in many respects that right differs from a usufruct: for example, the king must give security to enjoy the estates at the discretion of a good man, so that the form and appearance of the estates is not changed, and other matters of the same kind. However that may be, it is clear from this definition that there is a great difference between the patrimony and the royal domain. For the patrimony is the king's own property; the domain, however, belongs to the kingdom and, as the common people say, to the Crown itself. The patrimony belongs to the king with full right, and therefore he has full and supreme power to alienate it at his own will. Of the domain, the bare ownership lies with the whole body of the people, or the commonwealth, and only the usufruct with the king; for this reason he has no power of alienating it, as I have said. The opinion of the jurists on this matter is entirely true: the king's right over his domain is equal to that of a husband over his wife's dowry. Thus, among others, Lucas de Penna on the law "quacunque" in the Code, de annona agrorum deferenda, Paris de Puteo in de syndicatu, under the rubric de excessibus, Andreas of Isernia on the title of the feudal law quae sunt regalia, have taught. There is this further difference between the domain and the fisc: the domain was established for the use of the king himself, that is, for his revenue and for the food, clothing and maintenance befitting his majesty; the fisc was established for protecting and preserving the state and the commonwealth. If at any time this is not thought sufficient on account of wars and other such necessities, then at last taxes are levied on the whole nation, in aid, by the common decision of the estates in a public council. Moreover, there is no trade in the domain, whereas the fiscal goods are customarily and lawfully traded, as we showed a little earlier. The one is certain and definite; the other's extent is uncertain and unlimited, because the name of the fisc embraces not only all those things which are commonly called royal rights in the narrow sense, but fully called royal rights, but also countless other things granted to the royal majesty for the protection of the commonwealth.

units.la: Ac de Domanio quidem illud accipiendum est, quod Eguinarthus in eo libello, quem ad Caroli Magni & Carlouingorum gratiam, & ad imminuēdam Merouingorum existimationē conscripsit, his verbis tradidit: Cùm præter inutile Regis nomen & precarium vitæ stipendium, quod ei Præfectus aulæ exhibebat, nihil aliud proprij possideret, quàm vnam perparui redditus villam, in qua domum, ex qua famulos sibi necessaria ministrantes, atque obsequium exhibentes paucę numerositatis habebat. Hæc ille. Itaque postquam, recepta sensim consuetudine, Francogalliæ corona hereditaria esse cœpit, & vel filio, vel proximo agnato deferri, quamuis plures eiusdem gradus vel filij vel agnati essent: tamen vni tantum, seniori scilicet, ac natu maximo domanium illud attributum fuit reliquis omnibus eiusdem gradus vel filijs, vel agnatis ab illo exclusis; quorum tamen habita ratio est diligenter. Nam ad vitæ cultum & decus familiæ pro dignitate tuendū, institutum fuit, vt ijs possessiones quædam assignarentur, quæ vulgo appannagia dictæ sunt: ab antiquo & Francico (vt mihi persuasi) vocabulo Abbanně, quod Latine valet, excludere: itē vt Ausbannen & Forbannen: quasi ea portione accepta exclusos se à Regni successione intelligerent: quemadmodum Otto Frising. Chron. 5. c. 9. & Godfridus Viterbiensis scribunt, Dagobertum Lotharij filium, regem constitutum, fratri Heriberto vrbes & pagos aliquot propè Ligerim fruendos dedisse. quod idem Aimoinus lib. 4. cap. 17. commemorans, ita subiungit: Pactum cum ipso pepigit, vt priuato contentus habitu, nil amplius de paterno sperare deberet regno. Et Regino lib. 1. Dagobertus, inquit, monarchiā totius imperij obtinuit, excepto quòd fratri suo Heriberto cōtra Ligerim & limitem, quò tenditur partibus Vasconiæ, pagum scilicet Tholosanum, Caturcinum, Aganensem, Petragorium, & Sanctonicum, vel quod ab his versus Pyrenæos montes excluditur, concessit. Ex quibus intelligitur, quod Aimoinus illo loco scribit, Heribertum consortem regni factum, non de regni iure intelligendum esse, sed de regni ditionibus. Itaque paulo post scribit eundem Heribertum illa ditione non contentum, vi & armis regis nomen sibi sumpsisse: bellūque fratri contra pactionem intulisse. Similiter autem idem Aimoinus eo libro quarto cap. 61. de Pipino scribens, Grifonem fratrem, inquit, more Ducum xii. comitatibus donauit. Atque huc illud pertinet quod Greg. Turonen. lib. 7. cap. 32. ita scribit: Misit Gondobaldus duos legatos ad regem, cum virgis consecratis iuxta ritum Francorum, ut scilicet non contingerentur ab vllo. Et mox, Gondobaldus dicit se filium esse patris nostri regis Clotarij, & misit nos ut debita portione regni sui recipiat. Nunc ut ad propositā quaestione redeamus, quantum ad regni successionem attinet: certū hac de re ius Francogalliæ nullū reperio. quippe, cum hereditaria, ut dixi, non esset: ceteris autem in patrimonijs nobilibus, quæ Feuda nominantur, Otto Frising. lib. Frid. 2. c. 29. Mos est, inquit, in Burgundia, qui penè in omnib. Galliæ prouincijs seruatur, quòd semper seniori fratri, eiusq; liberis, seu maribus, seu fœminis, paternæ hæreditatis cedat auctoritas: ceteris ad illum tanquam ad dominum respicientibus. Quibus omnibus ex locis intelligendum est, res eas, quæ Apannagij titulo filijs natu minoribus attribuuntur, neq; regni, neque regiæ hereditatis partes esse, nō magis, quàm res certas legati aut hereditatis titulo relictas, hereditatis partes esse intelligūtur, L. pen. C. de hered. instit. L. quoties, 9. §. heredes. D. eod. L. qui fundum, 87.§. 3, D. ad leg. Falcid. L. quædam, 9. §. 1, D. de edend, non enim hereditas pars proprie in vna re intelligitur. L. quamuis, 14, D. si quis omis. causs. rest. Atque hoc idem iuris in gente Francorum vniuersa fuisse, multis verbis traditur à Petro de Vineis, lib. Epistol. 6. epist. 25. & alijs nonnullis locis. Sed in regni successione aliud iuris fuit. Nam primùm vetus lex fuit, vt quamuis deferendi regni iudicium arbitriumque summum penes Ordinum comitia, publicumque gentis totius Concilium esset, tamen si Regis defuncti filij annis xxiiii. minores essent, eos creari ius non esset: atque adeò alium aetatis legitimae creari necesse esset. Qua ex re de Maiorum nostrorum sapientia existimare licet: qui Reipublicae suae gubernacula ei aetati committenda non existimarunt, quae alieni consilij, etiam in priuatis rebus suis administrandis, indigeret. Verba autem Hunibaldi apud Iohan. Tritenhemium haec sunt: Anno Christi cccix. cum Rex Francorum Clogio incautius dimicaret, à Romanis interfectus & occisus est: duos relinquens filios: quorum natu maior Helenus annum tunc agebat xx: minor vero natu Richimer xviii. Lege autem Francorum erat interdictum, ne quis promoueretur in Regem, nisi xxiiii aetatis annum complesset. Hinc factum est, quod neuter filiorum Clogionis ad regnum potuit peruenire. sed patruus eorum Clodomer, electione principum, fuit in Regem coronatus. Haec ille: ex quibus perspicuum est, quod superius dicebamus, quod Agathius scribit Regum filios regnum à parentib. excepisse: nequaquam simpliciter & absolutè intelligendum esse: sed ita, si causa eorum, Ordinum comitijs, publicoque gentis Concilio probata esset: in cuius causa cognitione caput hoc fuit, An x xiiii annorum maiores essent. Quam ætatem si compleuerant, tum memoriæ proditum est, antiquis temporibus persæpe Francogalliæ Regnum Rege mortuo non vni filio ab Ordinum comitijs attributum, sed in viriles partes diuisum, atque assignatum fuisse. Itaque defuncto Clodoueo Rege secundo, anno D xv. qui liberos iiii. reliquerat, Theodoricum, Clodoueum, Childebertū, Chlotarium satis constat, Regnum inter eos ita diuisum fuisse, vt Theodoricus Metarum, Clodoeus Aureliæ, Chlotarius Sueffionum, Childebertus Lutetiæ regnum obtineret, auctoribus Agathio libro histor. i. Greg. Turon. libro tertio capite i. Aimoin.lib. 2. cap. 1. Reginone sub anno 421. Rursus post Chlotarij Regis iiii. excessum, Regnum inter quatuor ipsius filios ita partitum fuit, vt Cherebertus Lutetiæ, Guntrannus Aureliæ, Chilpericus Sueffionibus, Sigebertus Rhemis regni sui sedem arcemque collocaret: auctoribus Gregor. libro 4. cap. 22. Aimoi. libro tertio, cap. 1. Reginone sub anno 498. Contrà vero anno circiter D cxxx. mortuo Lothario Rege v ii. Otto Frising. Chr. 5. c. 9. & Godfrid. Viterb. ita scribunt: Dagobertus Clotarij filius solus in Francia regnabat. sed fratri suo Heribert. circa Ligerim fluuium pau-
units.tr: What is to be understood about the domain is what Eginhard said in that little book which he wrote to win the favour of Charlemagne and the Carolingians, and to diminish the reputation of the Merovingians, in these words: "Since the king, apart from the useless title of king and the precarious allowance for his life, which the steward of the household paid him, possessed nothing else of his own except one very small villa, in which he had a house and a small number of servants who supplied his necessities and attended him." So far he. Accordingly, after the crown of France gradually became hereditary, by custom received little by little, and was passed to a son or a nearest agnate, even though several sons or agnates of the same degree existed, that domain was nevertheless assigned to one only, namely the eldest and firstborn, all the other sons or agnates of the same degree being excluded from it; yet their claims were carefully considered. For it was established that, in order to maintain their way of life and the honour of the family in keeping with their rank, certain possessions should be assigned to them, which are commonly called appannagia. The word is ancient and Frankish (as I am persuaded) Abbanně, which in Latin means "to exclude"; so also Ausbannen and Forbannen, as if those who received that portion understood themselves to be excluded from the succession to the kingdom. Thus Otto of Freising in his Chronicle, book 5, chapter 9, and Godfrey of Viterbo write that Dagobert, son of Lothar, having been made king, gave his brother Heribert some towns and districts near the Loire to enjoy. Aimoin, recording the same, adds in book 4, chapter 17: "He made an agreement with him that, content with a private estate, he should expect nothing more from the paternal kingdom." And Regino, book 1: "Dagobert," he says, "obtained the monarchy of the whole empire, except that he granted to his brother Heribert the district of Toulouse, Cahors, Agen, Périgueux and Saintes, that is, the land along the Loire and the boundary which runs toward the parts of Gascony, or that which is shut off from these towards the Pyrenean mountains." From these passages it is understood that what Aimoin writes in that place, that Heribert was made a partner in the kingdom, is not to be understood of the right of the kingdom but of the lordships of the kingdom. Accordingly, a little later he writes that the same Heribert, not content with that lordship, assumed the name of king by force and arms, and waged war on his brother contrary to the agreement. In the same way Aimoin, writing in book 4, chapter 61 about Pepin, says: "He gave his brother Grifo twelve counties, in the manner of dukes." And to this pertains what Gregory of Tours writes in book 7, chapter 32: "Gondobald sent two envoys to the king, with consecrated rods according to the custom of the Franks, so that they should not be touched by anyone." And soon after: "Gondobald says that he is a son of our father, King Clotar, and has sent us so that he may receive his due portion of the kingdom." Now, to return to the question proposed, as far as the succession to the kingdom is concerned, I find no certain law of France on this matter; since, as I have said, it was not hereditary, and in the other noble patrimonies, which are called fiefs, Otto of Freising in the book on Frederick 2, chapter 29, says: "It is the custom in Burgundy, which is observed in almost all the provinces of Gaul, that the authority over the paternal inheritance always passes to the elder brother and his children, whether male or female, the others looking up to him as their lord." From all these passages it must be understood that the things which are assigned to the younger sons under the title of appanage are no more parts of the kingdom or of the royal inheritance than specific things left by legacy or by the title of inheritance are understood to be parts of an inheritance (Code, de heredibus instituendis, last law; Digest, ibid., law "quoties", section "heredes"; Digest, ad legem Falcidiam, law "qui fundum", section 3; Digest, de edendo, law "quaedam", section 1; for an inheritance is not properly understood as a part in one thing, Digest, si quis omissa causa testamenti, law "quamvis"). That this same law was in the whole nation of the Franks is related at length by Peter de Vinea, Epistles, book 6, letter 25, and in some other places. But in the succession to the kingdom the law was different. For first there was an old law that, although the power and the final judgement of appointing the king lay with the assembly of the estates and the public council of the whole nation, yet if the sons of the deceased king were under twenty-four years of age, they could not be created king, and it was necessary to create another of lawful age. From this matter one may judge the wisdom of our ancestors, who did not think that the government of their commonwealth should be entrusted to an age which needed the counsel of others even in managing its private affairs. The words of Hunibald, as given by Johannes Trithemius, are these: "In the year of Christ 509, when the King of the Franks, Clodio, fought too rashly, he was killed and slain by the Romans, leaving two sons: of whom the elder, Helenus, was then twenty years old, and the younger, Richimer, eighteen. But by the law of the Franks it was forbidden that anyone be raised to the kingship unless he had completed the twenty-fourth year of his age. Hence it came about that neither of Clodio's sons could attain the kingdom, but their uncle Clodomer was crowned king by the choice of the princes." So far he. From these things it is clear that what we said above, that Agathias writes that the sons of kings received the kingdom from their parents, must not be understood simply and absolutely, but only if their case was approved by the assembly of the estates and the public council of the nation; and in the examination of their case this was the point: whether they were of full age, that is, twenty-four years old. If they had completed that age, it has been recorded that in ancient times the kingdom of France, after the death of the king, was very often not assigned by the assembly of the estates to one son alone, but was divided among the sons in equal shares and assigned to them. Thus, when Clovis II, the second king, died in 515 leaving four children, Theodoric, Clodoveus, Childebert and Clotaire, it is quite certain that the kingdom was divided among them so that Theodoric held Metz, Clodoveus Orléans, Clotaire Soissons, and Childebert Paris, as Agathias relates in book 1 of his Histories, Gregory of Tours in book 3, chapter 1, Aimoin in book 2, chapter 1, and Regino under the year 421. Again, after the death of King Clotaire IV, the kingdom was divided among his four sons, so that Charibert set up his seat and citadel of the kingdom at Paris, Guntram at Orléans, Chilperic at Soissons, and Sigebert at Reims, as Gregory in book 4, chapter 22, Aimoin in book 3, chapter 1, and Regino under the year 498 relate. On the other hand, about the year 630, when Lothar II, the King, died, Otto of Freising, Chronicle 5, chapter 9, and Godfrey of Viterbo write thus: "Dagobert, son of Clotaire, alone reigned in France; but to his brother Heribert he had given a few towns and districts near the river Loire."

units.la: C25 cas vrbes & pagos dimiserat.à Clodoueo enim vsque ad id tempus regnum Francorum inter filios, filiorumque filios, multifariè diuiso confusè regnatum est. Terminus autem Regni Francorum erat iam ab Hispania vsque Pannoniam. Dagobertus itaque vnicus rex Francorū leges Bauaris dedit. Hæc Godefridus. neque, vt multi sapientes sæpe iudicarunt, iniuria. Nam (vt est apud Iustinum libro 21.) firmius est futurum regnum, si penes vnum remanserit, quam si portionibus inter plures fratres diuidatur. Aliquot tamen interiectis annis, cum Francorū Regnum longè lateque propagatum esset, Pipino rege mortuo, alia publico Gallorum consilio sententia placuit. quod valet ad confirmandum quod superius diximus, penes Ordinum & Concilij arbitrium, totum illud ius suisse. Nam Eguinarthus in vita Caroli Magni, sic loquitur: Mortuo Pipino, Franci facto solenniter generali conuentu, ambos sibi eius filios reges constituunt: ea conditione, vt totum Regni corpus ex æquo partirentur: & Carolus eam partem, quam pater eorum Pipinus tenuit: Carolomānus eā, cui patruus eorū præerat, regendam susciperet. Item Abbas Vrsperg. Mortuo Pipino, Carolus & Carolomannus filij eius, omnium Francorum consensu ambo reges creati sunt, ea conditione, vt totum regni corpus ex æquo partirentur. Simillima post Caroli Magni excessum in partiendo regno ratio fuit: quemadmodum ex ipsius testamento apud Iohan. Nauclerum, & Eguinarthi libello de ipsius vita cognosci licet: vbi tota propè Europa inter tres ipsius filios ita diuiditur, vt tamen filiabus nihil dotis, aut legitimæ portionis caussa tribuatur. sed earum collocandarum, dotisque constituendæ potestas fratrum fidei, charitati & prudentiæ permittatur. Neque iniuria. cùm principes, & proceres quibus illæ nuptum collocantur, non tam dotis spe, & magnitudine, quàm generis & familiæ dignitate ad earum matrimonium adducantur. Eandem in Orientali Francia partitionem post Ludouici mortem anno DCCCLXIIII. fuisse, testatur Otto Frisingensis Chron. 6. cap. 6. & Regino in Chron. anno 877. Rursus annis aliquot interiectis, post Ludouici Balbi Regis XXIII. excessum, anno DCCCLXXX. eadem quoque partiendi ratio seruata est, quam tamen non in Regum ipsorum, sed in Ordinum ac publici Concilij arbitrio fuisse, facilè, ex his Aimoini verbis cognosci licet, libro quinto, capite 40. Filij, inquit, Ludouici quondam Francorum Regis profecti sunt Ambianos, & sicut fideles eorum inuenerunt, Regnum paternum inter se diuiserunt. Ex quibus ita disputatis, perspicuum est, nullum antiquitus certum hac de re eius in Francogallia fuisse: sed totam eius rei potestatem in Ordinum & publico gentis concilio positam fuisse. postea verò Philippo tertio, Rege XLI. auctore constitutum est, vt ditio aliqua minoribus fratribus attribueretur. sed eius quoque iuris variæ interpretationes fuerunt: multæque natæ contentiones, propter filiarum rationem: vt plane nihil certi hac de re tradi à nobis possit: nisi, si res ad antiquum Maiorum nostrorum institutum reuocetur, totum eius rei ius publico Gentis & Ordinum Concilio committendum esse: vt pro liberorum numero certæ illis ditiones ad victum & cultum & dignitatem generis tuendam fruendæ attribuantur.
units.tr: ...a few cities and districts. From Clovis until that time, the kingdom of the Franks had been ruled in a confused way, divided among sons and grandsons in many parts. The boundary of the Frankish kingdom now ran from Spain to Pannonia. So Dagobert, as sole king of the Franks, gave laws to the Bavarians. Thus Godfrey, and not without reason, as many wise men have often judged. For (as Justin says in book 21) a kingdom will be more secure if it remains in the hands of one man than if it is divided into shares among several brothers. Some years later, however, when the kingdom of the Franks had spread far and wide, after King Pepin's death a different view was adopted by the public council of the Gauls. This helps to confirm what we said above: that the whole right lay in the judgement of the orders and the council. For Eginhard, in his life of Charlemagne, speaks thus: "After Pepin's death the Franks held a general assembly with due solemnity and made his two sons kings for themselves, on the condition that they should divide the whole body of the kingdom equally: Charles was to take the part which their father Pepin had held, and Carloman was to receive that which their uncle had governed." Likewise the Abbot of Urspergen: "After Pepin's death, Charles and Carloman, his sons, were both created kings with the consent of all the Franks, on the condition that they should divide the whole body of the kingdom equally." After Charlemagne's death the method of dividing the kingdom was very similar, as may be learned from his own will, as given by Johannes Naucler, and from Eginhard's little book on his life. There almost all of Europe is divided among his three sons, but no share of dowry or lawful portion is given to his daughters; the power of arranging their marriages and fixing their dowries is left to the good faith, love and prudence of their brothers. And rightly so, since the princes and nobles to whom the daughters were married were drawn to these marriages less by hope of dowry and its size than by the dignity of birth and family. Otto of Freising (Chronicle, book 6, chapter 6) and Regino (Chronicle, year 877) testify that the same partition took place in East Francia after the death of Louis in 864. Again, some years later, after the death of Louis the Stammerer, king for 23 years, in 880 the same method of division was observed. Yet this was done not by the kings themselves but by the judgement of the orders and the public council. This may easily be learned from the words of Aimoin, book 5, chapter 40: "The sons of Louis, once king of the Franks, went to Amiens, and, as their faithful men found them, divided their father's kingdom among themselves." From these arguments it is clear that in ancient times there was no fixed rule on this matter in Francogallia, but the whole power of it lay in the judgement of the orders and the public council of the people. Later, however, under Philip III, the forty-first king, it was decided on his authority that some domain should be assigned to the younger brothers. But even this law was interpreted in various ways, and many disputes arose over the position of daughters, so that nothing certain on this matter can be handed down by us, unless, if the matter is referred back to the ancient custom of our ancestors, the whole right in it is to be committed to the public council of the people and the orders, so that for the number of children fixed domains may be assigned to them, to be enjoyed for their support, their maintenance and the preservation of their dignity of birth.

units.la: De lege Salica,& iure mulierum in Regum parentum hæreditatibus. CAP. X.
units.tr: On the Salic law, and the right of women in the inheritances of kings' parents. CHAPTER X.

units.la: QVoniam de Regalis hereditatis iure dicere instituimus, non prætermittenda legis Salicæ commemoratio videtur: quæ cùm assiduè nostris hominibus in ore est, tum verò Maiorum nostrorum memoria maximam & periculosam de regni successione contentionē sedauit. Nam cùm anno 1328. rex Carolus Pulcher, Philippi Pulchri filius moriens vxoré prægnantem reliquisset, paucis intermissis mensibus agnata filia, Eduardus Angliæ Rex, ex Isabella Philippi Pulchri filia Caroli Regis sorore natus, hereditate auiti regni ad se pertinere contendit. At ex aduerso Philippus Valesius exortus est, Regis Caroli Pulcri frater patruelis, qui diceret, antiquam esse legem Regiam, Salicam nominatam, qua lege mulieres à Regni hæreditate tam, qua lege mulieres à Regni hæreditate arcerentur. Hanc porro legem Gaguinus & eiusdem generis scriptores à Faramundo scriptam tradunt: ad nostram, inquit, vsque ætatem nominatiffimam. Et in vita Philippi Valefij, Eduardo, inquit, obstabat lex Salica, quæ à Pharamundo Francis data in illos vsque dies obseruantiffima habebatur. Ea lege foli virilis sexus Reges à maioribus Regibus orti regnum administrant: nec ad eam dignitatem fœminæ admittuntur. cuius legis hæc sententia est. Nulla hereditatis portio de terra Salica ad mulierem venito. Terram autem Salicam, Francorum Iureconfulti eam dicunt, quæ solius Regis est: & à lege Alodij distat, quæ subditos comprehendit: quibus datur per hanc legem rei alicuius liberum dominium, non exclusa Principis maiestate. Hæc Gaguinus. In eandem autem sententiam Francogalli omnes non modò Historici, verumetiam Iurisconsulti & Pragmatici vsque ad hoc tempus scripserunt: teste Paponio Areft, lib. 4. cap. 1. vt iam communis error propemodum ius fecisse videatur. Verùm illud meminisse oportet, quod superiùs attigimus, Francorum duas sedes, duoque regna fuisse. Vnum in Gallia, quod ad hunc vsque diem permansit: alterum vltra Rhenum, ad flumen Salam, vnde Salij & Salici Franci coniunctè, plerunque autem Salici præcisè appellati, quorum & regnū & iam prope nomen obsoletum est. De Salijs superiùs ex Marc. Ammia. historia dictum est, demonstratumque illos Orientales, hos Occidentales appellatos fuisse. Quemadmodum autem duo Francorum regna fuerunt, ita duæ Francorum leges: Salica, quæ ad Salios: Francica, quæ ad Francogallos pertinebat. Eguinarth. in Carolo Magno: Post suscepturn Imperiale nomen, cùm animaduerteret multa legib. populi sui deesse (Nam Franci duas habent leges plurimis in locis valde diuersas) cogitauit quæ deerant addere. Auctor præfationis in Legem Salicam: Gens Francorum inclita, antequam ad fidem catholicam conuerteretur, dictauit Salicam legem per Proceres ipsius gentis, qui tùc temporis apud eandem erant rectores. Sunt autem electi de pluribus viri quatuor, Wisogast, Arbogast, Salogast, & Windogast: qui per tres mallos (id est comitia) conuenientes, omnes causarum origines solicitè discurrendo, tractates de singulis, iudicium decreuerunt hoc modo, &c. Ac fere ijsdem verbis vtitur Sigebertus in Chron. anni 422. Otto Frisin. lib.4.c. pen. Leges quoque Wisigastaldo & Salagasto auctoribus ex hinc habere cœpere. Ab hoc Salagasto legem, quæ ex nomine eius Salica vsque hodie vocatur, inuentam dicunt. Hac nobilissimi Francorum, qui Salici dicuntur, adhuc vtuntur. Atque hæc quidé veteres Chronographi: ex quib. eorū errorem coargui licet, qui Salicam legem vel à sale, id est, prudentia dictam, vel corruptâ vocem tradiderunt, pro Gallicam: quo dici absurdius nihil potuit. Sed longe maiores ex eodem fonte nati sunt errores. Primùm quod creditum est,Salicam legem ad ius publicum Imperij, & hereditariæ Regni successionis pertinuille. Nam illius legis Salicæ tabulæ non multis ab hinc annis repertæ,atq; in lucem editæ sunt, ex quarum inscriptione cognoscitur, eas primū circiter ætatem Faramundi Regis scriptas editasq; fuisse: deinde omnia & Salicæ legis & Fracicæ capita non de publico Regni & Imperij iure,sed de priuato tantùm constituta fuisse. In ijs autem vnū hoc caput extat tit.62. qui inscriptus est DE ALODIS, h.e. de ijs rebus, quę non feudi, sed patrimonij iure à priuatis possidentur:quod summè notandum est. DE TERRA SALICA IN MVLIEREM, NVLLA PORTIO HEREDITATIS TRANSIT: SED HOC VIRILIS SEXVS ACQVIRIT:hoc est,filij in hereditate succedũt. SED VBI INTER NEPOTES AVT PRONEPOTES POST LONGVM TEMPVS DE ALODE TERRÆ CONTENTIO SVSCITATVR, NON PER STIRPES, SED PER CAPITA DIVIDATVR. Cuius legis similis extat apud Ripuarios tit. ⁊ 8.Itemq; apud Anglos tit.7.vbi tantū abest, vt de Regnorum hereditatib.sanciatur,vt ne ad feudorū quidem,sed tantum ad alodiorum successiones eæ leges pertineant: vt facilè illorum imperitia coarguatur, qui lege illa aut nunquã lecta, aut non intellecta affirmare ausi sunt,lege Salica cautum fuisse,ne regia potestas ad mulieres transferatur. Vtcunque fit, primùm illud constat,etsi nullum nec Salicæ, nec Francicæ legis caput extet, quo mulieres à regni hereditate arcearceantur:tamen instituta & mores gentis tanto seculorū consensu conseruatos,ac præsertim contradictorijs iudicijs confirmatos, legis scripte vim obtinere.nam Childericus 3.rege mortuo,duabus filiabus superstitib.fratri eius Clothario regnum,illis exclusis,delatū est. Rursus Chereberto quinto Rege mortuo,tribus filiabus superstitibus, Sigeberto ipsius fratri successio delata est.Itē,Gontranno Burgundiæ & Aurelię rege mortuo,non Clotildæ filiæ ipsius, sed fratri Sigeberto regnum delatum est. Constat præterea multo consideratius & cautius illos Philippi Valesij cōsiliarios ex feudali iure disputaturos fuisse, quo iure feudorum hereditates liberis posterisq; virilis sexus tantummodo deferuntur,neque ad eas mulieres admittuntur. Vbi autem in ea stirpe, in qua feudum versatur, mares defecerunt, tū ad alteram stirpē feudum reuocatur, vt illo casu acciderat. Quæ verò seuda deprauato iure ad mulieres deferuntur, ea non proprie feuda, sed feudastra potius appellāda esse, alijs libris quos de illo iure scripsimus, abunde demonstrauimus.
units.tr: Since we have undertaken to speak of the right of royal inheritance, the mention of the Salic law seems not to be passed over. This law, though it is constantly on the lips of our people, has also calmed a very great and dangerous contest over the succession to the kingdom in our ancestors' time. For when King Charles the Fair, son of Philip the Fair, died in 1328 and left his wife pregnant, after a few months had passed a daughter was born. Edward, King of England, son of Isabella, daughter of Philip the Fair and sister of King Charles, claimed by hereditary right the kingdom of his grandfather. On the other side Philip of Valois arose, the paternal cousin of King Charles the Fair, who said that there was an ancient royal law, called the Salic law, by which women were excluded from the inheritance of the kingdom.
