Gaguin and writers of his kind hand down that this law was written by Pharamond, and that it was most famous down to our own age. And in the life of Philip of Valois it is said: "The Salic law, which was given to the Franks by Pharamond and was held in the highest observance down to those days, stood in the way of Edward." By this law only kings of the male sex, born of kings, administer the kingdom, and women are not admitted to that dignity. The sense of the law is this: "No portion of inheritance from Salic land shall come to a woman." The lawyers of the Franks call Salic land that which belongs to the king alone, and it differs from the law of allods, which embraces subjects, to whom by that law the free ownership of some property is given, without excluding the majesty of the prince. So Gaguin. Indeed all the Gallic writers, not only historians but also jurists and men of practice, have written to this same effect down to the present time, as Papon the Arles writer testifies (book 4, chapter 1), so that the common error now seems almost to have become law. But we must remember what we touched on above: the Franks had two seats and two kingdoms. One was in Gaul, and that has remained to this day; the other lay beyond the Rhine, by the river Sala, whence the Salians and Salic Franks, joined together, but more often the Salic Franks alone, were called, and their kingdom and even their name is now almost obsolete. We have said above, from Marcellinus Ammianus, that the Salians were called Eastern and the others Western. But just as there were two Frankish kingdoms, so there were two Frankish laws: the Salic, which belonged to the Salians, and the Frankish, which belonged to the Franco-Gauls. Eginhard, in his life of Charlemagne: "After he had taken up the imperial title, since he noticed that many things were lacking in the laws of his people (for the Franks have two laws, very different in many places), he thought to add what was missing." The author of the preface to the Salic law: "The famous race of the Franks, before it was converted to the Catholic faith, dictated the Salic law through the nobles of that people, who at that time were its rulers. Four men were chosen from among many: Wisogast, Arbogast, Salogast and Windogast; meeting through three mallos (that is, assemblies), and carefully examining the origins of all cases, they decided each matter by judgement in this way, etc." Sigebert, in his Chronicle under the year 422, uses almost the same words. Otto of Freising (book 4, last chapter): "The laws too began to be had from here, through Wisigastald and Salagast as authors. They say that the law which is called Salic after his name, Salagast, was devised by him. The most noble Franks, who are called Salians, still use it to this day." These are the words of the older chroniclers, from which we may refute the error of those who have said that the Salic law took its name from salt, that is, prudence, or from a corrupted word "Gallic", which could not be more absurd. But far greater errors have sprung from the same source. First, it has been believed that the Salic law pertained to the public right of the empire and to the hereditary succession of the kingdom. For the tablets of that Salic law were found and published not many years ago, and from their inscription it is known that they were first written and published around the time of King Pharamond. Then, all the chapters of both the Salic and the Frankish law were established concerning private right only, not the public right of kingdom and empire. Among them there is only one chapter, title 62, which is headed CONCERNING ALLODS, that is, concerning those things which are held by private persons under the right of patrimony, not of fief; this must be carefully noted. CONCERNING SALIC LAND, NO PORTION OF INHERITANCE PASSES TO A WOMAN, BUT THE MALE SEX ACQUIRES IT: that is, sons succeed to the inheritance. BUT WHERE, AFTER A LONG TIME, A DISPUTE ARISES CONCERNING ALLODIAL LAND BETWEEN GRANDCHILDREN OR GREAT-GRANDCHILDREN, IT IS DIVIDED NOT BY STOCKS BUT BY HEADS. A similar law exists among the Ripuarians, title 58, and likewise among the Angles, title 7, where it is so far from being decreed concerning the inheritance of kingdoms that these laws do not even concern the successions of fiefs, but only those of allods; so the ignorance of those is easily refuted who have dared to affirm, on the basis of that law, either never read or not understood, that by the Salic law it was provided that royal power should not pass to women. Be that as it may, this first point is certain: although no chapter of either the Salic or the Frankish law exists by which women are excluded from the inheritance of the kingdom, nevertheless institutions and customs of the people, preserved by such a long consensus of ages and especially confirmed by contested judgements, have the force of written law. For when King Childeric III died, with two daughters surviving, the kingdom was conferred on his brother Clothar, the daughters being excluded. Again, when Chilperic V, the fifth king, died with three daughters surviving, the succession was conferred on his brother Sigebert. Likewise, when Gontran, king of Burgundy and Orléans, died, the kingdom was given not to his daughter Clotilde but to his brother Sigebert. It is further established that Philip of Valois's counsellors argued from feudal law much more prudently and cautiously, by which hereditary fiefs are passed only to children and descendants of the male sex, and women are not admitted to them. Where in the line in which the fief lies the males have failed, the fief reverts to another line, as happened in that case. But those fiefs which, through corrupted law, pass to women, ought not properly to be called fiefs but rather pseudo-fiefs; we have amply demonstrated this in other books which we have written on that law.

units.la: De iure Regalis capillitij. CAP. XI.
units.tr: On the Royal Right to Long Hair. CHAP. XI.

units.la: HOc loco non alienum videtur, aliud Maiorum nostrorum institutum commemorare,de Regio capillitio. nam memoriæ proditum est, singulare quoddā ius capillitij apud maiores nostros fuisse, vt qui Reges à populo creati,aut regio genere prognati eflent,comam alerent: eamq; à fronte discriminatam, vnguētisque delibutam, decus atque insigne regium, regiæque stirpis haberent. reliqui ciues omnes quamuis illustri loco nati, tamen capillitij ius non haberent : sed propter assiduos ( vt credi par est ) in re militari labores, raso vel detonso capite incederent: quéadmodum de Iulio Cæsare & plerisque alijs, Romanæ historiæ commemorant. Aimoin. lib. 1.cap. 4. Regem verò ceterarum more nationum Franci sibi eligentes, Faramundum solio sublimant regio: cui filius successit Clodiocrinitus. illo enim tempore Francorum Reges criniti habebantur. Item libro 3. capite 6 1. Hic Gundoaldus more Regū à matre sua enutritus ( vti consuetudo antiquis fuit Franciæ Regibus) capitis comam gerebat profusam. Similiter Agathius lib. de bell.Goth. 1.vbi Regem Francorum Clodomirum à Burgundionibus in bello captum commemorat: Vt primum, inquit,ex equo lapsus est, Burgundiones conspicati capillitium, quod illi à tergo propendebat,ducem esse hostium animaduerterunt. Neq; .n. Francorum regib.coma carere licet: sed à pueris intonsi permanent, & profusum capillitium, atque in tergum reiectum habent. Quinetiam multis ex locis licet animaduertere, maioribus nostris in more fuisse,vt si cui vel Regnum abrogarent, vel adipiscendi Regni spem adimerent, ei capillitium abscinderent. Aimoinus illo eodem loco: Ille intuitus in eum, incidi eius precepit capillos, hunc suum negans filium fuisse. Item: Iterum incisis crinibus Coloniæ in custodiam traditur: unde suga elapsus succrescentibus capillis, ad Narlete- m transiens, &c. quam histor. Gregor. Turonen. lib. 6. cap. 24. commemorat. Item cap. 44. ubi de Thedorico Rege loquitur: Franci, inquit, super eum consurgunt, ac eum de regno ejiciunt, crinesque capitis eius vi abstrahentes incidunt. Item lib. 7. cap. 36. Tu ne es ille, qui plerumq; à regibus Francorum propter has præsumptiones quas profers, tonsoratus, & exilio datus es? Et mox: Quod me Chlotarius pater meus exosum habuerit, nulli est incognitum: quod autem ab eo, & deinceps à fratribus sim tonsoratus, manifestum est omnibus. Memorabilis autem ac potius horribilis historia extat apud Gregor. Turonen. de Regina matre Chrotilde, quæ duobus nepotibus caput abscindi, quàm comam maluit. Locus est lib. 3. capite 18. Mater nostra (inquibat Rex fratri suo) fratris nostri filios secum retinuit, & vult eos regno donari. Communi consilio pertractare oportet, quid de his fieri debeat: vtrùm incisa cæsarie, vt reliqua plebs habeantur: an his interfectis regnum germani nostri inter nos diuidatur. Et mox: Tunc miserè Archadium cum forcipe, atque euaginato gladio: qui veniens ostendit Reginæ vtrunque, dicens: Voluntatem tuam, ô gloriosissima Regina, filij tui domini nostri ex-
units.tr: Here it seems not out of place to mention another custom of our ancestors, concerning the royal long hair. For it is recorded that among our forefathers there was a peculiar right of hair: those who were created kings by the people, or were born of royal stock, let their hair grow, parted at the forehead and anointed with perfumed oils, and so had the adornment and mark of royalty and of the royal line. All the other citizens, however noble their birth, had no right to long hair but went with their heads shaved or cropped, presumably because of their constant labours in war, as the Roman histories tell of Julius Caesar and many others. Aimoin, book 1, chapter 4. The Franks, however, following the custom of the other nations, chose a king for themselves and raised Pharamond to the royal throne; his son Clodion succeeded him, for in that period the kings of the Franks were regarded as long-haired. Likewise book 3, chapter 6: "This Gundoald, reared by his mother in the manner of kings (as was the custom of the ancient kings of France), wore his hair long and flowing." Similarly Agathias, book 1 of the Gothic War, where he relates that King Clodomir of the Franks was captured by the Burgundians in battle: "As soon as he fell from his horse," he says, "the Burgundians, seeing the hair that hung down his back, recognised that he was the leader of the enemy." For the kings of the Franks may not lack long hair; from boyhood they remain unshorn and wear their hair flowing and thrown back. Indeed, in many places one may observe that it was the custom among our forefathers that if anyone was to be deprived of his kingdom or of the hope of obtaining it, his hair was cut off. Aimoin in the same place: "He looked at him and ordered his hair to be cut, denying that he was his son." Again: "With his hair cut a second time he was handed over to custody at Cologne; from there he escaped and, when his hair had grown back, passed to Narbonne," and so on, as Gregory of Tours relates, book 6, chapter 24. Also chapter 44, where he speaks of King Theuderic: "The Franks," he says, "rose up against him, drove him from the kingdom, and forcibly tore off and cut his hair." Also book 7, chapter 36: "Are you not the man who was often shorn and sent into exile by the kings of the Franks because of the presumptions you put forward?" And soon after: "That Chlothar my father hated me is known to no one; but that I was afterwards shorn by him and then by my brothers is plain to everyone." There is also a memorable, or rather horrifying, story in Gregory of Tours about Queen Mother Chrotilde, who preferred that the heads of her two grandsons be cut off rather than their hair. The passage is in book 3, chapter 18: "Our mother," said the king to his brother, "has kept our brother's sons with her and wishes them to be given the kingdom. We must consider together what ought to be done with them: whether they should be shorn, so that they may be counted as the common people, or whether, with them killed, our brother's kingdom should be divided between us." And soon after: "Then Archadius, wretched man, came with shears and a drawn sword, and showing both boys to the queen, said: 'Your will, most glorious queen, your sons, our lords, request...'" The sentence continues in what follows, as to what you think should be done with the boys: whether you order them to live with their hair cut, or both to be throttled. But she preferred to see them dead rather than shorn. Aimoin relates this story in book 2, chapter 12, introducing Chrotilde as speaking thus: "But however the matter stands..."

units.la: F petunt, quid de pueris agendum censeas: vtrũ incisis crinibus eos viuere iubeas, an vtrumque iugulari. Maluit autem illa interfectos videre, quàm tonsos. Quam historiam Aimoinus lib. 2, cap. 12. enarrans, Chrotildem ita loquentem inducit: Sed vtcunque se res habeat, nullatenus clericos fieri patiar. quasi ad clericatum tonsura puerorũ quæreretur. Quod cum à Gregorij verbis alienum est, tum etiam ab illa consuetudine vsitata, vt tonsura quasi abdicatio, & à regni hereditate exclusio quædam esset. Quin etiam moris fuisse animaduerto, vt cùm Reges prælio decertarent, nodatum cápillitium in galeam, quasi cristam erigerent: idque insigne in prælijs haberent. Itaque Aimoinus libro quarto, capite 18. vbi de Dagoberti Regis, cum Bertoaldo Saxonum Duce acerrimo, prælio commemorat: Rex, inquit, ense percussus in caput, decisos cum parte galeæ crines patri per armigerum mittit, vt sibi in auxilium properet. Huius autem instituti causam cùm apud me considero, hanc ferè reperio, quòd cùm & Gallorum & Francorum nationes comatæ essent (item vt Sicambrorum, ac ferè regionum illarum institutum fuisse constat) Maioribus nostris visum est, hoc proprium Regiæ dignitati decus atque insigne tribuere. Nam de Gallis quidem (vnde Comata Gallia dicta est) nemo mediocriter eruditus testimonium quærit: memor præsertim illius Claudiani ex lib. in Ruffinum 2. Inde truces flauo comitantur vertice Galli, Quos Rhodanus velox, Araris quos tardior abit, Et quos nascentes explorat gurgite Rhenus.
units.tr: ...what you think should be done with the boys: whether you order them to live with their hair cut, or whether both are to be slain. She preferred to see them killed rather than shorn. Aimoin, in book 2, chapter 12, retelling this story, introduces Chrotilde speaking thus: "However the matter stands, I shall by no means allow them to be made clerics," as if the tonsure were sought for the boys in order to enter the clergy. This is foreign both to Gregory's words and to that usual custom by which the tonsure was a kind of renunciation and a certain exclusion from the inheritance of the kingdom. Moreover, I observe that it was also the custom that when kings fought in battle they tied their hair into a knot on their helmet, as if raising a crest, and used this as a badge in battles. So Aimoin, book 4, chapter 18, where he records the battle of King Dagobert with Bertoald, a most fierce duke of the Saxons: "The king, struck on the head with a sword, sent his hair, cut off along with part of the helmet, to his father through an armour-bearer, so that he might hasten to his aid." Now when I consider the reason for this custom, I find it is mostly this: since both the Gallic and the Frankish peoples were long-haired (as it is established that the custom also prevailed among the Sicambri and nearly all those regions), it seemed fitting to our ancestors to bestow on royal dignity this distinction and badge as its own. For as to the Gauls (whence Gaul was called "long-haired"), no one of moderate learning needs to seek testimony, especially if he remembers that passage of Claudian from the second book against Rufinus: Inde truces flauo comitantur vertice Galli, Quos Rhodanus velox, Araris quos tardior abit, Et quos nascentes explorat gurgite Rhenus.

units.la: De Francis autem, quos ex Chaucis, siue Chaycis ortos demonstrauimus, vel vnus ille ex Lucani primo locus, testimonio esse potest:
units.tr: As for the Franks, whom we have shown to be descended from the Chauci, or Chaycians, that single passage from the first book of Lucan can serve as testimony:

units.la: Et vos crinigeros bellis arcere Chaycos Oppositi petitis Romam, &c.
units.tr: Et vos crinigeros bellis arcere Chaycos Oppositi petitis Romam, &c.

units.la: Quod cùm ita esset, animaduertimus, exteros qui animo in nostros inimico essent, reges capillatos, non modò contumelioso nomine Setatos appellasse: verùm cùm setæ leonum, equorum, & suum communes essent, (qui omnes propterea Setosi & Setigeri appellantur) etiam ad suillas setas nominis contumeliâ produxisse. Vnde & obscœna conficta fabula, & spurcû nomè <bl>τριχοεχάτων</bl>: de quo Georg. Cedrenus in histor. ita scribit: <bl>ἐλέγοντο δὲ οἱ ἐκ τῆς γένυς ἐκείνης καταγόμενοι κρισάτοι. ὁ ἐμψωνεύεται</bl> <bl>τριχοεχάτοι. εἶχον γὰρ κατὰ τὰς ῥάχεως αὐτῶν τρίχας ἀνφυομένας, ὡς χοῖροι</bl>: id est, qui regio erant prognati genere, dicebantur Cristati: quod interpretatur, Tergiferosi. Habebant enim in spina dorsi pilos enascentes, quasi porci. Quem tamen locum mendosum, ac depravatum esse arbitror: ac pro <bl>ΚΡΙΣΤΑΤΟΙ</bl> vel reponendum <bl>ΣΕΤΑΤΟΙ</bl>, vel utrunque certè coniungendum: vt à nonnullis festiuè Cristati, propter erectû in galea criniû flocculû: à maleuolis etiam cotumeliosè Setati, vel Setigeri appellaretur. Quod si clausula illatâ aperte Cedrenus non apposuisset, & Criftatorû nomen retinendum fuisset, dicendi potius τριχοχάραχτοι fuissent: vt cuiuis perspicuum esse arbitror: pro, Crinibus insignes. quanquam totũ illum Cedreni locum animaduerti iam ab auctore Hiftorię Miscellæ ad verbum ita conuersum, lib. xxii. Dicebantur sane ex genere illo descendere Cristati: quod interpretatur Trichorachati.pilos.n. habebát natos in spina, veluti porci. Vtcunque fit, ne illud quidem prætermittendum videtur, circiter Caroli Magni ætatem,consuetudinem quandam increbuiffe, vt regis filius ad exterum aliquem principem amicum ac fœderatum mitteretur, qui honoris caussa capillos ei præcideret: eoque facto Pater ipsius honorarius diceretur. Nam Paul.Diaconus libro sexto,capite decimoquinto, de Carolo Magno scribens: Carolus, inquit, Francorũ princeps filium suum ad Liutprandum Longobardorum regem misit, vt eius, iuxta morem, capillum susciperet. qui eius cæsariem incidens, ei pater effectus est: multisque regijs muneribus donatum genitori remisit. quam historiam Regino libro primo, sub anno DCLV. commemorat:apud quem prosvsciperet commodius legi videretur,INCIDERET. Verùm hæc quidẽ de regalis capillitij iure, hactenus. Quod verò nonnulli fabulantur, regnante Ludouico vii. Petri Lombardi Parifienfis Episcopi confilio atq; hortatu institutum fuisse, vt discrimen inter Gallos & Francos tolleretur, cum illi comam tantum,hi & comam & barbam colerét: indignum hominibus doctis videtur. quasi vero per annos amplius octingentos (totidem enim à Francogallici regni origine ad Ludouicū VII. numerantur) discrimen vllum inter Gallos & Francos durarit: ac non superius demonstratum fit, post Francogalliæ regnum constitutū, vnam è duabus quasi gemellam gentem, & vnius linguæ & eorundem institutorum ac morum conflatam fuisse.
units.tr: Since this was so, we observe that foreigners who were hostile to our people called the long-haired kings not only by the insulting name of Setati, but, since the bristles of lions, horses and swine are all alike (and are therefore all called bristly and setose), they also extended the insult to the bristles of swine. Hence also an obscene invented fable and a filthy name, trichoechatōn [τριχοεχάτων]. Georgius Cedrenus, in his history, writes of this thus: "Those descended from that race were called Kristatoi [κρισάτοι]; which is mocked as Trichoechatoi [τριχοεχάτοι], for they had hairs growing along the spine of their back, like pigs [ὡς χοῖροι]." That is, those who were born of royal stock were called Cristati, which is interpreted as "bristly-backed." For they had hairs growing on the backbone, like pigs. I think, however, that this passage is corrupt and faulty, and that instead of KRISTATOI either SETATOI should be restored, or certainly both should be joined together, so that by some they were called Cristati playfully, on account of the little tuft of hair standing up on the helmet, and by the malicious, insultingly, Setati or Setigeri. And if Cedrenus had not clearly added the clause that follows, and if the name Cristati had to be kept, they would more properly have been called trichocharaktoi [τριχοχάραχτοι], "distinguished by their hair," as I think is clear to anyone. Yet I have noticed that this whole passage of Cedrenus was already rendered word for word by the author of the Historia Miscella, book 22: "Indeed the Cristati were said to be descended from that race, which is interpreted Trichorachati; for they had hairs growing on the spine, like pigs." However that may be, it does not seem right to pass over this as well: about the time of Charlemagn, a certain custom grew up whereby a king's son was sent to some foreign prince who was a friend and ally, and he cut the boy's hair as a mark of honour, and by this act that prince was called the boy's honorary father. For Paul the Deacon, writing of Charlemagne in book 6, chapter 15, says: "Charles, prince of the Franks, sent his son to Liutprand, king of the Lombards, so that, according to custom, he might receive his hair; who, cutting his long hair, became his father, and sent him back to his parent, given many royal gifts." Regino records this same story in book 1, under the year 755, where the word "suscipere" would seem to read more suitably as "INCIDERET" (cut). But this, so far, concerns the law of the royal hair. As for what some fable, namely that under King Louis VII, on the advice and urging of Peter Lombard, Bishop of Paris, it was instituted so that the difference between the Gauls and the Franks might be removed, since the former wore only the hair while the latter wore both hair and beard, this seems unworthy of learned men. As if indeed any difference between the Gauls and the Franks had endured for more than eight hundred years (for so many are counted from the origin of the Gallo-Frankish kingdom down to Louis VII), and as if it had not been demonstrated above that, after the kingdom of Francogallia was established, the two peoples, like twins, became one nation, formed from one language and the same institutions and customs.

units.la: Qualis regni Francogallici constituendi forma fuerit.
units.tr: On what the form of the constitution of the Franco-Gallic kingdom was.

units.la: HIs ita breuiter expositis, deinceps qualis regni Francogallici constituendi forma fuerit, exponendū videtur. Ac superius quidem populū in comitijs nō modò creandi, verūetiā abdicandi regis potestatē sibi omnē retinuisse, docuimus. Quam eandē regnandi formā constat Gallos nostros, priusquam in Romanorum potestatem redigerentur, habuisse: vt populus non minus (inquit Cæsar) in regem, quàm rex in populū imperij ac potestatis retineret. Quanquam non à Gallis, sed à popularibus suis Germanis eam Reip. constituendæ formam Francos nostros sumpsisse, consentaneum est: de quibus Tacitus in lib. de moribus Germ. ita scribit: Regibus non est infinita aut libera potestas. Hac autem forma nullam à tyrannico dominatu remotiorem esse constat. Nam vt ait Aristoteles lib. Polit. v. cap. xi. quanto pauciorum rerū penes Regé potestas est, tantò diutius regnū maneat necesse est. Quinetiā è trib. tyrannidis notis, quas philosophi veteres indicarunt, nullam in regni nostri forma constituenda licet animaduertere. Primùm enim quantum ad coactum imperium attinet, hoc est, vt rex inuitis dominetur, docuimus iam antea, summam ordinum publicíque Concilij tum in deligendis, tum in abdicandis regibus potestatem suisse. Quantum ad peregrinam corporis custodiam, quam secundam tyrannidis notam numerant, tantum abest, vt Francogalliæ reges peregrinis & alienigenis mercenarijs ad præsidiariam cohortem vterentur, vt plerunque ne ciues quidem & indigenas ad corporis custodiam adhiberent. quippe, cum omnem in clientum suorum fide & beneuolentia præsidij sui fiduciam collocarent. Cuius rei argumento est, quod Gregor. Turon. lib. 7. capite 18. & Aimoinus libro tertio, cap. 63. scribunt, regem Gontrannum ab homine quodam tenui Lutetiæ admonitum, vt insidias sibi à Faraulpho paratas vitaret: continuò se armis & custodijs muniuisse: vt nusquam, inquit Gregorius, ac ne ad loca quidem sacra, nisi vallatus armatis atque custodibus procederet. Quinetiam extat Ludouici cognomento Diui præclara historia, & ab illustri viro Ioanne Ionuillæo scripta, qui cum illo rege perfamiliariter multos annos versatus est: qua in historia nullam planè satellitum, aut stipatorum, aut præsidiariæ
units.tr: Having set out these matters briefly, it seems right next to explain what form was given to the constitution of the Frankish kingdom. Earlier we showed that the people, in their assemblies, kept for themselves the entire power not only of creating the king but also of deposing him. It is well established that our Gauls had this same form of government before they were brought under the power of the Romans, so that the people, no less (as Caesar says) than the king, retained authority and power over the other. Although it is likely that our Franks took this form of constituting the commonwealth not from the Gauls but from their German kinsmen, Tacitus writes of them in his book on the customs of the Germans: "The power of kings is neither unlimited nor free." It is established that no form of government is further removed from tyrannical domination than this one. For, as Aristotle says in the fifth book of the Politics, chapter 11, the fewer the things over which a king's power extends, the longer the kingdom must necessarily last. Moreover, of the three marks of tyranny which the ancient philosophers pointed out, none can be discerned in the form of our kingdom. First, as far as forced rule is concerned, that is, a king ruling over unwilling subjects, we have shown above that the supreme power of choosing and of deposing kings lay with the orders and the public council. As for a foreign bodyguard, which they count as the second mark of tyranny, the Frankish kings were so far from using foreign and alien mercenaries as a garrison that they generally did not even employ citizens and natives as bodyguards, since they placed all confidence in their protection in the loyalty and goodwill of their clients. Evidence of this is that Gregory of Tours (book 7, chapter 18) and Aimoin (book 3, chapter 63) write that King Guntram, warned at Paris by a certain humble man to avoid the plots laid against him by Faraulf, at once fortified himself with arms and guards, so that, as Gregory says, he never went anywhere, not even to sacred places, unless surrounded by armed men and guards. Moreover, there is the famous history of Louis, surnamed the Saint, written by the illustrious man John of Joinville, who lived on very intimate terms with that king for many years. In that history one can find no mention at all of satellites, attendants or a bodyguard, but only of doorkeepers, whom he calls, in the vernacular, huissiers, that is, hostiarii.

units.la: pria riæ cohortis mentionem licet animaduertere: sed tantum Ianitorum, quos populari lingua Huiserios, id est, Hostiarios, appellat. Verùm, quid hæc tenuia & minuta diluci-dæ rei argumenta conquirimus? cùm perspicuum eius documentum extet, apud Wilhelmum Neunbrigensem, libro Rerum Anglicarum 4. capite 2. quod iccirco subscribemus, ne tam insignis Maiorum nostrorum sapientiæ memoria intercidat: & canibus aulicis, qui nobis antehac allatrarunt, ora obturemus. Scribit autem Neunbrigensis de rege Philippo, Ludouici filio, qui cum Richardo Anglorum rege ad recuperandas Hierosolymas profectus est: circiter annum mcxc. Sanè, inquit, postquam percrebuit apud regem Francorum quod Marchioni acciderat, de amici quidem indigno exitu doluit: sed mox hunc dolorem suscepta cum ingenti gaudio suggillandi regem Anglorum occasio compensauit. Cumque in proprijs esset tam longe finibus à Syria constitutus, illius in Oriente consistentis vel frustra timebat, vel potius se ad augendam inuidiam, timere fingebat insidias: & tanquâ ab eo subornati imminerent sicarij, præter morem Maiorum suorum non nisi firmata vallatus custodia procedebat: adeo vt quidam familiari ausu propius accedentes, non sine periculo hoc ausi dicantur. Miratib. hanc nouitate regiam plurimis, vt pro ea satisfaceret, gentéq; suam in regem Anglorum accenderet, Præsulum Procerumq; suorū Concilium Parisios conuocauit. Vbi allegans contra eundem regem plurima, tanquam certa, atque inter cetera, quòd virum illum nobilissimum nequiter per diros satellites peremisset, literas quoque protulit à quibusdam potentibus sibi (vt dicebat) transmissas, quibus monebatur propensiorem suimet habere cautelam: sciens quòd rex Anglorum insidiaturus animæ suæ ab Oriente iam direxisset sicarios. Quamobrem, inquit, nemo debet mirari, quòd praeter solitum diligentiorem mei ipsius curam habeam: quam tamen si reputatis vel indecentem, vel superfluam, decernite amouendam. Adiecit etiam cordi sibi esse de manifesto proditore proprias maturè vlcisci iniurias. Adhæc plurimi adulatoriè responderunt, bonum honestúmque esse, quod pro cautela faciebat: & quod pro vltione disponebat. Prudentes vero dixerunt, Cautelam quidem tuam, Rex, qua tibi contra incertos casus forte abundantiùs prospicis, non culpamus: præmaturæ verò vltionis propositum minimè approbamus. Nam etsi vera sint quę de rege Anglorum dicuntur, non tamen est petulanter & præmature agendum: sed respectum honesti sustinendum quousq; ad propria reuertatur, qui propter Christum peregrinari noscitur. Hæc Neunbrigensis. Deinceps alteram Maiorum nostrorum in regno constituendo sapientiam consideremus. Nam quæ tertia tyrannidis nota numeratur, vt non ad civitatis & subiectorum, sed ad ipsius dominantis tis commodum atque arbitrium omnia reserātur,eius nullam in nostra Repub. maculā multas per ætates hæsisse, ex eo intelligetur quòd quod paulo posterius docebimus, summam regni Francogállici administrationem penes publicum & solenne gentis Cõcilium fuisse: quod posterior ætas Conuentum trium Statuum appellauit. Cuius appellationis rationem Claudius Seyssellus in libello quem Franciæ monarchiam inscripsit, ad tres ciuium ordines referédam putat: quorum summum nobilitati, medium iuridicis & mercatoribus, tertium opificibus & agricolis attribuit. Verba illius capit. 13. hæc fere sunt: Est in hoc regno forma quædam Reip. magnopere & laudanda & retinenda: quoniam plurimum in ea momenti est ad ordinum omnium concordiam constabiliendam: neque dubium est, quin quandiu suum cuique ordini ius suaq; dignitas seruabitur, difficile sit regnum labefactari. Nam cuiusque ordinis certa est prærogatiua: neque, ea seruata, potest alter alterum euertere: ac ne tres quidem simul in Principem & Monarcham conspirare possunt. Horum porrò in ordinum trium numerum nequaquam repono Ecclesiasticos: qui per illos permixti sunt: sed tres status siue ordines numero, primùm Nobilitatem: tum medium populum, qui dici Opimus potest: postremò plebem infimam. Hæc Seyssellus. Sed videamus, ne cùm hæc tripartita distributio non ad vitæ communis rationem, sed ad publicum gentis Concilium referatur (qua de causa Concilium illud vulgo Trium statuum appellatur) ecquid commodius, ad illa tria genera referri possit, quibus id Concilium constat: hoc est, ad regalem, optimatum & popularem: quippe, cum huius regni status is fuerit, quem Philosophi veteres, (in his Plato & Aristoteles, quos Polybius & Tullius imitati sunt) optimum ac praestantissimum iudicarunt: nimirum qui e tribus generibus Regali, Optimatum, & Populari mixtus ac temperatus esset: quam Reipub. formam idem Tullius in suis de Repub. libris unam ex omnibus potissimam esse duxit. Nam cum regius & popularis dominatus natura inter se dissideant, adhiberi tertium aliquem oportet intermedium, & utriusque communem, qui est Principum, sive Optimatum: qui propter splendorem & antiquitatem generis, ad regiam dignitatem accedit: propter clientelam, & (ut vulgo loquimur) subiectionem a plebeio genere minus abhorret. Unum enim eundemque cum plebe populi universi Magistrum agnoscunt. Huius autem praeclari Reipub. status insignis extat Ciceronis laudatio, ex Platonis de Repub. libris expressa, quam propter singularem elegantiam subscribemus: Ut in fidibus, inquit, ac tibijs, atque cantu ipso, ac vocibus concentus est quidam tenendus ex distinctis sonis, quem immutatum ac discrepantem aures erudite ferre non possunt: isque concentus ex dissimillimarum vocum moderatione concors tamen efficitur, & congruens: sic ex summis, & medijs, & infimis & interiectis ordinibus, ut sonis, moderata ratione ciuitas, consensu dissimillimorum concinit: & quæ harmonia à musicis dicitur in cantu, ea est in ciuitate concordia: arctissimum atque optimum in Republica vinculum incolumitatis, quæ sine iustitia nullo pacto esse potest. Hæc Cicero, de Optimo Reip. statu: quem ex tribus permixtis generibus temperatū, Maiores nostri in Francogalliæ regno constituēdo tenuerūt, quod cum alijs argumentis demonstrari potest, tum vero vel maximè ex Oratione Regis Ludouici cognomento Pij, ad omnes Francogalliæ ordines habita: & ab Anfegilo in lib. Franc. leg. secundū relata, cuius ca. 3. verba hęc extant: Sed quanquā summa huius ministerij Regij in nostra persona cōsistere videatur: tamen & diuina auctoritate, & humana ordinatione ita per partes diuisum esse cognoscitur, ut vnufquifq; vestrum in suo loco & ordine parte nostri ministerij habere cognoscatur. vnde apparet, quod nimirum vestrum admonitor esse debeo: & omnes vos nostri adiutores esse debetis. nec enim ignoramus, quid vnicuique veftrum in sibi commissa portione conueniat. Itę c. 12. Et sicut diximus, vnusquisq; vestrum parte ministerij nostri per partes habere dignoscitur. Item cap. 6. Monemus vestram fidelitatem, vt memores sitis fidei nobis pmissæ, & in parte ministerij vestri vobis cōmissi. Hæc igitur mixtam tribus generibus Reipub. temperationem Maiores nostri secuti, sapientissimè constituerunt, vt quotannis publicum totius regni Concilium Kalendis Maij haberetur: quo in Concilio de summis quibusque Reip. negotijs communi ordinum omnium consilio ageretur: sic, vt vetus illa aurea lex valeret: SALVS POPVLI SVPREMA LEX ESTO. Cuius instituti sapientia & vtilitas tribus maximè reb. cernitur. primùm quòd in magno prudentium numero magnitudo cõfilij ac propterea salus populi versatur: vt Salomoni & alijs sapientibus placuit. deinde quia libertatis pars est, quorum periculo res geritur, vt illa eorum consilio atque auctoritate administretur: &, quemadmodum Imp. Iustinianus dixit, quod omnes tangit, ab omnibus approbetur. postremò vt qui apud regem in magna potentia sunt, & magnis imperijs præsunt, eius Concilij metu, in quo Ciuitatum postulata liberè audiuntur, in officio contineantur. Nam quòd regna quædam vnius regis arbitrio ac nutu gubernantur, quale hodie Turcicum esse cõstat, rectissimè Ariftoteles lib. Polit. 3. animaduertit, non hominum liberorum & lumine mentis ac rationis vtentium, sed pecudum potius & brutorum cõfilij expertium eam gubernationem esse. Sic enim fe res habet: vt pecudes, non ab vno è suo genere: vt pueri aut adolescentes, non ab vno è suis æqualibus, sed à præftantiore aliquo reguntur: sic hominum multitudo non ab vno è suo numero, qui minus fortasse,
units.tr: of a praetorian cohort. But why do we gather these slight and trivial proofs to clarify the matter, when a clear document of it survives in William of Newburgh, book 4 of his History of English Affairs, chapter 2? We shall set it down in full, so that the memory of such notable wisdom of our ancestors does not perish, and so that we may silence the courtly curs who have barked at us before now. Newburgh writes of King Philip, son of Louis, who set out with Richard, king of the English, to recover Jerusalem, around the year 1190. Indeed, he says, once it became widely known among the King of the Franks what had happened to the Marquis, he grieved at the unworthy end of his friend; but soon he made up for this grief by the great joy of seizing an opportunity to disgrace the King of the English. And although he was situated in his own territory so far from Syria, he feared, or rather pretended to fear, the plots of that king who was stationed in the East, in order to increase hatred of him; and, as if hired assassins were threatening him at the other king's bidding, contrary to the custom of his ancestors he went out only when surrounded by a strongly fortified guard, so much so that some who approached him too boldly are said to have done so at risk to themselves. Many were astonished at this novelty, and in order to answer for it, and to stir his people against the King of the English, he summoned a council of his bishops and nobles to Paris. There, arguing against the same king many things as if they were certain, and among other things that he had wickedly slain that most noble man by means of dire attendants, he also produced letters which had been sent to him (as he said) by certain powerful men, warning him to take greater care of himself, since the King of the English, knowing that he was about to lay snares for his life, had already sent assassins from the East. Therefore, he said, no one should wonder that he takes more careful thought for himself than usual; yet if you judge this to be unbecoming or excessive, decide that it should be dropped. He added that it was his heart's desire to avenge his own wrongs promptly on a manifest traitor. Then many replied with flattery that what he did for caution was good and honourable, and what he planned for revenge as well. But the wise said: "Your caution, O King, by which you perhaps look ahead more than enough against uncertain chances, we do not blame; but the purpose of hasty vengeance we by no means approve. For even if what is said about the King of the English is true, it must not be done wantonly and hastily, but regard for what is honourable must be maintained until he returns to his own land, he who is known to be wandering abroad for Christ's sake." This is Newburgh. Next let us consider the second wisdom of our ancestors in constituting the kingdom. As for the third mark of tyranny, which is counted as this: that everything is referred not to the advantage and will of the state and its subjects, but to the convenience and arbitrary will of the ruler himself, it will be understood from this that no stain of this kind stuck to our commonwealth through many ages, since, as we shall show a little later, the supreme administration of the Frankish kingdom lay with the public and solemn council of the nation, which later ages called the Assembly of the Three Estates. Claudius de Seyssel, in the little book which he entitled The Monarchy of France, thinks that the reason for this name is to be referred to the three orders of the citizens: he assigns the highest to the nobility, the middle to lawyers and merchants, and the third to craftsmen and farmers. His words in chapter 13 are roughly these: "In this kingdom there is a certain form of commonwealth which is greatly to be praised and retained, since it has the greatest weight in establishing the concord of all the orders; and there is no doubt that as long as each order keeps its right and its dignity, it will be difficult for the kingdom to be overthrown. For each order has its certain prerogative, and while it is preserved, one cannot overturn another; nor can all three together conspire against the Prince and the Monarch. Moreover, I by no means count the ecclesiastics among these three orders, since they are mingled among them; but I count three estates or orders by number: first the nobility, then the middle people, who may be called the well-to-do, and lastly the lowest common people." This is Seyssel. But let us see whether, since this tripartite division is referred not to the way of common life but to the public council of the nation (for which reason that council is commonly called the Assembly of the Three Estates), anything could be more fittingly referred to those three kinds of which that council consists: that is, the royal, the aristocratic and the popular. For the state of this kingdom was of that kind which the ancient philosophers (among them Plato and Aristotle, whom Polybius and Tully imitated) judged to be the best and most excellent, namely that which is mixed and tempered from the three kinds, royal, aristocratic and popular. Tully, in his books on the Commonwealth, judged this form of commonwealth to be the most powerful of all. For since royal and popular rule are naturally at odds with each other, some third intermediate power must be admitted, common to both, which is that of the princes or nobles: this rises to royal dignity by its splendour and antiquity, and by its clientage and, as we say in common speech, its subjection, it shrinks less from the plebeian kind. For they acknowledge one and the same master with the common people of the whole nation. Of this excellent kind of commonwealth there is a notable praise by Cicero, drawn from Plato's books on the Commonwealth, which, because of its singular elegance, we shall set down: "As in lyres and flutes, and in song itself and in voices, a certain harmony must be kept from distinct sounds, which trained ears cannot bear if it is altered and discordant; and this harmony, through the moderation of the most unlike voices, is nonetheless made agreeable and consonant; so from the highest, the middle, the lowest and the intermediate orders, as from sounds, a city, by moderate reason, harmonises through the agreement of the most unlike parts; and what musicians call harmony in song, that is concord in the state, the tightest and best bond of the commonwealth's safety, which can in no way exist without justice." This is Cicero, on the best state of the commonwealth, which our ancestors held to be tempered from three mixed kinds when they constituted the kingdom of France. This can be shown both by other arguments and above all by the speech of King Louis, surnamed the Pious, delivered to all the orders of France, and reported by Ansegisus in the book of the Frankish laws, book 2; chapter 3 of which contains these words: "But although the chief power of this royal office seems to reside in our person, yet it is recognised to be divided by divine authority and human ordinance into parts, so that each of you is known to have a part of our office in his own place and order. Whence it is evident that I ought indeed to be your admonisher, and that you all ought to be our helpers. For we are not ignorant of what befits each of you in the portion committed to him." Likewise chapter 12: "And as we have said, each of you is known to hold a part of our ministry in parts." Again chapter 6: "We admonish your loyalty, that you be mindful of the faith pledged to us, and of the part of your ministry committed to you." Our ancestors, therefore, following this mixed temperament of the commonwealth from three kinds, wisely arranged that a public council of the whole kingdom should be held every year on the first of May; in this council the highest affairs of the commonwealth were transacted by the common counsel of all the orders, so that that ancient golden law held good: THE SAFETY OF THE PEOPLE IS THE SUPREME LAW. The wisdom and usefulness of this institution are seen chiefly in three things. First, because the greatness of counsel, and therefore the safety of the people, lies in a large number of wise men, as it pleased Solomon and other sages. Second, because it is part of liberty that affairs be conducted at the risk of those whom they concern, so that they be administered by their counsel and authority; and, as the Emperor Justinian said, what touches all should be approved by all. Last, so that those who are in great power with the king and command great authorities may be kept in their duty by fear of that council, in which the demands of the cities are freely heard. For that some kingdoms are governed by the will and nod of one king alone, as the Turkish realm is today, Aristotle rightly observes in the third book of the Politics, that this is not the government of free men who use the light of mind and reason, but rather of cattle and brutes that lack counsel. For the matter stands thus: cattle are not ruled by one of their own kind, nor boys or youths by one of their equals, but by some superior; so a multitude of men must be ruled and governed not by one of their own number, who perhaps sees less than many others, but by a mind formed from many, that is, by the joined counsels of approved men.

units.la: Prouerb. II. & 15. fortasse, quàm alij complures, videret: sed à méte ex multis conflata, hoc est, coniunctis probatorum virorum consilijs, regeda & gubernanda est. Nam quòd Senatum assiduum & ordinarium plerique habent reges, cuius consilio in administranda Repub. sese vti dicunt: primùm aliud est regni, aliud regis consiliarium esse. Ille Reipub. vniuersæ, & in commune consulit: hic vnius hominis commodis atque vtilitatibus seruit. Deinde cum illi Senatores assidui vel vno in loco, vel certè in aula Principis perpetuò maneant, longinquarum ciuitatum nosse ac videre statum commodè non possunt. Præterea regalis & aulicæ vitæ illecebris inducti, facilè ad libidinem dominandi, ad ambitionem, & opes amplificandas deprauantur: vt ad extremum non regni, & Reip. consiliarij, sed regis vnius assentatores, & ministri cupiditatum & regiarum, & suarum quoque appareant. Qua de re extat insigne Imp. Aureliani elogium apud Fl. Vopiscum, quod subscribemus: Ego (inquit) à patre meo audiui, Diocletianum principem, iam priuatum dixisse, nihil esse difficilius, quàm bene imperare. Colligunt se quatuor vel quinque; atque vnum consilium ad decipiendum Imperatorem capiunt: dicunt quid probandum sit. Imperator qui domi clausus est, vera non nouit. cogitur hoc tantùm scire, quod illi loquuntur. Facit iudices, quos fieri non oportet. Amouet à Repub. quos debebat retinere. quid multa? vt Diocletianus ipse dicebat, Bonus, cautus, optimus venditur Imperator. Hactenus Vopiscus: apud quem tamen haud scio, an non rectius incautus legeretur. Vtcunque sit, haec incommoda veteres Romani metuentes, Regi quidem Senatum ordinarium attribuerunt: sed, vt salus populi suprema lex esset, summam Reip. non regi, aut eius senatui, sed ipsi populo & comitijs referuarunt. Quare sub omnibus regibus haec lex fuit: Vt populus in comitijs magistratus crearet, leges scisceret, bella decerneret: quemadmodum Dionysius Halic. lib. 2. testatur. Pomponius quidem iurisconsultus memoriae prodidit, populum R. primis temporibus in triginta partes diuisum, quae Curiae dictae sunt: propterea quod rex Reipublicae curam (vt ipse ait) per sententias partium earum expediebat, unde leges Curiatae dictae, & antiquissima omnium comitia, Curiata. quinetiam Seneca libro Epistol. decimonono scribit, se ex Ciceronis de Republica libris dedicisse, PROVOCATIONEM AD POPVLVM ETIAM A REGIBVS FVISSE. quod etiā Tullius initio libri Tusculanarum disputationum iv. his demonstrat verbis: Nam cum a primo vrbis ortu regijs institutis, partim etiam legibus, auspicia, cerimoniae, comitia, prouocationes, & cetera tota res militaris diuinitus esset constituta, &c. Sed & in Oratione quam pro domo sua habuit: Nego, inquit potuisse iure publico, legibus ijs quibus haec ciuitas vtitur, quenquam ciuem vlla eiusmodi calamitate affici sine iudicio. hoc iuris
units.tr: Prouerb. II. & 15. Perhaps it would not see as well as several others, but it must be ruled and governed by a council drawn from many, that is, by the united counsels of approved men. For although most kings have a permanent, ordinary senate, and say they use its counsel in administering the commonwealth, first, being a councillor of the kingdom is one thing and being the king's counsellor is another. The former consults for the whole commonwealth and for the common good; the latter serves the advantage and interests of one man. Second, since those constant senators remain always in one place, or at least in the prince's court, they cannot conveniently know or see the condition of distant cities. Moreover, lured by the allurements of royal and courtly life, they are easily corrupted by the lust to dominate, by ambition, and by the desire to increase their wealth, so that in the end they appear not as councillors of the kingdom and commonwealth but as flatterers of one king and as servants of his desires and their own. On this matter there is a notable saying of the Emperor Aurelian in Flavius Vopiscus, which I shall set down: "I heard from my father," he says, "that the Emperor Diocletian, while still a private man, said that nothing is more difficult than to rule well. Four or five men band together and agree on one plan to deceive the emperor: they tell him what is to be approved. The emperor, shut up at home, does not know the truth; he is forced to know only what they tell him. He makes judges whom he ought not to make. He removes from the commonwealth those whom he ought to keep. In short, as Diocletian himself used to say, a good, cautious, excellent emperor is sold." Thus far Vopiscus, though I do not know whether in him "incautus" ("unwary") should not rather be read. However that may be, the ancient Romans, fearing these inconveniences, did indeed assign to the king an ordinary senate; but, so that the welfare of the people might be the supreme law, they reserved the supreme power of the commonwealth not to the king or his senate but to the people itself and its assemblies. Hence under all kings this law held: that in the assemblies the people should create magistrates, pass laws, and decide on wars, as Dionysius of Halicarnassus testifies in book 2. Indeed the jurist Pomponius has recorded that the Roman people in its earliest times was divided into thirty parts, which were called curiae, because the king, as he himself says, conducted the care of the commonwealth through the opinions of those parts; whence the laws were called curiate and the most ancient of all assemblies curiate. Moreover, Seneca in book nineteen of the Epistles writes that he had learned from the books of Cicero's On the Republic that APPEAL TO THE PEOPLE WAS ALSO IN FORCE UNDER THE KINGS. Cicero also demonstrates this at the beginning of book four of the Tusculan Disputations, in these words: "For since from the first beginning of the city, by royal institutions and partly also by laws, the auspices, ceremonies, assemblies, appeals, and all the rest of military affairs were established by divine ordinance, etc." But also in the speech he delivered for his own house: "I deny," he says, "that under public law, by those laws which this state uses, any citizen could be subjected to any such calamity without trial. This right

units.la: Ciceronis de Republica; Seneca lib. Epistol. decimonono. iuris in hac ciuitate etiam tum cum Reges essent, dico fuisse, vt nihil de capite ciuis, aut de bonis fine iudicio senatus, aut populi, aut eorum qui de quaque re constituti iudices sunt, detrahi possit. Quibus ex locis perspicuum est, Romanos, etiam tum cum regibus parebant, hanc tamen sacrosanctam legem habuisse, quam superius commemorauimus:
units.tr: Cicero, On the Republic; Seneca, Epistles, book nineteen. A right in this state, even at the time when there were kings, I say was such that nothing could be taken from a citizen's life, or from his goods, without trial before the senate, or the people, or those judges appointed for each matter. From these passages it is clear that the Romans, even while they obeyed kings, nevertheless had this sacrosanct law which we mentioned above:

units.la: SALVS POPVLI SVPREMA LEX ES- TO.
units.tr: THE WELFARE OF THE PEOPLE SHALL BE THE SUPREME LAW.

units.la: neque vnquam regnum vllum fuisse arbitror, præter Turcicum, aut Turcici simile, in quo cives non aliquam libertatis imaginem retinerent, quæ in vnico comitiorum habendorum iure posita est. Itaque legem illam Maiores nostri summa sapientia secuti decreuerunt, Rempublicam communi omnium ordinum consilio gerendam esse: cuius consilij habendi causa certo anni tempore Rex, & principes & delecti ex singulis prouincijs conuentum agerent. Quod idem institutum, videmus etiam multis in alijs gentibus obseruatum fuisse. Primùm in Gallia nostra antiqua, & libera, quam superius ex Cæsaris commentarijs ostendimus communi Delectorũ Concilio administratam fuisse. Sed quoniam de Regno instituta cõmemoratio est, satis cõstat, antiquitus in Græcia Amphyctionũ Concilium fuisse ab rege Amphyctione (vt Suidas & alij testantur) Deucalionis filio institutũ, vt èx xı.Græcię ciuitatib.certo anni tepore delecti ad Thermopylas conuenirent, ibiq; de regni & Reip.summis rebus communi consilio deliberarent. qua de causa Cicero Commune, Plinius Publicum illud Græciæ Concilium appellat: sic Aristoteles lib. Ethicorum iii scribit, Homericis temporibus, quæ Reges suscipiebant, de iis prius ad populi Concilium referre solitos fuisse. Sic Herodotus memoriæ prodidit, duodecim Ioniæ ciuitates commune plerunque Concilium habuisse; quod iccirco πανιώνιον appellabant: sicuti Ætoliæ quoque ciuitates suum πανaιτώλιον habuere: quorum nominum exemplo Budæus noster Francogalliæ nostræ Concilium πανκέλπιον appellat. Sic Populus Lacedæmonius, etsi regem habebat, tamen de summa Repub. quidnam esset vtile & honestum deliberabat: vt ex Æschine scribit Gellius lib. 18. cap. 3. quinetiam Regibus suis Ephoros, tanquam custodes atq; obseruatores, imponebat, qui (quemadmodum Plato scribit) Regibus freni instar essent, quorumque consilio atque auctoritate Reges Repub. administrarent. Quam eandem in insula Taprobane regni rationem Plinius commemorat libro 6. cap. 22. vt Regi xxx Rectores attribuerentur à populo, quorum consilio in gubernanda Rep. vteretur, ne si immensa interminataque Regibus in ciues potestas permitteretur, eodem loco ac numero non modò suos ciues, sed etiam consanguineos, quo vel mancipia vel pecudes, haberent. quod in Turcico imperio accidisse constat, vbi non modò priuatos quosque ciues quasi pecudes mactare Tyranno ius est; verùm etiam cognatos, propinquos, affines,fratres denique consanguineos. Simillimam Germanorum in imperio Germanico constituendo sapientiam fuisse apparet,vbi Imperator, Monarchæ: Principes, Ariftocratiæ: ciüitatum vero legati,Democratię speciem obtinent.neque quicquam quod ad summã Rempubl.Germanicam pertineat, nisi in Ordinum conuentu constitutum,atque complacitum fit, ratum & firmum habetur. Quinetiam eandem apud Anglos Regni adminiftrādi formam esse, testis est Polyd. Verg. lib. Ang. Hift. 1 1.vbi sic scribit: Ante hæc tempora, (Regis autem Henrici I.vitam exponit)Reges non confuerant populi conuentum consultandi caussa, nisi perraro,facere:adeò vt ab Henrico id institutum manaffe iure dici possit,quod tam altis defixum,vt etiam nunc, radicibus semper stetit,vt deinceps quicquid ad Rempublicam bene gerendam, eiusque confseruationem deliberandum foret, illud ad Conciliũ deferretur, & fiquid aut Regis aut populi iussu decretū factumque effet,id totum pro nihilo haberetur, nisi eiusmodi Concilij auctoritate foret comprobatum. Ac ne imperitæ vulgi multitudinis, cuius proprium est nihil sapere,iudicio Cõcilium impediretur,certa lege exceptum fuit ab initio, qui ex Sacerdotum cœtu,quive,quotve ex reliquo populo vocari deberent ad Concilium.More Gallico vulgò Parlamentum appellant. quod vnusquisque Rex initio fui Regni habere solet: qui & deinde, quoties res postulat, suo arbitratu illud ipsum convocat. Hæc Vergilius. Et in eandem sententiam vetus quidam scriptor Angliæ Cancellarius in libello cui titulus est Alearned commendation: cap. 36. Neque Rex, inquit, ibidem per se aut ministros suos tallagia, subsidia, aut quaevis alia onera imponit legibus suis: aut leges eorum mutat, vel novas condit, sine concessione vel assensu totius Regni sui, in Parlamento suo expresso. Sed ex his gentium fere omnium institutis nullum æque insigne memoratur ut illud Hispanorum, qui cum in communi Aragoniæ Concilio Regem creant, rei memoriæque consignandæ causa fabulam per agunt: hominemque inducunt, cui Iuris Aragonici nomen imponunt: quem Rege maiorem ac potentiorem esse communi populi decreto sancinunt, tandemque Regem certis legibus & conditionibus creatum his affantur verbis, quæ propter eximiam ac planè singulare gentis illius in frenando Rege fortitudinem proferemus: NOS QVI VALEMOS TANTO COME VOS, Y PODEMOS MAS QVE VOS, VOS ELEGIMOS REY: CON ESTAS Y ESTAS CONDITIONES: INTRA VOS Y NOS, VN QVEMANDA MASQVE VOS. Id est, Nos qui tanti sumus, quanti vos, & plusquam vos possumus, Regem vos eligimus, his atque his conditionibus. Inter vos & nos unus maiore cum imperio est, quam vos. Eoq; illud pertinet Iohannis Vaffei in Chronicis Hispan. sub anno 839.
units.tr: Nor, I think, has there ever been any kingdom except the Turkish, or one like the Turkish, in which the citizens do not retain some image of liberty, which consists in the sole right of holding assemblies. Therefore our ancestors, following that law with the highest wisdom, decreed that the commonwealth should be governed by the common counsel of all orders; for the sake of holding this counsel, at a fixed time of year the king, the princes, and chosen men from each province would hold an assembly. We see the same institution observed among many other peoples. First in our ancient and free Gaul, which we showed above from Caesar's commentaries was administered by the common council of the chosen men. But since mention has been made of kingdoms, it is well established that in antiquity in Greece there was a council of the Amphictyons, instituted by King Amphictyon, son of Deucalion (as Suidas and others attest), so that chosen men from eleven Greek cities would gather at a fixed time of year at Thermopylae and there deliberate on the highest matters of kingdom and commonwealth by common counsel. For this reason Cicero calls it the Common council of Greece, and Pliny the Public council. So Aristotle writes in book 3 of the Ethics that in Homeric times, when kings undertook matters, they were accustomed to refer them first to the assembly of the people. So Herodotus has recorded that the twelve cities of Ionia usually held a common council, which for that reason they called the panionion [πανιώνιον]; just as the cities of Aetolia also had their panaetolion [παναιτώλιον]. Following the example of these names, our Budaeus calls the council of our Gaul the pankelpion [πανκέλπιον]. So the Lacedaemonian people, although it had a king, nevertheless deliberated on the highest matters of the commonwealth, what was expedient and honourable, as Gellius writes from Aeschines, book 18, chapter 3. Moreover, they imposed on their kings the Ephors as guardians and overseers, who (as Plato writes) were like a bridle for kings, and by whose counsel and authority the kings administered the commonwealth. Pliny records this same system of kingship on the island of Taprobane, book 6, chapter 22: thirty rulers were assigned to the king by the people, and he would use their counsel in governing the commonwealth; for if an immense and boundless power over citizens were granted to kings, they would hold not only their citizens but even their blood relations in the same position and number as slaves or cattle. It is certain that this has happened in the Turkish empire, where it is lawful for the tyrant to slaughter not only private citizens like cattle, but also kinsmen, relatives, connections, and finally brothers by blood. The Germans showed a very similar wisdom in establishing the German empire, where the emperor takes the form of a monarchy, the princes of an aristocracy, and the envoys of the cities of a democracy. Nor is anything that pertains to the German commonwealth as a whole regarded as valid and firm unless it has been settled and agreed in the assembly of the orders. Moreover, that the same form of governing the kingdom exists among the English is attested by Polydore Vergil, in book 11 of the English History, where he writes thus (he is describing the life of King Henry I): "Before these times the kings had not been accustomed to call an assembly of the people for consultation, except very rarely; so that it can rightly be said that this custom came from Henry, one that took so deep a root that it has still stood firm with ever-fixed roots, so that thenceforth whatever was to be deliberated for the good conduct and preservation of the commonwealth was referred to the council; and if anything had been decreed and done by the order of the king or the people, the whole was held to be nothing unless it had been approved by the authority of such a council. And lest the judgment of the council be hindered by the unskilled multitude of the common crowd, whose proper trait is to understand nothing, from the beginning it was settled by a fixed law who should be summoned to the council from the company of priests, and who, and how many, from the rest of the people. In the French manner they commonly call it the Parliament, which every king is accustomed to have at the beginning of his reign, and which afterwards, whenever the matter requires, he convenes at his own discretion." Thus Vergil. And to the same effect an old English writer, a Chancellor, in a little book entitled A Learned Commendation, chapter 36: "Nor does the king," he says, "there by himself or his ministers impose tallages, subsidies, or any other burdens on his subjects, nor change their laws or make new ones, without the concession and assent of the whole of his kingdom, expressed in his Parliament." But of all the institutions of almost all nations, none is recorded as more notable than that of the Spaniards, who, when they create their king in the common council of Aragon, perform a kind of play to commemorate the matter: they bring in a man whom they call by the title of the Law of Aragon, and whom they decree by common vote to be greater and more powerful than the king; and at last, having created the king under certain laws and conditions, they address him in these words, which we shall quote because of the singular and quite extraordinary courage of that people in restraining its king: "WE WHO ARE AS GREAT AS YOU, AND CAN DO MORE THAN YOU, CHOOSE YOU AS KING, WITH THESE AND THESE CONDITIONS: BETWEEN YOU AND US, THERE IS ONE WHO IS GREATER THAN YOU." That is: We, who are of such worth as you, and are able more than you, choose you as king on these and these conditions; between you and us there is one with greater power than you. To this refers also the passage of Juan Vasseo in his Chronicles of Spain under the year 839.

units.la: 839. Ermicus populari suffragio electus Rex, vnctus, & coronatus, sed certis conditionibus, nimirum, vt in eos æquis legibus vteretur, atq; vt vnus iudex esset medius inter Regem & populum, si quid controuersiæ oriretur, ISQVE ARAGONIÆ IVSTITIA appellaretur. Item Lucius Marinæus lib.8. Princeps, inquit, eligitur, propositis tamen nonnullis conditionibus, vt in eos æquis legibus vteretur, à quibus etiam iudex qui medius inter eos esset, petebatur, & ARAGONIÆ IVSTITIA vocabatur. Item Hieronymus Surita, sub anno DCCCXLIX. Ioannes Simenius Cerdanus, qui præfecturam, quam vocant Iustitiæ Aragonum, plures annos auorum ætate gessit, cuius præstantissimi viri magna est apud omnes, & in primis grauis auctoritas, prodidit eundem Magistratum, cui nostri summa rerum deferunt, initio regni constitutum: vt quemadmodum apud Lacedæmonios Ephori Regibus oppositi fuerant, sic apud Aragonios is magistratus vim maiorem, atque impotentiam Regiæ potestatis coerceret: & quodammodo præses atque custos libertatis haberetur. Inde enim magistratum introductum ferunt, præsidia communi libertati suppeditatem: cuius vis in libertate retinenda emineat: vt nemo ius suum amittere posset, nisi qui eum gerat auctor sit factus: & in posterum certum manssse perfugium aut intermissæ aut retetæ libertatis: adeoque integrum purumque esse voluerunt, vt ipsius IVSTITIÆ nomine insignitum produxerint. Aragonensium certè legum atque institutorũ serie liquido constat, magnis interdictorum præsidijs eam præfecturam fuisse, atq; communitam: cum, regno latiùs patente de libertate retinenda maiores paulatim cautum sibi decreuere: ne in posterum extraordinarijs potestatib. libertas adimeretur: néve quid de eius dignitate minueretur.
units.tr: 839. Ermicus, chosen king by popular vote, was anointed and crowned, but on certain conditions: namely, that he would rule them by equal laws, and that a single judge should stand between king and people, to whom appeal could be made if any dispute arose; and this judge was called the Justice of Aragon. Likewise Lucius Marinaeus, book 8: "A prince is chosen, though with certain conditions proposed, that he will rule them by equal laws; and from these also a judge who should stand between them was sought, and he was called the Justice of Aragon." Likewise Jerome Surita, under the year 849. John Simenius Cerdanus, who held the office which they call the Justice of Aragon for many years in his grandfathers' day, a man of outstanding worth, whose authority is great among everyone and especially weighty, has written that this same magistracy, to which our people entrust the highest affairs, was established at the beginning of the kingdom. Just as the ephors were set against the kings among the Lacedaemonians, so among the Aragonese this magistracy was to restrain the greater force and the excesses of royal power, and was regarded in some sense as the guardian and protector of liberty. For they say the magistracy was introduced to provide defences for common liberty, and its strength stands out in preserving liberty: so that no one could lose his right unless the holder of this office had been made its guarantor; and that there might be a sure refuge for liberty, whether it was interrupted or curtailed. They wished it to be so whole and pure that they put it forward marked with the very name of JUSTICE itself. From the sequence of Aragonese laws and institutions it is clear enough that this office was fortified by great safeguards of interdicts, since, as the kingdom spread more widely, their ancestors gradually took care to decree, for the retention of liberty, that in future liberty should not be taken away by extraordinary powers, nor anything be diminished from its dignity.

units.la: Item sub anno M C X I V, Petrus Simenius præfectus Iustitiæ Aragonũ. Is magistratus primo Maior Iustitia appellatus fuit: quod supremum ius ac potestatem à Regibus obtineret. postea verò legibus ita septus fuit, atque munitus, vt libertatis, à supremo dominatu vindicandæ atque tuendę commune perfugium atque præsidium esset.
units.tr: Likewise under the year 1114, Peter Simenius, prefect of the Justice of Aragon. This magistracy was first called the Greater Justice, because it held supreme right and power from the kings. Afterwards, however, it was so hemmed in and fortified by laws that it became the common refuge and protection for defending liberty against supreme domination.

units.la: Item sub anno M CCCXLIV. Rex prouentus omnes & vectigalia Athonis Foccij, militariaq; beneficia notari describiq́ue decernit: & Foccius Garciæ Ferdinandiç Castrensis Iustitię Aragonum præfecti intercessione atque interdicto notationem eam abrogandam contendit: summaque de iurisdictione controuersia suboritur. Regij enim aduocati eò actionem intenderunt, vt præfectum Iustitiæ Aragonum reiectione interpositą, iudicem aspernentur, atque repudient: id ius esse asseuerantes, vt in generali conuentu, de ijs controuersijs diiudicet, atque definiat, quæ cum Rege haberentur: neque illi ius fasque esse, extra conuentum Regem in iudicium deducere: neque aduersus regiam dignitatem, pro aliquo iudicium accipere: nisi, in ingenuitatis actionibus: aut in eis litibus, quib. Rex tanquam auctor obstrictus esset: & in his quæstionibus quæ aduersus Regios magistratus, & iudices constituerentur.
units.tr: Likewise under the year 1344. The king decrees that all the revenues, taxes and military benefices of Athon Foccius be noted and listed. Foccius, through the intercession and interdict of Garcia Ferdinand of Castro, prefect of the Justice of Aragon, contends that this listing must be annulled, and a great dispute over jurisdiction arises. For the royal advocates directed their action to this end: that, with the appeal against him interposed, they should spurn and reject the prefect of the Justice of Aragon as judge, asserting that it was their right that he should judge and decide, in the general assembly, those controversies which arose with the king; that it was not lawful or right for him to summon the king to trial outside the assembly, nor to admit a case against royal dignity on behalf of anyone, except in actions concerning freedom, or in those suits in which the king was bound as guarantor, and in those questions which were raised against royal magistrates and judges.

units.la: Item sub anno MCCCXLVIII. Ex eo magistratus & Præfectura Iustitiæ Aragonum stabiliendæ communis libertatis caussa, antiquitus legibus sepța, atque munita, in eo vires suas exercere cœpit, ne quis contra regiorum ministrorum extraordinariam potestatem iussa, atque imperia, auxilij egeret: aut potentiorum iniuria premeretur: ac fere de omnibus controuersijs publicis, priuatisque ne vis inferatur, constituit. Si quis aut priuatus aut publicus eius decreto non steterit, grauissima pœna afficitur: neque petenti ius redditur, aut vllus honos communicatur: eiusque auctoritas è ciuitate exterminatur: idque legibus habent sancitum. Institutum vero eius præfecturæ interdictis tale temperamentum fuit, vt tenuiores & qui locum infimum ciuitatis tenent, cum principib. viris æquari se arbitrentur: & eam scisscendarum legum rationem nostri secuti videntur, in eo magistratu muniendo, vt regijs iudicibus opponeretur: quemadmodum Lacedæmone Ephori à Theopompo Spartanis Regibus oppositi fuerant: & apud Romanos Consulibus Tribuni plebis. Sed ne existimatio atque auctoritas eius magistratus vnquam imminui posset, aut popularis fieret, atq; omnes iussis supremæ legis obtemperarent, & cum omnib.ea lex fem per vna atque eadé voce personaret, vt vere populi salus suprema lex esset, ac vinculum & firmamentum libertatis, atq; omnes, qᵱ dici solet, quasi sacræ legis cathenis constringerentur, ea cautio adhibita est, ne ex intimo ordine, aut popula ri suffragio, quispiam eum magistratū adipisceretur: sed militari decore cohonestatus & à Rege ascitus, atq; suffectus. Moderatione quoque ea prefectura, non ad popularem aurā proucta, sed tēperatior à maiorib.instituta est, quā Ephororū magistratus à Lacedæmonijs fertur introductus: qui se adeo insolenter esferre consueuerant, vt in more institutoq; positū esset, vt in tribunali sedētes Regib. ne allurgerent: néve eos venerarentur: & singulis mensibus iurisiurandi religione obstringerētur: Reges se patrijs legib.obtemperaturos: Ephori vero se Regum imperio obedientes fore: dū leges, ac scita institutaq; maiorū ab illis obseruarentur. Inde euenit vt nō dissēsione ac dissidio, sed more institutoq; in vnius Prefecturæ magistratu Resp. regijs magistratib. opposita, non imbecilla esset: sed magnū applausū assentiēte populo cōsequeretur: & turbidi cōcitatiq; mot⁹ in posterū cōprimerē tur: atq; intestinę dissēsiones sine vllo tumultu, aut motu sedarentur. Itē anno MCCCLXXXVI. Rex Iohannē filiū procuratione Regni priuat: imperatq; atq; edicit, ne qs primogenio pareat. Iohan. anxius exploratis in se patris nouercæq; odijs, vt aduersus regiā potestatem iuris implorarer raret auxilium, Dominicum Cerdanũ summo Iustitiæ Aragonum magistratui Præfectum appellat: atq; ad eum prouocat: eoq; perfugio & legum præsidio aduersus maiorem vim regiæ potestatis munitur. Præfectus, vt est consuetudo, de vi interdicit. Tantum communi libertati tribuitur, vt Princeps de suo iure, & de legibus disceptaturus ad eum potius magistratum venire, necesse habuerit: cum is magistratum gerat, qui à Rege creatus sit. Eius nanque magistratus interdictis appositis, nihil Regij imperij, aut summæ potestatis fit reliqui: quoad magistratus suum de interdicti iure iudicium pronunciet, & sententiam ferat: ne dignitatis Regiæ præstantia æquabilitatem communis iuris ttanseat: aut vi oppressos extraordinario imperio coërceat. Cerdanus in causa popuları, maximeque plausibili perpetua constantia in propósito, suscepto'que consilio permansit. Eam enim vim intercessionum, inhibitionemque Præfecturæ Iustitiæ Aragonum maiores esse voluerunt, vt nihil inuiolabilius, sanctiusve ducant: & ad eam summam omnia referri velint, vt ij restituantur, qui vi compressi, constricti aut depulsi deiective fuerint: eaque religione obseruant, & in ea positum fuit semper ratione atque sententia, vt eius magistratus ea vis sit, vt præscribat Regijs iudicibus, ne quid aduersus interdicta intercessionemque attentent, molianturve. Inde id perfugium, quasi præsidium communis salutis, legum, & institutorum venerantur, obseruant, arcte tenent, accurateque tuentur: ac primigenium regni heredem ad ea legis præsidia decurrisse, ciuitates omnes gloriantur. Quæ cum ita se habeant, cùm, inquam, gentium ac nationum omnium commune hoc institutum semper fuerit, quæ quidem regio ac non tyrannico imperio vterentur, vt SALVS POPVLI SVPREMA LEX ESSET: perspicuum est, non modò præclaram illam communis concilij habendi libertatem partem esse iuris gentium, verumetiā Reges qui malis artibus illam sacrosanctam libertatem opprimunt, quasi iuris gentium violatores, & humanæ societatis expertes, iam non pro Regibus, sed pro tyrannis habendos esse. Quanquam quid eos tyrannos appellemus, ac non etiam atrociore vocabulo vtamur? cùm Fl. Constantinus tyrannus, qui iuniore Honorio imperante tyrannidem in Gallia occupauit, vetus illud Galliæ nostræ institutum violare ausus nō fit, sed tanquam sacrosanctum conseruarit. Nam cùm Arelate regni sui sedem fixisset, eamque propterea Constantinam vrbem vocari statuisset, publicum gentis Concilium quotannis ex vetere instituto haberi solutum, in ea vrbe haberi statuit: hoc est, septem prouinciarum conuentus, Viennensis, vtriusque Narbonensis, vtriusque Aquitaniæ, Nouempopulaniæ, & Alpium maritimarum. quod ex ipsius Constitutione nuper duorum clarissimorum virorum beneficio in lucem edita, cognoscere licebit.
units.tr: Likewise under the year 1348. From that time the magistracy and prefecture of the Justice of Aragon, established of old for the sake of common liberty and long fenced in and protected by laws, began to exercise its powers in this way: that no one should need help against the extraordinary power of royal ministers, against their orders and commands, or be crushed by the wrong of the more powerful. It settles almost all public and private disputes, so that no violence is done. If anyone, private or public, does not abide by its decree, he is subjected to the gravest penalty: justice is not rendered to him who seeks it, no honour is granted to him, and his authority is driven out of the state; and their laws have sanctioned this. The institution of this prefecture by interdicts had such a moderation that the humbler and those who hold the lowest place in the state think themselves equal to the leading men. In fortifying this magistracy our forefathers seem to have followed the same reasoning as in framing their laws, so that it was set against the royal judges, just as the ephors were set against the Spartan kings by Theopompus, and the tribunes of the plebs against the consuls among the Romans. But lest the esteem and authority of this magistracy should ever be diminished or become popular, and so that all might obey the commands of the supreme law, and that law might sound with one and the same voice to all, so that the safety of the people truly is the supreme law and the bond and firmament of liberty, and all, as the saying goes, might be bound by the chains of a sacred law, this precaution was taken: no one was to attain that magistracy from the lowest rank or by popular vote, but he was to be graced with military distinction and chosen and appointed by the king. This prefecture was also established by the elders with a moderation not carried away on popular breezes, but more temperate than the magistracy of the ephors is said to have been introduced by the Spartans. The ephors used to bear themselves so insolently that it became custom and institution that, sitting on their tribunal, they should not rise for the kings nor show them reverence; and every month they were bound by the sanctity of an oath: the kings would obey the laws of their fathers, and the ephors would obey the king's command, as long as the laws, decrees and institutions of the ancestors were observed by them. Hence it came about that the commonwealth, set against the royal magistrates not by discord and dissension but by custom and institution in the magistracy of a single prefecture, was not feeble, but won great applause with the people assenting; and turbulent and agitated movements were held in check in future, and internal dissensions were settled without any tumult or upheaval. Likewise in the year 1386, the king deprived his son John of the regency of the kingdom, and commanded and ordered that no one should obey the first-born. John, anxious because of the hatred shown against him by his father and stepmother, and so that he might seek the aid of law against royal power, appeals to Dominic Cerdanus, prefect of the highest magistracy of the Justice of Aragon, and calls upon him; and by this refuge and the protection of the laws he is fortified against the greater force of royal power. The prefect, as is customary, issues an interdict concerning violence. So much authority is given to common liberty that the prince, who was about to dispute his right and the laws, was obliged to come before that magistracy, since that magistrate was created by the king. For once the interdicts are imposed, nothing of royal command or supreme power remains until his magistracy pronounces on the right of the interdict and passes sentence: lest the eminence of royal dignity override the evenness of common law, or restrain by extraordinary command those oppressed by force. Cerdanus persisted in this popular and most applauded cause with constant firmness of purpose and in the plan he had undertaken. For the ancestors wished the force of the intercessions and prohibitions of the prefecture of the Justice of Aragon to be such that they hold nothing more inviolable or sacred, and they want everything referred to this supreme power, so that those who have been forcibly restrained, bound or driven out should be restored. They observe this with such scruple, and it has always been held, in this reasoning and opinion, that the power of that magistracy is such that it prescribes to the royal judges that they must not attempt or undertake anything against the interdicts and intercession. Hence they revere, observe, hold fast and carefully guard that refuge as a protection of common safety, of laws and institutions; and all the cities boast that the first-born heir of the kingdom had recourse to these legal safeguards.
