Since these things stand so, since, I say, this common institution has always belonged to all peoples and nations which were governed by a kingly and not a tyrannical rule, so that THE SAFETY OF THE PEOPLE WOULD BE THE SUPREME LAW, it is plain that not only is that famous freedom of holding a common assembly part of the law of nations, but also that kings who by wicked arts oppress that most sacred liberty, as violators of the law of nations and strangers to human society, are no longer to be regarded as kings but as tyrants. Yet why should we not call them tyrants, and use an even harsher word? When Flavius Constantinus, the tyrant who seized power in Gaul while the younger Honorius was emperor, did not dare to violate that ancient institution of our Gaul, but preserved it as sacrosanct. For when he had fixed the seat of his kingdom at Arles, and had therefore decreed that the city should be called Constantina, he ordered that the public council of the nation, which by ancient custom was held every year, should be held in that city: that is, the assembly of the seven provinces of Vienne, both Narbonese, both Aquitaines, Novempopulania and the Maritime Alps. This may be learned from his own Constitution, lately brought to light through the kindness of two most distinguished men.

units.la: IMP. CONSTANTINVS AD AGRICOLAM PRÆFECTVM PRÆTORIO GALLIARVM.
units.tr: The Emperor Constantine to Agricola, Praetorian Prefect of Gaul.

units.la: Saluberrima magnificētiæ tuæ suggestione inter reliquas Reip. vtilitates euidenter instructi, obseruanda prouincialibus nostris.id est,per feptem Prouincias mansura in æuum auctoritate decernimus,quod sperari planè ab ipsis prouincialibus debuisset. Nam cum propter priuatas & publicas necessitates de singulis ciuitatibus, non solùm de singulis Prouincijs vel Honoratos confluere,vel mitti legatos aut possessorum vtilitas,aut publicarum ratio exigat functionū: maximè opportunum & conducibile iudicauimus,vt seruata posthac quotannis confuetudine, in constituto tempore, in Metropolitana, id est,in Arelatenfi vrbe incipiat septe Prouincie habere conciliū.In quo planè tā in singulis q̄ in cōmune consulimus: primum, vt optimorū conuentus sub illustri præsentia præfecturæ, fi id tamen ratio publicæ dispositionis obtulerit, saluberrima de singulis rebus possint esse confilia. Tum quicquid tractatum fuerit,& difcufsum ratiocinijs constitutum, nec latere potiores Prouincias poterit, vt parem necesse est inter absentes æquitatis formam, iustitiæque feruari. Hinc planè præter necessitates etiam humanæ conuersationi non parum credimus cōmoditatis accedere,quod in Conftantina vrbe iubemus annis singulis esse concilium. Tanta est enim loci opportunitas, tanta est copia cōmerciorum,tanta illic frequentia commeantium, vt quicquid vsquam nascitur, illic commodius distrahatur. Neq; enim vlla Prouincia fructus sui facultate lætatur, vt non nisi hæc propria Arelatensi, soli credatur esse fœcunditas. Quicquid enim diues Oriens, quicquid odoratus Atalis, quicquid delicatus Assyrius, quod Africa fertilis, quod speciosa Hispania, quod fœcūda Gallia potest habere præclarum, ita illi exhibetur affatim, quasi sibi nascantur omnia, quæ vbiq; constat esse magnifica. Iam verò de cursu Rhodani, & Turoni recursu, necesse est, vt vicinum faciant, & penè conterminum, vel quod iste præterfluit, vel ille quod circuit. Cum ergo huic seruiat ciuitati quicquid habet terra præcipuum: ad hanc vel naui, vel vehiculo, terra, mari, flumine deferatur quidqd in singulis nascitur: quomodo non multū sibi Galliæ nostræ præstitum credant, cùm in eadem ciuitate præcipiamus esse conuentum, in qua diuino quodam munere commoditatum & commerciorum opportunitas tanta præstatur? Siquidem hoc rationabili planè, probatoque consilio iam & vir illustris Petronius obseruari debere præceperit. Quod interpolatum vel iniuria temporum, vel desidia Tyrannorum reparari solita prudentiæ nostræ auctoritate decernimus, Agricola Parens charissime, atque amantissime. Vnde & illustris magnificentia tua & hanc præceptionem nostram, & priorem sedis suæ dispositionem per septem prouincias uinciasin perpetuo faciet custodiri. vt ab Idib. Augusti quibuscunque medijs diebus in Idus Septemb. in Arelatensi vrbe nouerint Honorati, vel Possessores iudices singulare̅ Prouinciarum annis singulis Concilium esse seruādum, ita vt de Nouempopulonia, & de secunda Aquitania, quæ Prouinciæ longius constituræ sunt, si eorum Iudices occupatio certa detinuerit,sciant legatos iuxta consuetudinem esse mittendos. Qua prouisione plurimum & provincialibus nostris nos intelligimus, vtilitatisque præstare: & Arelatensis vrbis, cuius fidei secundum testimonia atque suffragia Patritij parentisque nostri multa debemus, non parvum adijcere nos cōstat ornatum. Sciat autem magnificentia tua, quinis auri libris Iudicem mulćtandum esse: ternis Honoratos, vel Curiales,qui ad constitutum locum intra definitū tempus venire distulerint.
units.tr: Having been clearly instructed, by your most wholesome suggestion, in the advantages that the commonwealth may derive from this, we decree with lasting authority, to be observed by our provincials throughout the seven provinces, what the provincials themselves ought to have hoped for. For whereas, on account of private and public necessities, the advantage of the property owners or the requirements of public business demand that honorati from each city, and not only from each province, should gather together or that envoys should be sent, we have judged it most opportune and advantageous that, with the custom observed each year from now on, at the appointed time, the seven provinces should begin to hold a council in the metropolis, that is, in the city of Arles. In this council we shall deliberate both on individual matters and on common concerns: first, so that the best men, under the illustrious presence of the prefecture (if the arrangement of public business allows it), may be able to hold the most salutary deliberations on each matter; then, whatever has been discussed and settled by reasoned argument will not be hidden from the more powerful provinces, so that the form of equity and justice may necessarily be kept equal even for those who are absent. Hence, beyond the necessities, we believe no small convenience also accrues to human intercourse from our ordering that a council be held each year in the city of Constantina. For the location is so favourable, the supply of trade so great, and the crowd of travellers there so large, that whatever is produced anywhere is sold more conveniently there. For no province rejoices in the abundance of its produce in such a way that the fertility of its own soil is thought to belong only to Arles. Whatever the rich East, whatever fragrant Arabia, whatever luxurious Assyria, whatever fertile Africa, whatever beautiful Spain, whatever fruitful Gaul can have that is excellent, is supplied there in abundance, as if everything were born for it, though it is well known that all these things are splendid everywhere. Now, as to the course of the Rhône and the return of the Turonus, they must make it near and almost adjacent, either because the one flows past it or because the other encircles it. Since, then, whatever is outstanding in the land serves this city, whatever is produced in each place is carried to it by ship, by carriage, by land, by sea, or by river: how can our Gaul not think that a great favour has been shown to it, when we order the assembly to be held in that same city in which, by a certain divine gift, such great advantage of convenience and commerce is provided? Indeed, the illustrious Petronius had already ordered this to be observed, as a plainly reasonable and approved plan. Since it had been corrupted either by the injury of the times or by the sloth of tyrants, we, by the authority of our prudence, decree that it be restored, Agricola, most dear and most beloved father. Whence your illustrious magnificence will also cause both this our injunction and the earlier arrangement of its seat to be maintained throughout the seven provinces in perpetuity: so that the honorati and the possessores who are judges of the individual provinces may know that, from the Ides of August to the Ides of September, in whatever middle days, a council must be kept each year in the city of Arles; but that, concerning Novempopulania and Second Aquitaine, which are constituted as more distant provinces, if their judges are detained by fixed business, they should know that envoys must be sent according to custom. We understand that this provision is of great benefit and advantage both to our provincials, and it is clear that it adds no small distinction to the city of Arles, to which we owe much on account of the loyalty and services of the Patrician and of our father. Know, moreover, your magnificence, that a judge is to be fined five pounds of gold, and honorati or curiales who have delayed coming to the appointed place within the set time are to be fined three pounds.

units.la: De Regia maiestate & annuo gentis Franco- gallica conuentu, placito, curia, Parlamento.
units.tr: On the Royal Majesty and the Annual Assembly, Plea, Court and Parliament of the Gallic Nation.

units.la: VErum vt ad institutum redeamus, cum illa, quam superiùs exposuimus forma, Respub. nostra sapientissimo maiorū instituto temperata è tribus generibus fuisset, constitutū est vt quotannis, atque adeò quoties maior aliqua res incideret, solēne & publicum Concilių indiceretur: quod propterea Trium statuum Parlamentum appellatum est: cùm eo vocabulo colloquium & conuentus hominum intelligeretur, varijs ex locis vnum in locum communi de re deliberandi caussa coeuntium. Nam colloquia inter hostes pacis aut inducciarū caussa instituta, semper in Chronicis nostris vetusto illo Parlamenti nomine appellantur. Huic porro Concilio rex in aureo tribunali sedens, præerat: cui primùm Principes Regníque magistratus, tum inferiore loco Delecti ex singulis ciuitatibus subsidebant: quos populari lingua Deputatos appellamus. Nam vbi dies Concilij venerat, Rex in atrium constitutum, quasi in augustissimum & religiosissimum Iustitiæ Gallicæ templum, ea pompa deducebatur, quę magis ad popularem moderationem, quam ad Regalem magnificentiam accommodata videbatur. Quam etsi perditis hisce temporibus aulicis assentatoribus irrisui fore non dubitamus, tamen quoniam pietatis pars est, Maiorum sapientia delectari, ex antiquis monimentis exponemus. Carpento igitur Rex in atrium ac potius in Reipub. sacrarium vehebatur bubus tracto, quos auriga stimulo agebat. Vbi verò in eum locum ventum erat, tum Principes Regē in aureo solio collocabant: reliquique (vt iam diximus) suo quisque loco atque ordine subsidebant. Eoque demum in statu atque sacrario Regia Maiestas dicebatur. cuius rei etiam nunc insigne monimentum animaduertere licet in typo Regio, quod Magnum Cancellariæ sigillum vulgò nominamus, vbi Rex non equo militari insidens, aut triumphali more quadrigis inuehens: sed togatus & coronatus, sedens in solio, dextraque sceptrum regale, sinistra sceptrum Iustitiæ tenens, folennique concilio prælidens conspicitur. Et profecto ita est, vt ibi demum Regalis maiestas verè proprieq; dicatur, vbi de summa Reipub. consilium agitur: non, vt imperitum vulgus hodie vsurpare solet, siue rex pila ludat siue saltet ac tripudiet, siue cū mulierculis garriat, ac nugas agat denique, vt semper Maiestatem Regiam nominet. Harum autem rerum omnium testimonia è multis pauca proferemus. Primum ex historia Eguinarthi, qui Caroli Magni Cancellarius fuit, eiusque vitam conscripsit, & Hunibaldi Appendice apud Iohan. Tritenhemium: Quocunque, inquit, eundum erat, carpento ibat, quod bubus iunctis & bubulco rustico more agente trahebatur. Sic ad palatium, sic ad publicum populi sui conuentum, qui ad Kalendas Maij annuatim ob Regni vtilitatem celebrabatur, ire, sic domum redire folebat. Quod idem totidem propè verbis Iohannes Nauclerus in Chronologia Generat. 2 6. commemorat. Itemque auctor magni Chronici sub initium vitæ Caroli Magni, sol. 177. Neque vero nimiopere admirandum id videtur. nam huc temporum illorum morem fuisse, vt & Reges & Reginæ, & Regij liberi bubus veherentur, argumento est etiam ille Gregorij Turon. locus lib. 3. cap. 26. Deuteria vero (hæc Childeberti regis vxor erat) cernens filiam suam ex superiore marito suscep-tam, adultam valde esse, timens ne eam cōcupiscens Rex sibi adsumeret, in basterna positam indomitis bobus coniunctis eam de ponte præcipitauit. Iam vero de Tribunali aureo Aimoinus lib. 4. cap. 30. ita scribit, vbi de Rege Dagoberto commemorat: Generale indixit placitum in loco nuncupato Bigargio: ad quod properè conuenientibus cunctis Franciæ Primoribus Kal. Maijs Rex solio residens aureo, hoc apud eos habuit orationis exordium. Item cap. 41. vbi de Clodoueo Rege loquitur: Medius inter eos solio residens aureo hoc habuit orationis exordium. Item Sigebertus. in Chron. anni 662. Francorum, inquit, Regibus moris erat, Kal. Maij præsidere coram tota gente, & salutare, & salutari, obsequia & dona accipere. Quod Georg. Cedrenus totidem propè verbis sic exponit: Κατὰ ὃ τὴν Μάϊον μῆνα προσκαθέσθαι ὅπῃ πάντῶν τῶν ἐθνῶν καὶ προσκυνεῖν αὐτῷ, καὶ αὐτοπροσκυνεῖσθαι ὑπ᾽ αὐτῶν, διαφοροφορεῖσθαι τε κῆ σωνῄδιαν, καὶ ἀπὸ δίδοσθαι αὐτῷ. Iam vero de popularium, qui ad Concilium conuenerant, auctoritate, testimonium hoc extat apud Aimoinum lib. 4. cap. 41. vbi de Clodoueo secundo loquitur: Quanquā (inquit rex) Francigenæ ciues, terreni nos cura principatus admoneat, publicis vos consultores rebus aduocare. Idem eodem lib. cap. 74. Æstatis initio in Saxonia eundem, & ibi (in Fran-cia cia quotannis folebat) generalem conuentum quotannis habuit. Item lib. 4. capite 13. vbi de Carolo Magno loquitur: Peracta venatione Aquisgrani, rediens generalem populi sui conuentum more solenni habuit. Cap. 16. Imperator autem duobus conuentibus habitis, vno apud Nouiomagum, altero apud Compendiu, in quo & annua dona suscepit. Item capite 17. Mense Augusto Wormaciam venit, atq; habito generali conuentu, & oblata sibi annua dona more solenni suscepit, & legationes plurimas audiuit. Item lib. 5. cap. 31. Generale PLACITVM Idibus Iunijs in villa Duziaco tenuit: vbi & annua dona sua suscepit. Atque haec quidem de solenni Concilio, quod Historici & Galli & Germani depravata Latini sermonis consuetudine modo Curiam modo Conuentum generalem, plerunque autem PLACITVM appellarunt. Gregor. lib. 7. cap. 14. Igitur adueniente PLACITO directi sunt a Childeberto rege, &c. & lib. & cap. 21. Sed cum ad PLACITVM Childebertus cum proceribus suis conueniret, &c. Aimoinus libro 4. capite centesimo nono. Medio mense Conuentus generalis apud Theodonis villam magna populi Francorum frequetia celebrauit. Et mox: Eminuit in hoc PLACITO piissimi Imperatoris misericordia singularis. Nam moris fuit vt in illo Concilio munera vndiq; Regi mitterentur, quod & aliis multis locis traditur: quibus Concilium illud, Conuentus generalis appellatur. Aimoilib.4.cap.64.vbi de Pipino Rege loquitur: Coëgit vt promitterent se omnem voluntatem illius esse facturos: & annis singulis honoris causa ad generalem conuentum equos trecentos pro munere daturos. Item cap. 85.Saxonum perfidiæ non immemor, conuentum generale trans Rhenum in villa Cuffensten more solenni habuit. Iam verò Concilium illud alio quoque vocabulo Curia dicebatur. vnde nata popularis locutio, cùm ad aulam & Regiam itur, vt,iri ad Curiam dicatur: propterea quòd raro ad regem, nisi indicto publico gentis concilio & parlamento, magnisque de rebus adibatur. Iuo Carnotenf. epist. 206. Rex concessit, vt eū ad Curiam suam, quæ Aurelianis in Natali domini congreganda erat, securè adduceremus: & ibi cum eo, & cum Principibus regni de hoc negotio, quantū fieri posset salua regni integritate tractaremus. Factum est, vt cōdictum erat, & conuenientes in Curiam petitionem nostrā replicauimus. Sed reclamante Curia plenariam pacē impetrare nequiuimus, nisi prædictus Metropolitanus per manum & sacramentum eam fidelitatem Regi faceret, quam prædecessoribus suis Regibus Francorum antea fecerant omnes Remenses Archiepiscopi,& ceteri regni Francorum episcopi. Quod persuadentibus omnibus Curiæ optimatibus factum est. Aimoin.lib. 5.cap.50. Carolus, inquit, Danorum Regis filius Flandriæ Proceres quosdam iudicio Curiæ conuenienter petebat. Item c. sequenti: Defuncto Henrico Romanorum Rege, in ea quæ maxima & generalis est habita Maguntiæ Curia.Item Otto Frising. libro Frider. 1,cap.40. Post hæc Princeps Bauariam ingreditur, ibique mense Februario generalem Curiam celebrauit.Item cap.43.Conradus Romanorum Rex, Principes conuocans in oppido Orientalis Frãciæ Franconofurt generalem curiam celebrat. Posterioribus autem seculis dicta est Franciæ Curia: interdum Curia Parlamenti trium statuum: interdum curia Regis Franciæ: interdū præcisè Parlamétum statuum, vt posterius docebimus. Hinc illud Speculatoris Iurisconf. sub titulo De ferijs, ad finem: Potest excusari consuetudo CVRIÆ REGIS FRANCIÆ, quæ tempore Parlamentorum omni die ius reddit:vt venientes de longinquis partibus citius expediantur. Item illud Ioannis Fabri in Auth. hoc nisi.C.de folut.Curia Francię consueuit statuere,quod quando rex monetam debilitat, recipitur pro forti: quando fortificat, habetur respectus ad tempus contractus. Thomas Walsingham Historiæ Angl. sub anno 1275. Sub ijsdem diebus Gasco de Bierna à Rege Anglorum obsessus, super eo negotio quod inter Regem Eduardum & ipsum verrebatur, appellationem interponit ad curiam Regis Francorū. cui deferens Rex Eduardus, nolens Regem Francorum (quem nuper dominum suum pro terris in Francia recognouerat) contra se partem facere, ministris suis commisit, vt in curia Regis Franciæ caussam prosequerentur contra Gasconem.
units.tr: But to return to our subject: when our commonwealth, in the form we have described above, had been tempered by the three kinds of men under the most wise institution of our ancestors, it was ordained that every year, and indeed whenever some greater matter arose, a solemn and public council should be convened. For this reason it was called the Parliament of the Three Estates, since by that word was understood a conference and assembly of men gathering from various places into one place to deliberate on a common matter. For the conferences held between enemies for the sake of peace or a truce are always called by that old name of Parliament in our Chronicles. In this council the king presided, seated on a golden tribunal, and beside him first sat the princes and the magistrates of the realm, and then in a lower place the deputies chosen from each city, whom in the vernacular we call Deputies. When the day of the council had come, the king was led into the courtyard set apart, as into the most august and sacred temple of French justice, with a ceremony better suited to popular moderation than to royal magnificence. Although we do not doubt that in these degenerate times it will be laughed at by court flatterers, nevertheless, since it is part of piety to take delight in the wisdom of our ancestors, we shall set it out from the ancient records. The king was therefore carried in a wagon into the courtyard, or rather into the sanctuary of the commonwealth, drawn by oxen which a carter drove with a goad. When they had come to that place, the princes set the king on a golden throne, and the rest (as we have already said) sat each in his own place and order. And it was then, in that state and sanctuary, that the royal majesty was said to be present. A notable monument of this matter can still be seen today in the royal emblem which we commonly call the Great Seal of the Chancery, where the king is shown not riding a warhorse, nor borne in a chariot in triumphal fashion, but robed and crowned, sitting on a throne, holding the royal sceptre in his right hand and the sceptre of justice in his left, and presiding over a solemn council. And indeed it is truly and properly the case that royal majesty exists only where the highest counsel of the commonwealth is being held, and not, as the ignorant crowd is wont to use the phrase today, whether the king plays at ball or dances and capers, or chatters with little women and finally does trifles, and yet always calls it royal majesty. We shall set forth a few of the many testimonies to all these matters. First, from the history of Eginhard, who was chancellor of Charlemagne and wrote his life, and from the Appendix of Hunibald in Johannes Trithemius: "Wherever he had to go," he says, "he went in a wagon, which was drawn by oxen yoked together and driven in rustic fashion by an ox-driver. Thus he was accustomed to go to the palace, thus to the public assembly of his people, which was held annually on the first of May for the good of the realm, and thus to return home." The same thing, in almost the same words, is recorded by Johannes Nauclerus in his Chronology, generation 26. Likewise the author of the Great Chronicle, at the beginning of the life of Charlemagne, page 177. Nor does this seem to be something to wonder at too much, for that such was the custom of those times, that kings and queens and royal children were all carried by oxen, is shown also by that passage of Gregory of Tours, book 3, chapter 26: Deuteria (she was the wife of King Childebert), seeing her daughter, born of an earlier husband, grown up to a great age and fearing that the king, desiring her, would take her for himself, placed her in a litter, yoked to unbroken oxen, and cast her down from the bridge. Now concerning the golden tribunal, Aimoin in book 4, chapter 30, writes as follows, where he mentions King Dagobert: "He called a general plea in a place named Bigargium; and when all the chief men of France had hastened to assemble there on the first of May, the king, sitting on a golden throne, began his address to them in this manner." Likewise chapter 41, where he speaks of King Clovis: "Sitting on a golden throne in the middle of them, he began his address in this manner." Also Sigebert in the Chronicle, under the year 662: "It was the custom for the kings of the Franks," he says, "to preside before the whole nation on the first of May, and to greet and be greeted, and to receive homage and gifts." Georgius Cedrenus sets this out in almost the same words, thus: "In the month of May, to sit before all the nations and to receive their homage, and to be worshipped by them, and to be carried in procession and to be given gifts" [Κατὰ ὃ τὴν Μάϊον μῆνα προσκαθέσθαι ὅπῃ πάντῶν τῶν ἐθνῶν καὶ προσκυνεῖν αὐτῷ, καὶ αὐτοπροσκυνεῖσθαι ὑπ᾽ αὐτῶν, διαφοροφορεῖσθαι τε κῆ σωνῄδιαν, καὶ ἀπὸ δίδοσθαι αὐτῷ]. Now concerning the authority of the common people who had gathered for the council, this testimony is found in Aimoin, book 4, chapter 41, where he speaks of the second Clovis: "Although," said the king, "the citizens of France, the care of earthly rule admonishes us, we summon you as counsellors in public affairs." The same author, in the same book, chapter 74: "At the beginning of summer he held in Saxony, and there (as he used to do every year in France), a general assembly every year." Also book 4, chapter 13, where he speaks of Charlemagne: "When the hunting at Aachen was finished, returning, he held a general assembly of his people in the customary solemn manner." Chapter 16: "The emperor, however, having held two assemblies, one at Noyon and the other at Compiègne, in which he also received the yearly gifts." Likewise chapter 17: "In the month of August he came to Worms, and having held a general assembly, and having received the yearly gifts offered to him in the customary solemn manner, he heard many embassies." Also book 5, chapter 31: "He held a GENERAL PLEA on the Ides of June in the village of Duziacum, where he also received his yearly gifts." And these things indeed concerning the solemn council, which the historians, both French and German, through a corrupted usage of Latin, called sometimes Court, sometimes General Assembly, but most often PLEA. Gregory, book 7, chapter 14: "Therefore, when the PLEA drew near, envoys were sent by King Childebert, etc." and book 7, chapter 21: "But when Childebert was to meet with his nobles at the PLEA, etc." Aimoin, book 4, chapter 109: "In the middle of the month a general assembly was held at the villa of Theodo, with a great crowd of the Frankish people." And soon after: "In this PLEA the singular mercy of the most pious emperor stood out. For it was the custom that at that council gifts were sent to the king from every quarter, as is recorded also in many other places; that council is accordingly called a general assembly." Aimoin, book 4, chapter 64, where he speaks of King Pepin: "He compelled them to promise that they would do all his will; and, as a mark of honour, to give three hundred horses each year as a gift at the general assembly." Likewise chapter 85: "Not unmindful of the treachery of the Saxons, he held a general assembly in the customary solemn manner beyond the Rhine, in the village of Cuffenstein." Now indeed that council was also called by another name, Court. Whence the popular expression arose, that when one goes to the royal household one is said to go "to Court," because the king was seldom approached, except when a public assembly of the nation and a parliament had been summoned, and then only on great affairs. Ivo of Chartres, letter 206: "The king granted that we might safely bring him to his Court, which was to be gathered at Orléans at Christmas; and there, with him and with the princes of the realm, we might treat of this business as far as could be done with the integrity of the realm preserved. It came about, as had been agreed, and when we had assembled at the Court we renewed our petition. But with the Court objecting, we could not obtain full peace, unless the aforesaid Metropolitan made that fidelity to the king by hand and oath which all the Archbishops of Reims and the other bishops of the realm of the Franks had formerly made to the kings of the Franks, his predecessors. This was done, all the nobles of the Court urging it." Aimoin, book 5, chapter 50: "Charles, son of the King of the Danes," he says, "by the judgment of the Court, rightly sought certain nobles of Flanders." Likewise the next chapter: "Henry, King of the Romans, having died, in the Court held at Mainz, which was the greatest and general one." Also Otto of Freising, Life of Frederick 1, chapter 40: "After this the prince entered Bavaria, and there in the month of February he held a general Court." Likewise chapter 43: "Conrad, King of the Romans, summoning the princes to the town of Frankfurt in eastern Franconia, holds a general Court." In later centuries, however, the name of France's Court was used in various ways: sometimes Court of the Parliament of the Three Estates, sometimes Court of the King of France, and sometimes simply Parliament of the Estates, as we shall show later. Hence that passage of the jurist Speculator under the title On Holidays, near the end: "The custom of the COURT OF THE KING OF FRANCE, which on every day of the Parliaments renders justice, may be excused, so that those coming from distant parts may be dispatched more quickly." Likewise that of John Faber on Authentica "hoc nisi", Code, on payment: "The Court of France is accustomed to decide that when the king debases the coinage it is accepted at its face value, and when he strengthens it, regard is had to the time of the contract." Thomas Walsingham, History of England, under the year 1275: "About the same days, Gascon de Bierne, besieged by the King of the English, on account of that business which was being disputed between King Edward and himself, lodged an appeal to the Court of the King of the Franks. King Edward, hearing of it, and unwilling to take the side of the King of the Franks (whom he had lately acknowledged as his lord for his lands in France) against himself, commissioned his officials to pursue the case against Gascon in the Court of the King of France."

units.la: De sacrosanƈta publici Concilij auƈtoritate: & quibus de rebus in eo ageretur. CAP. XIIII.
units.tr: On the most sacred authority of the public Council, and the matters that were dealt with in it. CHAP. XIIII.

units.la: DEinceps locus postulat, vt quibus de rebus in illo solenni Concilio ageretur, consideremus: Maiorumque nostrorum in constituenda Rep. sapientiam admiremur. Summatim autem has fere obseruauimus. Primum de creando vel abdicando Rege: tum de pace & bello: de legibus publicis: de summis honoribus, præfecturis, & procurationibus Reip. de assignanda patrimonij parte liberis defuncti Regis, vel dote filiab. constituenda: de re numaria, & monetæ rationibus: denique de iis rebus omnibus, quæ vulgus etiam nunc Negotia Statuum populari verbo appellat, quoniam summo multarum ætatum consensu de nulla (vt dixi) Reipubl. parte, nisi in Statuum siue Ordinum Concilio agi ius esset. Ac de creandis quidè aut abdicandis Regibus superius, tū ex Caroli Magni testamento tum etiam ex alijs auƈtoribus satis multa testimonia protulimus. Neque tamen illud prætermittemus, ex Reginonis li. 2. sub anno DCCCVI. vbi de Carolo Magno scribens: Cum primoribus, inquit, & optimatib. Francorum de pace constituenda & conseruãda inter filios suos, & de partitione regni placitum habuit. Quo eodem modo Aimoinus li. 5. c.17. vbi de rege Carolo Caluo commemorat: Generali (inquit) conuentu in Carisiaco habito filium suum Carolum armis virilibus, id est ense, cinxit: corona Regali caput insigniuit, & Neustriam ei attribuit: Pipino, Aquitaniam. Nam (vt superius dictum est) prærogatiuam quidem regis filij magnam in illis comitijs habebant: sed tamen etiam si à parentibus in suo testamento designati heredes erant, à populo tamen eos confirmari oportebat: ex quo intelligitur, nullam Regibus de suo Regno testamenti factionem fuisse: neque ipso iure illam patris institutionem valuisse: sed à populo in communi Ordinum conuentu confirmandā fuisse: quemadmodū in iure Romano dicere solemus, quia curator testamento patris inutiliter datur, iccirco datum à Prætore confirmandā esse. Hunc autem morē non modo Occidentales nostri, sed etiam Orientales Franci retinuerunt. cuius rei cùm alia pleraque apud alios testimonia extant, tum illud singulare apud Vitichindum Sax. lib. 2. vbi cùm paulò antè scripsisset Henricum Imp. filiū suum Oddonē regni sui successorem designasse, ita infert: Defuncto Henrico, omnis populus Francorum atque Saxonum iam olim designatum regem à patre, filium eius Oddonem, elegit sibi in principem: vniuersalisque electionis notantes locum, iusserunt ad Aquisgrani palatium. Et mox, Vbi Magontini Episcopi, qui cum infulis occursum illius in pompa & processione expectabat, orationem ad populum exponit: En, inquit, adduco vobis à domino Henrico olim designatum, nunc vero à cunctis Principibus regem factum Oddonem. Si vobis ista electio placeat, dextris in cœlum leuatis significate. Adhæc omnis populus dextras in excelsum leuans, cum clamore valido imprecati sunt prospera nouo Regi.
units.tr: NEXT, the subject requires us to consider what matters were dealt with in that solemn Council, and to admire the wisdom of our ancestors in establishing the commonwealth. I have observed these in summary, and they are roughly as follows. First, the creation or deposition of the king; then war and peace; public laws; the highest honours, offices and administrations of the commonwealth; the assignment of a share of the estate of a deceased king to his sons, or the provision of dowries for his daughters; money and the management of the coinage; and finally all those matters which even now the common people call by the popular name "affairs of the Estates," because by the long-standing agreement of many ages, as I have said, no part of the commonwealth had a right to be dealt with except in the Council of the Estates or Orders. As for the creation or deposition of kings, I have already brought forward quite a few testimonies above, both from the will of Charles the Great and from other authors. Nor shall we pass over this passage from Reginon, book 2, under the year 806, where, writing of Charles the Great, he says: "He held a meeting with the leading men and nobles of the Franks about establishing and keeping peace among his sons and about the division of the kingdom." In the same way Aimoin, book 5, chapter 17, where he mentions King Charles the Bald, says: "At a general assembly held at Quierzy he girded his son Charles with the manly arms, that is, with a sword, adorned his head with the royal crown, and assigned Neustria to him, and Aquitaine to Pepin." For (as was said above) the king's sons indeed had a great pre-eminence in those assemblies; yet even if they had been designated as heirs by their parents in their wills, they still had to be confirmed by the people. From this it is understood that kings had no power to make a testament concerning their kingdom, and that such an appointment by a father had no validity in law, but had to be confirmed by the people in a common assembly of the Estates. Just as in Roman law we are accustomed to say that, because a guardian is given to a son in his father's will ineffectively, he must therefore be confirmed by the Praetor. Moreover, this custom was retained not only by our Western Franks but also by the Eastern Franks. Of this there are many other testimonies among other authors, but this one in particular in Widukind, book 2, where, having written a little earlier that the Emperor Henry had designated his son Otto as successor to his kingdom, he goes on to say: "Henry being dead, the whole people of the Franks and Saxons elected as their prince Otto, the son of the man whom his father had long before designated as king. And they ordered that the place of this general election be marked, at the palace of Aachen." And soon after: "Where the Bishop of Mainz, who was waiting for him in procession with the mitres to meet him, addressed the people: 'Behold,' he said, 'I bring to you Otto, who was designated by Lord Henry long ago, and who has now been made king by all the Princes. If this election pleases you, signify it by raising your right hands to heaven.' Thereupon all the people, raising their right hands on high, with a loud shout invoked good fortune on the new king."

units.la: Quib. & similibus aliis ex locis facile intellectu est, idem Francorum Orientalium & Occidentalium institutum in suis regibus deligendis fuisse: quippe, qui & vnis ex sedibus patriaque olim profecti, & perquandiu sub ijsdem regibus ac principibus ijsdem legibus ac moribus vterentur. Iam de regni procuratione, insigne illud testimonium apud eundem auctorem extat, lib. 5. cap. 35. vbi de eodem Carolo Caluo loquitur: Carolus, inquit, Romam proficiscés, Compendij Placitum generale Kalend. Iunij habuit: vbi per capitula, qualiter regnum Franciæ filius suus Ludouicus cum fidelibus eius & regni primoribus regeret, vsque dum ipse Roma rediret, ordinat. Idem eodem lib. cap. 42. Cuius ætatem (de Carolo Simplice loquitur) Franciæ primores incongruam, vt erat, exercendæ dominationi arbitrati, concilium de summis ineunt rebus: Franci, Burgundiones, Aquitaniensesque proceres congregati in vnum, Odonem tutorem Caroli, regnique elegere gubernatorem. Iam vero de legibus & constitutionibus, vel vnus ille Gaguini locus in vita Ludouici cognomento Sancti, testimonio esse potest: Cùm Parisium, inquit, Ludouicus venisset, conuentu generali habito, Remp. reformauit, statutis optimis legibus de iure à iudicibus dicendo, & de officijs non emédis, &c. Porrò de summis honoribus, & præfecturis ad probatos viros deferendis, testimonium apud Aimoinum extat, libro 5.cap. 36. vbi de Carolo Caluo loquitur: qui cùm ante inaugurationem regni præfecturas arbitratu suo distribuisset, Proceres solenne Concilium indicere cœperunt, legatosque ad regem mittere: neque prius regem coronari passi sunt, quàm illorum Concilio atque auctoritate in illis mandandis magistratibus vsus esset. Regni primores, indignati, quia quibusdam honores dederat sine illorum consensu, & ob id aduersum ipsum conspirarunt, & conuentum suum in villa Witmariû conduxerunt: indeq; legatos suos ad Ludouicû direxerunt. sed & Ludouicus legatos suos ad illos direxit, &c. Item Regino lib. 2. Carolus placitum habuit in Compendio, ibiq; cum optimatum consilio Rodiberto Comiti ducatum inter Ligerim & Sequanam commédauit. Item Appendix Gregor. Turon. lib. 11, cap. 54. Eo anno, inquit, Clotharius cum proceribus & leudibus Burgundię Trecassinis coniungitur: cum eos solicitasset, si vellent, mortuo iam Warnhario alium in eius honoris gradum sublimare: sed omnes vnanimiter denegantes, se nequaquam velle Maiorem domus eligere, Regis gratiam obnixè petétes, cum rege transegere. Et cap. 101. Mortuo Theodorico rege, Franci Clodoueum filium eius paruulum elegerunt in regem. quo non multos post annos mortuo, Childebertus frater eius in regnū redfedit: Grimoaldus autem cū Childeberto rege Maior domus palatij super Francos electus est. Ad eundem numerum referendæ sunt Principum contentiones, quæ Reip. perniciosæ futuræ videbantur, de quibus in eodem illo Concilio disceptabatur. Nam Aimoinus lib. 4. cap. 1. vbi de Clotario Chilperici filio commemorat, à quo Brunechildis Austrasiæ regnum postulabat, ita loquitur: Clotarius respondit, conuentum nobilium debere eam aggregare Francorum, & communi tractatu de comunibus consulere rebus. Se vero iudicio illorum in omnibus pariturum, nec præceptis promisit obstaturum. Quod idem Appendix Gregor. lib. 11. commemorans: Clotarius, inquit, respondebat, iudicio Francorum electorum quicquid procedente domino à Fracis inter eosdem iudicabitur, pollicitum esse implere. Eodemque modo apud eundem Gregorium lib. 8. ca. 21. Bofo Gunthranus sepulchri violati in publico Francorum Concilio accusatus damnatusque dicitur. Cum ad placitum, inquit, Childebertus cum proceribus suis conuenisset & Gunthranus de his interpellatus clam aufugisset, ablateque sunt ei ones res, quas in Aruerno de fisci munere promeruerat. Item Aimoi. lib. 5. ca. 12. vbi de rege Ludouico Pio loquitur, quē filij odijs & contentionib. exagitabant: bant: Cùm autem instaret Autumnalis temperies,ij qui Imperatori contraria sentiebant, alicubi in Francia conuentū fieri generalem volebant. Item cap. 13. In Theodonis villam conuenire generaliter suum populum præcepit. Et paulò post:Sed post paucum tempus idem ad se stum Sancti Martini populum conuocauit: filiumq; Pipinum fugientem ad se quoquomodo reuocare voluit.sed ille id refugiebat. Eademq; ipsa de re Gaguinus cōmemorans: At coniurati, inquit, cùm intelligerent absq; procerum conuentu regem se deijcere non posse,magnis viribus enituntur Conciliū in Francia habere. Repugnabat tamen Ludouicus, quòd sciret Francos ab inimicis aduersum se persuasos esse, Maguntiæ propterea conuentum indixit: mandatque neminem in Concilio cum armis admitti. At ne publico auctoramento coniurati aduersus patrem filij destituerentur, coacto apud Compendium ex toto regni Episcoporum Procerumque Concilio,Lotharius eductum de custodia patrem Compendium perduxit. Rursus Aimoinus lib. 5. capite 38. vbi de rege Ludouico Balbo scribit, qui Concilium Marsuæ agebat, & de pace cum suo consobrino conferebat: In ipso quidem placito,inquit, hæc quæ sequuntur inter eos consensu fidelium suorum seruanda conuenerunt. Nunc cetera videamus.Nā illud pręterea reperio moris fuisse,vt si quis Princeps atque illustriore loco natus criminis alicuius insimularetur, iniudicium ad illud Concilium vocaretur, ibique caussam dicere cogeretur. Itaque regis Clotarij tempore cùm Brunechildis multorum capitalium criminum accusata & damnata est, rex Concilio Francogalliæ indiĉto, ita cum ordinibus loquitur, apud Aimoinum lib.4. cap. 1. Vos dulcissimi commilitones, & præeminentes Francię primores, decernite cui subiaceat supplicio tanti obnoxia sceleris. Et Ado Ætat. v1. sub anno 583. In præsentia, inquit, regis iudicantibus Francis, indomitis equis religata discinditur. De regalis verò patrimonij partitionibus & appannagijs, testimonium extat apud Aimoi. libro 5. ca. 94. vbi de Carolo Magno commemorans ita loquitur: Illis absolutis conuentum habuit Imperator cum primoribus & optimatibus Francorum de pace constituenda, & conferuanda inter filios suos, & diuisione regni faciendain partes tres, vt vnusquisq; illorū suam partem tueri & regere debuisset, si superstes illi eueniret. Item eo loco vbi de partitione inter Ludouici liberos facta loquitur, libro 5. cap. 40. Profecti Ambianos, & sicut fideles illorum inuenerunt, regnum paternum inter se diuiserūt: Item cap. 41. vbi de Carolomanno scribit, qui Wormaciæ Concilium agebat. Ad quod Placitum Hugo profectus pro petitione partis regni, quam frater suus Ludouicus in locarium acceperat. Quinetiam ex alijs locis licet animaduertere, si quando rex maiores sumptus facere instituisset, velut in templis ædificandis & monasterijs fundandis, his de rebus ordinū consilium exquirebat. Nam Aimoinus libro 4. cap. 41. vbi de Clodoueo secundo loquitur, qui in tribunali pro solenni Concilio sedebat: Hoc habuit, inquit, sermonis exordium: Quanquam Francigenæ ciues, terreni nos cura principatus admonet, publicis vos consultores rebus aduocare. Atque hæc quidem hactenus. Ex quibus perspicuum esse arbitramur, quod initio diximus, Maiores nostros, qui verè Franci ac libertatis custodes fuerunt, non Tyrannū sibi aut carnificem imposuisse, qui suos ciues in pecudū loco ac numero haberet: sed ab omni tyrannica & Turcica dominādi libidine abhorruisse: diuinumq; illud præceptum arcte retinuisse: SALVS POPVLI SVPREMA LEX ESTO. quippe, qui omnem plane regni administrandi potestatem penes maximum comitiatum, & ordinum Concilium collocarunt: quod, vt ante diximus, Placitū appellabant. velut apud scriptorem Chronici Besnenfis: Anno DCCLXIIII Pipinus Rex placitum magnum habuit cum Francis apud villam Carisiacum. Huius autem vocabuli origo hinc fluxit, quod Latina consuetudine Placitum id proprie dicitur, quod re in multorum consilio quæsita & deliberata, tandem inter ipsos conuenit: vnde Placita philosophorum apud Ciceronē, & alios auctores dicta sunt. Gellius li. 18. ca. 3. Populus, inquit, Lacedæmonius de summa Rep. quidnam esset vtile & honestum deliberabat. Et mox: Consiliū quod dabat acceptũ ab vniuersis & complacitũ est.Sic Romæ quæ Senatus de maioris Senatorũ partis sententia decreuerat, his perscribebantur verbis: PLACERE SENATVI: vt cum ex alijs veteribus S.C. cuiuis notum est, tum etiam ex ijs quę in libris nostris extant: velut in l.itern veniunt, 20. §. præter hæc. D. de hered.petit. & l. 2. D.ad Velleian. neque quicquam in ijsdem libris frequentius est, quàm Placitum appellari,quod inter aliquos conuenit. velut in l. vlt. C. de pignorib.Pro tenore communis militantium placiti vnde Placitum,pro conuentione in l. 33. C. de transact. l j. C. de pact. l. 4. D. de feruitut.& alijs sexcentis locis, Quæ cùm ita se habeant, non absurda, opinor, coniectura nostra videbitur, quam alijs iam quibusdā in libris nostris exposuimus, vulgatam formulâ, qua etiam nūc regij scribæ in legum & constitutionum clausulis vtuntur, ex illo PLACITI vocabulo, natam esse: QVIA TALE EST NOSTRVM PLACITVM. Nam cùm illæ Latinis litteris scriberentur(quod ex Aimoino & Capitulari Caroli Magni,& omnibus archijs, monimentisque Gallicis satis constat) postea scribæ regii, vbi populari sermone vti cœperunt, ita vel ignorantia, vel malitia potius conuerterunt: Car tel est nostre plaisir: Quoniam ita nobis placet. Nam de populi quoque potestate argumentum in Caroli Capitulari hoc extat: Vt populus interrogetur de capitulis, quæ in lege nouiter addita sunt: & postquam omnes consensefenferint, fubfcriptiones & manufirmationes fuas in ipfis capitulis faciant. Quibus ex verbis patet, populos Franciæ, iis demum olim legibus aftringi folitos quas in comitiis suffragiis suis sanxerant, quod ei legis definitioni confentaneum eft, quam iuris confultus Marcianus ex Demofthene protulit in l. 2. D. de Legib. νόμος ἐςὶ πόλεως συνθήκη κοινή: lex eft pactio & conuentio ciuium, Reipubl. bonoq; publico confulentium. Eodemq; illud pertinet in fine Legis Alemanicæ: Hoc decretum eft apud Regem, & Principes eius, & apud cunctum populū Christianum, qui infra regnum Merouingorū confiftunt. Item apud Aimon. lib. 5. cap. 38. In ipfo Placito hæc quæ fequuntur, inter cos confenfu fidelium fuorum feruanda conuenerunt. Conuentio quæ inter gloriosos reges &c. & ipsis & communibus fidelium ipforum fauentibus & confentientibus facta eft. Sed nullum certius eius rei documentum eft, quam quod fuperius ex libro Legis Frācicæ II protulimus: vbi Ludouicus Pius vniuerfos Regni fui Ordines fic affatur: Quanquam fumma minifterij Regij in noftra perfona confiftere videatur, tamen & diuina auctoritate, & humana ordinatione ita per partes diuifum effe dignofcitur, vt vnufquifque veftrum in fuo loco & ordine partem minifterij noftri habere cognofcatur. Item capite duodecimo, Vnufquifque veftrum partem minifterij noftri per partes habere dignofcitur. Item capite vigefimo fecundo, In nostro Capitulari de hac re communi confultu fidelium nostrorum ordinauimus. & cap. 24. Volumus etiam, vt capitula quæ nunc & alio tempore consultu fidelium nostrorum à nobis constituta sunt,à Cancellario nostro Archiepiscopi & Comites accipiant. Postremò ne illud quidem prætermittendum est, tantam huius Concilij apud exteras gentes auctoritatē fuisse, vt etiam Principes exteri si quid controuersiæ haberent, id interdum illius Concilij iudicio permitterent. Appendix Gregor. Turon. lib. 11.cap.37. Anno xii. regni Theodorici cū Alsaciones, vbi fuerat enutritus, præcepto patris sui Childeberti tenebat, ad Theodebertum barbarico ritu peruaditur: vnde placitum inter hos duos reges, vt Francorum iudicio finiretur, Saloisso castro instituunt.
units.tr: From these and similar passages it is easy to see that the Franks of both East and West followed the same custom in choosing their kings. They had come originally from the same seats and homeland, and for as long as they lived under the same kings, princes, laws and customs. As for the management of the kingdom, a notable witness is found in the same author, book 5, chapter 35, where he speaks of Charles the Bald: "Charles, setting out for Rome, held a general assembly at Compiègne on the Kalends of June, where he laid down by chapters how his son Louis should govern the kingdom of France with his faithful men and the chief men of the realm until he himself returned from Rome." The same author, in the same book, chapter 42, speaks of Charles the Simple: "The chief men of France, judging his age unfit, as it was, for exercising rule, entered into a council on the highest matters. The Franks, Burgundians and Aquitanian nobles, gathered together into one body, chose Odo, guardian of Charles, as governor of the kingdom." Regarding laws and constitutions, that one passage of Gaguin in the life of Louis, surnamed the Saint, can serve as testimony: "When Louis had come to Paris, a general assembly was held, and he reformed the commonwealth, establishing excellent laws concerning the administration of justice by judges, and concerning the non-sale of offices, and so on." Further, concerning the highest honours and prefectures being conferred on proven men, there is testimony in Aimoin, book 5, chapter 36, where he speaks of Charles the Bald: "Charles, who before his inauguration as king had distributed the prefectures at his own discretion, the nobles began to call a solemn council and to send envoys to the king; nor would they allow him to be crowned until he had used their council and authority in committing those magistracies. The chief men of the realm, indignant because he had given some honours without their consent, conspired against him and gathered their assembly in the town of Witmar; from there they sent envoys to Louis. But Louis also sent his envoys to them, etc." Likewise Regino, book 2: "Charles held an assembly at Compiègne, and there, with the counsel of the nobles, he committed to Count Robert the duchy between the Loire and the Seine." Likewise the Appendix to Gregory of Tours, book 11, chapter 54: "In that year, says the text, Clotaire joined with the chief men and vassals of Burgundy at Troyes, when he had urged them, if they were willing, to raise another man in place of the now dead Warnarius to that rank of honour; but all of them unanimously refused, saying they would by no means choose a mayor of the palace, and earnestly seeking the king's favour, they came to terms with the king." And chapter 101: "When King Theuderic died, the Franks chose his young son Clodoveus as king. Not many years later, when he died, his brother Childebert was restored to the kingdom; Grimoald, however, was chosen mayor of the palace over the Franks together with King Childebert." To the same category belong the disputes among the princes, which seemed likely to prove harmful to the commonwealth, and which were debated in that same council. For Aimoin, book 4, chapter 1, where he records Clotaire, son of Chilperic, from whom Brunhild demanded the kingdom of Austrasia, speaks thus: "Clotaire replied that she ought to gather an assembly of the Frankish nobles and consult them on common affairs by common deliberation. He promised that he would abide by their judgement in all things, and would not oppose their commands." The same Appendix to Gregory, book 11, recording this, says: "Clotaire, they say, replied that he had promised to carry out whatever should be decided among them by the judgement of the chosen Franks, by the Lord's leading." And in the same way, in Gregory, book 8, chapter 21, Bosso Gunthram is said to have been accused and condemned in a public council of the Franks for violating a tomb. "When Childebert had come together with his nobles for an assembly, says the text, and Gunthram, having been summoned concerning these matters, had secretly fled, his goods were taken away, which he had earned in Auvergne as a gift from the treasury." Again, Aimoin, book 5, chapter 12, where he speaks of King Louis the Pious, whom his sons harassed with hatred and quarrels: "When autumn weather was coming on, those who were opposed to the Emperor wished that a general assembly be held somewhere in France." Again, chapter 13: "He ordered his people to meet in general at the villa of Theodo." And shortly after: "But after a short time he called his people together again at the holy Martin's, and tried in some way to recall his son Pippin, who was fleeing to him, but the son refused." Gaguin, recalling this same matter, says: "But the conspirators, when they understood that they could not depose the king without the assembly of the nobles, strove with great effort to hold a council in France. Louis resisted nonetheless, because he knew the Franks had been persuaded against him by his enemies; therefore he called an assembly at Mainz, and ordered that no one be admitted to the council under arms. But lest the conspirators, with public sanction, should set the sons against their father, a council of bishops and nobles from the whole kingdom was gathered at Compiègne, and Lothar led his father, released from custody, to Compiègne." Again Aimoin, book 5, chapter 38, where he writes of King Louis the Bald, who held a council at Marsuas and was conferring with his cousin about peace: "In that very assembly, says the text, these things that follow were agreed between them to be kept with the consent of their faithful men. Now let us look at the rest." For I find it was also a custom that if any prince or one of higher birth were accused of some crime, he was summoned to judgement before that council and compelled to plead his cause there. So in the time of King Clotaire, when Brunhild was accused and condemned of many capital crimes, the king, with a council of France summoned, spoke to the orders thus, as in Aimoin, book 4, chapter 1: "You, most sweet comrades, and eminent chief men of France, decide to what punishment one bound by so great a crime is to be subjected." And Ado, Sixth Age, under the year 583: "In the presence of the king, with the Franks judging, she was tied to untamed horses and torn apart." Concerning the divisions of the royal patrimony and the appanages, there is testimony in Aimoin, book 5, chapter 94, where, speaking of Charlemagne, he says: "Those matters settled, the Emperor held an assembly with the chief men and nobles of the Franks to establish peace and to keep it among his sons, and to divide the kingdom into three parts, so that each of them should defend and rule his own part, if he survived him." Likewise, in the place where he speaks of the division made among the children of Louis, book 5, chapter 40: "They set out for Amiens, and, as their faithful men found them, divided the paternal kingdom among themselves." Likewise chapter 41, where he writes of Carloman, who was holding a council at Worms: "Hugh went to that assembly to ask for the part of the kingdom which his brother Louis had received in tenure." Moreover, from other passages one may observe that if a king intended to make greater expenditures, as in building temples or founding monasteries, he sought the counsel of the orders on these matters. For Aimoin, book 4, chapter 41, where he speaks of Clovis II, who sat on the tribunal at a solemn council, says: "He began his speech thus: Although the cares of earthly rule admonish us, Frankish citizens, to call you as counsellors on public affairs..." So far so good. From these things we think it is clear, as we said at the beginning, that our ancestors, who were truly Franks and guardians of liberty, did not set over themselves a tyrant or executioner who would hold their citizens in the place and number of cattle, but shrank from every tyrannical and Turkish lust for domination, and kept closely to that divine precept: THE SAFETY OF THE PEOPLE IS THE SUPREME LAW. For they placed the whole power of administering the kingdom in the greatest assembly and council of the orders, which, as we said before, they called the Placitum. So in the writer of the Chronicle of Besançon: "In the year 764 King Pippin held a great Placitum with the Franks at the village of Quierzy." The origin of this word, however, arose from this: in Latin usage the Placitum is properly that which, having been sought and deliberated in the counsel of many, at last is agreed upon among them; whence the "placita" of the philosophers in Cicero and other authors. Gellius, book 18, chapter 3: "The Lacedaemonian people, says the text, deliberated on what was useful and honourable for the commonwealth." And soon after: "The counsel that was given was accepted by all and found pleasing." Thus at Rome what the Senate had decreed by the opinion of the greater part of the senators was written down in these words: IT PLEASES THE SENATE, as is known to anyone both from other old senatorial decrees and from those things which are extant in our books, as in the law "Item veniunt," 20, §. "praeter haec," D. de hered. petit., and in law 2, D. ad Velleian., and nothing is more frequent in these same books than to be called a Placitum what has been agreed among some; as in law last, C. de pignorib.; "according to the tenor of the common military placitum," whence Placitum; for a convention in law 33, C. de transact.; law 11, C. de pact.; law 4, D. de servitut., and in six hundred other places. Since these things stand thus, our conjecture, which we have already set forth in some other books of ours, will not, I think, seem absurd: that the common formula, which the royal scribes even now use in the clauses of laws and constitutions, arose from that word PLACITUM: BECAUSE SUCH IS OUR PLACITUM. For when those documents were written in Latin letters (as is sufficiently clear from Aimoin and the Capitulary of Charlemagne, and from all the archives and monuments of Gaul), afterwards the royal scribes, when they began to use the vernacular, converted it thus, either through ignorance or rather through malice: Such is our pleasure: that is, because it so pleases us. For there is also an argument concerning the power of the people in the Capitulary of Charlemagne: "The people shall be asked about the chapters that have been newly added to the law; and after all have consented, they shall make their subscriptions and confirmations on those same chapters." From these words it is plain that the peoples of France were accustomed to be bound by those laws which they had sanctioned by their votes in the assemblies; this agrees with the definition of law which the jurist Marcian drew from Demosthenes in law 2, D. de legibus: "Law is a common compact of the city" [νόμος ἐστὶ πόλεως συνθήκη κοινή]: law is a pact and agreement of citizens, consulting the commonwealth and the public good. To the same effect is what stands at the end of the Alemannic Law: "This decree was made by the King and his princes, and by the whole Christian people who dwell within the kingdom of the Merovingians." Likewise in Aimoin, book 5, chapter 38: "In that very Placitum, these things that follow were agreed between them to be kept with the consent of their faithful men. The convention which was made between the glorious kings, etc., was made with the consent and approval of their faithful men and of the common people." But there is no surer proof of this matter than what we above quoted from the second book of the Law of the Franks, where Louis the Pious addresses all the orders of his kingdom thus: "Although the sum of royal ministry seems to consist in our person, yet it is known to be divided into parts both by divine authority and by human ordinance, so that each of you is known to have a part of our ministry in his own place and rank." Likewise in chapter 12: "Each of you is known to hold a part of our ministry in parts." Likewise in chapter 22: "In our Capitulary we have ordained on this matter by the common counsel of our faithful men." And chapter 24: "We also wish that the chapters which have now and at another time been established by us with the counsel of our faithful men be received by our Chancellor, the archbishops and the counts." Finally, this too must not be passed over: this council had such authority among foreign nations that even foreign princes, if they had any dispute, sometimes submitted it to the judgement of that council. Appendix to Gregory of Tours, book 11, chapter 37: "In the twelfth year of the reign of Theuderic, when Alsatia, where he had been brought up, was held by Theudebert under the command of his father Childebert, he was assailed in barbarous fashion; whence the two kings agreed to settle the dispute by the judgement of the Franks, at the fortress of Saloisso."

units.la: De Prafectis Regijs,qui Maiores do- mus dicebantur. CAP. XV.
units.tr: On the Royal Prefects, who were called Mayors of the Palace. CHAPTER XV.

units.la: PRiusquam de continuata Publici Concilij auctoritate plura exponamus,non prætermittenda commemoratio est de Regijs Præfectis,qui Merouingicis temporibus Maiores domus, hoc est, Magistri Palatij dicebantur: qui cum regiam potestatem aliquādiu obsedissent, aliquando tandem facultatem nacti, eam pro sua occuparunt. Eorum video eandem propè apud reges nostros dignitatem fuisse, qualis quondam apud Imperatores Romanos erat Præfectorum Prætorio: qui etiam Aulæ præfecti dicebantur. Creari autem eodem in Concilio & conuentu, quo reges ipsi solebant: publicique postea consilij auctores ac principes erant. Itaque passim apud Historicos nostros illa occurrunt: In principatum Maioris domus elegerunt. Item: Herchinoldo Maiore domus defuncto, Franci Ebroinū in hac dignitate, vt Maior esset in Aula regia, constituunt. Item: Hilderichum super se regem leuant, Maiorem domus, Wolfoldum. Quod ad superiorem proximam tractationem pertinet, vbi docuimus maiores quosq; magistratus non à rege pro suo arbitrio mādari, sed in soleni Concilio fidelissimis & probatissimis viris deferri solitos fuisse. Verùm in hoc magistratu idem plane vsuenit, quod Plutarchus in Lysandri vita tum accidisse scribit, cùm Agesilaus à Lacedæmonijs ad exercitum Imperator missus est: Lysander autem legatus: Vt in tragœdijs, inquit, plerunque vsuenit histrionibus, vt qui nuncij vel famuli personam sustinent, pluris fiant, primasque partes agant: illius verò qui sceptrum & diadema gestat, ne vox quidem exaudiatur: sic penes legatum Lysandrum maiestas imperij versabatur: penes Regem verò, nudum atque inane nomé manebat. Quod eodem modo in Francogallia nostra tū accidit: oblata videlicet occasione, & crescendi facultate ex regum aliquot inertia, de fidiaque: in quibus Dagobertus, Clodoueus, Clotarius, Childericus & Theodoricus numerari possunt. Nam Paulus Diaconus libro de gestis Langobardorum sexto capite quinto. Hoc tempore, inquit, apud Gallias Francorum regibus à solita fortitudine & scientia degenerantibus, ij qui Maiores domus regalis esse videbantur, administrare regis potentiam, & quicquid regib. agere mos est, coeperunt. Et in eandem sententiam auctor historiæ Francorum, quem Venericus Vercellensis aliquoties, sine nomine tamen, profert, ita scribit: Tempore Clotarij patris Dagoberti regnum Francorum regi cœptum est, & administrari ab his, qui Prouisores aulæ regiæ, vel Maiores domus esse videbantur. Quod idé Godfridus Viterbien. parte Chronic. 16. testatur. Itemque scriptor Chronici Besnensis monasterij: In illo tempore, inquit, deficientibus iam à pristino vigore regibus, cura totius regni administrabatur per duces & Principes domus. Itaque dum illi Magistri Palatij omnia Reipub. munera obirent, & siquod gerendum esset bellum, exercitibus præessent, hi domi nudo atque inani Regum nomine contenti, propter desidiam in otio viuebant. Tandemque eò progressa res est, vt Childerico rege xviii. regnum obtinente, Pipinus Magister Palatij, qui regis nomine magna diuturnaque bella gesserat, Saxones deuicerat, suamque in potestatem redegerat, oblatam regij nominis occupandi facultatem non repudiarit: exercitu præsertim, eoque victore & glorioso instructus. Quarum rerum apud Auctores testimonia hæc extant. Primum apud Ottonem Frisingensem Chronic. 5. capite 12. & imitatorem ipsius Godfridum Viterbiensem, part. 16. vbi sic scribunt: Reges Franciæ ante tempora Pipini Magni, qui Maior domus erat, expertes omnis administrationis & regiminis, solo nomine regnabant: sed Maiores domus vniuersam regni administrationem habebant. In eandem sententiam Sigebertus sub anno 662. & Lothario Clodouei filio ita loquitur: Ab hinc Francorum regibus à solita fortitudine & scientia degenerantibus, regni potentia disponebatur per Maiorem domus, regibus solo nomine regnantibus: quibus moris erat principari quidem secundum genus, & nil agere, vel disponere.
units.tr: Before I set out more on the continuing authority of the public council, I must not pass over a mention of the royal prefects, who in Merovingian times were called Mayors of the Palace, that is, Masters of the Palace. After they had for some time besieged the royal power, they at last gained the opportunity and seized it for themselves. I find that their dignity under our kings was nearly the same as that once held under the Roman emperors by the Prefects of the Praetorium, who were also called prefects of the court. They were created in the same council and assembly in which the kings themselves were customarily made, and afterwards they became the authors and leaders of public counsel. Thus our historians everywhere record such things as: "They chose him to the principate of the Mayor of the Palace." Also: "When Herchinoald, Mayor of the Palace, had died, the Franks set Ebroin in this office, so that he might be Mayor in the royal court." Also: "They raised Hilderich as king over themselves, and Wolfold as Mayor of the Palace." This bears on my previous discussion, where I showed that the greater magistrates were not appointed by the king at his own pleasure, but were customarily conferred in a solemn council upon the most faithful and approved men. But in this office the very same thing happened that Plutarch writes happened in the life of Lysander, when Agesilaus was sent by the Lacedaemonians as commander of the army and Lysander was his legate. "As often happens to actors in tragedies," he says, "those who play the messengers or servants become more important and take the leading parts, while the voice of the one who bears the sceptre and diadem is not even heard. So the majesty of command rested with the legate Lysander, while the king was left with a bare and empty name." The same thing happened in our Gaul at that time: the opportunity was offered, and the chance to grow arose from the sluggishness and weakness of some kings. Among these Dagobert, Clovis, Clothar, Childeric and Theuderic may be counted. For Paul the Deacon, in his book on the deeds of the Lombards, book 6, chapter 5: "At this time," he says, "in Gaul, the kings of the Franks, degenerating from their accustomed strength and wisdom, began to be governed by those who seemed to be the Mayors of the royal household, and they began to exercise the king's power and to do whatever it is customary for kings to do." To the same effect the author of the history of the Franks, whom Venerius of Vercelli cites several times though without naming him, writes thus: "In the time of Clothar, father of Dagobert, the kingdom of the Franks began to be ruled by those who seemed to be the stewards of the royal court or Mayors of the household." Godfrey of Viterbo attests the same in part 16 of his Chronicle, and so does the writer of the Chronicle of the monastery of Besnes: "At that time," he says, "the kings now having fallen from their former vigour, the care of the whole kingdom was administered by the dukes and princes of the household." So while those Masters of the Palace discharged all the public offices, and if any war had to be waged, commanded the armies, these kings, content at home with the bare and empty name of king, lived in idleness through sloth. At last matters went so far that, while Childeric held the kingdom in the eighteenth year, Pepin, Master of the Palace, who had waged great and long wars in the king's name, had conquered the Saxons and brought them under his power, did not refuse the opportunity offered him of seizing the royal name, especially as he had an army, and that a victorious and glorious one. Testimonies to these facts are extant among the authors. First in Otto of Freising, Chronicle book 5, chapter 12, and in his imitator Godfrey of Viterbo, part 16, where they write thus: "The kings of France before the times of Pepin the Great, who was Mayor of the household, were without any share in administration and government and reigned in name only; but the Mayors of the household had the whole administration of the kingdom." To the same effect Sigebert, under the year 662, speaks thus of Lothar, son of Clovis: "From then on, the kings of the Franks, degenerating from their accustomed strength and wisdom, saw the power of the kingdom disposed by the Mayor of the household, the kings reigning in name only; for it was their custom to rule by right of birth, and to do or arrange nothing."

units.la: Quanquā in hac commemoratione cautio adhibenda est. nam cùm & Pipinus & eius filij ob ereptum regi Childerico regnū inuidia (vt credi par est) laborarent, reperti sunt homines ingeniosi, qui & Childerici, & superiorum regum desidiam verbis maiorem facerent: inertiamq; grauius accusarent. In his Eguinarthus Caroli Magni Cācellarius, qui suo Imperatori strenuā in ea re operam nauauit. Nam initio sui libri ita scribit: Gens Merouingorum, de qua Franci reges sibi creari soliti erant, vsque in Hildericum regem, qui iussu Stephani Rom. Pontificis depositus ac detonsus, atque in monasterium trusus est, durasse putatur: quæ licet in illo finita pos-
units.tr: Yet caution must be used in this mention. For since both Pepin and his sons laboured under the envy (as is fitting to believe) of having snatched the kingdom from King Childeric, there were found clever men who made the sloth of Childeric and of the earlier kings greater in their words, and accused their inertia more severely. Among these was Eginhard, the chancellor of Charlemagne, who in this matter laboured strenuously for his emperor. For at the beginning of his book he writes thus: "The race of the Merovingians, from which the Franks were accustomed to create their kings, is thought to have lasted until King Childeric, who by order of Stephen, Roman Pontiff, was deposed and shorn and thrust into a monastery; and although this may seem to have ended then..."

units.la: fit videri, tamen iamdudum nullius vigoris erat, nec quicquam in se clarum, praeter inane regis vocabulum, praeferebat. Nam & opes & potentia Regni penes Palatij Praefectos, qui Maiores domus dicebantur, & ad quos summa imperij pertinebat, tenebantur: neque aliud Regi relinquebatur: quàm vt Regio tantùm nomine contentus, crine profuso, barba submissa, solio resideret, ac speciem dominatis effingeret, legatos undecunque venientes audiret, eisque abeuntibus responsa, quae erat doctus, vel etiam iussus, ex sua velut potestate redderet: cùm praeter inutile Regis nomen & precarium vitae stipendium quod ei praefectus Aulae, prout videbatur, exhibebat, nihil aliud proprij possideret, quàm vnam praeparui reditus villam: in qua & domum, ex qua famulos sibi necessaria ministrantes, atq; obsequium exhibentes paucae numerositatis habebat. His Eguinarthi verbis, quae in Appendice quoque Hunibaldi apud Tritenhemium reperio, inductus Sigebertus sub anno 662. eadem prope verborum contumelia superiores Reges insectatur: Quibus, inquit, moris erat principari quidem secundum genus, & nihil agere vel disponere, quàm irrationabiliter edere & bibere, domique morari. Quasi vero haec eadem Regum superiorum ratio, atque inertia fuerit: ac non potius virtus ac fortitudo animi singularis, qualem scriptores omnes in Clodoneo commemorant, qui non modò innumerabiles Germanorum copias, in Galliam irrumpentes, prælio propè Tolbiacum commisso, profligauit: verùm etiam Romanorum reliquias è Galliæ finibus propulsauit. Iam verò quid de Childeberto, & Clothario dicemus, qui Wisigothos & Ostrogothos è Provincia & Aquitania, vbi sedes fixerant, exterminarunt? Quorum omnium in historijs nulla Magistri Palatij, ne minima quidem mentio fit: nisi forte cursim atque obiter, & tanquam vnius è Regij Imperij administris, velut apud Gregor. lib.5. cap.18. vbi de Gucilio loquitur: & lib.6. cap.9. & cap.45. & lib.7.cap.29. itaque honosille non tantùm in Regis, verùm etiam in Reginæ aula & comitatu versabatur. Nam idem Gregor.lib.7.cap.27. Wadonem quendam nominat Maiorem domus in aula Reginæ Rigunthæ: alijsque locis compluribus idem Gregor. & Aimoinus Magistros aulæ domusque Regiæ commemorant. Tantæ autem illorum Regiorum præfectorum potentiæ initium (vt modò diximus) cœpit tempore Clotharij II. circiter annū Christi DLXXXVIII. id est, circiter CXXX. annis post Regnum Francogalliæ constitutum. Quod ex eo, quem Venericus aliquoties profert, historico licet cognoscere. Sunt tamen alij duo historici, sed nequaquam tantæ auctoritatis, Sigebertus & Tritenhemius, qui tantæ potentiæ initium ad Clotharij III. Regnum referunt: cuius Magister Palatij Ebroinus nominatur, homo nequitia & crudelitate insignis. Vtcunque fit, Historici alijs quoque nominibus præfectos illos appellabant: nimirum Magistros Regij palatij, Comites domus Regiæ, Præfectos aulæ, Comites Palatij, Duces & Principes domus: quinetiam aliquot post seculis Senefchalli Franciæ appellati sunt. Sigebertus sub anno MCLXX. In purificatione beatæ Mariæ fuit filius Regis Anglorum Parisijs, & seruiuit Regi Francorum ad mensam, vt Senefchallus Franciæ. Hanc Senefchalciam, vel (vt antiquitus dicebatur) Maioratum domus Regiæ Robertus Rex Francorum dedit Gaufrido, &c.
units.tr: "...yet for a long time it had been of no vigour, and showed nothing bright in itself beyond the empty title of king. For both the wealth and the power of the kingdom were held by the prefects of the palace, who were called Mayors of the household and to whom the supreme command belonged; nor was anything left to the king but that, content with the royal name alone, with his hair flowing loose and his beard long, he should sit on the throne and give the appearance of ruling, hear envoys coming from wherever, and give back to them on their departure the answers which he, as if from his own authority, had been taught or even ordered to give. Besides the useless name of king and the precarious allowance of life which the prefect of the court gave him as seemed fit, he possessed nothing of his own except one villa of small revenue, in which he had a house and a few servants supplying his needs and rendering service. Moved by these words of Eginhard, which I also find in the Appendix of Hunibald in Trithemius, Sigebert, under the year 662, assails the earlier kings with almost the same insulting language: "To whom," he says, "it was customary to rule by right of birth, and to do or arrange nothing, but to eat and drink without reason and to stay at home." As if this same conduct and inertia had indeed belonged to the earlier kings, and not rather the singular virtue and courage of spirit which all writers record of Clovis, who not only routed the innumerable German forces that broke into Gaul in a battle fought near Tolbiac, but also drove the remnants of the Romans from the borders of Gaul. What shall we say of Childebert and Clothar, who drove the Visigoths and Ostrogoths out of Provence and Aquitaine, where they had fixed their seats? Of all these deeds there is no mention in the histories of any Master of the Palace, not even the slightest, unless perhaps cursorily and in passing, and as of one of the ministers of the royal power, as in Gregory of Tours, book 5, chapter 18, where he speaks of Gucilio; and book 6, chapters 9 and 45; and book 7, chapter 29. So that office was found not only in the court and retinue of the king, but also in that of the queen. For the same Gregory, book 7, chapter 27, names a certain Wado as Mayor of the household in the court of Queen Brunhild; and in several other places Gregory and Aimoin mention the masters of the court and of the royal household. The beginning of the great power of those royal prefects (as I have just said) came in the time of Clothar II, about the year of Christ 588, that is, about 130 years after the kingdom of Gaul had been established. This may be learned from that historian whom Venerius cites several times. There are, however, two other historians, but of no such authority, Sigebert and Trithemius, who date the beginning of such great power to the reign of Clothar III, under whom Ebroin is named as Master of the Palace, a man notable for wickedness and cruelty. However that may be, historians called those prefects by other names as well: namely Masters of the royal palace, Counts of the royal household, Prefects of the court, Counts of the palace, Dukes and Princes of the household; and even some centuries later they were called Seneschals of France. Sigebert, under the year 1170: "On the feast of the purification of the blessed Mary, the son of the King of the English was at Paris, and he served the King of the Franks at table as Seneschal of France." This seneschalship, or (as it was called in ancient times) mayoralty of the royal household, King Robert of the Franks gave to Geoffrey, &c.

units.la: Utrum Pipinus Papa, an concilij Francogallici auctoritate Rex factus fuerit. CAP. XVI.
units.tr: Whether Pippin was made king by the authority of the Pope, or by the authority of the Gallic council. CHAPTER XVI.

units.la: QVoniam superius dictum est, Pipinum ex magistro Palatij Regem esse factum, exacto Childerico Rege stupido, in eoque Childerico Merouingiorum stirpem defecisse: non alienum est, hoc loco exquirere, cuiusnam auctoritate Regnum illi delatum fuerit. Nam Gelasius Papa in can. alius. 15. quæst. 6. Alius, inquit, Romanus Pontifex, Zacharias scilicet, Regem Francorum non tam pro suis iniquitatibus, quàm pro eo quòd tantæ potestati erat inutilis, à regno depositit: & Pipinum Caroli Imperatoris patrem in eius locum substituit: omnesque Francigenas à iuramento fidelitatis absoluit. Neque ferè quisquam est, qui non illud Papæ de semetipso testimonium approbarit: Ado, Lambertus, Regino, Sigebertus, Aimoinus, Landulphus. Quinetiam Venericus Vercellensis, in eo quem superius protulimus libro verba haec ex episto. Gregorij Papae v i i. ad Hermannum Metensem Episcopum profert. Quidam Romanus Pontifex Regem Francorum non tam pro suis iniquitatibus, quam pro eo quod tantae potestati non erat utilis, a regno depositi, & Pipinum in eius loco substituit, omnesque Francigenas a iuramento fidelitatis, quam illi fecerant, absoluit. Haec ille. Quod idem Otto Frising, commemorans libro Chronic. 5. capite 23. itemque Godfrid. Chronic. parte 17. ita exclamant: Ex hoc facto Romani Pontifices Regna mutandi auctoritatem trahunt. Sed videamus, ne huius historiae veritas non satis constet. nam primum omnium ex tanto Regum Francorum numero, quos vel creatos, vel abdicatos docuimus, neminem esse constat, Papae auctoritate vel creatum, vel abdicatum: contra vero docuimus ius illud omne & creandorum, & abdicandorum Regum, penes solenne gentis Concilium fuisse. ut plane incredibile videatur, Francos in hoc uno ius illud suum neglexisse. Quid verbis opus est? Venericus ille Vercellensis testimonium profert historici veteris, qui de gestis Francorum conscripserat: quo tota illa narratio mendacij coarguitur: dilucideq; affirmatur, & Childericum & Pipinum visitato Francorum more, veteriq; instituto, illum abdicatum: hunc autem in illius locum suffectum fuisse: hoc est, solenni gentis concilio: cuius solius tantum fuisse potestatem superius demonstrauimus. Illius autem historici verba haec sunt: Quòd vnà cum consilio & consensu omnium Francorum missa relatione ad sedem Apostolicam,& auctoritate percepta, praecelsus Pipinus electione totius gentis sublimatus sit in sedem Regni, cum consecratione Episcoporū,& subiectione Principum.Quibus ex verbis satis patet, Pipinum non à Papa,sed à populo ipso & Ordinibus ac Statibus Regni delectum, inauguratumque fuisse. Quod etiam paulò ante dilucidius idem Venericus ex eodem Historico sic exponit: Pipinum Maiorem Palatij cùm ad illum spectaret summa Regiae potestatis & officij,electum fuisse primùm ex praefectis palatij in Regem, atque ordinatum fuisse: prius super hoc experto Zachariae Papę iudicio: quia consensus & auctoritas Romani Pontificis necessaria huic videbatur negotio. Et mox: Quorum legatorum postulationem cùm aequâ atque vtilem Zacharias Papa iudicassset, ad ea quae postulabant consensit,& Pipinus factus est Rex communi suffragio Principum. In eandem sententiam Ado Viennensis Æt. vi. sub anno 727. ita scribit: Missi legati ad Zachariam, vt interrogarent eum, si ita manere deberent Reges Francorum, cùm penè nullius potestatis essent, iam solo Regio nomine contenti. Quibus Zacharias Pontifex responsum dedit, Regem potius illum debere vocari,qui Remp. regeret. Reuersis legatis, abiectoque Childerico, qui tunc Regium nomen habebat, Franci per consilium legatorum & Zachariæ Pontificis electum Pipinum Regem sibi constituunt. Præter illos superiores extat Aimoini testimonium in eandem sententiam lib. 4. cap. 61. vbi ad extremum ita concludit: Hoc anno Pipinus Rex Francorum appellatus est, & more Francorū eleuatus in solio Regni, in Sueßionū ciuitate. Sed & Godfrid. Viterbiē. Chro. parte 17. c. 4. Pipinus, inquit, per Papā Zachariā ex electione Francorū rex factus est Francorum, Hildrico ignauo Rege per Francos in monasterium missō. Horum similia dilucidè scripserunt Sigebertus sub anno 752. auctores historiæ Miscell. lib. 22.
