Item Otto Frising. lib. 5. cap. 21. 22. 23. & auctor libri cui titulus est, Fasciculus temporum: Ex quibus omnibus facilè intellectu est, Non si Franci Pipinum exquisita Papæ sententia Regé crearunt, iccirco illum Papæ imperio atque auctoritate creatum fuisse. Aliud est enim Regem creare, aliud creandi consilium dare; aliud ius creandi habere, aliud ius consilij dandi. quanquam consilij in huiusmodi rebus dandi ius nemo habet, nisi is à quo petitur. Proseram etiam testimonium insigne, quod mihi ex veteri quodā manuscripto incerti auctoris libro missum est, in quo hæc Archiepiscopi Maguntinensis ad Pipinum oratio profertur: Galli omnium ordinum consensu hoc diadema regium cum oneris, tum honoris insigne capiti tuo mea manu inferunt: teque spolijs Childerici exornant, cuius non familiam aut maiorum memoriam, sed perditissimos mores oderunt, tu? virtutis lucem suspiciunt & amant. Quod si tantum lumen in te extingui superbia, aut obscurari ignauia ferferint, quid de te illos facturos putas, quorum beneficio stabis, qui in eum qui suo iure, non alieno beneficio regnum obtinebat, tam seuerum exercuerunt iudicium? Disce igitur Pipine, alieno exemplo, atque periculo, Regem agere, hoc est omnem curam & cogitationem in salute populi tui collocare. Denique nemo dilucidius totam hanc rem explicat Marsilio Patauino, qui imperante Ludouico Bauaro librum de translatione imperij conscripsit: in quo, cap. 6. ita loquitur: Pipinus filius Caroli Martelli, vir in rebus bellicis strenuus, legitur à Zacharia Papa in Regni Francorum excellentiam sublimatus. Sed Aimoinus in Gestis Francorum scribit, & verius, Pipinum per Francos legitimè in Regem electum, & per Regni Proceres leuatum. Childericus verò, qui tum sub nomine Regio in delitijs marcescebat, fuit in monachum tonsoratus. Vnde non illum Zacharias depositi, sed deponentibus (vt quidam aiunt) consensit. Nam talis depositio Regis, & alterius institutio, propter rationabilem causam, non ad Episcopum tantummodo, neque ad clericum aliquem, aut clericorum collegium pertinet, sed ad vniuersitatem ciuium inhabitantium regionem, vel nobilium, vel ipsorum valentiorem multitudinem. Hæc Marsilius. quibus consentaneum postea reperi locum in Appendice Hunibaldi, apud Iohann. Tritenhemium: vbi scriptum ita est: Eodem anno proceres totius Regni conuenientes in vnum super abrogatione Regis Hildericiinutilis,cœperunt habere consilium. placuit autem in commune omnibus, vt Regem Hildericum nullam regnandi vel peritiam, vel potestatem habentem deponerent: & Pipinum penes quem totius regni summa manebat auctoritas, in regem sublimarent. Sed Pipinus in hanc rem consentire noluit, nisi prius consilium Romani Pontificis Zachariæ inquiratur, causas allegans se monentes. Hæc ille. Paparum igitur commentum impudens de iure Regum vel creandorum, vel abdicandorum, perspicuum omnibus esse arbitror. Sed præter commentum, quod improbitatis & impudentiæ documentum est certissimum, operæpretium est,insignem quandam Stephani Papæ epistolam ad hanc fabulam accommodatam proponere, ex qua de veteratoris illius stoliditate & vesania existimare liceat.
units.tr: Since I have said above that Pippin was made king from the office of mayor of the palace, after King Childeric, a dull man, had been deposed, and that the line of the Merovingians ended with Childeric, it is not out of place to inquire here by whose authority the kingdom was offered to him. For Pope Gelasius, in can. alius, 15. quaest. 6, says: "Another Roman Pontiff, namely Zachary, deposed the King of the Franks from his kingdom, not so much for his wrongdoings as because he was useless for so great a power, and he put Pippin, father of the Emperor Charles, in his place, and absolved all the Franks from their oath of fidelity." Almost nobody fails to approve this testimony of the Pope about himself: Ado, Lambert, Regino, Sigebert, Aimoin, Landulf. Moreover, Venericus of Vercelli, in the book I cited above, gives these words from the letter of Pope Gregory VII to Hermann, Bishop of Metz: "A certain Roman Pontiff deposed the King of the Franks from the kingdom, not so much for his wrongdoings as because he was not useful for so great a power, and put Pippin in his place, and absolved all the Franks from the oath of fidelity which they had sworn to him." So he. Otto of Freising, recalling this in book 5 of his Chronicle, chapter 23, and likewise Godfrey in part 17 of his Chronicle, cry out: "From this deed the Roman Pontiffs derive their authority to change kingdoms." But let us see that the truth of this history is not left insufficiently established. For first of all, out of so great a number of kings of the Franks, whom I have shown to have been either created or deposed, it is agreed that none was created or deposed by the Pope's authority; on the contrary, I have shown that all that right of creating and deposing kings rested with the solemn council of the nation. So it seems wholly incredible that the Franks, alone in this matter, neglected their right. Why need I say more? That Venericus of Vercelli produces the testimony of an ancient historian who had written about the deeds of the Franks, by which whole tale of that story is refuted as a lie, and it is clearly affirmed that both Childeric and Pippin were deposed and installed respectively according to the custom and ancient institution of the Franks, that is, by the solemn council of the nation, whose sole power I have shown above. The words of that historian are these: "Because, together with the counsel and consent of all the Franks, a report having been sent to the Apostolic See and authority received, the most exalted Pippin was raised by the election of the whole nation to the throne of the kingdom, with the consecration of bishops and the submission of the nobles." From these words it is sufficiently clear that Pippin was chosen and inaugurated not by the Pope but by the people itself and by the orders and estates of the kingdom. The same Venericus, a little earlier, sets this out even more clearly from the same historian: "Pippin, the mayor of the palace, to whom the supreme power and office of the royal authority belonged, was first chosen from the prefects of the palace and made king, and this was done only after the judgment of Pope Zachary had been obtained, because the consent and authority of the Roman Pontiff seemed necessary to this matter." And soon after: "When Pope Zachary judged the request of these envoys to be fair and useful, he agreed to what they asked, and Pippin was made king by the common suffrage of the nobles." Ado of Vienne, in his Sixth Age, under the year 727, writes to the same effect: "Envoys were sent to Zachary to ask him whether the kings of the Franks ought to remain as they were, since they had almost no power, being content now with the royal name alone. To them Zachary the Pontiff gave the answer that he ought rather to be called king who governs the commonwealth. When the envoys returned, Childeric, who then bore the royal name, being cast off, the Franks, by the counsel of the envoys and of Pope Zachary, set up Pippin as king for themselves." Besides these, there is the testimony of Aimoin to the same effect in book 4, chapter 61, where at the end he concludes thus: "In this year Pippin was called King of the Franks, and, after the manner of the Franks, was raised on the throne of the kingdom, in the city of Soissons." But also Godfrey of Viterbo, Chronicle part 17, chapter 4: "Pippin," he says, "was made king of the Franks by Pope Zachary, by the election of the Franks, Childeric the sluggard being sent by the Franks into a monastery." Sigebert under the year 752, the authors of the Historia Miscella in book 22, likewise Otto of Freising in book 5, chapters 21, 22 and 23, and the author of the book entitled Fasciculus Temporum have written similar things clearly. From all these it is easily understood that it does not follow, because the Franks created Pippin king after seeking the Pope's opinion, that he was therefore created by the Pope's command and authority. For it is one thing to create a king, another to give counsel about creating him; one thing to have the right of creating, another the right of giving counsel. Although, indeed, no one has the right of giving counsel in such matters except the one from whom it is sought. I shall also set forth a notable testimony, which was sent to me from an old manuscript book by an unknown author, in which the following speech of the Archbishop of Mainz to Pippin is recorded: "The Gauls, with the consent of all orders, place this royal diadem on your head with my hand, a sign both of burden and of honour; and they adorn you with the spoils of Childeric, whose family and ancestral memory they do not care for, but whose utterly depraved morals they hate. They look up to you and love you as the light of virtue. But if they have seen that such light in you is to be quenched by pride or dimmed by sloth, what do you think they will do to you, by whose favour you stand, who exercised so severe a judgment upon him who held the kingdom by his own right and not by another's favour? Learn therefore, Pippin, from another's example and danger, to act as king, that is, to place all your care and thought in the welfare of your people." Finally, no one explains this whole matter more clearly than Marsilius of Padua, who wrote the book on the transfer of empire under the reign of Louis of Bavaria. In it, in chapter 6, he speaks thus: "Pippin, son of Charles Martel, a man vigorous in warlike affairs, is read to have been raised by Pope Zachary to the eminence of the kingdom of the Franks. But Aimoin in his Deeds of the Franks writes, and more truly, that Pippin was lawfully chosen king by the Franks and raised up by the nobles of the kingdom. Childeric, however, who then languished in pleasures under the royal name, was shorn as a monk. Hence it was not Zachary who deposed him, but he consented to his deposition by those who deposed him (as some say). For such a deposition of a king, and the installation of another, for a reasonable cause, belongs not to a bishop alone, nor to any cleric or college of clerics, but to the whole body of citizens inhabiting the region, or to its nobles, or to the greater part of them." So Marsilius. With these things there is agreement in a passage I later found in the Appendix to Hunibald, in Johannes Trithemius, where it is written thus: "In that same year the nobles of the whole kingdom, assembling together, began to take counsel about removing King Childeric, who was useless. It pleased all in common that they should depose King Childeric, who had neither skill nor power in ruling, and raise Pippin, in whom the highest authority of the whole kingdom remained, to be king. But Pippin was unwilling to consent to this matter unless first the counsel of the Roman Pontiff Zachary were sought, giving as his reasons that they should consult him." So he. I think, therefore, that the shameless fiction of the Popes concerning the right of creating or deposing kings is clear to all. But besides this fiction, which is a most certain proof of impudence and shamelessness, it is worth while to set forth a notable letter of Pope Stephen, adapted to this fable, from which one may judge the stupidity and madness of that deceiver.

units.la: Extat autem apud Reginonem, monachum ordinis Benedictini, Abbatem Pruniacensem, testem in hoc genere irrefragabilem: in Chronic. anni DCCCLIII.
units.tr: This is found in Regino, a monk of the Benedictine order and abbot of Prüm, an unanswerable witness in this matter, in his Chronicle for the year 853.

units.la: STEPHANVS Episcopus, seruus seruorum Dei. Sicut nemo se debet iactare de suis meritis, sic non debent opera Dei, quæ in illo per suos sanctos fiunt, sine suis meritis sileri, sed prædicari: sicut angelus admonet Thobiam. Vnde ego pro oppressione sanctæ Ecclesiæ à Rege atrocissimo & blasphemo & nec dicendo Haistolpho, ad optimum & Sancti Petri fidelë Dominum Pipinum, Christianissimum Regem, in Franciam veni: vbi ægrotaui vsque ad mortem: & mansi aliquod tempus apud pagum Parisiacum, in venerabili monasterio Sancti Dionysij martyris: quem, cùm iam medici desperarent, fui sicut in oratione in Ecclesia eiusdem beati martyris subtus campanis: & vidi ante altare Dominum Petrum, & Magistrum gentiũ Dominum Paulum: & tota mente illos recognoui de illorum surcarijs: & tunc Beatum Dominum Dionysium ad dextram Domini Petri, subtilem & longiorem. dixitque bonus Pastor Dominus Petrus: Hic frater noster postulat sanitatē: & dixit beatus Paulus: Modò sanabitur. & appropinquās misit manum suam ad pectus Domini Dionysij amicabiliter, respexitque ad Dominum Petrum: & dixit Dominus Petrus ad Dominum Dionysium hilariter: Tua gratia est sanitas eius. Et statim Dominus Dionysius thuribulum incensi, & palmam in manu tenens cum presbytero & diacono, qui in parte stabat, venit ad me, & dixit: Pax tecum frater, noli timere. non morieris donec ad sedem tuam prosperè reuertaris: Surge sanus, & hoc altare in honorem Dei & Apostolorum Petri & Pauli, quos vides, dedica. missas gratiarū agens, moxque factus sum sanus: & volebā implere, quod mihi præceptum erat, & dicebant, qui ibi aderant, quòd dementabam. Quapropter retuli illis & Regi, suisque omnibus ex ordine quæ videram, & quomodo sanatus fuerim, & impleui quæ visa sunt mihi omnia. Gesta sunt autem hæc anno ab incarnatione Domini DCCLIII. v. Id. Aug. quo Christi roboratus virtute, inter celebrationem consecrationis prefati altaris, & oblationem sacrificij vnxi in Reges Francorum Regem Pipinum, & duos filios eius, Carolum & Carolomannum. Sed & Bertrandam coniugem ipsius Regis, indutam cycladibus regijs, & gratia spiritus sancti septiformis consignaui in Dei nomine: atque Francorum proceres Apostolica benedictione sanctificans, auctoritate S. Petri sibi à Christo tradita obligauit, & obtestatus est, vt nunquam de altera stirpe per succedentium temporum curricula, ipsi vel quique ex eorum progenie orti, Regem super se præsumant aliquo modo constituere nisi de eorū progenie. Hæc Papa Stephanus: cuius cū ridicula bonis omnibus vesania videri debet, tum etiam detestanda illa execratio, qua in eorum caput vtitur, qui non ex Caroli Magni stirpe pgnati regnum obtinerent. vt vel vnicus ille locus insignem eius libelli stoliditatem coarguat, quem Matharellus nescio quis, rabula impudes & impurus, aduersus hanc nostram Francogalliam nuper edidit: & in quo stultissimam illam Papæ Stephani epistolam comprobat, dignissimumque & illum & alterum nescio quem Papirium Massonum, Iesuitam Bardocucullum, & Sycophantâ mercede conductum ostendat, qui in Mathurini Parisiensis fano, vbi eiusmodi fanatici curantur, flagris ad necem cedantur.
units.tr: STEPHEN, bishop, servant of the servants of God. Just as no one ought to boast of his own merits, so the works of God that are done in him through his saints ought not to be passed over in silence without their merits being proclaimed, as the angel admonished Tobias. Therefore, because of the oppression of the holy Church by the most savage and blasphemous king, whom I will not even name, Haistolphus, I came into France to the most excellent Lord Pippin, the Christian King and faithful to Saint Peter. There I fell ill unto death and stayed for some time in the district of Paris, in the venerable monastery of Saint Dionysius the martyr. When the physicians had already given up hope, I prayed in the church of that blessed martyr, beneath the bells, and I saw before the altar Lord Peter and the teacher of the nations, Lord Paul. With my whole mind I recognised them by their vestments. Then the blessed Lord Dionysius stood at the right hand of Lord Peter, tall and slender. The good Shepherd, Lord Peter, said: "This brother of ours asks for health." And blessed Paul said: "He shall now be healed." Drawing near, he laid his hand kindly on the breast of Lord Dionysius and looked toward Lord Peter, and Lord Peter said cheerfully to Lord Dionysius: "His health is by your grace." Immediately Lord Dionysius, holding a censer and a palm in his hand, came to me with a priest and a deacon who stood on one side, and said: "Peace be with you, brother; do not fear. You shall not die until you return prosperously to your see. Rise up healed, and dedicate this altar to the honour of God and of the Apostles Peter and Paul, whom you see." I gave thanks and celebrated Mass, and at once I was made whole. I wished to carry out what had been commanded me, but those who were present said that I was raving. Therefore I related to them and to the King, and to all his people, in order, what I had seen and how I was healed, and I carried out everything that had been shown to me. These things were done in the year of the Lord's incarnation 753, on the fifth day before the Ides of August, when, strengthened by the power of Christ, during the celebration of the consecration of the aforesaid altar and the offering of the sacrifice, I anointed Pippin as King of the Franks, and his two sons, Charles and Carloman. I also signed with the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit, in the name of God, the wife of the same King, Bertrada, clothed in royal robes. Sanctifying the nobles of the Franks with Apostolic blessing, by the authority of Saint Peter delivered to him by Christ, I bound them and adjured them that never, through the course of succeeding times, should they or any of their descendants presume in any way to set over themselves a king who was not of their line. Thus Pope Stephen. This is a fantasy that must seem ridiculous to all good men, and that curse which he pronounces upon the heads of those who should obtain the kingdom without being born of the stock of Charlemagne is no less detestable. Indeed that single passage alone refutes the remarkable stupidity of that pamphlet which some Matharellus, I know not who, an impudent and impure wrangler, lately published against this our France of the Gauls, and in which he vouches for that most foolish letter of Pope Stephen. It shows him, and another I know not who, Papirius Masson, the Jesuit Bardocucullus, a sycophant hired for pay, to be most worthy of being whipped to death in the shrine of Saint Mathurin of Paris, where people of this kind of frenzy are cured.
On the Constable and the Peers of France.

units.la: PRæter illam Magistri Palatij dignitatem, de qua superius diximus, fuit & altera, de qua iccirco dicendum hoc loco est, quia non multis ab hinc seculis, sed prope Maiorum nostrorum memoria, videtur in illius locum successisse. Erant enim Comites stabuli Regij, vnde Comestabuli, ad extremum Connestablij postea, corrupto nomine, dicti sunt. Comites autem posteriorum Imperatorum Romanorum ætate vulgò dicebantur omnes, qui amplissimos quosque honores in Regia obtinebant: & Rempublicam pro parte administrabant: à qua consuetudine veteres non abhorruisse, alijs quibusdam libris nostris docuimus. Sic enim Cicero Callisthenem Alexandri Magni Comitem non vno loco appellat. Erat autem Comes stabuli, fere is, qui apud Romanos Magister equitum dicebatur: hoc est, qui equitatui præerat: cui custodes regiorum equorum subërât, quos vulgo Scutieros appellamus. Gregor. Turon. lib. 5. cap. 39. Thesaurarius Clodouei à Cuppane Stabuli comite de Biturigo retractus, vinctus Reginæ transmissus est. Et rursus capite 48. vbi de Leudaste loquitur: Quæ libenter eum colligens provocat, equorumque meliorum deputat esse custodem. Hinc iam obsessus vanitate, & superbiæ deditus, Comitatum ambit stabulorum: quo accepto, cunctos despicit ac postponit. Quibus ex locis apparet, custodiam equorum præfecturam fuisse honestissimam, sed multo ampliorem Comitatum Stabulorum. Cuius rei Aimoinus quoque auctor est libro 3. capite 43. ubi de eodem Leudaste loquitur: Reginæ familiarissimus factus, custos equorum efficitur. Inde Comitatum super ceteros nactus custodes, post mortem Reginæ Comitatum Thuronicum à Chariberto percepit. Et rursus capite 70. Leudegisilus Regalium præfectus equorum, quem vulgo Connestabilem vocant, quemque Rex ei præfecerat expeditioni, machinamenta deduci imperat. Item libro quarto capite 95. ubi de Carolo Magno loquitur: Eodemque anno Burchardü Comite Stabuli sui cum classe misit in Corsicam. Quod Regino libro 2. commemorans: Eodem anno, inquit, Burchardum Comitem Stabuli sui, quem corrupte Constabulum appellamus, cum classe misit in Corsicam. Hunc autem Appendix Gregorij Comestabulum appellat, libro undecimo: Brunechildis, inquit, ab Erporre Comestabulo de pago producitur. Quod cum ita esset, Albert. Krantzius lib. Suet. 5. capite 41. ausus est Connestablium affirmare, eundem esse, quem Germani Marschallum appellant. Gubernatorem, inquit, appellauere ex Optimis militem, qui conuocandis
units.tr: Besides that office of Master of the Palace, of which we spoke above, there was another, which must be discussed here because it seems to have taken the place of the former not many centuries ago, but within the memory of our forefathers. For there were Counts of the Stable (comites stabuli regii), whence the Comestables, and finally, with the name corrupted, the Connestables. In the age of the later Roman emperors, all who held the highest offices at court and administered some part of the state were commonly called counts. We have shown in other books of ours that the ancients did not shrink from this usage. Thus Cicero calls Callisthenes, the companion of Alexander the Great, a count in more than one place. The Count of the Stable was generally the one who among the Romans was called Master of the Horse, that is, the commander of the cavalry, and under him were the keepers of the royal horses, whom we commonly call esquires. Gregory of Tours, book 5, chapter 39: Chlodovech's treasurer was taken from Count of the Stable Cuppanus of Bourges, bound, and sent to the queen. And again, chapter 48, where he speaks of Leudast: Gathering him up gladly, she summons him and appoints him keeper of the better horses. Already possessed by vanity and given over to pride, he now aspires to the countship of the stables; having obtained it, he looks down on and disregards everyone. From these passages it appears that the keeping of the horses was a most honourable charge, but the countship of the stables was much greater. Aimoin also vouches for this, book 3, chapter 43, where he speaks of the same Leudast: Made most intimate with the queen, he becomes keeper of the horses. Then, having obtained the countship over the other keepers, after the queen's death he received from Charibert the countship of Tours. And again, chapter 70: Leudegisil, prefect of the royal horses, whom they commonly call the Connestable, and whom the king had set over that expedition, orders the siege engines to be brought up. Likewise book 4, chapter 95, where he speaks of Charlemagne: In the same year he sent Burchard, Count of his Stable, with a fleet to Corsica. Regino, recalling this in book 2, says: In the same year, he says, he sent Burchard, Count of his Stable, whom we corruptly call the Constable, with a fleet to Corsica. The Appendix to Gregory, however, calls him Comestable in book 11: Brunechildis, he says, is led out from the district by Erporr the Comestable. Since this was so, Albert Krantz, in book 5 of the Suevic history, chapter 41, ventured to assert that the Connestable is the same as what the Germans call the Marschall. Among the best men, he says, they called a soldier a governor, who has the power of convening the assemblies of the kingdom and of managing all affairs in the place of the prince. Our people call him the Marefchal; the French call him the Connestable. So he writes, and these views may perhaps seem more probable for this reason, that I observe no mention of Marshals in our France in ancient times; so that it is likely that the later kings instituted that office...

units.la: Regni cœtibus & omnia vice Principis gerendi habeat potestatem. Marefchalcum nostri vocant: Galli Connestabulum. Hæc ille, quæ fortassis eo probabiliora videri possunt, quod Marefchallorum nullam in Francogallia nostra mentionem antiquitus animaduerto: vt verisimile sit, Regum posteriorum institutum illud fuisse, ad Germanorum consuetudinem accómodatum. Vtcunque sit, vetus hoc verbum esse patet etiam ex Annalib. Anglicis Thomæ Walsinghamij: vbi sub anno 1293. ita scribit: Moxque Rex Francorum præcepit constabulario Franciæ, vt in manu armata ducatum Aquitaniæ regis Francorum nomine occuparet. Hūc autem stabulorum Comitatum non dubito à Romanorum Imperat. instituto natum fuisse: etsi ex paruis initijs tandem moribus nostris ad præfecturæ prætoriæ dignitatem excreuit. Erat autem per illa tempora dignitas hæc tanquam militaris Tribunatus. Ammia. li. 26. vbi de Imp. Valentiniano loquitur: Nicomediam itineribus certis ingressus, Kalen. Martijs Valentem fratrem stabulo suo cum Tribunatus dignitate præfecit. Eius dignitatis in Cod. Iustiniani mentio fit l. 1. C. de comitibus & tribunis schol. vbi magni honoris loco illis tribuitur, vt Imperatoris epulis præesse, & purpuram eius adorare possint. Itemque in l. 3. C. Theodos. de annon. & tribut. & l. perpensa, 29. Cod. Theodos. de equor. collat. & l. 1. C. Theo. qui à præbit. tyron. vbi ius illis conceditur sportulas exigendi à prouincialibus, qui militares equos ad vsum Imperatoris conferebant. Superest, vt de ijs magistratibus differamus, qui vulgo PARES FRANCIÆ nominantur: quanquam nobis quidem non studium, sed monimentorum facultas deest. Nam ex tanto librorum numero, qui Francogalliæ Annales & Chronica dicuntur, ne vnus quidem adhuc editus est, in quo probabilis aliqua illius instituti ratio pferatur. Quod enim Guaguinus & Italus quidam Paulus Æmilius non tam Regum Gallię historicus, quam Paparum assentator mercenarius, & alij nescio qui vulgo scribunt, magistratus illos vel à Pipino, vel à Carolo Magno institutos fuisse: id plane abfurdū esse, vel hinc licet intelligatur, quòd ex tam multis Germanis Historicis, qui regum illorum ætate, aut paulò infra eorum ætatem historias scripserunt, nullus plane Magiftratum illorum mentionem vel tenuissimam interponit. Quinetiam Aimoini de Francorum institutis & rebus gestis historia, vsque ad Ludouici Pij, eiufq; Appendix ad Ludouici Iunioris Regis xxxvii. ætatem perducta, nusquam horum Pariūm mentionem facit. Quare tantisper dum certius aliquid afferatur, institutū ad illud Hugonis Capetti regnum referendum arbitrabor: qui cùm remoto herede legitimo regnum occupasset, proceres aliquot nouo quodam honore ac beneficio sibi deuinciendos putauit. nam eiusmodi aliquid ab illo factum omnes consentiunt. Eius autem instituti exemplum facilè intelligitur ex Feudali iure sumptū fuisse: quo iure Vassalli qui ab eodem Seniore ac patrono feuda receperunt, Pares inter se, hoc est, quasi ὁμότιμοι, appellantur. quorum triplex hæc potestas est: primum, vt qui in vassallorum ordinem cooptantur, pro eorum collegio cooptentur: lib. Feud. 2. titul. 2. tum vt rogati testimonium de investitura dicant: libro 2. titulo decimonono. postremò, vt si qua vel inter ipsos, vel inter Seniorem & inter ipsos controuersia exoriatur, ipsi iudicium & ciuile & criminale exerceant. libro secundo, titul. 46. & titul. 52. & titul. 55. Et profectò ita est, vt Pares Franciæ hoc iure sint: primum vt neque inaugurari, nisi pro collegio, neque abdicari, nisi causa in consilio cognita, neque ad aliud vllum nisi ad collegarum iudicium, vocari possint. quanquam Parisiensis Senatus hanc sibi auctoritatem asciuit, vt Pares causam apud se dicere iubeat. Ac Budæus quidem vir longè doctissimus, Pares illos Patritiorum nomine appellat: scribitque videri sibi ab vno aliquo Rege institutos, ex eorum numero, qui Germanicum Imperium obtinuerunt: propter ea quod Iustinianus Patres eos ab imperatore delectos esse ait, quasi Reipubl. patronos, tutoresque. Ego verò doctissimi viri sententiam non aspernor: præsertim à Parium dignitate non alienam. Fuit enim Romanorum Imperat. posteriorum ætate Patritiatus, dignitas ab illa Parium non admodum dissimilis: partim quòd Reipublicæ quodammodo patres erant, vt Suidas testatur: & de summis quibusque rebus ab Imperatore consulebantur: insignibusq; ijsdem, quibus Consules, vtebantur: ac maiorem quidem Præfecto Prætorio, minorem autem Consule, honorem atque auctoritatem habebant. Quod ex Iustiniani Nouellis, & Sidonio Apollinari, & Claudiano, & Cassiodoro præsertim cognosci potest. Sed translato in Germanos Imperij nomine, vsurpatum hunc honorem non arbitror. neque verisimile est, vllos eiusmodi Patritios ab aliquo Germanico Imperatore, qui idem Francogalliæ Rex esset, institutos fuisse, vt non aliquis ex Germanis historicis eius mentionem fecisset. Denique idem Budæus, eodem loco haesitans, commemorat eiusmodi Parium dignitatem apud ceteras quoque vicinas gentes fuisse: atque in Regijs Commentarijs scriptum esse, anno MCCXXIIII. Ioannem quendam Nigellanum Flandrum, cui controuersia in Flandria illata esset à Comitissa Flandriæ, ad Pares Franciæ appellasse: quòd æquo iudicio apud Pares Flandriæ certare se non posse iurasset. cumque à Comitissa ad Patium Flandriæ iudicium revocaretur, tandem certis de causis decretum fuisse, vt ea controuersia ad Pares Franciæ introduceretur. Causa autem translati iudicij cuiusmodi fuerit, neque Budæus exponit: & qui in iure feudali versatus fuisset, nunquâ praetermisisset. Verù vt iâ huius magistratus institutum paulo planius ac certius exponamus: primum omnium, vt iam antè dixi, constare inter omnes arbitror, nullam Parium nominis, neque apud Germanos, neq; apud Gallos historicos ante Capeuingiorum regum métionem inueniri. Sed quoniam eruta quædam nuper vetustatis monimenta video, atque in lucem edita, in quibus illorum Parium iura nō minima ex parte designantur, operæpretium esse arbitror quæ ex illis commentarijs obseruauimus, breuiter exponere: idque eo lubentius, quod ab eo ipso, à quo illi commentarij nuper euulgati sunt, in aliam partem ac veritas & ratio postulat, contorquentur. Ergo eorum quidem instituendorum caussam duplicem video fuisse: primùm, vt regis inauguration i atque (vt tum loquebantur) inuestituræ præessent. hoc est, vt regem imperij sui insignibus, atque insulis, solenniter in Principum atque Optimatum conuentu exornarent. deinde vt si quis è Potentium & Principum Franciæ numero fraudis capitalis reus fieret, iudicium illud exercerent. nā cùm antiquitus ea iudicia in publico Gentis Có cilio exercerentur (vt superius copiosè demonstratum est) atque is mos Maiorum paulatim Capeuingiorum instituto ad iuridiciale parlamētum (de quo posterius dicemus) traduci cœpisset: neq; Principes regni facilè illi parlamento suas fortunas committendas putaret, Regibus illis ad suas rationes commodissimum fore visum est, præter illius parlamenti curiam, suū hunc Parium confessum instituere, quæ Parium curia vocitata est: quorum tamen ordo ac numerus aliquandiu varius fuit. neque enim Duodecim viri semper fuerunt, vt eos ipsos à quibus hæc monimenta prolata sunt, ariolari video: sed interdum plures, interdum pauciores erant: prout Regi, à quo in summi honoris ac beneficij loco magistratus ille deferebatur, commodum videbatur. Id quod ex infrascriptis monimentis cognoscere licebit: quorum antiquissimum est sub anno MCCXVI. hoc est sub Rege Ludouico Crasso: Iudicatum est à Paribus Regni nostri, videlicet à Rhemensi Archiepiscopo, Wilel. Lingonen. Guillelmo Catha-launensi, Ph. Beluacensi, Stephano Noviomensi episcopis, & Odone Duce Burgundiæ, & à multis aliis Episcopis & Baronibus nostris, videlicet Altisiod. R. Carnot. G. Siluanect. & I. Lexouiensi Episcopis, & Comite Pontiui, R. Comite Drocarum, B. Comite Britanniæ, C. Comite S. Pauli, Wil. de rupibus. Senesc. Andeg. Wil. Comite Iuuigniaci, I. Comite Bellimontis, & R. Comite Alencon. nobis audientibus, & iudicium adprobantibus, &c. Quibus ex verbis cognosci potest, non eosdem fuisse per id tempus Pares Franciæ, qui posteriorib. temporibus fuerunt: magnamque illorum partem, pro illorum temporum superstitione, Archiepisc. & Episcopos fuisse. Nam cum Episcopales sedes ijs in locis constituerentur, quibus opima & fructuosa prædia & tanquam satrapiæ attributæ Regum liberalitate fuerant, facilè cum illis opibus superbia Sacerdotum creuit: ac tum præsertim cum sacerdotia & Episcopatus non propter muneris Ecclesiastici functionem, sed propter opum & potentiæ magnitudinem ad homines illustri familia natos deferri cœpti sunt. Hinc illud Sigeberti sub anno D. Collatis à Clodoueo rege multis prædiis Ecclesiæ Rhemensi, Remigius multa eorum parte data Ecclesiæ Laudunénsi sedem Episcopatus ibi esse constituit. Sed ad Parium institutum redeamus. nam ex aliis commentariis aliud Parium iudicium aduersus Petrum Mauclerum, (id est, maledoctum) Armoricæ Britanniæ Principem, his profertur verbis: Ex anno MCCXXX. Galterus Dei gratia Senonensis Archiepiscopus, Galterus eadem gratia Carnotensis & Guillelmus Parisiensis Episcopi, Comes Flandriæ, Th. Comes Campaniæ, Comes Niuernensis, Comes Blesensis, Comes Carnotensis, Comes Montisfortis, Comes Vindocinensis, Comes Rociacæ, Matthæus de Montmorencio Franciæ Constabularius, Iohannes Sueffionensis, Stephanus de Sacrocæsare, Vicecomes Bellimontis, &c. notum facimus, quòd nos coram charissimo domino nostro Ludovico Rege Franciæ iudicauimus vnanimiter, quod Petrus quondam Britanniæ Comes, propter ea quæ eidem domino Regi fors fecerat, Baillium Britanniæ per iustitiam amisit, & quod Barones Britanniæ & alij qui ei fecerunt fidelitatem vel homagium ratione illius Baillij, sunt penitus absoluti, & quicti ab illa fidelitate & homagio, &c. Sed aliud insignius profertur, ex anno MCCCXV. sub Rege Ludouico Hutino, ex quo intelligitur, primùm quàm sæpe Pariun dignitas variis Principibus attributa fuerit: deinde ad illorum iudicia nonnullos insuper alios è Franciæ proceribus & satrapis Episcopis adhiberi solitos: postremò in illorum numero interdum etiam Reges ac principes exteros fuisse, siquidem satrapiam aliquam ex iis, quibus Pariatus dignitas attributa fuerat, possidebant.
units.tr: …of the assemblies of the realm, and has the power to conduct all affairs in place of the Prince. Our people call him the Marshal; the French call him the Constable. So he writes. These words may seem more credible for this reason: I notice that no mention of Marshals is found in our France in ancient times, so it is likely that this office was a later institution of the kings, adapted to German custom. However that may be, the word is evidently old, as is also clear from the English Annals of Thomas Walsingham, where under the year 1293 he writes: "And presently the King of the Franks ordered the Constable of France to occupy the duchy of Aquitaine with an armed force in the name of the King of the Franks." I do not doubt that this office of Count of the Stables was born from the institution of the Roman Emperors, although from small beginnings it at last grew under our customs to the dignity of the Praetorian Prefecture. In those times, moreover, this dignity was like a military tribuneship. Ammianus, book 26, where he speaks of the Emperor Valentinian: "Having entered Nicomedia by fixed stages, on the Kalends of March he placed his brother Valens in charge of his stables with the dignity of tribune." Mention of this dignity is made in the Code of Justinian, law 1, C. de comitibus et tribunis scholarum, where it is granted to them as a mark of great honour, that they may preside over the Emperor's banquets and adore his purple. Likewise in law 3, C. Theodosianus, de annona et tributis; in law "Perpensa," 29, Cod. Theodosianus, de equorum collatione; and in law 1, C. Theodosianus, qui a praebitione tyronum, where the right is granted to them of exacting fees (sportulae) from the provincials who contributed military horses for the Emperor's use. It remains for us to discuss those magistrates who are commonly called PEERS OF FRANCE, although I certainly lack not the will but the means of documents. For out of so great a number of books, which are called Annals and Chronicles of France, not even one has yet been published in which any probable account of that institution is put forward. For that Gaguin, and a certain Italian, Paulus Aemilius, not so much a historian of the kings of France as a mercenary flatterer of the Popes, and others I know not who, commonly write that those magistrates were instituted either by Pepin or by Charlemagne, is plainly absurd, and this may be understood even from this: that among so many German historians who wrote histories in the age of those kings, or a little after their age, not one at all makes the least mention of those magistrates. Indeed the history of Aimoin on the institutions and deeds of the Franks, brought down to the time of Louis the Pious, and the Appendix to it, carried down to the thirty-seventh year of the reign of King Louis the Younger, nowhere mentions these Peers. Therefore, until something more certain is brought forward, I shall think the institution should be referred to the reign of Hugh Capet, who, when he had seized the kingdom with the lawful heir set aside, thought that some nobles should be bound to himself by a new kind of honour and favour. For all agree that something of this kind was done by him. Now an example of this institution is easily understood to have been taken from feudal law, under which the vassals who received fiefs from the same lord and patron are called peers among themselves, that is, as it were, ὁμότιμοι [equals in honour]. Of these there is this threefold power: first, that those who are admitted into the order of vassals are admitted by the college of them (Lib. Feud. 2, tit. 2); then, that when asked they give testimony concerning an investiture (book 2, title 19); lastly, that if any controversy arises either among themselves, or between the lord and them, they themselves exercise jurisdiction both civil and criminal (book 2, title 46, and title 52, and title 55). And indeed it is so, that the Peers of France have this right: first, that they cannot be inaugurated except as a college, nor deposed except for a cause heard in council, nor summoned to any other judgment except that of their colleagues. Although the Parisian Senate has claimed for itself the authority to order the Peers to plead their cause before it. And Budé, a man by far the most learned, calls those Peers by the name of Patricians, and writes that they seem to him to have been instituted by one king from the number of those who held the German Empire, because Justinian says that the Fathers were chosen by the Emperor as patrons and guardians of the Commonwealth. Yet I do not scorn the opinion of that most learned man, especially since it is not foreign to the dignity of the Peers. For in the later age of the Roman Emperors there was the rank of Patrician, a dignity not very unlike that of the Peers: partly because they were in some measure the fathers of the Commonwealth, as Suidas bears witness, and were consulted by the Emperor on the highest matters; they used the same insignia as the Consuls, and held greater honour and authority than the Praetorian Prefect, or less than the Consul. This can be learned especially from the Novels of Justinian, and from Sidonius Apollinaris, and Claudian, and Cassiodorus. But I do not think this honour was adopted once the name of the Empire had been transferred to the Germans; nor is it likely that any such Patricians were instituted by some German Emperor who was at the same time King of France, without some German historian making mention of him. Lastly, Budé himself, hesitating in the same place, recalls that a dignity of this kind of Peers existed also among the other neighbouring peoples; and that it is written in the Royal Commentaries that in the year 1224 a certain John of Nigella, a Fleming, against whom a controversy had been brought in Flanders by the Countess of Flanders, appealed to the Peers of France, because he had sworn that he could not contend before the Peers of Flanders in a fair judgment; and when he was called back by the Countess to the judgment of the Peers of Flanders, it was at last decreed for certain reasons that this controversy should be brought before the Peers of France. But what the cause of the transferred judgment was, Budé does not set out; and one who had been versed in feudal law would never have passed it over. But so that we may now set out the institution of this magistracy a little more plainly and more certainly: first of all, as I said before, I think it is agreed by all that no mention of the name of Peers is found, either among German or French historians, before the reign of the Capetian kings. But since I see that certain monuments of antiquity have lately been dug out and brought into the light, in which the rights of those Peers are in no small part set forth, I think it worth while to set out briefly what we have observed from those commentaries; and this the more willingly because, from the very man by whom those commentaries have recently been published, they are twisted in another direction than truth and reason demand. Therefore I see that the reason for instituting them was twofold: first, that they might preside over the inauguration of the king and (as they then spoke) the investiture, that is, that they might solemnly adorn the king with the insignia of his rule and with the crown, in the assembly of princes and nobles. Then, that if anyone from the number of the powerful and princes of France were guilty of capital treason, they might exercise judgment upon him. For since in ancient times those judgments were exercised in the public council of the people (as has been demonstrated at length above), and that custom of our ancestors had gradually begun to be transferred, by the institution of the Capetians, to the judicial parliament (of which we shall speak later), and since the princes of the realm did not readily think their fortunes should be committed to that parliament, it seemed to those kings most convenient for their purposes that, besides the court of that parliament, they should establish this assembly of their Peers, which was called the court of the Peers; yet its order and number varied for some time. For they were not always twelve men, as I see those very men from whom these monuments have been brought forward are conjecturing: sometimes there were more, sometimes fewer, as seemed fitting to the king, by whom that magistracy was conferred as a mark of the highest honour and favour. This will be recognised from the following monuments: the oldest of which is under the year 1216, that is, under King Louis the Fat: "It was judged by the Peers of our kingdom, namely by the Archbishop of Reims, William of Langres, William of Châlons, Philip of Beauvais, Stephen of Noyon, bishops, and Odo Duke of Burgundy, and by many other bishops and barons of ours, namely the bishops of Auxerre, R. of Chartres, G. of Senlis, and I. of Lisieux, and the Count of Ponthieu, R. Count of Dreux, B. Count of Brittany, C. Count of Saint-Pol, William de Roches, the Seneschal of Anjou, William Count of Joigny, J. Count of Beaumont, and R. Count of Alençon, we hearing and approving the judgment," etc. From these words it can be known that the Peers of France at that time were not the same as those who were later, and that a great part of them, according to the superstition of those times, were archbishops and bishops. For when episcopal seats were established in those places to which rich and fruitful estates had been assigned as, as it were, satrapies by the royal liberality, the pride of the priests easily grew with those riches; and especially when priesthoods and bishoprics began to be conferred on men born of illustrious families, not for the performance of an ecclesiastical office, but for the greatness of their wealth and power. Hence that statement of Sigebert under the year 4?? (D.): when King Clovis had bestowed many estates on the Church of Reims, Remigius, with a large part of them given to the Church of Laon, established an episcopal seat there. But let us return to the institution of the Peers. For from other commentaries another judgment of the Peers against Peter Mauclerc (that is, badly taught), Prince of Armorican Brittany, is produced in these words: "In the year 1230, Walter, by the grace of God Archbishop of Sens, Walter by the same grace Bishop of Chartres, and William Bishop of Paris, the Count of Flanders, T. Count of Champagne, the Count of Nevers, the Count of Blois, the Count of Chartres, the Count of Montfort, the Count of Vendôme, the Count of Rocroi, Matthew de Montmorency, Constable of France, John of Soissons, Stephen de Sacrocaesare, Viscount of Beaumont, etc., make known that we, before our most dear lord Louis, King of France, have unanimously judged that Peter, once Count of Brittany, on account of those things which he had done to the same lord King, has lost the bailiwick of Brittany by justice, and that the barons of Brittany and the others who did fealty or homage to him by reason of that bailiwick are wholly absolved and released from that fealty and homage, etc." But another more notable one is produced, from the year 1315 under King Louis the Hutin, from which it is understood, first, how often the dignity of the Peers was conferred on various princes; then, that besides them some others from among the nobles and satraps of France, and bishops, were customarily admitted to their judgments; lastly, that among their number at times even foreign kings and princes were included, since they held some satrapy from among those to whom the dignity of Peer had been conferred.

units.la: Verba autem illius Commentarij hæc sunt: Nos Pares supradicti ad requestam & mandatum Regis venimus in suam curiam Parisius, & fecimus & tenuimus curiam cum duodecim aliis personis, prælatis, & aliis altis hominibus, Archiepiscopo Rothomagi, Episcopis Briocensi & Maclouiensi, Philippo filio Regis Franciæ, Comite Pictauiensi, Ludouico Ebroicarum Comite, Carolo Comite Marchiæ, Guydone Comite S. Pauli, Gaucherio dom. Castellionis & Portiani, Comestabili Franciæ, primogenito Comitiis Claromontis, Io.dom. Claromontis & Carolesij, dom. de Marcueil, & Milone dom. de Noyers, à nobis electis ad iudicandum nobiscum, tanquam curia Paribus munita regis auctoritate: qui dixit se non posse plures Pares habere: quia Dux Aquitaniæ, nëpe rex Angliæ, qui vocatus fuerat, se excusauit ob bellū Scotorum: Dux Burg. quoq; excusauit se propter certam exoniā: Episc. Nouiodunī mortuus erat: & Cathalaunen. Episco. pro certis caussis in carceribus detinebatur, &c. His insignibus vetustatis testimonijs accedat etiam illud quod ex commentarijs anno MCCCLX. prolatum est: unde intelligi potest, primum quod iam aliquoties diximus, certum quidem ac definitum Parium numerum fuisse, sed eius arbitrium summum penes regiam potestatem fuisse: deinde honorem illum non Patriciatus, vt Budæus & Budæum secuti crediderunt: sed Pariatus nomine appellatum fuisse: quanquam posterioribus seculis Paritatis quoque & ex Gallicę linguæ consuetudine Perria nomen illi tributum est. Verba autem illius commentarij hæc sunt: Et cum huiusmodi Ducatus dignitatis nomine, honorem superaddentes honori, Parem Franciæ ipsum fecimus, statuentes auctoritate prædicta vt ipse, quamdiu vixerit in humanis, & dicti eius heredes masculi de matrimonio legitimo procreati, post eius obitum Duces Bituricenses & Aruernię ac Pares Franciæ nominentur, omniaque Ducatus & Pariatus honore cum nomine, iure, & quacunque alia prærogatiua lætentur, &c. Eiusdemmodi ferè illud diploma est regis Iohann. sub anno 1363. vbi honos ille non Patriciatus sed Pariatus appellatur: Ducatum Burg. in Pariatu, & quicquid iuris & proprietatis habemus in eodem, nec non in Comitatu Burg. ex successione Philippi vltimi, ducis consanguinei nostri, charissimo Philip. filio nostro concessimus tenenda & possidenda per eum, & & heredes suos in legitimo matrimonio, ex proprio corpore procreandos, perpetuò, hereditariè, pacificè & quietè. Sed posterioribus temporibus Paritatis & Perria verbum (vt superius diximus) ex popularis linguæ consuetudine vsurpari cœpit: vt ex commentarijs anni M C C C C X I I I. cognosci potest, in quibus ita scriptum est: Eundem Iohannem consanguineum nostrum ampliori volentes fulgere dignitate, & Comitis titulum supradictum in maiorem excelsioremque mutantes, dictum Iohannem consanguineum nostrum, in Ducem tenore præsentium sublimamus: dictumque Comitatum Alenconij erigimus in Ducatum, volentes vt prædictus Ducatus in Perria seu Paritate nobis teneatur: sub forma tamen & modis quibus antea idem Iohannes sæpedictum tenebat Comitatum. Atque hæc quidem ex Commentarijs Gallicis, vt dixi, prolata sunt: in quibus illud quoque notatione dignum est, quod dici & commemorari video: sed tamen sine teste: cùm Dux Armoricus læsæ maiestatis reus factus esset, magnopere quæsitum, à quibus iudicium illud exerceretur: ac tandem cùm Philippus Audax Burgundus idem ex Rege quæsiffet, Regem de consilij sententia pronunciasse, Parem nonnisi in Parium iudicium adduci posse. VI. Non. Mart. ann. M C C C X X X V I. ac rursus Regi Carolo septimo quærenti à Senatu Parisiensi, apud quos Pares rei capitalis rei fieri possent, idem respondsum fuisse: XII. Kal. Maij, ann. MCCCCLVIII. quod (vt superius diximus iuri feudali plane consentaneum est. Sed iam tempus est ad institutum nostrum redire.
units.tr: The words of that commentary are these: "We, the aforesaid Peers, at the request and command of the King, came to his court at Paris. We held court with twelve other persons, prelates and other men of high rank: the Archbishop of Rouen, the Bishops of Brieuc and Maclou, Philip, the son of the King of France, the Count of Poitiers, Louis, Count of Évreux, Charles, Count of La Marche, Guy, Count of Saint-Pol, Gaucher, lord of Châtillon and Porcien, Constable of France, the eldest son of the Count of Clermont, John, lord of Clermont and Charolais, the lord of Marcueil, and Milo, lord of Noyers, all chosen by us to judge with us as a court strengthened with the Peers' authority under the king's authority. He said that he could not have more Peers, because the Duke of Aquitaine, namely the King of England, who had been summoned, excused himself on account of the war with the Scots; the Duke of Burgundy also excused himself for a certain reason; the Bishop of Noyon had died; and the Bishop of Châlons was being held in prison for certain causes, etc." Besides these weighty testimonies of antiquity, there should be added also that which was brought forward from the commentaries of the year 1360. From it one can understand, first, what we have already said several times: that the number of Peers was certain and fixed, but that the decision of the matter rested chiefly with the royal power. Second, that the honour was not called Patriciatus, as Budé and those who followed Budé believed, but was named Pariatus; although in later centuries it was also called Perria, from the usage of the French language, as Paritas too. The words of that commentary are these: "And since we have added honour to honour by bestowing upon him the title of the Duchy, we have made him Peer of France, decreeing by the aforesaid authority that he himself, as long as he lives among men, and his legitimate male heirs born of lawful marriage, shall after his death be called Dukes of Bourges and of Auvergne and Peers of France, and that they shall enjoy all the honour, name, right and every other prerogative of Duchy and Pariatus, etc." A similar diploma is that of King John under the year 1363, where that honour is called not Patriciatus but Pariatus: "We have granted to our dearest son Philip the Duchy of Burgundy in the Pariatus, and whatever right and property we have in the same, as also in the County of Burgundy, by the succession of Philip the last, our kinsman, to be held and possessed by him and his heirs born in lawful marriage of his own body, forever, by hereditary right, peacefully and quietly." But in later times the word Paritatis and Perria (as we said above) began to be used from the custom of the common tongue. This can be seen from the commentaries of the year 1413, in which it is written thus: "Wishing to make our kinsman John shine with a greater dignity, and changing the aforesaid title of Count into a greater and loftier one, we raise the said John, our kinsman, to the rank of Duke by the tenor of these presents, and we erect the County of Alençon into a Duchy, wishing that the aforesaid Duchy be held of us in the Perria or Parity, yet under the form and conditions by which the same John previously held the aforesaid County." These things, as I said, are taken from the French commentaries. In them there is also a point worth noting, which I see is said and recalled, but without a witness. When the Duke of Brittany was made guilty of treason, it was much debated by whom that trial should be conducted. At last, when Philip the Bold of Burgundy had asked the king about this, the king, by the advice of his council, declared that a Peer could be brought before no court except the court of Peers, on the sixth day before the Nones of March in the year 1336. And again, when King Charles VII asked the Parisian Senate before whom Peers could be tried for a capital crime, the same answer was given on the twelfth day before the Kalends of May in the year 1458. This (as I said above) is entirely in accord with feudal law. But now it is time to return to our purpose.

units.la: De continuata Sacrosancti Concilij auctoritate sub Carlouingiorum Regno. CAP. XVIII.
units.tr: On the continued authority of the Sacred Council under the reign of the Carolingians. CHAPTER XVIII.

units.la: CViusmodi regnantibus Merouingiis Reip. nostrae forma fuerit, quantáque Concilij publici auctoritas, satis iam explicatum arbitramur. nunc consequens est, vt qualis sub Carlouingiis fuerit, exponamus. Quantum enim ex omnibus & nostris, & Germanicis historiis existimare licet, eadem prorsus Ordinum, sive Statuum auctoritas conseruata est: vt non penes Pipinum aut Carolum, aut Ludouicum, sed penes regiam Maiestatem summum rerum omnium iudicium arbitriumque esset: cuius Maiestatis veram propriamque sedem summo multarum aetatum consensu in solenni Concilio fuisse, superius demonstrauimus. Huius autem rei documento est, primum, Regino lib. Chron. 2. sub anno DCCCVI. vbi de Carolo Magno loquens: Imperator, inquit, cum primoribus & optimatibus Francorum, de pace constituenda & conseruanda inter filios suos & de partitione regni placitum habuit. Et mox: De hac diuisione testamentum interpositum fecit, quod per sacramentum à Francis confirmatum est. Eiusdemmodi est Eguinarthi testimonium, in eo quem aliquoties iam laudauimus libello: vbi cùm ea quæ post Pipini mortem acciderunt exponit, ita loquitur: Franci siquidem facto solenniter generali conuentu ambos sibi reges constituunt: ea conditione præmissa, vt totum regni corpus ex æquo partirentur: & Carolus eam partem quam pater eorum Pipinus tenuerat, Carolomanus vero eam cui patruus eorum Carolomanus præerat, regendi gratia susciperet, &c. Quibus ex verbis perspicuum est, quam potestatem antea trecentis paulo minus annis sub Merouingiis regni ordines habuerant, eandem post illius interitum sibi retinuisse: vt quauis defuncti regis filij extarent, tamen non tam hereditario iure, quam ordinum iudicio & voluntate ad regnum peruenirent. Itaque si regis filius impubes relictus erat, Tutor ei in populi comitiis creabatur. Aimoinus lib. 5. c. 42. Ludouico, inquit, diem suum obeunte, Carolus filius eius, qui Simplex postea dictus est, in cunis æuum agens patre orbatus remansit. Cuius ætatem Franciæ primores incongruam (vt erat) exercendæ dominationi arbitrati, consilium de summis ineunt rebus. Ibi Odonem Franci, Burgundi Aquitanienses q; proceres congregati in vnum, tutorem Caroli pueri, regniq; gubernatorem elegere. Iam vero cetera quoq; maiora regni negotia ad illud idem Cociliū referri solita, testimonio est Regino l. Chr. 2. Anno, inquit, DCCLXIII. rex Pipinus habuit placitum suum in Niuernis. Et mox: Anno 864. rex Pipin habuit placitu suu in Wormacia. Ite ann. 866. rex Pipinus habuit placitu suu apud Attiniacum. Et mox: Habuit placitum suum in Aurelianis ciuitate. Sed & Aimoinus lib. 4. cap. 71. vbi de Saxonum bello loquitur: Rex, inquit, prima veris aspirante temperie, Noviomagum profectus est, & ad locum, qui Padabruno vocatur, generalem populi sui conuentum habiturus cum ingenti exercitu in Saxoniam profectus est. Et rursus cap. 77. Transacta tandem hyeme, publicum populi sui conuentum in loco qui Padabruno vocatur, more solenni habuit. Item, cap. 79. Et cum vxorem suam Wormaciæ inuenisset, generalem populi sui conuentum ibi habere statuit. Quo loco & alijs superioribus perpetuò de Carolo rege loquitur: qui cum Europæ ferè totius regnum magnis suis rebus gestis adeptus esset, Magniq; cognomentum gentium omnium consensu consecutus, Francis tamen pristinum illud suum ius ac libertatem eripere non potuit: ac ne conatus quidem vnquam est, maiorem vllam rem sine populi iudicio & Optimatum auctoritate suscipere. Iam verò post Caroli Magni è vita excessum, non dubium est, quin Ludouicus eius filius eadem conditione regnum administrarit. Nam Appendix Aimoini lib. 5. c. 10. Mortuo, inquit, Carolo, Ludouicus Imperator concilium populi generale, quasi quodam indixerat præfagio, in loco Theotuadi. Rursus cap. 38. vbi pactionem pacis commemorat factæ inter Ludouicum regem, & Ludouicum ipsius consobrinum: Condixerunt, inquit, placitum, & in ipso placito hæc quæ sequuntur inter eos consensu fidelium suorū seruanda conuenerunt: in quo placito communi consensu inuentum est, vt ipsi reges redirent cum scara,&c. Item ca.41. vbi de Carolomanno Ludouici Balbi filio loquitur: Et sic, inquit, reuersus Wormaciam placitum suum Kal. Nouemb. habiturus à Normannis recessit. Item auctor Annalium Rhemensium, sub anno DCCCCXXXV. Hoc rege Rudolpho Laudani degête tumultus ipso die sancti Paschę inter Regios & Episcopi milites exoritur: vbi nonnulli non modo laici, verūm etiam clerici vulnerati, & interempti. Vnde Rex placitum Sueffionis cum Regni primatibus habuit. Sed multo planius sub anno DCCCCXLVI. cum de Rege in Regnum restituendo ageretur: Edmūdus, inquit, Anglorum Rex legatos ad Hugonem principem pro restitutione Ludouici Regis dirigit: & idem princeps proinde conuentus publicos cum nepotibus suis aliisque regni primatibus agit. Et paulò post: Hugo Dux Francorum accito secum Hugone filio Richardi, ceterisq; regni primatibus, Ludouicum Regem, qui ferè per annum sub custodia detinebatur, in regnum restituit. Quin ne illud quidem praetermittendum est, quod eorumdem Annalium auctor PLACITVM REGALE hoc publicū Gentis Concilium appellat: veluti sub anno 961: Otto filius Hugonis quondam Principis ad Regem Lotharium in ipsis festi paschalis diebus Laudunum venit. sed & à nonnullis tam
units.tr: How our commonwealth was constituted while the Merovingians reigned, and how great the authority of the public council was, we think has been sufficiently explained already. It now follows that we set out what it was like under the Carolingians. For as far as one may judge from all our histories and the German ones, the same authority of the Orders, or Estates, was preserved entirely, so that the supreme judgment and decision of all affairs lay not with Pepin, Charles or Louis, but with the royal majesty; and we have shown above that the true and proper seat of that majesty, by the long-standing agreement of many ages, was in the solemn Council. A proof of this is, first, Regino, book 2 of the Chronicle, under the year 806, where, speaking of Charlemagne: "The Emperor," he says, "together with the chief men and nobles of the Franks, held a council about establishing and keeping the peace between his sons and about the division of the kingdom." And soon after: "He made a will concerning this division, which was confirmed by an oath from the Franks." Of the same kind is the testimony of Eginhard, in the little book we have quoted several times already, where, when he sets out what happened after the death of Pepin, he speaks thus: "The Franks, indeed, having held a general assembly with due solemnity, set up both of them as kings, on the condition set down beforehand that they should divide the whole body of the kingdom equally, and that Charles should take the part which their father Pepin had held, and Carloman that over which their uncle Carloman had presided, to rule, etc." From these words it is clear that the power which the orders of the kingdom had held under the Merovingians, a little less than three hundred years before, they kept for themselves after that line perished. So even though the sons of the dead king survived, they did not come to the kingdom by hereditary right so much as by the judgment and will of the Orders. Thus, if a king's son was left under age, a guardian was appointed for him in the assembly of the people. Aimoin, book 5, chapter 42: "When Louis died," he says, "his son Charles, who was afterwards called the Simple, was left fatherless while still in the cradle. The chief men of France, judging his age unsuitable (as it was) for exercising rule, took counsel about the highest matters. There the Franks, the Burgundians and the Aquitanian nobles, gathered into one body, chose Odo as guardian of the boy Charles and governor of the kingdom." Moreover, that the other greater affairs of the kingdom were also customarily referred to that same Council is witnessed by Regino, book 2 of the Chronicle: "In the year 763," he says, "King Pepin held his assembly at Nevers." And soon after: "In the year 864 King Pepin held his assembly at Worms. Again, in the year 866, King Pepin held his assembly at Attigny." And soon after: "He held his assembly in the city of Orléans." And Aimoin, book 4, chapter 71, where he speaks of the war against the Saxons: "The king," he says, "when the first mildness of spring was blowing, set out for Nijmegen, and, intending to hold a general assembly of his people at the place called Paderborn, went into Saxony with a great army." And again, chapter 77: "When winter was at last over, he held, in the customary solemn manner, a public assembly of his people at the place called Paderborn." Likewise, chapter 79: "And when he had found his wife at Worms, he decided to hold a general assembly of his people there." In that passage, and in others above, he speaks throughout of King Charles, who, although he had gained by his great deeds almost the whole kingdom of Europe, and had obtained the name Great by the consent of all peoples, could not take away from the Franks their ancient right and liberty; nor did he ever even try to undertake any greater matter without the judgment of the people and the authority of the nobles. Now, after the death of Charlemagne, there is no doubt that his son Louis governed the kingdom on the same terms. For the Appendix to Aimoin, book 5, chapter 10: "Charles being dead," it says, "the Emperor Louis, as if by some presentiment, had summoned a general council of the people at the place called Theotuadi." Again, chapter 38, where he records the agreement of peace made between King Louis and Louis, his cousin: "They agreed upon an assembly," he says, "and in that assembly the following matters were settled between them to be kept with the consent of their faithful men; in that assembly it was found by common consent that the kings themselves should return with their retinue, etc." Likewise chapter 41, where he speaks of Carloman, son of Louis the Stammerer: "And so," he says, "having returned to Worms, he withdrew from the Normans, intending to hold his assembly on the Kalends of November." Likewise the author of the Annals of Reims, under the year 935: "While King Rudolf was staying at Laon, a tumult broke out on the very day of holy Easter between the king's soldiers and the bishop's soldiers, where several were wounded and killed, not only laymen but also clergy. Whereupon the king held an assembly at Soissons with the chief men of the kingdom." But much more plainly under the year 946, when the restoration of a king to the kingdom was under discussion: "Edmund," he says, "King of the English, sent envoys to Duke Hugh to bring about the restoration of King Louis; and the same prince, for this purpose, held public assemblies with his nephews and other chief men of the kingdom." And a little later: "Hugh, Duke of the Franks, taking with him Hugh, son of Richard, and the other chief men of the kingdom, restored King Louis to the kingdom, who had been kept in custody for almost a year." Nor must we pass over the fact that the same author of the Annals calls this public assembly of the nation a ROYAL COUNCIL (PLACITUM REGALE). Thus under the year 961: "Otto, son of the late Prince Hugh, came to King Lothar at Laon, on the very days of the Paschal feast." But also by some of the nobles of both France and Burgundy a ROYAL COUNCIL (PLACITUM REGALE) and assemblies of princes were held at Soissons. To hinder this (if it could be done), Richard, son of William the Norman, went there, but was set upon by some of the king's loyal men, and after several of his followers were killed he turned to flight. But to pursue each testimony one by one would be a labour…

units.la: Franciæ quàm Burgundiæ PLACITVM REGALE, diuersorúmque conuentus principum Suefsionis habetur. ad quod impediendum (si fieri potest) Richardus filius Wilhelmi Nortmanni accedens, à fidelibus Regis quibusdam peruasus, & interemptis suorum nonnullis in fugam conuersus est. Sed singula testimonia persequi laboris esset infiniti, &, vt opinor, superuacanei. Nam ex iis quę vsque adhuc protulimus patere cuiuis arbitramur, iudicium arbitriúmque summæ Reipub. vsque ad Carolum Simplicem, hoc est, per annos amplius quingentos & quinquaginta penes populi comitia, & (vt nunc loquimur) statuum siue Ordinum conuentum suisse: idque Maiorum nostrorum institutum pro sacrosanćto habitum tot seculis fuisse: vt iam Scriptorum quorundam recentium satis admirari iudicium non possim, quos non est puditum, suis in libellis tradere, Concilij publici institutum Pipino Regi accepto ferendum esse: cùm Eguinarthus Caroli Magni Cancellarius tam dilucidè testetur, Merouingiorum omniū institutum fuisse, vt quotannis Kalend. Maij publicum populi sui conuétum agerent, ad eumque conuentnm carpento bobus tracto veheŗentur.
units.tr: The royal assembly (PLACITVM REGALE) of France and Burgundy is held at Soissons, along with gatherings of various princes. To hinder it, if it could be done, Richard, son of William the Norman, came up, but he was set upon by certain of the king's loyal men, and after some of his own followers were killed he was put to flight. But to pursue each testimony would be an endless labour and, I think, a pointless one. For from what we have brought forward so far, we believe it is clear to anyone that the judgment and decision of the supreme commonwealth, down to Charles the Simple, that is, for more than five hundred and fifty years, lay with the assemblies of the people and, as we would say now, with the convention of the estates or orders; and that this institution of our ancestors was regarded as sacrosanct for so many centuries. So I cannot sufficiently wonder at the judgment of certain recent writers, who are not ashamed to state in their little books that the institution of a public council is to be credited to King Pepin, when Eginhard, the chancellor of Charlemagne, bears witness so clearly that it was the custom of all the Merovingians to hold a public assembly of their people every year on the first of May, and to be carried to that assembly in a cart drawn by oxen.

units.la: De summa inter Regem & Re- gnum differentia.
units.tr: On the great difference between the King and the Kingdom.

units.la: VErum vt maiore in argumento operam ponamus, atq; in illo instituto maiorum nostrorum sapientiam, tanquam in speculo contemplemur, an non ex iis quae hactenus dicta sunt perspicuum est, quantam illi inter Regem & regnum differentiam constituerint? Etenim sic se res habet: Rex, princeps est vnicus ac singularis, ac tanquam caput Reipublicæ; Regnum vero ipsa ciuium ac subiectorum vniuersitas, & quasi corpus Reipublicæ. quam distinctionem Iurisconsulti quoque obseruant. Nam perduellem Vlpianus definit, qui hostili animo aduersus Rempublicam vel Principem animatus est. Item in Institut. tit. vlti. lex Iulia maiestatis in eos qui contra Imperatorem vel Rempublicam aliquid moliti sunt, vigorem suum ostendit. Paulus lib. Sent. v. Qui de salute Principis, vel de summa Reipub. vaticinatores consulit, cum eo qui responderit, capite punitur. Sic in legibus Saxonicis titulo tertio. Qui in Regnum, vel in Regem Francorum conspiliatus fuerit, capite punitur. praeterea Rex eandem cum Regno rationem habet, quam Pater cum familia: Tutor, cum pupillo: Curator, cum adolescente: Gubernator, cum nauigante & vectoribus onusta naue: pastor cum grege: Imperator, cum exercitu. Vt igitur non
units.tr: But that we may devote greater effort to this argument, and contemplate the wisdom of our ancestors in that institution as in a mirror, does it not clearly follow from what has been said so far how great a difference they established between the King and the kingdom? For the matter stands thus: the King is the sole and singular prince, as it were the head of the commonwealth; the kingdom, however, is the whole body of citizens and subjects, as it were the body of the commonwealth. The jurists also observe this distinction. For Ulpian defines a public enemy as one who is moved by hostile intent against the commonwealth or the prince. Likewise, in the Institutes, last title, the Julian law of majesty shows its force against those who have plotted anything against the Emperor or the commonwealth. Paulus, Sentences, book 5: whoever consults fortune-tellers about the safety of the prince or the welfare of the commonwealth is punished with death, together with the one who gives the answer. So too in the Saxon laws, title three: whoever conspires against the kingdom or the King of the Franks is punished with death. Moreover, the King stands in the same relation to the kingdom as a father to his household, a guardian to his ward, a curator to a young man, a helmsman to a ship laden with passengers, a shepherd to his flock, a commander to his army. Therefore, just as

units.la: pupillus tutoris, non nauis gubernatoris, non grex pastoris, non exercitus imperatoris: sed contrà hi caussa illorum instituti sunt: ita non populus Regis, sed Rex populi caussa, quæsitus ac repertus est. Potest enim populus sine Rege esse, veluti qui optimatum aut suo ipsius consilio paret, itemque in interregno. At sine populo ne fingi quidem cogitando Rex potest: non magis quàm pastor sine grege. Quamobrem (inquit apud Xenophontem Socrates ἀπομν. γ.) existimas Homerum appellasse Agamemnonem ποιμένα λαῶν? id est pastorem populorum. an nō ideo, quia sicuti pastor curare debet, ut oves sint incolumes, neq; ijs quicquam deest: ita Regis officium est, curare ut sui cives beati ac fortunati sint. Agè, ceteras differentias videamus. Rex æquè ut quiuis priuatus, mortalis est: Regnum per petuum, & certè (vel ominis caussa) immortale: ut Isocrates in Orat. de pace, de Ciuitatibus locutus est: Iurisconsulti autem de collegijs & vniuersitatibus: Rex mentis errore, insaniaque affici potest, ut noster Carolus vi, qui temere Regnum suum Anglis donauit: neque vlli sunt homines, qui facilius voluptatum blanditijs & mulierculuarum illecebris infatuentur, atque adeo de statu mentis deturbentur. At regnum suam habet in suis Senioribus & Optimatibus, & vsu rerum peritis propriam certamque, tanquam in capite ciuitatis, sapientiam. Rex uno prælio, uno inquam die, vinci, capi etiam, atque in hostium potestatem cadere, & vinctus in eorum fines abduci potest: quod in Ludovico Sancto, & Iohanne & Francisco primo, vsuuenisse nemo ignorat. Regnum amisso Rege incolume tamen manet: tantoque accepto incommodo repente publicum Concilium indicitur, primores conueniunt: & communi consilio praesentibus incommodis remedium ac subsidium quaerunt. quod etiam illis casibus factum constat. Rex vel ob aetatis infirmitatem, vel ob ingenij leuitatem, non modo ab vno & altero consiliario auaro, rapaci, libidinoso: non modo à lasciuis aliquot adolescentibus aequalibus induci ac deprauari potest: verumetiam à muliercula infatuari, sic vt omnem prope administrandi regni potestatem ei committat. cuius mali exempla quàm saepe acciderint, pauci, vt opinor, in nostris Annalibus versati ignorat. At regnum, Seniorum suorum consilio & sapientia, perpetuò fretum est. Salomon sapientissimus, tamen à mulierculis, etiam in summa senectute corruptus est. Roboamus ab adolescentibus: Ninus à matre Semiramide: Ptolomaeus, Auletes cognomento dictus, à tibicinib. & citharoedis. Maiores nostri Regibus suis priuatos suos consiliarios, qui priuata ipsorum negotia curarent, reliquerunt. Seniores, qui Rempubl. administrarent, & in commune consulerent, Regiqué administrandi Regni rationem ostenderent, ad conuentum publicum retulerunt. Anno MCCCLVI. cum Rege Iohanne capto ab Anglis, & in Angliam abducto, publicum Regni Concilium Lutetiæ haberetur: eoque nonnulli ex Regis consiliariis couenissent: iussi sunt è conuentu excedere: denunciatúmque illis fuit, publici Concilij delectos nó amplius conuenturos, nisi illi ad augustum illud Regni sacrarium adire desinerent. cuius rei testimonium extat in Magno Chron.Gallicè scripto vol.2. sub rege Ioanne,sol. 169 Neque verò vlla vnquam ætas fuit, quæ non certam illam atque animaduertendam inter Regem & Regnum differentiam notaret. Rex Lacedæmoniorum (vt Xenophon testatur) & Ephori qui tanquam custodes & obseruatores ipsius erant, singulis mensibus iureiurando fidem inter se dabant: Rex,se ex legum præscripto regnaturû: Ephori,se Regium dominatum conseruaturos, si modo ipse iusiurandum seruasset. Cicero in Epist.ad Brutum,Scis mihi semper placuisse, nó Rege solùm, sed regno liberari Rempu. Idem libr. De legib.3. Sed quoniam Regale Ciuitatis genus probatum quondam,postea nó tam Regni quam Regis vitiis repudiatum est, nomen videbitur tantum Regis repudiatum,&c. Idem Philipp.11. Si enim assuissem,nó solum Regem, sed etiam regnum de Rep. sustulissem. Sed eius differentiæ nullum nobis planius Maiores nostri documentum reliquerunt, quàm in Magistratuum iure & appellatione. nam qui à Rege dignitatem aliquam in Regia obtinent, & Regis ministri appellantur, & eo vel mortuo vel abdicato, repente dignitatem amittunt, Regis deniq; arbitrio sua illis dignitas, quasi precario tantum concessa, adimitur. Cuiusmodi sunt qui vulgo Magistri Hospitij REGIS appellantur, & Camerarij REGIS & Magnus venator Regis & alij aulæ regiæ officiales. At qui regni & Reipubl. vniuersæ magistratus erant, eos Maiores nostri adiecto amplissimo FRANCIÆ nomine designarunt: quem morem etiam nunc retinemus: vt cùm dicimus Comestabulum FRANCIÆ: Amiralium FRANCIÆ: Cancellarium FRANCIÆ. & cum antiquitus non à Rege, sed à populo eas dignitates acciperent, neque ipsius morte aut mutatione desinebant: neque ipsius arbitrio abdicabantur. itaque ne nunc quidem magistratus illi summi quos vulgus CORONÆ OFFICIALES appellat, Rege mortuo magistratus esse desinunt: neq; iis adimi dignitas, nisi cū vita, hoc est, nisi rei capitalis damnatis potest. quin ne illud quidem summæ populi potestatis argumentum prætermittendum est, quòd quibus tribus in rebus Reip. summa consistit, remi litari, iurisdictione, & ærario, iis rebus qui cum summo imperio præfecti sunt, non à rege, sed à Regno & Francia denominatur. nam vt modo diximus is ad quem rei militaris summa pertinet, Comestabulus, aut Marescallus, aut (vt Sigebertus testatur) Senescha llus FRANCIÆ dicitur: qui vero classi & maritimis copiis præest, Amiralius FRANCIÆ: qui iurisdictioni, Cancellarius FRANCIÆ: qui tributis & ærario, Quæstor generalis FRANCIÆ.
units.tr: the ward does not exist for the guardian, nor the ship for the helmsman, nor the flock for the shepherd, nor the army for the commander, but on the contrary these were instituted for the sake of those others, so the people does not exist for the King, but the King was sought out and appointed for the sake of the people. For the people can exist without a King, as when it obeys the best men or its own counsel, and likewise during an interregnum. But a King cannot even be imagined, even in thought, without a people, no more than a shepherd without a flock. Wherefore, says Socrates in Xenophon, Memorabilia, book 3 [ἀπομν. γ.], do you think Homer called Agamemnon "shepherd of the peoples" [ποιμένα λαῶν]? That is, shepherd of the people? Is it not because, just as a shepherd must take care that his sheep are unharmed and lack nothing, so the office of a King is to take care that his citizens are happy and prosperous? Come now, let us look at the other differences. The King, like any private person, is mortal; the kingdom is perpetual and, at least for the sake of omen, immortal, as Isocrates spoke of cities in his oration on peace; and the jurists speak likewise of colleges and corporations. The King can be afflicted with a derangement and insanity of mind, as our Charles VI was, who rashly gave his kingdom to the English; and there are no men more easily infatuated by the flatteries of pleasures and the allurements of little women, and so driven from a sound state of mind. But the kingdom has its own sure wisdom in its Seniors and Optimates, who are skilled in affairs, as if in the head of the state. A King can be defeated in one battle, in one day I should say, can even be captured and fall into the power of enemies, and be led off in chains into their territory; as nobody is unaware happened to Louis the Saint, and to John and Francis I. The kingdom, with its King lost, nevertheless remains intact; and at once, having received so great a blow, a public council is summoned, the chief men assemble, and by common counsel they seek a remedy and relief for the present troubles. That this too has been done in such crises is established. A King, either through infirmity of age or through lightness of mind, can be led and corrupted not only by one or another greedy, rapacious, lustful counsellor, not only by some wanton young companions, but can even be infatuated by a little woman, so that he commits to her almost all the power of governing the kingdom. How often examples of this evil have occurred, few, I think, who are versed in our annals are ignorant. But the kingdom has always relied on the counsel and wisdom of its Seniors. Solomon, the wisest of men, was nevertheless corrupted by women, even in his extreme old age. Rehoboam by young men; Ninus by his mother Semiramis; Ptolemy, surnamed Auletes, by flute-players and lyre-players. Our ancestors left their Kings private counsellors, to attend to the Kings' private affairs; the Seniors, who would administer the commonwealth and deliberate for the common good, and show the King the manner of governing the kingdom, they referred to the public assembly. In the year 1356, when King John had been captured by the English and led off to England, a public council of the kingdom was held at Paris; and some of the King's counsellors having come together there, they were ordered to leave the assembly, and it was announced to them that the chosen members of the public council would no longer meet unless they ceased to approach that august sanctuary of the kingdom. Evidence of this matter is found in the Great Chronicle written in French, volume 2, under King John, page 169. Indeed there has never been an age that did not mark this certain and noteworthy difference between the King and the kingdom.
