The King of the Lacedaemonians (as Xenophon attests), and the Ephors, who were as it were guardians and observers of him, every month pledged faith to one another by oath: the King, that he would rule according to the law's prescription; the Ephors, that they would preserve his royal rule, provided that he himself kept the oath. Cicero, in his letter to Brutus: You know that it has always pleased me that the commonwealth should be freed not only from the King but from the kingdom. The same, in On the Laws, book 3: But since the royal form of a state was once approved, but afterwards was rejected not so much for the faults of the kingdom as for those of the King, the name only of King will seem to have been rejected, and so on. The same, Philippics, book 11: For if I had been accustomed, I would have removed from the commonwealth not only the King but also the kingdom. But our ancestors left us no clearer proof of this difference than in the law and the name of the magistrates. For those who hold some dignity in the royal household from the King, and are called ministers of the King, lose their dignity at once when he dies or abdicates; indeed, their dignity, granted to them as if merely on sufferance, is taken away at the King's pleasure. Such are those who are commonly called Masters of the King's Household, the King's Chamberlains, the King's Grand Huntsman, and the other officials of the royal court. But those who were magistrates of the whole kingdom and commonwealth, our ancestors designated by adding the most ample name of FRANCE; a custom we still retain, as when we say Constable of France, Admiral of France, Chancellor of France. And since formerly they received these dignities not from the King but from the people, they did not cease with his death, nor were they removed at his pleasure. Thus even now those highest magistrates whom the common people call OFFICERS OF THE CROWN do not cease to be magistrates when the King dies, nor can their dignity be taken from them except with their life, that is, unless they are condemned for a capital crime. Nor must we omit this proof of the sovereignty of the people: the three things on which the sum of the commonwealth rests, war, justice and the treasury, those who are set in charge of these with supreme power are named not from the King but from the Kingdom and France. For, as we have just said, he to whom the supreme command of war belongs is called Constable, or Marshal, or (as Sigebert attests) Seneschal of France; he who presides over the fleet and maritime forces is called Admiral of France; he who has justice, Chancellor of France; he who has taxes and the treasury, Receiver-General of France.

units.la: De Capeu'ngiorum familia, & Regno Fran- cogallia in illam translato.
units.tr: On the Capetingian family, and the Kingdom of France transferred to it.

units.la: DEmonstratum est superiùs, Regnum Francogalliæ his mille ducentis annis in tribus tantùm familiarum nominibus versatum esse: quarum prima Merouingia, altera Carolouingia, ex auctorum & capitum nominibus appellata est. Nam etsi non hæreditate (vt iam sæpe docuimus) sed Concilij iudicio Regni successio deferretur, libenter tamen Franci Germanorum suorum institutum retinebant, vt Reges ex nobilitate, (quemadmodum Tacitus loquitur) Duces ex virtute sumerent: ac plerumque Reges eos sibi deligerent, qui Regali sanguine prognati, regaliter instituti, educatiqué fuerant: siue illi ex liberorum, siue ex propinquorum numero & gradu essent. At anno 987. mortuo Ludouico v. Rege Francogalliæ xxxi, & ex Carlouingiorum stirpe, xii. migratio sceptri, regniqué mutatio contigit. Nam cùm ex illa familia Carolus Lotharingiæ Dux superesset, regis demortui patruus, ad quem instituto Gentis regni successio deferenda videbatur: exortus est Hugo Capetus, Imper. Ottonis I. sororis Hauuidis nepos, Hugonis Comitis Parisiensis filius: vir militari laude insignis, qui se præsentem absenti: bene de regno meritum, alieno, vt ipse loquebatur, præferri voluit. nam cùm inter Germaniæ imperium & regnū Galliæ liæ controuersiæ aliquot extitissent, Carolus partium se imperij studiosum, & à Galliæ regno alieniorem ostenderat. Qua de caussa Gallorū complurium animos ac voluntates ab se abalienauerat. Itaque Carolus comparato exercitu, in Galliam irrupit, ciuitatesque aliquot deditione accepit. Capetus Francorum Principum fauore atque amicitia fretus, ad Laudunum oppidum, quod est in Campaniæ finibus, coactis quibus potuit copijs, progressus est. neque ita multò post prælium atrox committitur: quo Capetus superatus, in interiorem Galliam profugit, bellumque nouis coactis copijs, redintegrare instituit. Carolus interea in oppido Laudano cum vxore, dimisso exercitu, quiescebat. Anno insequenti circumuentus à Capeto, magnisque copijs ibidem circumsessus est. Erat in oppido Anselmus quidam, eius ciuitatis Episcopus. Huc Capetus præmijs & pollicitationibus ad regis & oppidi proditionem induxit. Ita oppido & victoria potitus, Carolum cum vxore comprehensum Aureliam mittit: custodesque vtrique attribuit. Cùm in ea custodia Rex biennium retentus esset, duo ei filij, Ludouicus, & Carolus, nati sunt, neque longo interiecto tempore omnes interierunt. Ita Capetus liberè ac sine controuersia totius Galliæ regno potitus, Robertum filium regni consortem asciuit: eumque sibi successorem designandum curauit. Atque hoc facto Carlouingiorum familiæ dignitas memoriaque interijt: anno ab ipsorum regni primordio ducentisimo trigesimo septimo. quam historiam Sigebertus in Chron.ann.987.commemorat. Itémq; appendix Aimoini lib.5.c.42.& c.45.ex quibus cognosci potest,Hugonem Capetum,Hugonis magni Francorum Ducis filium, ex Roberto natum, Odonis illius filio, cui superius diximus Francos Carolo Crasso mortuo,regnum extra ordinem detulisse,pronepotem Roberti Andium Ducis fuisse,clari & magni principis. Ex quibus etiam & ex Vitichindo Saxone intelligitur,Hugonem Capetum non sordida & obscura (vt Italici quidam scriptores tradunt) sed illustrissima familia natum fuisse. nam Roberti Andegauorum comitis abnepos fuit, quem Aimoinus Saxonici generis fuisse scribit. Ex eo natus Odo, siue Otto,tantæ virtutis fuit,vt cū à Rege Carolo Crasso Dux Francorum exercitus aduersus Danos creatus,hostium centum millia vno prælio deleuisset,Franci ei,repudiato Crassi filio, Carolo Simplice puero,regnū detulerint:quemadmodum alio loco superiùs demonstratum est. Huius Odonis filius fuit Robertus: ex quo Hugo magnus Dux quoque Francorũ natus est: cuius filius Hugo Capetus dictus, regnũ eo quem superiùs diximus modo adeptus est. Memorabile est autem quod idem Vitichindus scribit, cùm Odo Carolo Simplici regnum restituisset, Arnulphum Imperatorem armis Galliæ regnum occupasse:eíque Odoni(sic legendū,nonODA) diadema & sceptrum & cetera regalia ornamēta obtulisse, & Odonem imperium domini sui, gratia Arnulphi Imperatoris obtinuisse. Vnde (inquit Vitichin.) vsque hodie certamen est de Regno Carolorum stirpi & posteris Odonis. Nam Hugo cuius pater Robertus filius Odonis ab exercitu Caroli occisus est, dolo eum cepit, posuitque in custodia publica, donec vitam finiret. Neque vero silentio praetereundum videtur altutum Capeti in novo regno constabiliendo consilium. Nam cum Magistratus & dignitates regni, quos Ducatus & comitatus appellant, ita mandari antiquitus in populi comitiis, certis ac delectis viris solerent, ut in beneficij tantum loco, & (ut Iurisconsulti loquuntur) precario tenerentur: quemadmodum in exponenda concilij publici auctoritate demonstratum est: primus Hugo Capetus ad conciliandos retinendosque sibi Procerum animos, has, quae temporariae erant, dignitates, fecit perpetuas: constituitque, ut qui eas obtinebat, patrimonij iure retineret: atque ad suos liberos posterosq; cum reliqua hereditate, transferret: teste Francisco Connano Iurisconsulto Com. 1. c. 9. quo facinore non minimam publici concilij auctoritatem ab ipso imminutam constat: quam tamen imminui ab ipso, sine concilij ipsius consensu potuisse, temporum illorum rationem consideranti consentaneum non videtur.
units.tr: It has been shown above that the Kingdom of France, for these twelve hundred years, passed through only three families, which were named after their founders and their chiefs: the first Merovingian, the second Carolingian. For although the succession to the kingdom was conferred not by hereditary right (as I have often shown) but by the judgement of the Council, the Franks nonetheless willingly kept the custom of their German ancestors, by which, as Tacitus puts it, they took their kings from the nobility and their leaders from their courage. And for the most part they chose as kings those who had been born of royal blood and brought up and trained as princes, whether they belonged to the number and rank of the children or of the kinsmen. But in the year 987, when Louis V, the thirty-first king of France and the twelfth of the Carolingian line, had died, the sceptre passed to another house and the kingdom changed hands. For although Charles, Duke of Lorraine, the uncle of the dead king, was still alive from that family, and to him the succession of the kingdom seemed by the custom of the nation to be due, there arose Hugh Capet, the grandson of Hadwig, sister of the Emperor Otto I, and son of Hugh, Count of Paris: a man distinguished by military renown, who wished that he himself, present and having deserved well of the kingdom, be preferred to an absent man who, as he himself put it, was a foreigner. For although several disputes had arisen between the empire of Germany and the kingdom of Gaul, Charles had shown himself a partisan of the imperial cause and rather alien to the kingdom of France. For this reason he had estranged from himself the minds and goodwill of many Gauls. Therefore Charles, having assembled an army, broke into France and received the surrender of several cities. Capet, relying on the favour and friendship of the princes of France, advanced towards the town of Laon, which lies on the borders of Champagne, with whatever forces he could muster. Not long after, a fierce battle was joined, in which Capet was defeated and fled into the interior of Gaul, and set about renewing the war with fresh forces. Meanwhile Charles remained at Laon with his wife, having dismissed his army, and rested there. In the following year he was surrounded by Capet and besieged there with great forces. In the town there was a certain Anselm, bishop of that city. Capet induced him by rewards and promises to betray both the king and the town. Thus, having gained the town and the victory, he sent Charles, seized together with his wife, to Orléans, and assigned guards to each of them. While the king was kept in that custody for two years, two sons were born to him, Louis and Charles, and before long they all died. So Capet, having taken possession of the kingdom of all Gaul freely and without dispute, associated his son Robert with him in the kingdom and saw to it that he should be designated as his successor. And by this act the dignity and memory of the Carolingian family perished, in the two hundred and thirty-seventh year from the beginning of their reign. Sigebert records this history in his Chronicle, under the year 987; likewise the appendix to Aimoin, book 5, chapters 42 and 45, from which it can be learned that Hugh Capet, son of Hugh the Great, Duke of the Franks, was born of Robert, the son of that Odo to whom I said above the Franks had transferred the kingdom outside the ordinary succession after Charles the Fat died; and that he was great-grandson of Robert, Duke of Anjou, a famous and great prince. From these same sources, and from Widukind of Saxony, it is also understood that Hugh Capet was born not of a mean and obscure family (as some Italian writers hand down) but of a most illustrious one. For he was the great-grandson of Robert, Count of Anjou, whom Aimoin writes was of Saxon stock. From him was born Odo, or Otto, of such great courage that when he had been made by King Charles the Fat commander of the Frankish army against the Danes and had destroyed a hundred thousand enemies in one battle, the Franks, rejecting Charles's son, the boy Charles the Simple, conferred the kingdom upon him, as has been shown elsewhere above. The son of this Odo was Robert, and from him was born Hugh the Great, also Duke of the Franks; his son, called Hugh Capet, obtained the kingdom in the way I have described above. It is worth remembering, moreover, what the same Widukind writes: when Odo had restored the kingdom to Charles the Simple, Arnulf the Emperor by arms seized the kingdom of Gaul, and offered to that Odo (so read, not "ODA") the diadem, the sceptre and the other royal ornaments, and Odo obtained the rule of his lord through the favour of Emperor Arnulf. Hence (says Widukind) even today there is a contest over the kingdom between the stock of Charles and the descendants of Odo. For Hugh, whose father Robert, son of Odo, was slain by the army of Charles, Charles seized by treachery and put in public custody, until he ended his life. Nor does it seem right to pass over in silence the cunning of Capet in establishing his new kingdom. For although the magistracies and dignities of the kingdom, which they call duchies and counties, had anciently been conferred in the assemblies of the people upon certain chosen men, so that they were held only as a benefice and (as the jurists put it) by precarious tenure, as has been shown in the explanation of the authority of the public council, Hugh Capet was the first to make these offices, which had been temporary, perpetual, in order to win over and keep the minds of the nobles to himself. He established that whoever held them should keep them by hereditary right, and should pass them on to his own children and descendants along with the rest of the inheritance; the witness is Francis Connan, jurist, Commentaries, book 1, chapter 9. By this deed it is plain that no small part of the authority of the public council was diminished by him; yet that this could have been diminished by him without the consent of that council does not seem consistent with a consideration of the circumstances of those times.

units.la: De continuata Concilii publici auctoritate in Capeuingiorum familia.
units.tr: On the continued authority of the public Council in the Capetian family.

units.la: NAm quemadmodum ex Froffardo, Monstrelletto, Guaguino, Cominio, Gillio, & alijs historicis omnibus cognosci licet, nihilo propè minor in Capeuingiorum familia, quàm in superioribus duabus, publici concilij auctoritas fuit: valuitque apud illos præceptum illud, tam sæpe & tam valde, nunquam tamen fatis commemoratum: SALVS POPVLI SVPREMA LEX ESTO: neq; vllum tam tyrannicum dominatum vnquam post homines natos fuisse arbitror, præter vnum Turcicum, in quo ciues pro pecudibus, non pro hominibus haberentur. Neque fatis eorum hominum imperitiam admirari possum, qui cùm primoribus labris ius ciuile deguftaffent, & in libris nostris legissent, lata lege Regia populum Imperatori omne suum imperium & potestatem concessisse: continuò liberam quandam & infinitam Regum omnium potestatem commenti sunt, quam Absolutam barbaro & inepto nomine appellant. quasi verò non etiam Romani Reges Reipublicæ curam (vt Pomponius Iurifc. loquitur) per Curiata comitia expedirent: aut, fi liberam Imperatores Romani potestate habuerunt, continuò verum fit Regibus omnibus eandem à populo potestatem tributam effe. neque enim ex vno particulari rectè de vniuersis concluditur: & hac ætate longè diffimillimam esse regum Poloniæ, Daniæ, Sueciæ, Hispaniæ rationem, nemo nisi rerum omnium imperitus ignorat. Regibus Germanorum (inquit Tacitus) nō est infinita, aut libera potestas. Rex Angliæ (inquit libro quarto Cominæus) tributa exigendi nullam habet sine Ordinum & Statuum consensu potestatem. quod idem de ceteris omnibus affirmat libro quinto, capite decimo octauo. denique, satis constat, nullā esse Galliæ regionem, siue (vt vulgus loquitur) prouinciam, quæ Regi serua aut deditia fit, omnemq; in se (vt quondam populus Romanus Imperatoribus) potestatem ei permiserit. quinimo nulla est, quæ non iura quædam sua propria habeat, ijs pactionibus & conditionibus retenta, quibus se in Regis fidem ac ditionem commisit. cuius rei insigne illud argumentum est, quod vnaquęq; Regio, cùm vsus & publicæ vtilitatis ratio postulat, sua comitia indicit, quæ ad vniuersæ prouinciæ commodum pertinent, publico consilio prouideat. Itaque cum generale vniuersi Regni ac patriæ totius Concilium indictum est, cum ex illo conuentu vnus aut alter deligatur, qui cum Prouinciæ suæ mandatis eò ad dicendam sententiam proficiscatur. Exemplo erimus contenti vno, quod ex celeberrimi Doctoris Tholosani verbis proferemus. Willelmi nimirum Benedicti, qui in c. raynutius, ad verbum, & vxorem, num. 499. ita scribit: & laudatur à Nicol. Boerio nobili Iurisconsult. & Prætore Burdegal. Decif. 126. De vnione, inquit, comitatus Tholosani, & patriæ Occitanæ cum Regno Franciæ habetur plenè in documentis inter chartas statuum dictæ patriæ repositis: in qua vnione tria fuerunt, inter Regē & patriam in forma cōtractus passata. primo quod omnia priuilegia patriæ & ius commune illibata seruarentur: secundo, quod nunquam Rex gubernatorem instituet, nisi qui sit de sanguine regio: tertio quòd Rex tallias vel alia subsidia indicere patriæ non poterit SINE CONSENSV STATVVM EIVSDEM: prout nunquam fecit, neq; facit. quinimo annis singulis commissarium ad partes mittit, necessitatem Regni toti patriæ explicaturum, vt pro modo negotiorum Regno pro tempore emergentium subsidium præbeatur: quod obediens patria annuere consueuit, in seruando per Regem priuilegia patriæ, & cetera in dicta vnione contenta, & pro illa vice dutaxat:ita quod non trahatur in consequētiā. Sed quoniam persequi testimonia singula nimis laboriosum, ac planè infinitum esset, pauca quædam illustriora è magno numero, quasi exempli loco, subscribemus. Primum exemplum sumi licet ex anno MCCCXXVIII. quo tempore, mortuo (vt superius diximus) Rege Carolo Pulchro, qui sine liberis virilis sexus, atque postuma filia relicta decesserat, Angliæ Rex Eduardus tertius natus ex Isabella Caroli sorore, Galliæ Regnum ad se hereditate redisse contendebat. Qua controuersia nulla neq; maior, neque illustrior ad publicum Concilium deferri potuit. Quinetiam quòd ad publicū Conciliū introducta est, perspicuo argumento esse potest, maiore Concilij, quàm Regis auctoritate esse: cùm eius se iudicio arq; arbitrio ambo illi Reges subiecissent quod non modo historici nostri omnes testatur, verumetiā Polyd. Vergilius Angl. Histor. lib.19. & Thomas Walsimgamius in historia Anglic. sub Eduard. tertio. Eduardo & Philippo de successione contendentibus (inquit Guaguinus) Conuetus Francorum habitus est, quē TRIVM STATVVM COMITIA vulgo vocât, ibi de cōtendētiū iure diu multumq; disceptatū est. ad extremū ij qui cōmuni auctoritate concilij habebāt, multis rationibus edocti Philippo regnū adiudi cauerūt: cui iudicio nec Eduardus rex detraxit: fide post paucos annos Philippo de Aquitaniæ feudo præstita. Quinetiam Claudius Seyssellus Massilien fis Archiepiscopus in libello quē Franciæ Monarchiam inscripsit, affirmat vtrumque Regem in eo Cōcilio præsentem affuisse. Cùm res in contentionem prope adducta esset, Optimatum consilio, populi atque Ordinum comitia indicta sunt. De maioris partis sententia placuit, præferri agnatū: prægnātisq; reginæ custodiā Valesio attribui. Et, si filiā pareret, eidem Valesio regnū adiudicatum est. quā historiā Frossardus exposuit vol.1.c.22. Paponius Areft. lib.4. ca.1.artic.2. Guaguinus in Philippo Valesio. sed copiosissimè omnium Seyssellus, in eo quē modo nominaui libello. Alterum exemplum supnpeditat annus M C C C L VI. quo tempore Rex
units.tr: For, as can be learned from Froissart, Monstrelet, Guaguin, Commines, Gilles and all the other historians, the authority of the public Council in the Capetian family was nearly no less than in the two preceding families. That precept, so often and so emphatically invoked yet never sufficiently remembered, prevailed among them: THE WELFARE OF THE PEOPLE IS THE SUPREME LAW. I do not think there has ever been, since men were born, a tyranny so harsh, except the one Turkish rule in which citizens are regarded as cattle rather than as men. Nor can I sufficiently wonder at the ignorance of those men who, having tasted civil law only with the tips of their lips, and having read in our books that by the royal law the people granted the emperor all its power and authority, straightway invented a kind of free and unlimited power belonging to all kings, which they call "absolute" by a barbarous and clumsy name. As if the Roman kings did not also manage the care of the commonwealth through the curiate assemblies (as the jurist Pomponius puts it); or as if, supposing the Roman emperors held free power, it would follow at once that the same power had been granted by the people to all kings. For one cannot rightly conclude about all from one particular case, and that the situation of the kings of Poland, Denmark, Sweden and Spain is in this age very different, no one ignorant of public affairs fails to know. "The kings of the Germans," says Tacitus, "do not have an unlimited or free power." "The king of England," says Commines in book four, "has no power to levy taxes without the consent of the Orders and Estates." He affirms the same of all the others in book five, chapter eighteen. Finally, it is quite certain that there is no region of Gaul, or (as the common people say) province, which is subject or surrendered to the king and has granted him all power over itself, as the Roman people once did to the emperors. Indeed there is none that does not have certain rights of its own, retained by those pacts and conditions on which it committed itself to the king's faith and rule. A notable proof of this is that each region, whenever custom and the reason of public advantage require it, summons its own assemblies, which provide by common counsel for what pertains to the good of the whole province. Thus, when a general council of the whole kingdom and of the entire fatherland is summoned, one or another man is chosen from that gathering, who goes there with the mandates of his own province to deliver an opinion. We shall be content with one example, which we take from the words of the most celebrated teacher of Toulouse, Guillaume Benoît, who in c. Raynutius, under the words "and his wife," no. 499, writes thus; he is praised by Nicolas Boerius, noble jurist and praetor of Bordeaux, Decision 126. "Concerning the union of the county of Toulouse and the land of Occitania with the kingdom of France," he says, "it is fully set out in the documents kept among the charters of the Estates of that land. In this union there were three terms, agreed between the king and the land in the form of a contract. First, that all the privileges of the land and the common law should be preserved unimpaired. Second, that the king should never appoint a governor unless he were of royal blood. Third, that the king could not impose tallies or other subsidies on the land WITHOUT THE CONSENT OF THE SAME ESTATES, as he never did and does not now. Moreover, every year he sends a commissioner into the provinces to explain to the whole land the needs of the kingdom, so that aid may be given according to the measure of the affairs that arise for the kingdom at the time; and the dutiful land has been accustomed to grant this, while the king keeps the land's privileges and the other terms contained in that union, and only for that occasion, so that it is not drawn into a precedent." But since to pursue each testimony singly would be too laborious and quite endless, we will set down a few of the more illustrious from a great number, by way of example. The first can be taken from the year 1328, when, King Charles the Fair having died (as we said above) leaving no children of the male sex but a posthumous daughter, Edward III, King of England, born of Isabella, sister of Charles, claimed that the kingdom of France had returned to him by hereditary right. No controversy greater or more illustrious could be brought before the public Council. Moreover, that it was brought before the public Council can be a clear argument that the authority of the Council is greater than that of the king, since both those kings had submitted themselves to its judgment and decision. This is attested not only by all our historians but also by Polydore Vergil, English History, book 19, and Thomas Walsingham in his English history under Edward III. "When Edward and Philip contended over the succession," says Gaguin, "an assembly of the French was held, which people call the Assembly of the Three Estates; there the right of the contenders was long and much debated. At last those who held authority in the common council, instructed by many reasons, adjudged the kingdom to Philip; nor did King Edward disparage this judgment, since a few years later he did homage to Philip for the fief of Aquitaine." Moreover, Claude de Seyssel, Archbishop of Marseille, in the little book he entitled The Monarchy of France, affirms that both kings were present at that Council. When the matter had nearly come to armed contention, the assemblies of the Nobles, of the people and of the Orders were summoned by counsel. By the opinion of the greater part it was decided that the agnate should be preferred, and that the custody of the pregnant queen be assigned to Valois; and if she should bear a daughter, the kingdom was likewise adjudged to Valois. Froissart has set out this history, vol. 1, ch. 22; Papon, Arrêts, book 4, ch. 1, art. 2; Gaguin under Philip of Valois; but most fully of all, Seyssel, in the little book I have just named. The second example is supplied by the year 1356, when King

units.la: Iohannes commisso cum Anglis prope Pictauium prælio captus, atque in Angliam abductus fuit. Tanta calamitate accepta, vnica in Concilij auctoritate spes erat reliqua. Itaque comitia continuò Lutetiam indicta sunt: & quanquam tres regis filij extarent, Carolus, Ludouicus, & Iohannes, quorum natu maximus iustâ administrandi ætatem haberet: tamen delecti alij sunt, ex vnoquoque ordine duodeni probati viri, quibus regni procuratio mandata est: de- cretaq; in Angliam legatio de pace cum Anglis reconcilianda. auctoribus Frossardo vol. 1. cap. 170. Iohanne Bucheto lib. 4. sol. 118. Nicol. Gillio in Chronicis regis Iohannis. Tertium suppeditat annus MCCCLXXV. cum Caroli V. cognomento Sapientis testamentum prolatū est: quo testamento filiorum suorum tutorem instituerat Philippum Ducem Borboniū, vxoris suæ fratrem: Regni autem procuratorem, Ludouicum Ducem Andicum, fratrem suum: tantisper dum Carolus ipsius filius in suam tutelam veniret. Concilium enim Lutetiæ nihilominus actum est, irritoque habito testamento, decretum est, vt regni administratio Ludouico pueri patruo committeretur: ea lege, vt eam administrationem de certorum virorum in eo Concilio probatorum sententia gereret: pueri autem tutela & educatio Borbonio permitteretur. simulque lata regia lex est, vt qui regni heres annum ætatis XIIII. implesset, ei corona imponeretur, hominiaque & fidelitatum iuramenta præstarentur: auctore Froff. vol. 2. cap.60. Buchet. libro 4. sol. 124. Chron. Brit. cap. Quartum suppeditat annus MCCCXCII. cùm idem ille rex Carolus VI. repentino mentis errore affectus, primùm Cenomanum, tum deinde Lutetiam delatus est: ibique Concilium habitum: Ordinumque auctoritate decretum, vt Bituricæ & Burgundiæ Ducibus regni administratio deferretur: aucto re Froffardo vol. 4. c. 44. Neque vero prætermittendum est, quod Paponius Areft. lib. 5. tit. 10. artic. 4. nostra memoria in parlamento Parisiensi commemoratum testatur, cum rex Franciscus primus dominij sui partem alienare vellet, omnes eiusmodi alienationes à superioribus regibus factas eo solo nomine irritas fuisse, quòd sine Concilij & (vt ipse loquitur) trium Statuum auctoritate factæ fuissent. Sextum exemplū extitit anno MCCCCXXVI. cùm Philippus Dux Burgundiæ, & Hanfredus Dux Clocestræ capitales inimicitias magno Reipub. detrimento perquandiu exercuissent: tandemque inter eos conuenisset, vt controuersijs omnibus finem duello commisso imponerent. Nam in ea contentione Concilium se interposuit: decreuitque, vt arma vterque deponeret, deque suis controuersijs iure apud se potius, quàm ferro disceptarent. quam historiam copiosè exponit Paradinus in Chron. Burgund. libro tertio, anno MCCCCXXVI. Septimum exemplum suppeditat annus MCCCCLXVIII, cum dissidio inter regem Ludouicum xi. & Carolũ ipsius fratrem exorto, Cōcilium publicum indictum est Turones, ad Kal. Decembr. quo in Concilio decretum est, vt rex fratri suo Apannagij nomine Ducatum aliquem cederet: cuius annui fructus non minoris essent, quam xii. millium libellarum: insuperque rex è suo fisco lx. libellarũ millia quotannis ei adnumeráda curaret. quam historiam copiose auctor Chron. Britan. Armor. commemorat, lib. 4. sol. 200. Octauum exemplum editum est anno MCCCCLXXXXIIII. cùm Ludouico xi. mortuo superstite Carolo filio annorũ xiii. Concilium Turonib. habitum est, decretumque vt pueri educatio Annę sorori regis committeretur: Regni verò procuratio certis viris in eo Concilio probatis & delectis mandaretur: quamuis Ludouicus Dux Aurelianus proximus agnatus eam postula.ret. Cuius rei testimonium extat in actis eius Concilij Lutetiæ impressis, & apud Philipp. Cominæum lib. 5. ca. 18. itemque in Chron. Britan. lib. 4. & apud Ioan. Bucchetum lib. 4. sol. 167.
units.tr: John, captured in battle with the English near Poitiers and carried off into England, was led away. With so great a calamity received, the only hope left lay in the authority of the Council. Therefore assemblies were immediately summoned at Paris; and although the king had three sons, Charles, Louis and John, of whom the eldest was of an age fit to administer, nevertheless men were chosen from each order, twelve approved men, to whom the management of the kingdom was entrusted; and an embassy was decreed to England to negotiate peace with the English. Authorities: Froissart, vol. 1, ch. 170; John Bouchet, book 4, p. 118; Nicolas Gilles, in the Chronicles of King John. The third example is supplied by the year 1375, when the will of Charles V, called the Wise, was produced. In this will he had appointed as guardian of his sons Philip, Duke of Bourbon, his wife's brother, and as procurator of the kingdom his own brother Louis, Duke of Anjou, until Charles, his son, should come into his own guardianship. Nevertheless a Council was held at Paris, and, the will being set aside as void, it was decreed that the administration of the kingdom should be committed to Louis, the boy's uncle, on the condition that he conduct that administration by the judgment of certain men approved in that Council, while the guardianship and upbringing of the boy should be left to Bourbon. At the same time a royal law was passed that whoever was heir to the kingdom, on completing the fourteenth year of his age, should be crowned, and oaths of homage and fidelity should be rendered to him. Authorities: Froissart, vol. 2, ch. 60; Bouchet, book 4, p. 124; Chronicle of Britain, ch. The fourth example is supplied by the year 1392, when the same King Charles VI, struck by a sudden derangement of mind, was first carried to Le Mans and then to Paris; and there a Council was held, and by the authority of the Orders it was decreed that the administration of the kingdom should be handed over to the Dukes of Berry and Burgundy. Froissart, vol. 4, ch. 44, may be consulted. Nor must it be passed over that Papon, Arrêts, book 5, title 10, art. 4, records as recalled in our own memory in the Parlement of Paris, that when King Francis I wished to alienate a part of his domain, all such alienations made by earlier kings were annulled on this sole ground, that they had been made without the authority of the Council and (as he himself puts it) of the three Estates. The sixth example occurred in the year 1426, when Philip, Duke of Burgundy, and Humphrey, Duke of Gloucester, had for a long time carried on deadly enmity to the great detriment of the commonwealth, and at last it was agreed between them that they would end all their disputes by a duel. But in that contention the Council interposed itself; it decreed that both should lay down their arms, and that they should settle their disputes before it by law rather than by the sword. Paradin sets out this history fully in his Chronicle of Burgundy, book 3, year 1426. The seventh example is supplied by the year 1468, when, a quarrel having arisen between King Louis XI and his brother Charles, a public Council was summoned at Tours for the first day of December. In this Council it was decreed that the king should cede to his brother some duchy by way of an appanage, whose yearly revenues should be not less than twelve thousand livres; and moreover that the king should arrange to pay him sixty thousand livres a year from his own treasury. The author of the Chronicle of Brittany and Armorica records this history at length, book 4, p. 200. The eighth example was given in the year 1494, when, Louis XI having died and his son Charles, aged thirteen, surviving, a Council was held at Tours, and it was decreed that the upbringing of the boy should be committed to Anne, the king's sister, while the management of the kingdom should be entrusted to certain men approved and chosen in that Council, although Louis, Duke of Orléans, the nearest agnate, demanded it. Evidence of this matter exists in the acts of that Council printed at Paris, and in Philippe de Commines, book 5, ch. 18; likewise in the Chronicle of Brittany, book 4; and in John Bouchet, book 4, p. 167.

units.la: De publici Concilij auctoritate in maximis religionis negotiis. CAP. XXII.
units.tr: On the authority of the public Assembly in the greatest matters of religion. CHAP. XXII.

units.la: HActenus demonstratum est, summam in grauissimis quibusq; Reip. nostræ negotiis summo per multorum seculorũ consensu Concilij publici potestatem fuisse. Deinceps videamus, ecqua eiusdem in Religionis negotiis auctoriᵒoritas fuerit. Cuius rei documentum nobis præbent Annales nostri, sub anno M C C C. quo Bonifacius octauus, Papa Romanus, missis ad regem Philippum Pulcrum legatis, ei denūtiauit, se non modò spiritualem, (verba hæc Historici sunt omnia) verum etiam temporale omnium regnorum ac ditionum, quę in orbe Christiano sunt, dominū esse. pro eo iure postulare, vt rex Philippus eum pro domino ac Principe summo agnoscer et: eíque suum regnum acceptum ferret, ac fateretur se illud ipsius beneficio & liberalitate obtinere: si id facere recuset, futurū, vt eum hæreticum pronunciaret, & sacris suis interdiceret. Qua legatione audita, rex publicum Concilium Lutetiam indicit. in eo Concilio Papales literæ recitantur, his verbis: Bonifacius Episcopus, seruus seruorum Dei Philippo Francorum regi: Deum time, & mandata eius obserua.
units.tr: So far it has been shown that, by the long-standing consensus of many centuries, the public Assembly held supreme power in the most serious affairs of our commonwealth. Next let us see what authority it had in matters of religion. Our annals provide evidence of this under the year 1300, when Pope Boniface VIII sent envoys to King Philip the Fair and declared to him that he was lord not only of the spiritual but also of the temporal domain of all the kingdoms and lands in the Christian world. (These are the historian's own words.) By this claim he demanded that King Philip acknowledge him as lord and supreme prince, and that he receive his kingdom as a gift from the Pope and confess that he held it by the Pope's benefit and generosity. If he refused to do so, the Pope would declare him a heretic and bar him from the sacraments. When this embassy had been heard, the King summoned a public Assembly to Paris. In that Assembly the papal letter was read, in these words: "Boniface, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Philip, king of the Franks: fear God and keep his commandments.

units.la: Scire te volumus, quod in spiritualibus, & temporalibus nobis subes: beneficiorum atq; præbendarum ad te collatio nulla spectat. & si aliquorū vacantium custodiam habeas, vsumfructum earum successoribus referues: & si quas contulisti, collationem haberi irritam decreuimus: & quatenus processerit, reuocamus. Aliud credentes, fatuos reputamus. Datum Laterani, IIII. Non. Decemb. pontificatus nostri anno VI.
units.tr: "We wish you to know that you are subject to us in spiritual and in temporal matters. The conferring of benefices and prebends does not belong to you at all. If you have the guardianship of any vacant benefices, you are to reserve their revenues for successors; and whatever you have conferred, we have decreed that the collation shall be void, and as far as it has gone, we revoke it. Whoever believes otherwise we count as fools. Given at the Lateran, on the fourth day before the Nones of December, in the sixth year of our pontificate."

units.la: His literis recitatis, auditaque procerum sententia, ac deliberatare, primum decretum est, vt Epistola Papæ in area Palatij Parisiensi coram ipsius legatis & nuntiis cremaretur. tum vt legati mitellati, turpificati, sordidati, & à carnifice in illam aream lutulento plaustro aduecti, plebis totius ludibrio & conuicijs exponerentur: postremò vt regis nomine literæ ad Papá his verbis scriberentur: Philippus Dei gratia Francorũ rex Bonifacio se gerenti pro summo pontifice, salutem modicam, siue nullam. Sciat tua maxima FATVITAS, in temporalibus nos alicui non subesse. aliquarum Ecclesiarum & prebendarum vacantem collationem ad nos iure regio pertinere, & percipere: fructus earū contra omnes possessores vtiliter nos tueri: secus autem credentes fatuos reputamus, atque dementes. Cuius historiæ testes sunt auctor Chronic.Brittan.Armoric.libro 4.cap. 14. & Nicol.Gillius in Chron.Gallic. quibus adiungendus est pragmaticus Paponius in lib. Arestorum 1.tit.5.art. 27. sed multo magis Iohannes Tilianus Parisiensis Parlamenti scriba, homo ceteroqui ab hoc historiarum genere alienissimus. Cardinalis quidam, inquit, pag.172. denuntiauit inducias imperatas à Papa Bonifacio octauo inter Philippum Pulchrum, & Reges Romanorum atque Anglorum: adiecta pœna siue comminatione censuræ Philippus Pulcher anno 1297, consilio suorum Principum & cõsiliariorum, respondit se paratum esse, Sedi Apostolicæ parere, in ijs rebus quæ ad suam animam & spiritualitatem pertinerent: sed neminem præter Deum agnoscere superiorem se in ijs quæ ad res sui regni temporales pertinerent: neque velle se in rebus sui regni temporalibus cuiquam mortali subijcere. Quibus rebus cognitis Bonifacius bulla Regi Philippo missa, denuntiauit eum sibi subiectum esse æque in temporalibus, vt in spiritualibus: simulque pronũciauit hereticos esse, qui aliter crederent. cui denuntiationi fortiter reclamatum est: simul bulla Lutetiæ combusta, in præsentia Regis, & Principum, atque consiliariorum. Quę, malum, ista est hodie Principum & summorum Magistratuũ, vt ita dicam, Papimania? qui cum tantam ac tam nefariam illius Tyranni superbiam atque arrogantiam videant, tamen, quasi Circæo poculo dementati, nihilominus sese ad illius exosculados pedes prouoluunt, quasi Deum aliquē de cœlo delapsum intuerētur. sed nemo totam hanc historiam commodius exponit, quàm Tho. Walsinghamius, Angl. Historicus, monachus ceteroqui papisticis superstitionibus addictissimus, & ad tuendam Paparum amplitudinem præter ceteros deuotissimus. Itaq; cum is liber venalis (vt audio) in Gallia nostra non reperiatur, operæ pretium fore arbitror, totam illam historiam eiusdem illius monachi verbis exponere.
units.tr: After these letters were read and the opinion of the nobles had been heard and debated, it was first decreed that the Pope's letter be burned in the courtyard of the Parisian palace in the presence of his legates and messengers. Next, that the legates, dressed in mitres, disgraced, filthy and sordid, and brought into that courtyard by the executioner on a muddy cart, be exposed to the mockery and jeers of the whole populace. Last, that in the King's name a letter be written to the Pope in these words: "Philip, by the grace of God king of the Franks, to Boniface, who calls himself supreme pontiff, little or no greeting. Let your most foolish Highness know that in temporal matters we are subject to no one. The collation of certain churches and vacant prebends belongs to us by royal right, and we take their revenues; against all possessors we rightly defend ourselves in this. Whoever believes otherwise we count as foolish and mad." The witnesses to this history are the author of the Chronicle of Brittany and Armorica, book 4, chapter 14, and Nicolas Gilles in his Chronicle of Gaul. To these must be added the lawyer Papon in the book of Arrêts, title 1, article 27. Yet much more so, John Tillet, clerk of the Parisian Parlement, a man otherwise most alien to this kind of history. "A certain cardinal," he says on page 172, "announced a truce imposed by Pope Boniface VIII between Philip the Fair and the kings of the Romans and of the English, with a penalty or threat of censure added. In 1297 Philip the Fair, by the counsel of his princes and counsellors, replied that he was ready to obey the Apostolic See in those matters which pertained to his soul and spiritual welfare; but that he acknowledged no superior except God in those matters which pertained to the temporal affairs of his kingdom, and that he did not wish to submit the temporal affairs of his kingdom to any mortal." When these things became known, Boniface sent a bull to King Philip, declaring that he was subject to him in temporal matters just as in spiritual, and at the same time pronounced that those who believed otherwise were heretics. Against this declaration strong protest was made, and at the same time the bull was burned at Paris in the presence of the King, the princes and the counsellors. Good heavens, what is this Papomania today among princes and the highest magistrates, if I may so put it? When they see the so great and so wicked pride and arrogance of that tyrant, yet, as if driven mad by a Circean cup, they nevertheless throw themselves down at his kissable feet, as if they were gazing upon some god fallen from heaven. But no one sets out this whole history more fittingly than Thomas Walsingham, the English historian, a monk otherwise most devoted to papist superstitions and, beyond others, most devoted to defending the greatness of the Popes. Since this book (as I hear) cannot be found for sale in our France, I think it worth while to set out that whole history in the words of that same monk.

units.la: Celestinus Papa, vir vitæ anachoriticæ, subdole à Benedicto Caietano inductus est, vt ei Papatum cederet: & constitutionem ederet, vt Papa quilibet cedere suum Papatum posset: quam tamen constitutionem Benedictus ille (postea Bonifacius Papa factus) revocauit, de quo vere Celestinus prophetauit
units.tr: Pope Celestine, a man of anchoritic life, was craftily induced by Benedict Gaetani to resign the papacy, and he issued a constitution that any pope might resign his papacy. Yet that same Benedict (afterwards made Pope Boniface) revoked this constitution. Concerning him Celestine truly prophesied

units.la: in hunc modum, Ascendisti vt vulpes: regnabis vt leo: morieris, vt canis. Bonifacio Papæ creato Rex Francorum Philippus in multis resistebat. Papæ fauebat Gallus Appamésis Episcopus, qui propterea de conspiratione contra Regé Franciæ accusatus, & ad Regis vocatus curiam, in custodia detentus est. Mense vero Februario ad mandatum Domini Papæ liberatus, iubetur vnà cum nuncio domini Papæ regnum euacuare.
units.tr: in this manner: "You have climbed up like a fox; you will reign like a lion; you will die like a dog." When Boniface had been created Pope, King Philip of the Franks resisted him in many things. Gallus, bishop of Appamea, favoured the Pope; for this reason he was accused of conspiracy against the King of France, summoned to the King's court and held in custody. But in February, at the Pope's command, he was released, and he was ordered to leave the kingdom together with the Pope's messenger.

units.la: Papa talibus nouis exasperatus, omnes gratias à se, vel suis prædecessoribus Francorum regibus concessas reuocauit: & in eundem Regem cito post excommunicationis sententiam fulminauit. Quam tamen Regi nemo est ausus nuntiare: vel in regno Franciæ publicare. Fecit etiam citari prælatos omnes de regno Franciæ, necnon & omnes magistros in Theologia, & in iure, tam canonico, quam ciuili, vt coram eo Romæ Kalend. Nouemb. comparerent. Rex vero Franciæ publico prohibuit edicto, nequis aurū, vel argentum seu merces quascunque Romam asportaret de regno suo: fecit etiam omnes exitus & introitus diligentissime custodiri.
units.tr: Exasperated by such new events, the Pope revoked all the favours granted by himself or by his predecessors to the kings of the Franks, and soon afterwards he hurled a sentence of excommunication against that same King. Yet no one dared to announce it to the King or to publish it in the kingdom of France. He also had all the prelates of the kingdom of France summoned, and all the masters in theology and in law, both canon and civil, to appear before him at Rome on the Kalends of November. The King of France, however, by public edict forbade anyone to carry gold, silver or any goods whatever out of his kingdom to Rome; and he had all the exits and entrances most diligently guarded.

units.la: Prælati Franciæ, missis ad Papam tribus Episcopis, de nó veniendo ad diē citationis præfixū, se p eosdem excusarunt. Papa vero Prælatis Fráciæ nó comparentibus, misit in Franciā Ioānē Monachum Cardinalē, q cōuocatis prælatis Parisiis, secretū consiliū habuit cū eisdē. Postea circa festū S.Ioā. Baptistę milites qdā in psentia cleri & populi Parisiis cōgregati, Papæ Bonifacio multa imposuerūt enormia, puta hæresim, simoniā, homicidia, propter quæ per Regem Franciæ appellatū est contra eum, ad illum cuius interest: donec, convocato consilio, se à criminibus purgaret obiectis. Circa festum natiuitatis beatæ Virginis, videlicet in vigilia natiuitatis eiusdem, venit summo manè magnus exercitus hominū armatorū missus ex parte Regis Franciæ repēte ad portas ciuitatis Anaguinæ, in quā Papa confugerat pro tutela: quia ibidem natus fuerat. Inueniētes igitur portas apertas ingressi sunt ciuitatē, & mox dederunt insultum Palatio domini Papę. Communitas vero villę cōperto, quòd Willelmus de Longaretto, (legendū est Nogaretto) senescha-lus Regis Frāciæ aduenisset, vt Papā deponeret, vel necaret, statim pulsata cōmuni campana, & tractatu habito, elegerunt sibi capitaneū quēdā Adnulphū, qui quidē illis ignorātibus extitit domini Papæ capitalis inimicus. Hi omnes cōmunibus votis tātū irruerūt in Papā, & nepotē suū, & tres Cardinales (q à tergo p latrinā euaserūt) q; diu (vt putabatur) eis resistere nō valeret. Ob q; cū Dns Papa timēs sibi, treugas petiit. Quib. finitis, exercit⁹ p vim ad papā est ingressus, quē tūc plurimi verbis contumeliosis sunt aggressi. Cū aūt ad rationē posit⁹ esset, an vellet renūtiare Papatui, cōstārer respōdit, Nō: imò citi⁹ vellet pdere caput suū, dicēs in suo vulgari: Ecco il collo: Ecco il capo: q; est dicere, ecce collū, ecce caput. Et statim, ptelstatus est coram omnib⁹, q; Papatui nūq; renūtiaret, quādiu posset habere vitā. exercitus vero postquā irrupit palatiū, mox despoliauit Papā, & eius cameram, atq; thesauria suam, & asportauit vestimenta cum ornamentis, & aurum atque argentum, cum omnibus alijs rebus inuentis ibidem. Et reuera creditur quod omnes reges mundi non possent tantum de thesauro reddere, infra vnum annum, quantum fuit de Papali palatio asportatū. Remansit autem Papa sub custodia militum & custodum vsq; ad diem tertiam. sed populus Anagum, facta conuocatione secreta vsque ad decem milia hominum concurrunt, & Papam deliberauerunt. sed ante haec omnia sciendum, quod cū illi primo Papam comprehendissent, in equum posuerunt effrenem, facie ad caudam versa, & sic coegerunt discurrere, fere ad nouissimum halitum, & tandem pene fame necauerunt: donec eum populus Anagum (vt praēmittitur) liberasset. Tunc populus fecit Papam deportari in magnam plateam, vbi Papa lacrymando populo prædicauit: & tandem in fine sermonis dixit: Boni homines & mulieres, constat vobis, qualiter inimici mei venerunt, & abstulerunt omnia bona mea, & non tantum mea, sed etiā bona Ecclesiæ, & me ita pauperem, sicut Iob fuerat, dimiserunt. propter quod dico vobis veraciter, quod nihil habeo ad comedendum vel bibendum, & ieiunus remansi, vsque ad præsens. Et si sit aliqua bona mulier, quæ me velit de sua iuuare eleemosyna, in pane vel vino, & si vinum non habuerit, de aqua permodica, dabo ei benedictionem Dei & meam, & omnes qui quicquam portauerint, quantulumcumq; modicum, absoluo eos ab omnibus peccatis suis. Tunc omnes hęc audientes ex ore Papæ, clamabant, Vivas pater sancte. Et mox cernere s mulieres currere certatim ad Palatium, ad offerendum sibi panem, vinum, vel aquam: in tantum, quòd statim camera Papæ victualibus repleta fuit. Et cum non inuenirentur vasa ad capiendum allata, fundebant vinum & aquâ in area cameræ Papæ, in maxima quantitate. Et tunc potuit quisque ingredi, & cum Papa loqui, sicut cum alio paupere, qui volebat. Tunc Papa exiens absoluit omnes existentes in ciuitate ab omnibus peccatis eorum. His itaque gestis, Papa subitò & inopinatè, recessit de villa Anagum, progrediens versus Romam: cum maxima multitudine armatorum. Et cum peruenisset ad sanctum Petrum, ex timore, quem conceperat, quando fuit captus, & mærore rerum inæstimabilium perditarum, cito defecit: & sic completa est prophetia prædecessoris sui, quæ dixit: Ascendisti vt vulpes: regnabis vt leo: morieris, vt canis. Hæc Walsinghamius, totidem verbis: primùm in Historia sub Eduardo primo, deinde in Annalib. quinetiam sub anno 1307. hæc adscribit: Rex Franciæ per hoc tempus petiit per suos nuntios à domino Papa Benedicto, ossa prædecessoris sui Bonifacij, ad comburendum, tanquam hæretici.
units.tr: The prelates of France, having sent three bishops to the Pope, excused themselves through them for not coming on the day fixed for the summons. The Pope, since the prelates of France did not appear, sent into France John the Cardinal Monk, who, having summoned the prelates to Paris, held a secret council with them. Afterwards, about the feast of St John the Baptist, certain soldiers, gathered in Paris in the presence of the clergy and people, charged Pope Boniface with many enormities: heresy, simony, homicides; on account of these, an appeal was lodged by the King of France against him to the one whose concern it was, until, a council being convened, he should purge himself of the charges laid against him. Around the feast of the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin, that is on the eve of her Nativity, early in the morning a great army of armed men, sent on behalf of the King of France, suddenly came to the gates of the city of Anagni, where the Pope had taken refuge for protection, because he had been born there. Finding the gates open, they entered the city and at once assaulted the palace of the lord Pope. But when the commune of the town learned that William of Longaret (read Nogaret), seneschal of the King of France, had come to depose or kill the Pope, at once the common bell was rung, and after a discussion they chose for themselves a certain captain, Adenulf, who indeed, unknown to them, had been the lord Pope's mortal enemy. All of them, with common consent, rushed upon the Pope and his nephew and three cardinals (who escaped through the latrine from behind), and for some time, as was thought, they could not resist them. Because of this, the lord Pope, fearing for himself, asked for a truce. When this was concluded, the army forced its way into the Pope's presence, and many of them then attacked him with insulting words. When he was called to account, whether he would resign the papacy, he firmly replied, No; rather, he would sooner lose his head, saying in his own vernacular: "Here is my neck; here is my head." And at once he declared in the presence of all that he would never resign the papacy as long as he had life. But after the army had broken into the palace, they at once plundered the Pope, his chamber and his treasury, and carried off the vestments with their ornaments, the gold and silver, and all the other things found there. And indeed it is believed that all the kings of the world could not restore so much treasure within a single year as was carried off from the papal palace. The Pope remained under the custody of soldiers and guards until the third day. But the people of Anagni, after a secret summons, gathered up to ten thousand men and deliberated about the Pope. Yet before all this one must know that when they first seized the Pope, they set him on an unbridled horse, facing the tail, and so forced him to run about almost to his last breath, and finally nearly starved him to death, until the people of Anagni (as was said above) freed him. Then the people had the Pope carried into a great square, where the Pope, weeping, addressed the people; and at last, at the end of his speech, he said: "Good men and women, you know how my enemies came and carried off all my goods, and not only mine but also the goods of the Church, and left me as poor as Job was. Therefore I tell you truthfully that I have nothing to eat or drink, and I have remained fasting until now. And if there is any good woman who would wish to help me from her alms, with bread or wine, or, if she has no wine, with a little water, I will give her the blessing of God and my own, and I absolve from all their sins all who have brought anything, however small." Then all who heard these words from the Pope's mouth cried out, "Long live the holy father!" And at once women could be seen running eagerly to the palace to offer him bread, wine or water, to such an extent that the Pope's chamber was at once filled with provisions. And since no vessels were found to hold what was brought, they poured the wine and water into the courtyard of the Pope's chamber in great quantity. Then anyone who wished could enter and speak with the Pope, just as with any other poor man. Then the Pope, going out, absolved all in the city from all their sins. With these things done, the Pope suddenly and unexpectedly left the town of Anagni, making his way towards Rome with a great crowd of armed men. And when he had reached St Peter's, from the fear he had conceived when he was taken, and from grief over the incalculable goods lost, he quickly sank; and so the prophecy of his predecessor was fulfilled, which said: "You have climbed up like a fox; you will reign like a lion; you will die like a dog." These things Walsingham writes, in these very words: first in his History under Edward I, then in his Annals, and moreover under the year 1307 he adds this: "At this time the King of France sought, through his messengers, from the lord Pope Benedict the bones of his predecessor Boniface, to burn them as those of a heretic."

units.la: MAgna igitur ac planè sacrosancta Concilij & Ordinum coactorum vis & potestas ex superioribus testimoniis apparuit. sed quoniam hoc in argumento & quasi campo versamur, non praetermittenda videtur eiusdem Concilij auctoritas, patrum nostrorum memoria interposita contra Regem Ludovicum XI. qui superiorum regum omnium versutissimus & callidissimus est habitus. ex quo intelligi facile poterit, quod iam saepe diximus, maiores nostros non sibi ferum aliquem tyrannum aut carnificem imposuisse, qui suos cives in pecudum loco ac numero haberet: sed Regem iuris ac libertatis suae custodem asciuisse qui iustitiae praeses esset. Anno igitur MCCCCLX. cum ita regnum ab illo Ludovico gereretur, ut multis in rebus boni Principis & patriam amantis ossicium desideraretur, coepta est Concilij auctoritas requiri, ut in eo Boni publici ratio haberetur. Et quoniam ei rex minimè sese subiecturus putabatur, Proceres regni, assiduis plebis querimoniis & expostulationibus incitati, manus cogere, exercitusque comparare instituerunt: ut Bonū publicum procurare, & regi perditam Reipub. administrationem (verba sunt Philippi Cominij lib.1.cap.2.) vi demonstrare possent. Instructi enim & parati cum exercitu esse volebant, bànt,vt fi rex consulere Bono publico,& bonis consilijs parere detractaret, vi cogere inuitum possent.qua de caussa bellum illud Bono publico susceptum dicebatur, vulgóque Bellum boni publici appellatum est. Procerum nomina idem Cominius, Gillius, Lamarcius hæc prodiderunt: Dux Borbonius, Dux Biturigum regis frater, Comites Dunensis, Niuernensis, Armeniacus, Albretius,&is ad quem summa imperij respiciebat, Dux Carolensis. Quacunque autem iter faciebant, pronuntiari iubebant, se bellum illud Bono publico instituere, tributorumque & vectigalium immunitatem indicebant(quæ omnia Gillij verba sunt lib. 4.sol.152.) legatóque & literas Lutetiam ad Parlamétum, Ecclesiasticos & Academiæ rectorem miserunt (verba hæc eiuldem Gillij sunt sol. eodem) ne putarent exercitum illum in regis perniciem comparatum fuisse: verùm vt illum ad boni regis officium reuocarent, sicuti boni publici ratio postulabat. Verba autem Annalium, qui Chronica Ludouici x i.inscripti sunt, Lutetiæ à Gallioto impressa,hæc fere sunt,sol.27.Primum & summum Postulatorum caput hoc fuit, vt Trium ordinum conuentus haberetur:quippe, quòd vnicum omnibus seculis, malorū omniū remedium fuisset, vimque semper eiusmodi incommodis medendi habuisset. Rursus pag.28. Procerum legatis Senatus datus est Lutetiæ, die xxiiii. in Curia quæ Domus ciuitatis dicitur, in quo affuerunt delecti ex Academia, ex parlamento,& ex Magistratibus.Respõsum est, eorum postulatum æquissimum videri, concilиumq; Trium ordinum indictum est. Hæc, inquam, Historici verba sunt, sol. 28. ex quibus verissimum istud M. Antonij vetus verbum esse apparet:Etsi omnes molestæ semper seditiones sunt,iustas tamen esse nonnullas, & propè necessarias. Eas verò iustissimas, maximéque necessarias quis non dicet, cùm populus Tyranni sæuitia oppressus, auxilium à legitimo Ciuium conuentu implorat? Quid? deteriórne Ciuium conditio esse debet, quàm olim seruorum fuit? qui sæuitia dominorum pressi ad vrbis præfectum confugiebant, & de suis dominis verecūdè(vt ait Vlpianus) expostulabant. Itaque Guaguinus in vita eiusdem Ludouici, vbi respósum Caroli Burgundiæ Ducis ad regis legatos exponit : his vtitur verbis,pag. 265. Audiuit, inquit, Carolus legatos. verùm ad pacem nihil commodius esse respondit, quàm trium Ordinum conuentum:vbi tantas animorum & belli discordias componi oporteret. quod postquam per nuntios Legati Ludouico retulerunt,ipse in dilatione spem reponens, concilium apud Turones ad Kal. Aprilanni MCCCCLXVII. indixit. Conuentionis definito tempore,affuere ex toto regno,&c. Quod idem totidem verbis traditur in iis quæ diximus Annalibus, sol. 64. & in Magno Chron.vol.4.sol.242. vbi etiam illud additum est, quod memoria dignum & summoperè obseruandum videtur,placuisse in eo concilio, cilio, vt certi probatique viri ex singulis ordinibus deligerentur, qui Remp. constituerent, & (vt ad verbum interpretemur) iuri ac iustitiæ prouiderent. At N. Gillius, eo quem ostendimus loco: Post prælium, inquit, Montlerinum, delecti sunt complures egregiè cordati & prudentes viri, qui boni publici curatores essent: quemadmodum inter regem & supradictos Proceres conuenerat: primúsque in eo numero fuit Comes Dunensis, qui primus discessionis illius auctor fuerat. Erat autem (vt superius dictum est) antiquæ consuetudinis, postquam Ecclesiasticorum opes in tantam potentiam excreuerant, vt populus in tres ordines describeretur, quorum vnum Ecclesiastici obtinerent: cúmque Reip. curatores constituerentur, duodeni ex vnoquoque ordine deligerentur. Itaque in eo Concilio constitutum fuit, vt xxxv i. Reipubli. curatores crearentur, qui communi consilio publicis incommodis mederétur. Qua dè re Monstrelletus vol. 4. sol. 150. ita scribit: Principio decretum est, vt ad Rempub. constituendam, plebémque tributis & detrimentis subleuandam x xxv i. viri auctoritate regia deligerentur: duodeni ex clero, totidem ex equitibus, & totidem iuris & iustitiæ periti: quibus potestas permitteretur videndi, quibus vitiis atque incommodis regnum laboraret, iisq; vitiis remedium adhibendi: fidemque rex regali dicto promissoque dedit (ad verbum, Et promisit rex in verbo regis) ratum se habiturum, quicquid illi xxxvi. viri constituerent. Hæc Mõftrelletus: cui Oliuerius Lamarcius Belga, in historiæ suæ cap. 35. totidem propè verbis subscribit, eundémque xxxvi. Curatorum Reipubl. numerum prodit: firmulque alscrib t, cùm rex ei dicto promissoque non stetisset, fideinque publicam & publicè iuratâ violasset, miserrimum in Francogallia bellum exartisse, quod annos propè xiii. duravit. Ita regis periurium cùm ipsius infamia, tum etiam populi pernicie expiatum est. Vtcunque fit, perspicuum est, nondum centesimum annum abiisse, ex quo Francogalliæ libertas, solennisque Concilij auctoritas vigebat: & vigebat aduersus regem, neque ætate, neque animo imbecillum: id & iam annorum xl. maiorem, & tanta ingenij magnitudine praeditum, quantam nunquam in vllo rege nostro fuisse constat. Vt facile intelligatur, Remp. nostram libertate fundatam & stabilitam, annos amplius centum & mille statum illum suum liberum & sacrosanctum, etiam vi & armis adversus Tyrannorum potentiam, retinuisse. Neque vero præclarum hac de re Philippi Cominæi clarissimi viri & ornatissimi historici elogium prætermittendum videtur: qui lib. Hist. 5. ca. 18. in hac scribit sententiam, quam ad verbum couertemus. Quare vt in instituto sermone pergamus, ecquis est in orbe terrarum rex, aut Princeps, cui ius sit tributum vnius teruncij subiectis suis sine ipsorum consensu & voluntate imponere? nisi violetia & tyrannide vti velit. Atenim (dixerit aliquis) potest tempus incidere, cùm publicum populi concilium expectandum non est: neque tantam moram res patitur. Sanè in bello suscipiendo nihil tanta celeritate est opus. satis ad eam rem temporis suppeditat. Addo etiam illud, cùm reges & Principes bellum ciuiũ suorum consensu suscipiunt, multò & potétiores sunt,& hostibus suis formidabiliores. Et rursus aliquantò post: Regem Galliæ minimè omnium decet his vti verbis: Habeo potestatem exigendi à meis ciuibus, quàtum mihi libet. Nã neque ipse,neque quisquam alius eam potestatem habet. Qui verò his vtuntur verbis,nullum ei honorem tribuũt: neque illius auctoritatem & existimationem apud exteras nationes augent. verùm ex contrario, terrorem finitimis iniiciunt:qui nulla cõditione dominatum illius subire vellent. At si rex noster, aut ij qui potentiam eius prædicant, ita loquerentur : Habeo subiectos ita mansuetos & obsequentes, vt nihil eorum quæ impero facere detrectêt, neque quisquam Princeps subiectos habet æquè obsequentes, quíque calamitatum & incommodorum suorum facilius obliuiscantur: hæc oratio magnę illi laudi,atque ornamento esset. Verùm illa regem non decet:Exigo,quantum volo: eiusque rei potestatem habeo, quam mihi conseruatam volo. Rex Carolus quintus hac oratione non vtebatur. Neque sanè regem vllum nostrum illis vtentem verbis audiui: sed quosdam ipsorum comites & ministros: qui sibi bonam regibus nauare operam videbātur. Verùm meo iudicio aduersus illos peccabant: & tātum assentandi causa ita loquebantur: neque satis quid dicerent, considerabant. Atque vt certius mansueti Gallorum ingenij argumentum proferamus, consideremus concilium trium Ordinum Turonibus, post regis nostri Ludouici xı. excessum, habitum: anno nimirum 1484. Existimari per id tempus poterat, bonū illum Ordinum conuentum periculosum esse. dicebántque nescio qui, non magni pretij homines, sæpiusque post id tempus dixerűt, crimen esse læsæ maiestatis, siquis de trium Ordinum concilio conuocando verba faciat. Id enim ad minuendam regis auctoritatem pertinere. Verùm illi ipsi sunt, qui crimen illud aduersus Deum, & regem & Remp. committunt. Neque verba eiusmodi aliis prosunt, quàm iis, qui nullo suo merito gradus honorum & dignitatum obtinent: neque ad illos obtinendos sunt idonei: sed assentari & seruire auribus didicerunt, & nugatoriis de rebus verba facere: magnósque conuentus hominum reformidant, ne quales sunt, tales agnoscantur: eorumque opera vituperétur. Hæc ad verbum Cominæus: ex quibus aliisque quæ superius de retenta publici concilij in Ludouicum xı. auctoritate diximus, perspicuè intelligitur, etiam vsque ad id tempus nobile illud præceptum, à Turcica tyrannide alienum, viguisse: SALVS POPVLI SVPREMA LEX ESTO. sed hanc conuentus publici libertatem palpatores aulici, regum assentatores, & qui malis artibus honores adepti sunt (vt Cominæus scribit) omni studio & contentione auersantur. Qua de re Budæus quoque libro de Asse iiii. sic scribit: Quare, si moribus iam nostris, qui rerum summam tenent, tenebúntque in posterū, In DISQVISITIONEM CONVENTVVM ali quando vocentur, nonnulli sæpe qui sese nasutos videri volunt, haud dubie (quod aiunt) apprime simi, atque ea parte deformes ab omnibus cernerentur. Hæc Budæus: circiter illud tempus, quo Rex Franciscus primus ex Hispania (quò captiuus abductus fuerat) reuersus, vt redemptionis suæ nomine pecuniam conficeret, tributum Ordinibus sui Regni non pro suo iure imperauit, sed (vt auctores omnes affirmant) ab iisbona sine gratia, sine venia impetrauit. qua de re Nic. Boerius Decif. cxxvi. ita scribit: Anno Dominic ɪɔɪɔxxvii. Princeps noster in mense Decemb. conuocauit prælatos, nec non nobiles de eius sanguine, & alios regni sui, & ex quolibet Parlamēto vnum præsidentē, & duos cōsiliarios, qui omnes ita REGI ANNVERVNT TALLIAM, VSQVE AD SVMMAM DVORVM MILLIONVM, pro redemptione sua, imponere & leuare posse.
units.tr: The great and truly sacred power and authority of the Assembly and the Estates gathered together has thus appeared from the testimonies above. But since we are working within this subject, as it were on a field of its own, the authority of the same Assembly should not be passed over. It was exercised in our fathers' time against King Louis XI, who was regarded as the most crafty and cunning of all the kings before him. From this it can easily be understood, as we have often said already, that our forebears did not set over themselves some savage tyrant or executioner who would hold his citizens in the place and number of cattle. They took instead a king as guardian of their law and liberty, to preside over justice. So in the year 1460, when the kingdom was being governed by Louis in such a way that in many matters the duty of a good prince who loved his country was missing, the authority of the Assembly began to be sought, so that the public good might be taken into account in it. And since the king was not thought likely to submit to it of his own accord, the nobles of the realm, roused by the constant complaints and protests of the common people, began to gather forces and raise an army, so that they might look after the public good and, by force, show the king the ruin of the government of the commonwealth (these are the words of Philippe de Commynes, book 1, chapter 2). For they wished to be armed and ready with an army, so that if the king refused to consult the public good and to obey good counsel, they could compel him against his will. For this reason that war was said to be undertaken for the public good, and it was commonly called the War of the Public Good. Commynes, Gilles and Lamarck have handed down the names of the nobles: the Duke of Bourbon, the Duke of Berry, the king's brother, the Counts of Dunois, Nevers and Armagnac, Albret, and he to whom the chief command was looked to, the Duke of Calabria. Wherever they went, they ordered it to be proclaimed that they were undertaking that war for the public good, and they announced an exemption from taxes and duties (all these are the words of Gilles, book 4, p. 152). They also sent envoys and letters to Paris, to the Parlement, the clergy and the rector of the University (these are the same Gilles's words, same page), so that they should not think that army had been raised for the king's ruin, but rather to recall him to the duty of a good king, as the public good demanded. The words of the Annals, which are entitled the Chronicles of Louis XI and were printed at Paris by Galliot, are roughly these, p. 27: "The first and chief demand of the petitioners was that a meeting of the three Estates be held, since this alone had always been the remedy for all evils and had always had the power to heal such troubles." Again, p. 28: "The envoys of the nobles were given an audience with the Senate at Paris on the 24th day, in the court called the House of the City, where there were present chosen men from the University, from the Parlement and from the magistrates. It was answered that their demand seemed most fair, and a meeting of the three Estates was announced." These, I say, are the words of the historian, p. 28, from which it appears that that old saying of Marcus Antonius is most true: "Although all seditions are troublesome, yet some are just and almost necessary." And who would not call those most just and most necessary, when a people oppressed by the cruelty of a tyrant implores help from a lawful assembly of its citizens? What? Ought the condition of citizens to be worse than that of slaves once were, who, oppressed by the cruelty of their masters, fled to the city prefect and, as Ulpian says, complained of their masters with respect? So Gaguin, in the life of the same Louis, where he sets out the reply of Charles, Duke of Burgundy, to the king's envoys, uses these words, p. 265: "Charles, he says, heard the envoys. But he replied that nothing was more suitable for peace than a meeting of the three Estates, where such great discords of minds and of war ought to be settled." When the envoys reported this to Louis through messengers, he, placing his hope in delay, announced an assembly at Tours for the Kalends of April in the year 1467. At the appointed time there came from the whole kingdom, etc. The same is handed down word for word in the Annals I have cited, p. 64, and in the Great Chronicle, vol. 4, p. 242, where this also is added, which seems worthy of remembrance and to be most carefully observed: it was agreed in that assembly that certain tested men should be chosen from each order, who would set the commonwealth in order and (to translate word for word) provide for law and justice. But N. Gilles, in the passage I have pointed to: "After the battle of Montlhéry," he says, "several very wise and prudent men were chosen, who were to be curators of the public good, as had been agreed between the king and the aforesaid nobles. First in that number was the Count of Dunois, who had been the first author of that dissension. Now there was (as was said above) an ancient custom, dating from the time when the wealth of the clergy had grown to such power that the people was divided into three orders, of which the clergy held one, that when curators of the commonwealth were appointed, twelve were chosen from each order." Accordingly, in that assembly it was decided that thirty-six curators of the commonwealth should be created, who by common counsel would remedy public ills. Concerning this matter Monstrelet, vol. 4, p. 150, writes thus: "First it was decided that thirty-six men should be chosen by royal authority to set the commonwealth in order and to relieve the common people of taxes and losses: twelve from the clergy, as many from the knights, and as many skilled in law and justice; to these power was to be given of seeing what vices and troubles the kingdom laboured under, and of applying remedies to those vices; and the king gave his faith by his royal word and promise (word for word, 'and the king promised on his word as king') that he would hold as ratified whatever those thirty-six men should decide." So Monstrelet; and Olivier de Lamarck, the Belgian, in chapter 35 of his history, agrees with him in almost the same words, and gives the same number of thirty-six curators of the commonwealth, and firmly adds that when the king did not abide by his word and promise, and violated his public and publicly sworn faith, the most wretched war broke out in France, which lasted almost thirteen years. Thus the king's perjury was expiated both by his own infamy and by the destruction of the people. However that may be, it is clear that not yet a hundred years had passed since the liberty of France and the solemn authority of the Assembly were in force, and were in force against the king, who was neither weak in age nor in spirit, being then forty years old and endowed with a greatness of mind such as is known never to have been in any of our kings. So it is easily understood that our commonwealth, founded and established in liberty, preserved for more than a hundred and a thousand years that its free and sacred condition, even by force and arms against the power of tyrants. Nor should the excellent judgement on this matter of Philippe de Commynes, a most distinguished man and most accomplished historian, be passed over; in book 5, chapter 18 of his History he writes an opinion which we shall render word for word. "Therefore, to go on with the subject at hand: what king or prince is there in the world who has the right to impose a single farthing on his subjects without their consent and will, unless he wishes to use violence and tyranny? But (someone may say) a time may come when a public assembly of the people cannot be awaited, and the matter does not admit such delay. Certainly, in undertaking war nothing needs such haste; there is time enough for that. I add also that when kings and princes undertake war with the consent of their citizens, they are much more powerful and more formidable to their enemies." And again, a little later: "It least of all befits the King of France to use these words: 'I have power to exact from my citizens as much as I please.' For neither he nor anyone else has such power. Those who use such words give him no honour, nor do they increase his authority and reputation among foreign nations; on the contrary, they strike terror into his neighbours, who would not wish to submit to his domination on any condition. But if our king, or those who extol his power, spoke thus: 'I have subjects so gentle and obedient that they refuse nothing I command, and no prince has subjects so obedient, who forget their calamities and losses more easily,' that speech would be a great praise and ornament to him. But this is not fitting for a king: 'I exact as much as I wish, and I have the power to keep for myself what I wish to keep.' King Charles the Fifth did not use that language. Indeed I have never heard any of our kings using those words, but some of their counts and ministers, who thought they were doing the kings a good service by it. But in my judgement they were wrong in this, and they spoke so only for the sake of flattery, and did not consider well enough what they were saying." And so that we may bring forward more certain evidence of the gentle temper of the French, let us consider the assembly of the three Estates held at Tours after the death of our King Louis XI, namely in the year 1484. At that time it could be thought that that good assembly of the Estates was dangerous, and certain men, I know not who, of no great worth, both then and often afterwards said that it was a crime of treason to speak of convoking an assembly of the three Estates, since that tended to diminish the king's authority. But it is precisely those men who commit that crime against God, the king and the commonwealth. Nor do words of that kind profit anyone except those who hold rank and dignity without any merit of their own, and are not fit to hold them, but have learned to flatter and to serve by their ears, and to speak about trifles; and they dread great gatherings of men, lest they be recognised for what they are, and their work be censured. So Commynes writes. From these words and from what we have said above about the retained authority of the public Assembly against Louis XI, it is plainly understood that even down to that time that noble precept, foreign to Turkish tyranny, flourished: "LET THE SAFETY OF THE PEOPLE BE THE SUPREME LAW." But this liberty of public assembly the court flatterers, the sycophants of kings, and those who have obtained honours by bad arts (as Commynes writes) avoid with all zeal and effort. On this matter Budé also writes thus in book 4 of his work On the As: "Wherefore, if with our present customs those who hold, and will hold in future, the chief power of affairs, are ever summoned to an inquiry into an assembly, some who like to appear keen-scented will undoubtedly, as they say, be seen by all to be most similar and most deformed in that respect." So Budé. Around the time when King Francis I, returning from Spain (where he had been led away as a captive), in order to raise money in the name of his ransom, imposed a tax on the orders of his kingdom not by his own right, but (as all authors affirm) obtained it from them as a good without grace and without pardon. Concerning this Nicolas Boerius, Decision 126, writes thus: "In the year of the Lord 1527 our prince, in the month of December, summoned the prelates, the nobles of his blood, and others of his kingdom, and from each Parlement one president and two counsellors, who all agreed that they could impose and levy on the king a tax, up to the sum of two million crowns, for his ransom."

units.la: Alterum eiusdem publici Concilij facinus insi- gne in Papa Benedicto XIII. damnando & repudiando. CAP. XXIIII.
units.tr: Another notable deed of the same public council, in condemning and repudiating Pope Benedict XIII. CHAP. XXIIII.

units.la: HActenus quanta publici Francogalliæ cō- cilijauctoritas in damnanda Papæ Bonifacij v iii. insania fuerit, satis explicatum arbitramur. Nunc alterum eiusdé auctoritatis exemplum in Papa Benedicto XIII damnádo ac repudiádo proponamus. Quo tempore Rex Carolus VI Galliæ gubernacula tenebat, circiter illud tempus mirificum quoddam Antipaparū aliquot certamen extitit, quod annos amplius xxx factionibus exitiosis, summa cũ omniū rerū perturbatione & piorū animorū cruciatu, mœrore ac prope desperatione duravit: neque vllus in orbe Christiano Princeps fuit, neq; Rex, neque Imperator, qui non omne suum studium in illa funesta & calamitosa Antipaparū cōtentione sedanda interposuerit, quam historiam Platina, Krantzius & Guaguinus memoriæ prodiderunt. sed omnium copiosissime is, qui assiduus tragœdiarum illarū spectator fuit, Theodor. Nyhemius, lib. de schismate tertio. Sed quoniam hanc operam Gallis nostris potissimum navamus, commodius fore arbitramur, vnius Enguerrantij Monstreletti, qui Gallorum prope omnium manibus teritur, testimonium sequi, totamque ipsius hac de re narratione breviter comprehendere. Sic enim fere ad verbum sub cap. xl. & aliquot insequentibus scriptum reliquit: Rex Carolus v i. per legatos denuntiavit Petro de Luna, Bonifacio xiii. per papificationem nominato, nisi intra tempus illud quod de communi Christianorum Principum sententia præstitutum erat, finem illi funesto certamini imponeret, ac de papatu cum æmulo suo transigeret, fore, vt ipse, suiqué omnes Galliæ populi sibi consilium caperent: ac neutri Antipaparum obedientiam præstarent. Hac denuntiatione Papa Benedictus grauiter indignatus, animi tamen offensionem vultu atque oratione tegés, blanda oratione legatos dimisit, confirmans se propediem responsum per certum hominem ac nuncium Regi missurum.
