Pauculis post diebus diploma quam Bullam appellát, Regi per emissarium quemdam misit, qua & Regem & omnes ipsius imperio subiectos excommunicabat, sacrisque omnibus tanquam impios ac profanos arcebat. Ea bulla perfecta, eiusque rei fama per vniuersam Galliá disseminata, Rex Concilium publicum Lutetiam Parisiorum indicit: quo in conuentu de communi ordinum sententia decreta hæc fuerút: primùm vt Benedictus Papa deinceps pro schismatico, hæretico, & Ecclesiæ Christianæ perturbatore haberetur: néve illi obedientia vlla præstaretur: vtiq; acta illius omnia irrita essent: tum vt bulla Regi missa pronuntiaretur impia, scelerata, & in regiam Maiestatem contumeliosa: atque iccirco palam inspectáte populo lacerarețur. postremò, vt tam atrox illata Regi & regno iniuria tum aduersus Papam, ipsius auctorem, tú etiam aduersus omnes ipsius factionis socios vindicaretur. His decretis palam in conuentu pronuntiatis confestim Rector Academiæ Parisiensis è sella exsurgés bullam cepit, eamque inspectante Rege in procerum delectorumque omnium conspectu suis manibus discidit. Nuntius autem Papæ qui eam attulerat, atque alter quidā eiusdem Pōtificis emissarius talaribus amicti togis, in quibus inuersa Papæ insignia depicta erant, mitra capitibus imposita, in qua grandibus literis elogium hoc scriptum erat: HI SVNT IN ECCLESIAM ET REGEM PERFIDI: è carcere vsque ad palatij Parisiensis aream aduecti sunt: atque in contabulato ex tempore extructo destituti, summa cum Papæ infamia ac dedecore catamidiati, omniū irrisui ac ludibrio expositi, ioculare Parisiensibus spectaculum præbuerūt. Tertio denique post die iterum in plaustrū impositi, ac per vrbis vias circunuecti, conuitiis, sibilis, clamoribus omnium vexati, vix è populi insultantibus manibus effugerunt.
units.tr: Thus far we think we have sufficiently shown how great was the authority of the public council of France in condemning the madness of Pope Boniface VIII. Now let us set out another example of that authority, in condemning and repudiating Pope Benedict XIII. At the time when Charles VI held the reins of the French realm, there arose a remarkable contest among several anti-popes, which lasted more than thirty years, with ruinous factions, with the complete upheaval of all affairs, and with the torment, grief and near despair of pious souls. No prince in the Christian world, neither king nor emperor, failed to devote all his zeal to settling that deadly and calamitous contention of the anti-popes. Platina, Krantz and Gaguin have handed down the story, but most copiously of all Theodoricus Niem, who was a constant spectator of those tragedies, in his book on the third schism. Since, however, we are devoting this labour chiefly to our French, we think it more convenient to follow the testimony of one man alone, Enguerrand de Monstrelet, whose work is worn in the hands of nearly all the French, and to summarise briefly his whole account of the matter. For he wrote roughly thus, word for word, under chapter 40 and some following: King Charles VI sent word through envoys to Peter de Luna, called Benedict XIII by the Papists, that unless within the time fixed by the common judgment of the Christian princes he put an end to that deadly contest and came to terms with his rival over the papacy, the king himself and all the people of France would take counsel for themselves and would render obedience to neither of the anti-popes. Pope Benedict, gravely offended by this declaration, yet concealing his offence in face and speech, dismissed the envoys with smooth words, assuring them that he would shortly send the king a reply through a certain man and messenger. A few days later he sent the king, through a certain emissary, what he calls a diploma, but what is commonly called a bull, by which he excommunicated both the king and all who were subject to his rule, and barred them from all sacred rites as impious and profane. When this bull was completed, and the report of it had spread through all of France, the king summoned a public council at Paris. At that assembly, by the common opinion of the orders, these decrees were made: first, that Benedict should henceforth be held as a schismatic, a heretic and a disturber of the Christian Church, that no obedience be rendered to him, and that all his acts be void; then, that the bull sent to the king be pronounced impious, wicked and insulting to the royal majesty, and that it be torn in pieces in the sight of the people; lastly, that so atrocious an injury done to the king and kingdom be avenged both against the pope, its author, and against all the allies of his faction. When these decrees had been announced openly in the assembly, the rector of the University of Paris at once rose from his seat, took up the bull, and tore it with his own hands, in the sight of the king and of all the nobles and chosen men. The papal messenger who had brought it, and another emissary of the same pontiff, dressed in long robes on which the papal insignia were painted upside down, with a mitre placed on their heads bearing this inscription in large letters: THESE ARE PERFIDIOUS TOWARDS THE CHURCH AND THE KING, were brought from prison to the courtyard of the Paris palace. Set down on a platform hastily built, they were shamed to the great infamy and disgrace of the pope, exposed to the derision and mockery of all, and provided a comical spectacle for the Parisians. Finally, three days later, they were again placed in a cart and carried round the streets of the city, tormented by the abuse, hisses and shouts of everyone, and they barely escaped from the hands of the jeering people.

units.la: Regem Francogalliæ non infinitam in suo regno dominationem habere, sed certo iure certisque legibus circumscriptam. CAP. XXV.
units.tr: That the King of France does not have unlimited dominion in his kingdom, but is bounded by a certain right and certain laws. CAP. XXV.

units.la: SAtis igitur demonstratum esse arbitramur, Regibus Francogalliæ non immensam atque infinitam potestatem à suis ciuibus permissam fuisse: vt legibus omnibus soluti dici possint: sed eos certis legibus & pactionibus obligatos esse; quarum primam esse summā hanc fuisse ostendimus. Vt publici Concilij auctoritate sanctam inuiolatamque seruarent: eumq; conuentum, quoties vtilitas Reip. postularet, sua præsentia concelebrarent. Ac leges quidem quibus Reges astrictos esse constat, permultæ sunt. Verùm nos eas solas de quibus nemo nisi ametissimus, nemo nisi patriæ, parentũ ac liberorum suorum hostis ambigit, vt quæque memoratu dignæ videbuntur, exponemus. Prima igitur hæc esto: Vt ne quid quod ad statum Reip. in vniuersum pertineat, Regi sine publici Concilij auctoritate statuere liceat, cuius rei cum antea certissima testimonia protulimus, tum etiam expressissimum & euidentissimum vsque ad hanc ætatem nostram vestigium illud manet, quòd senatus Parisiensis, qui veteris illius Parlamenti auctoritatem sibi magna ex parte asciuit, nullas Regis constitutiones, nulla edicta rata esse patitur, nisi quæ apud se pro consilio cognita, & consiliariorum suorum sententiis comprobata fuerint: vt non incommodè dici possit, similem hoc quidem in genere videri Senatus illius auctoritatem veterum Tribunorum plebis potestati, quos Val. Maximus scribit, in vestibulo Senatus expectare solitos, dum ad se decreta eius ordinis afferrentur, quæ ipsi pro Concilio cognoscerent: vt si plebi vtilia videretur, literam T quasi assensus sui notam atq; indicem subscriberet: sin minus, vetarent, atque intercederent. quanquam Budæus, vir doctissimus, aliunde similitudinem sumit: sicuti populo R. (inquit) scisçente aliquid, Senatum auctore fieri oportebat, quod nunc verbo Græco Homologare dicimus, ita Principum nostrorum constitutionibus, vt vim sanctionum habeat, huiusmodi actis ad Reipub. pertinentibus auctorem Curiam fieri hodie necesse est, easque in curia promulgari. Et paulo post: In hac curia pro factis provinciarum ac iuridici, quos Balliuos, Seneschallos, & huiusmodi nominibus vocamus, in leges iurare soleat. In huius acta referri diplomata, regiaque beneficia solent, ut perpetua esse possint, ac nunquam antiquabilia. Huius auctoritate rata irritave Principum acta, ne ipsis quidem recusantibus, fiunt. Una hęc curia est, à qua sibi ius dari Principes (legibus soluti) ciuili animo ferunt: quam auctorem fieri sacrandis promulgandisque sanctionibus suis volunt. Cuius concilij censurae constitutiones suas eximi, edictaque sua nolint, imo cuius decretis acta sua consecrari æternitati velint. Hęc Budæus. Vt igitur hanc sibi potestatem Senatus ille tyrannicè vsurpauit, vt Regiis edictis atque imperiis intercederet: quod certe credibile non est: aut illud fateamur necesse est, Regibus non liberam & infinitam rerum omnium potestatem permissam antiquitus fuisse, quod etiam Auffrerius, Boerius, Montanius, Chassanæus aliique summæ apud Gallias auctoritatis pragmatici, vna voce, sine vlla varietate, attestantur.
units.tr: We think it has therefore been sufficiently shown that the kings of France were not granted by their citizens an immense and unlimited power, such that they could be called free of all laws; rather, they are bound by certain laws and compacts. We have shown that the first of these was this: that they should keep the public council holy and inviolate, and attend that assembly in person whenever the interest of the commonwealth required it. There are indeed very many laws by which the kings are known to be bound. But we will set out, as each seems worthy of mention, only those few which no one except the most ungrateful, and no one except an enemy of his country, his parents and his children, would question. The first, then, shall be this: that the king may not establish anything that pertains to the state of the commonwealth as a whole without the authority of the public council. Of this we have already brought forward the most certain testimonies, and there also remains, down to our own age, a most express and evident trace of it: the Parliament of Paris, which has largely appropriated to itself the authority of that old Parliament, allows no royal constitutions or edicts to be valid unless they have first been examined by it as a council and approved by the opinions of its counsellors. So it may not unfairly be said that the authority of that Senate, in this respect, seems similar to the power of the old tribunes of the plebs, whom Valerius Maximus writes used to wait in the vestibule of the Senate until the decrees of that order were brought to them, to be examined by them as a council, so that if they seemed useful to the plebs they would subscribe the letter T as a note and sign of their assent, but if not, they would forbid and veto them. Budé, a most learned man, draws the comparison from elsewhere: just as, he says, when the Roman people passed a resolution, the Senate had to be made the authority for it, which we now call in Greek homologare [ὁμολογεῖν], so today, for the constitutions of our princes to have the force of sanctions, it is necessary that the court be made the authority for such acts as pertain to the commonwealth, and that they be promulgated in the court. And a little later: in this court it is customary for the officers of the provinces and the judges, whom we call bailiffs, seneschals and by such names, to swear to the laws. In this court the royal letters and royal grants are customarily entered, so that they may be perpetual and never repealable. By its authority the acts of the princes are made valid or invalid, and this takes place even without their objection. This is the one court from which princes, though released from the laws, acknowledge in a civil spirit that they are given their right; it is the court they wish to be made the authority for consecrating and promulgating their sanctions. They do not want their constitutions and edicts to be exempt from the censure of this council; indeed they wish their acts to be consecrated to eternity by its decrees. So Budé. Therefore, if that Senate usurped this power tyrannically, so as to interpose its veto against royal edicts and commands (which indeed is not credible), we must either admit that the kings were not granted from of old a free and unlimited power over all things, which also Auffrerius, Boerius, Montanius, Chassanaeus and other jurists of the highest authority in Gaul attest with one voice, without any dissent.

units.la: Age, reliquas leges regias videamus: atque hanc in primis, Vt Regi ius non sit neq; filiu adoptare, neque de suo regno, vel inter viuos, vel per testamentum disponere: sed in regni successione maiorum instituta & antiqua consuetudo seruea feruetur. Nam Ioannes de terra rubea tracta. 1. concil.9.ita scribit:Reges Franciæ non potuerunt vnquam, neq; posset Rex modernus facere testamentum de regno,nec primogenitū aut alterum heredem facere in illo. Item,adeo ex vi cōsuetudinis in regno Franciæ succeditur,quòd sicut nec ex voluntate dispositiua, & testamentaria regis successio defertur eius successori,nec deferri potest:sic nec ex tacita voluntate eius ab intestato dispositiua ei succedi potest:sed solum Consuetudo succedenti defert regnum. Hæc Territubrius. Cuius sententiam cum omnis cōprobat antiquitas, tū vero vel maxime historia hæc memorabilis,quam subiungam. Anno cIↄ cccccxx. cùm Rex Carolus vi. Hérico Angliæ Regi suum regnū mortis caussa donasset,eumq; sibi successorem designasset, repéte populus ad publicum gentis concilium provocauit: in quo summa omnium consensione pronuntiatū est, donationem illam ipso iure nullam,inutilé atq; irritam fuisse:neque Regi Galliæ fas esse, vllam sui regni partem sine publico gentis suæ cōsensu alienare. cuius rei autores sunt Enguer. Mōstrel.cap.hist.22 s.& aliis infeqq.itemque Guill. Benedict. in cap. Raynut. in verb. nume. 188. Cum Carolus sextus,inquit,ex matrimonio iusto filium haberet, cui regnum debebatur,non potuit Regem Angliæ adoptare in filium, in præiudicium filij sui legitimi, & naturalis: nec adoptio valuit,nec tenuit:quinimo regnum dicto Carolo septimo delatum fuit.Item in verb.
units.tr: Come, let us look at the remaining royal laws; and first this one: that the king has no right either to adopt a son, or to dispose of his kingdom either between living persons or by testament; but in the succession to the kingdom the institutions of our ancestors and the ancient custom are to be kept. For John of Terrevermeille, in his tract, first council, ninth, writes thus: the kings of France never could, nor can the present king, make a testament concerning the kingdom, nor make a firstborn or another heir in it. Likewise: so strongly by the force of custom does succession take place in the kingdom of France, that just as the succession of the king is neither conferred on his successor by his dispositive and testamentary will, nor can be conferred, so neither can he succeed by his tacit will, dispositive without a testament; but custom alone confers the kingdom on the successor. So Terrevermeille. Not only does all antiquity approve his opinion, but especially this memorable history which I shall add. In the year 1420, when King Charles VI had given his kingdom to Henry, King of England, on his death, and had designated him as his successor, the people at once appealed to the public council of the nation; in it, with the complete consent of all, it was pronounced that the donation was in law null, void and of no effect, and that it was not lawful for the King of France to alienate any part of his realm without the public consent of his nation. The authors of this are Enguerrand de Monstrelet, in the historical chapter 22 and following, and likewise Guillaume Benoît, in the chapter Raynutius, under the word "numero" 188. "When Charles VI," he says, "had a son by a lawful marriage, to whom the kingdom was owed, he could not adopt the King of England as a son to the prejudice of his legitimate and natural son; nor did the adoption hold good or stand; rather the kingdom was conferred on the said Charles VII." Likewise under the word…

units.la: In eodem testamento:num.1 5 1. Ex quibus,inquit, confutatur,& penitus confunditur,vt ipso iure nihil valuerit ille tractatus paçis,quem Anglì prætendunt passatum fuisse inter Carolum sextum,Francorum regem,& Henricum quintum,Regem Angliæ,per quem dictus Carolus dominam Catharinam filiam suam nuptui dedit præfato Henrico, eumque sibi adoptauit in filium: nec non sine proceribus solus existens declarauit coronam Franciæ eidem pertinere, & post sui decessum totum Franciæ regnum ad ipsum peruenturum.Sed dictus tractatus à proceribus regni reprobatus fuit, qui Carolum eius filium vngi & coronari fecerunt. Hæc Bened.Secunda igitur Regni Francogalliæ illa lex esto.Deinceps tertiam videamus, quam esse constat huiusmodi: vt rege mortuo regni hereditas filio ipsius natu maximo deferatur, neque regi vel natu minorem maiori anteferre, vel alium sibi successorē instituere liceat. Cuius hæc ratio est certissima: quoniam parentes ea demũ adimere suis liberis possunt, quæ ab ipsis prosiciscûtur: quæ vero vel natura,vel lege atque institutis maiorum iis addicta sunt, in iis parentes ius nullum habent.l.si arrogator. 22.D.de arrogat.l. 3.D.de interd. & releg. Filius autem natu maximus suitatem & spem hereditatis, non parẽtis sed legis communis beneficio adeptus est: neque illam suo patri acceptam ferre debet, sed legibus atque institutis maiorum. itaque rectissime doctores omnes vno consensu affirmant, ReRegem Francorum non posse auferre primogenito ius primogenituræ, sine spe regni, & dare secundo genito, vel alteri. Ioan. Andr. in c. licet, de voto. Bald. de prohib. feud. alien. per Frid. §. illud. Panorm. conf. 3. nitar in præsenti, lib. 2. Iason in l. nemo potest, De legat. 1. Bald. in c. 1. De feud. March. ducat. sed præcipue Ioan. Terrirubius tract. 1. concl. 9. vbi sic scribit: Reges Franciæ nunquam consueuerunt de regno testari, sed solum ex vi consuetudinis defertur successio primogenitis maribus ex linea recta eorum, quibus succeditur: & illa definente succedunt mares trâsuersales iuxta gradus prærogatiuam. Item, cócl. 9. 10. 11. & 12. vbi sic loquitur: In regno Franciæ non habetur successio hereditaria siue patrimonialis, sed simplex successio, siue subrogatio primogeniti, vel proximioris agnati, cui regnum debetur ex sola lege vel consuetudine regni, à qua sola ius accipit, & nō à patre vel alio prædecessore: & sic ius primogenituræ, quantum ad tale regnum non habetur à patre, sed à lege regni: vnde nec est hereditarium, nec patrimoniale, sed mero iure filiationis, vel sanguinis competit. Ita quod non posset Rex de regno testari, etiam primogenitum, vel proximiorem, cui regnum debetur, instituendo: quia nullo modo posset institutus capere regnum vi testamenti, vel alterius dispositionis paternæ, quæ non valuit: sed solum virtute legis immutabilis regni, à qua vocatur. Et in eandem sententiam Guill. Benedict. in c. Raynutius, in verb. In eodem testamento: num. 148. ita scribit: Natura regni Franciæ, inquit, requirit, & exigit, ne de eo fiant testamenta, legata, vel aliæ dispositiones. Vnde Ioan. de terra rub. in quodam libro, quem intitulauit Vinea Ecclesiæ, tract. 1. q. 9. concludit, dicens, quia regnum Franciæ debetur primogenito ex sola regni consuetudine, nunquam consueuerunt Reges de ipso regno testari: quod vi & medio consuetudinis defertur primogenito. Nam Reges Franciæ nunquam potuerunt, neque posset Carolus octauus Rex noster modernus testamentum facere de regno, etiam heredem instituendo dominum Delphinum eius primogenitum. quia regnum Franciæ non debetur primogenito, ex successione testamentaria, vel ab intestato, sed solum ex lege & consuetudine regni. Igitur Rex ipsum dare nō potest primogenito, neque auferre per alienationes inter viuos, testamenta, neque debita voluntaria, legata exheredationis, ex caussa: quia primogenitus Franciæ non habet regnum à patre, sed ab ipsa regni lege & consuetudine: & sic pater potestatem non habet ipsum grauare: & de tali dignitate testamento disponi non potest, vel alius in præiudicium primogeniti, qui cùm ius illud habeat, non patris iudicio, sed legis beneficio, per eum grauari non potest, à quo beneficium non habet, nec commodū sentit. Hæc ad verbum Bened. Sequitur quarta lex regni, de qua tamen superius ca. 1 o. disseruimus. Ne virgo, neve mulier ad regni hereditatem admittatur, sed agnatus defuncto Regi proximus, quamuis gradu fœmina posterior, ei tamen præferatur. qua de lege nobilis Pragmaticus Iacob. Petr. in sua Pract. capit. 63. ita scribit: Carolo qui rex Franciæ & Nauarræ fuerat mortuo, filia Ludouici, sui quondam fratris successit in regno Nauarræ, quia illud regnum venerat per fœminam: sed in regno Franciæ non successit: quia non admittitur fœmina, quamdiu masculus de genere inuenitur: successit ergo Philippus filius Caroli, qui erat ei in quarto gradu: quamuis dicta fratris filia tantū esset in tertio. Item Guill. Bened. in verb. duas habens, num. 78. unde restat, inquit, neq; filias, neque masculos ex ipsis descendentes in regno Franciæ secundum ipsius leges & consuetudinem succedere, quinimo liberis masculis non existentibus reliqui parentes & consanguinei in regno succederent, seruata gradus prærogatiua. Hæc Bened. quæ multo copiosius confirmat nume. 119. & 120. Item Cosm. Guim. in proœmio pragmat. sanct. vbi sic scribit: Regnum Franciæ est ita nobile, & clarum, quod in eo nunquam succedit fœmina, licet bene in regno Nauarræ. & huiusmodi quæstio orta fuit post mortem Philippi Pulchri, Regis Francorum, qui habuit vnam filiam, nomine Isabellam: & tres filios: dictam Isabellam duxit in vxorem Eduardus Rex Angliæ, ex qua habuit vnum filium, qui similiter dictus est Eduardus, qui successit in regno Angliæ, defuncto dicto Philippo. Tres eius filij fuerunt reges Franciæ sigillatim: qui tandem decesserunt sine liberis: quibus successit in regno Franciæ Philippus, filius Caroli de Valesio, fratris dicti Philippi, de consensu & approbatione x ii. Parium Franciæ, qui noluerunt dare regnum dictæ Isabellæ, Reginæ Angliæ, nec filio eius Eduardo: unde ortæ sunt magnæ guerræ, inter Reges Angliæ & Franciæ, & iniustè. quia sicut filia Regis non succedit in regno Francorum, ita nec natus ex ea. §. hoc autè. qui feud. dar. possit. De gradib. succes. in feud. c. i. §. ad filias. Exclusò enim ascendente, excluduntur descendentes ex persona ascendentis. l. sin. C. de natur. lib. l. si viua, C. de bon. matern. Ideo non potuit d. Eduardus filius d. Isabellæ prætendere aliquod ius in regno Franciæ: dicit Bald. in repet. l. i. C. de summa trinit. Sed nemo verius hanc historiam exponit, quam Claudius Seyssellus, archiepisc. Taurin. in lib. de lege Salica: ubi utriusque Regis Angliæ & Franciæ iusta copiosè exponit: & ad extremum publici concilij, siue trium statuum iudicium subiungit.
units.tr: In the same will, number 151: "From these points," he says, "it is refuted and utterly overturned that the treaty of peace which the English claim was concluded between Charles VI, king of the French, and Henry V, king of England, had any legal force at all. By that treaty Charles gave his daughter Catherine in marriage to the said Henry and adopted him as his son, and, although he acted without the nobles, declared that the crown of France belonged to him and that the whole kingdom of France would pass to him after Charles's death. But that treaty was rejected by the nobles of the kingdom, who had Charles, his son, anointed and crowned." Thus Benedict. The second law of the kingdom of France, then, is this. Let us next consider the third, which is of this kind: that when the king dies, the inheritance of the kingdom passes to his eldest son, and it is not permitted to the king to prefer a younger son to an elder, or to appoint any other successor for himself. The reason for this is most certain: parents can take away from their children only what comes from themselves; but what has been assigned to the children by nature, or by law and the institutions of their ancestors, parents have no right over. (Law "Si arrogator" 22, D. de arrogatione; law 3, D. de interdictis et relegatis.) The eldest son has obtained the right and the hope of the inheritance not by the favour of his father but by the benefit of common law; nor ought he to owe it to his father, but to the laws and institutions of his ancestors. Therefore all the teachers most rightly affirm with one voice that the King of the French cannot take the right of primogeniture away from the firstborn, leaving him without hope of the kingdom, and give it to a second-born son or to another. (Giovanni d'Andrea on c. "Licet", de voto; Baldus, de prohibita feudi alienatione, per Fridericum, §. "Illud"; Panormitanus, consilium 3; I shall rely on Niccolò in the present work, book 2; Jason on l. "Nemo potest", De legatis 1; Baldus on c. 1, De feudis; March of Ducat.) But above all John Terrarubia, tract. 1, concl. 9, where he writes thus: "The kings of France have never been accustomed to make a will concerning the kingdom; rather, by force of custom alone the succession passes to the firstborn male of the direct line of those whom they succeed; and when that line fails, the male collateral relatives succeed according to the precedence of degree." Likewise, concl. 9, 10, 11 and 12, where he speaks thus: "In the kingdom of France there is no hereditary or patrimonial succession, but a simple succession, or substitution, of the firstborn or the nearest agnate, to whom the kingdom is owed by the law or custom of the kingdom alone, from which alone he receives his right, and not from his father or any other predecessor. Thus the right of primogeniture, as far as such a kingdom is concerned, is held not from the father but from the law of the kingdom; hence it is neither hereditary nor patrimonial, but belongs by pure right of filiation, or of blood." So the king could not make a will concerning the kingdom, even by appointing the firstborn or nearest heir to whom the kingdom is owed, because the appointee could in no way take the kingdom by virtue of a will or of any other paternal disposition, which has no force; he takes it only by virtue of the unchangeable law of the kingdom, by which he is called. Benedict, in c. "Raynutius", in the words "In eodem testamento", number 148, writes to the same effect: "The nature of the kingdom of France," he says, "requires and demands that no testaments, legacies or other dispositions be made concerning it." Hence John of Terrarubia, in a certain book which he entitled The Vineyard of the Church, tract. 1, q. 9, concludes, saying: "Because the kingdom of France is owed to the firstborn by the custom of the kingdom alone, the kings have never been accustomed to make a will concerning the kingdom itself; it passes to the firstborn by force and by the means of custom." For the kings of France never could make, nor could our present king, Charles VIII, make a will concerning the kingdom, even by appointing his firstborn, the lord Dauphin, as heir; because the kingdom of France is owed to the firstborn not by testamentary succession or by intestate succession, but only by the law and custom of the kingdom. Therefore the king cannot give it to the firstborn, nor take it away from him by alienations inter vivos, by wills, by voluntary debts, by legacies or by disinheritance, for any cause; because the firstborn of France does not hold the kingdom from his father but from the very law and custom of the kingdom; and so the father has no power to burden him, and no disposition by will can be made about such a dignity to the prejudice of the firstborn, who, since he has that right not by the judgment of his father but by the benefit of the law, cannot be burdened by the one from whom he has no benefit and feels no advantage. Thus far Benedict, word for word. There follows the fourth law of the kingdom, which however I have discussed above in chapter 10: that neither a virgin nor a woman is admitted to the inheritance of the kingdom, but the agnate nearest to the deceased king is preferred to her, although he is a more remote woman in degree. Concerning this law the noble practitioner Jacques de Petra writes in his Practice, chapter 63, thus: "When Charles, who had been king of France and Navarre, died, the daughter of Louis, his late brother, succeeded in the kingdom of Navarre, because that kingdom had come through a woman; but she did not succeed in the kingdom of France, because a woman is not admitted as long as a male of the family can be found; so Philip, son of Charles, succeeded, who was in the fourth degree, although the said daughter of the brother was only in the third." Likewise Guillaume Benedict, in the words "duas habens", number 78: "Hence it remains," he says, "that neither daughters nor males descended from them succeed in the kingdom of France according to its laws and custom; rather, if there were no male children, the remaining parents and blood relatives would succeed in the kingdom, observing the precedence of degree." Thus Benedict, whom he confirms much more fully at numbers 119 and 120. Likewise Cosme Guymier, in the preface to the Pragmatic Sanction, where he writes thus: "The kingdom of France is so noble and illustrious that a woman never succeeds in it, although she does succeed in the kingdom of Navarre." And a question of this kind arose after the death of Philip the Fair, king of the French, who had one daughter, named Isabella, and three sons. Isabella was married to Edward, king of England, and by her he had a son, likewise called Edward, who succeeded in the kingdom of England when the said Philip died. Three of Philip's sons were kings of France in turn; they died at last without children; and the kingdom of France passed to Philip, son of Charles of Valois, brother of the said Philip, with the consent and approval of the twelve peers of France, who were unwilling to give the kingdom either to the said Isabella, queen of England, or to her son Edward. From this there arose great wars between the kings of England and France, and unjust ones; for just as the daughter of a king does not succeed to the kingdom of the French, so neither does the son born of her. (§. "Hoc autem", "Qui feudum dare possit"; "De gradibus successionis in feudis", c. 1, §. "Ad filias".) For when the ascendant is excluded, the descendants through that ascendant are excluded. (Law "Sin", C. de naturalibus liberis; law "Si viva", C. de bonis maternis.) Therefore the said Edward, son of the said Isabella, could not claim any right to the kingdom of France, as Baldus says in his repetition on law 1, C. de summa trinitate. But no one has explained this history more truthfully than Claude de Seyssel, archbishop of Turin, in his book on the Salic law, where he expounds at length the just claims of both kings, of England and of France, and at the end adds the judgment of the public council, or of the three estates.

units.la: Quinta ex ad Regis domanium pertinet de qua superius suo loco commemorauimus. Ne videlicet Regi ius sit, vllam domanij sui partem sine publici Concilij auctoritate alienare; quippe, quod ei ad tuendam tantum regiam dignitatem fruendum datum est vt parem in eo potestatem habeat, atque marito in vxoris dote conceditur. Itaque anno cıɔ cccxcix. cum Rex Carolus vi. Comiti Sampaulino particulam quādā fui domanij fiue donasset, fiue alia ex caussa cessisset, Senatus Parisiensis pro vetere veteris Parlamenti iure intercessit: ac pronuntiauit alienationem regij dominij nullius esse momenti, nisi cuius author Senatus ille Parisiensis fuisset, quod decretum Paponius inter Aresta sua retulit. lib. 5. tit. 10. vbi alia complura generis eiusdem senatusconsulta commemorat: quibus omnibus definitum hoc ius est, alienationem dominij à Rege, sine caussa in illo Senatu cognita & probata, factam, ipso iure nullam esse. qua in cognitione hæc potissimum exquiruntur. At non aliunde confici pecunia possit? ecqua necessitas vrgeat? an pretium sit idoneū? & auctione cōstituta summum illud ac postremum oblatum. Sed operæpretium est Claudij Seyssellij testimonium in hanc rem exponere: cuius verba ex lib. de monarch. Franc. 1. cap. 10. sic conuertimus. Tertium frenum quo Reges Franciæ coercentur est politia, hoc est instituta & mores regni multas per ætates cōprobati, & longinqua consuetudine retēti: quorum abrogationem non suscipiunt: & si forte susciperent, frustra id tentarent: quoniam eorum imperio non pareretur: quod vel ex dominio & patrimonio regali cognosci licet, cuius alienandi ius, sine caussis magnis & necessariis, non habent, quas caussas cognosci & probari oportet in cōsilio & curia parlamenti & Rationalium: qua in cognitione ita caute & diligenter, tantaq; cum disquisitione proceditur, vt pauci admodum reperiātur, qui eiusmodi alienationes expetant. Etsi autem Reges ius habent disponendi de fructibus & reditibus regni pro sui arbitrio, quandiu regni administrationem obtinent: tamen ratio sumptuum tum ordinariorum tum extraordinariorum ad Rationalium curiam & notionem reuocatur. Hi rationales sumptus illos regios, si inconsulte facti videntur, coercent. Quae sane lex Reipub. perquam utilis est, ad Regij dominij conseruationem, quia tum demum ad tributa & indictiones extraordinarias, quibus plebs oneratur, decurri tanquam ad subsidium solet, cum illud dominium regiu exhaustum est: ut omittam, quod hac praeclara Regni lege nimia Principis liberalitas quae ad prodigalitate accedit, coercetur. Haec Seyssellus, sed lib. II. cap. 11. insuper haec addit: Iterum dico: Regem non posse gratius obsequium Deo praestare, aut suorum ciuium utilitati, aut suae dignitati atque existimationi melius consulere, quam illas Regni leges obseruando. Tum enim boni & Christianissimi Regis & Patris patriae cognomentum acquirit: ceteraque omnia nomina, quae sibi magnus aliquis & gloriosus Princeps poterit acquirere. Ex contrario vero simulatq; limites & fines illos sibi praescriptos egreditur, & voluntate pro ratione uti instituit, habetur ac numeratur improbus, tyrannus, crudelis, & intolerandus, quibus de caussis in Dei & ciuium suorum odium incurrit. Hactenus Seyssellus Taurinensis Archiepiscopus, & Regis Ludovici XII. intimus consiliarius. In eandemq; sententiam, de Rege Frácie, cui nó licet vrbes Regni sui alienare, scribūt Hosti. & Io. Andr. in c. dilecti. De maior. & obed. Martin. Laud. in trac. de cōfœd. q. 13.
units.tr: The fifth law of the realm concerns the royal domain, which I mentioned earlier in its proper place. This is that the King has no right to alienate any part of his domain without the authority of the public council. The domain was given to him only to maintain the royal dignity and to enjoy its use, and in this respect he has the same position as a husband who is granted the use of his wife's dowry. Accordingly, in the year 1399, when King Charles VI had either given or otherwise ceded a small part of his domain to the Count of Sampaulino, the Parlement of Paris, by the ancient right of the old Parlement, interposed its authority. It declared that the alienation of royal property was of no effect unless the Parlement of Paris itself had authorised it. Papon records this decree in his Arrêts, book 5, title 10, where he also mentions many other decrees of the Senate of the same kind. By all of these it has been settled as law that an alienation of the King's property made without a cause heard and approved in that Senate is void in law. In such an inquiry the chief questions are these: whether the money cannot be raised in some other way; whether any necessity presses; whether the price is fair; and whether, after an auction has been held, the highest and final offer was accepted. It is worth setting out the testimony of Claude de Seyssel on this matter. We have translated his words from the book On the Monarchy of France, book 1, chapter 10, as follows. The third bridle by which the Kings of France are restrained is the polity, that is, the institutions and customs of the realm, approved through many ages and kept by long usage. The Kings do not undertake to abrogate these, and if they did undertake it they would attempt it in vain, since they would not be obeyed. This can be known even from the royal domain and patrimony, whose alienation they have no right to make without great and necessary causes. These causes must be known and approved in the council and court of the Parlement and of the Chambre des comptes. In that inquiry the proceedings are so careful and diligent, and with such scrutiny, that very few are found who seek such alienations. Although the Kings have the right to dispose of the fruits and revenues of the realm at their own discretion for as long as they hold the administration of the realm, nevertheless the account of expenditure, both ordinary and extraordinary, is referred to the court and reckoning of the Chambre des comptes. These auditors restrain the royal expenditures if they appear to have been made without counsel. Surely this law is most useful to the commonwealth for the preservation of the royal domain, because recourse is then had, as a last aid, to taxes and extraordinary levies, with which the common people are burdened, only when that royal domain has been exhausted. I say nothing of the fact that by this excellent law of the realm the excessive liberality of the Prince, which borders on prodigality, is restrained. Thus far Seyssel. But in book 2, chapter 11, he adds the following: I say again that the King cannot render a more acceptable obedience to God, nor better consult the advantage of his citizens, or his own dignity and reputation, than by observing those laws of the realm. For then he acquires the title of a good and most Christian King and Father of his country, and all the other names which some great and glorious Prince might acquire. On the contrary, as soon as he goes beyond those limits and boundaries prescribed for him, and begins to govern by will rather than by reason, he is regarded and counted as wicked, a tyrant, cruel and intolerable, and for these reasons he incurs the hatred of God and of his citizens. Thus far Seyssel, Archbishop of Turin and intimate counsellor of King Louis XII. To the same effect, concerning the King of France, to whom it is not lawful to alienate the cities of his realm, write Hostiensis and Johannes Andreae on the chapter Dilecti, De maioritate et obedientia, and Martinus Laudensis in the treatise De confoederatione, question 13.

units.la: Sexta Regni lex numerari hæc potest, vt Regi abolendi criminis & capitalis pœnæ, sine parlamenti auctoritate, remittendæ ius non sit in hoc regno, inquit Boerius, criminosus deferens literas remissionis aut abolitionis, siue pardonij, debet incarcerari, & suas literas offerre Parlamento, &c. Hæc ille Decif. Burdegal. 65.
units.tr: The sixth law of the realm may be reckoned as this: in this kingdom it is not within the King's right to remit a capital crime or its punishment without the authority of the Parlement. Boerius says: a criminal who presents letters of remission, abolition or pardon must be imprisoned and must offer his letters to the Parlement, and so on. Thus he writes in Decisiones Burdegalenses 65.

units.la: Septima est, vt Regi non liceat magistratū aliquē Regni, siue Reip. Franciæ, nisi caussa in Parium consilio cognita & probata, exauctorare. Quæ lex ita passim tota Gallia nota & decantata est, vt testimonij non egeat.
units.tr: The seventh law is that it is not lawful for the King to dismiss any magistrate of the realm, or of the French commonwealth, unless the cause has been heard and approved in the council of the Peers. This law is so widely known and proclaimed throughout the whole of Gaul that it needs no testimony.

units.la: Octaua Regni lex numerari hæc potest. Ne Regi sine publici concilij auctoritate monetæ mutandæ ius sit. Nam Guill. Budæus lib. de Asse 3. & 5. testatur ex antiquis omnibus quæ viderat monimētis cōstare rei nūmariæ ius, hoc est potestatis nūmorum vel augendæ vel imminuendæ semper penes populum fuisse. Quinetiā Carol. Molin. diligētissimus monetalium ratiociniorum inuestigator, extremo cōmentario de cōtract. & vsur. scribit se in archiuis parlamenti & monetalium præfectorū quāplurimas leges Francicas reperisse, quibus sancitū erat, ne qua rei nūmariæ mutatio sine populi consensu fieret: semperq; in eiusmodi mutationibus populi cōsensum (quippe cui plurimi intererat) interuenisse. quemadmodum à Iurisconsultis dici solet. Quorum quid fieri interest, eorum in eo negotio gerendo requiritur assensus: vel hoc modo, quod aliquos tangit, debet ab iis approbari. Quinetiā Hostiensis Canonista celebris & magnæ inter suos auctoritatis, in summa de censibus, ita scribit. Quæritur, nūquid Rex Franciæ habeat privilegium concedendi pedagia, vel mutandi novam monetam. Respondeo, sicut Papa in simili quæstione, sic videretur aliquibus. c. per venerabilem, qui fil. sint legit. Mihi verò non videtur nisi populus ei potestatem illam dederit: quæ & Imperatori data est. argu. l. 2. §. deinde, D. de orig. iur.
units.tr: The eighth law of the realm may be reckoned as this: the King has no right to change the coinage without the authority of the public council. For Guillaume Budé, in his book On the As, books 3 and 5, testifies that from all the ancient monuments he had seen it is clear that the right over money, that is, the power of either increasing or diminishing the value of coins, has always rested with the people. Moreover, Charles Dumoulin, the most diligent investigator of monetary accounts, in his final commentary On Contracts and Usury, writes that he found in the archives of the Parlement and of the officers of the mint very many Frankish laws by which it was decreed that no alteration of the currency should be made without the consent of the people, and that in such alterations the consent of the people (to whom very many were concerned) had always intervened, as the jurists are wont to say: whatever concerns all must be approved by all, or in that transaction the assent of those whom it touches must be sought. Also Hostiensis, the famous canonist of great authority among his own people, writes in his Summa, On Censuses, as follows. It is asked whether the King of France has the privilege of granting tolls or of changing the coinage. I answer that, as the Pope was thought to be in a similar question, so it seems to some (see chapter Per venerabilem, on those who are legitimate sons). But to me it does not seem that he has that power unless the people has given it to him, which power was also given to the Emperor (compare the law 2, section Deinde, Digest, On the origin of law).

units.la: An mulieres, non vt ab hereditate Regni, sic ab eius procuratione, Francogallico iure, arceantur. CAP. XXVI.
units.tr: Whether women are excluded from the administration of the kingdom by Frankish law, just as they are excluded from its inheritance. CHAPTER XXVI.

units.la: SEd quoniam de regni procuratione & summa Reip. administrandæ instituta disputatio est, non prætereunda quæstio videtur, An mulieres non vt ab hereditate Regni, sic etiam ab eius procuratione arceantur. Primùm autem illud apertè testatum volumus, nos neq; de Romanorum, neque de aliarum gentium iure, sed tantùm de huius nostræ Francogalliæ institutis differere. Nam, vt notū omnibus est, Romanorum institutis mulieres propter infirmitatem consilij in perpetua tutorum potestate fuisse, atque ab omnibus non modò publicis, verùm etiam ciuilibus negotiis exclusas esse ita nonnullis aliis in gĕtibus mulieres summam imperij vetustis moribus obtinent. Britanni sexum in imperiis non discernunt: inquit Tacitus in Agric. vita. Hoc igitur constituto, & testificatione nostra planè ac dilucidè proposita, deinceps ad quæstionem accedamus. Nam ei causam præbuisse superiorum aliquot temporum exempla videntur: quibus constat, Regnum Francogalliæ à Reginis, præsertim viduis, & regū vel puerorum vel absentium matribus administratum fuisse. In quibus haud scio an vllum ad mulierem audaciâ insignius commemorari possit, quàm illud reginæ Blancæ, Ludouici Transmarini matris, de qua posterius dicemus: quæ Regi filio in Africam ad bellum gerendum prosecto, summam sibi potestatē non modò in Reip. sed etiam in Ecclesiarum & Episcopatuum administratione asciuit: quemadmodum ex veteribus quibusdam monimentis nuper in lucem editis cognosci potest: Nos carissima Domina nostra & matri Regina concessimus, & voluimus, quòd ipsa in hac nostra peregrinationis absentia plenariam habeat potestatem recipiendi & attrahendi ad regni nostri negotia, quæs sibi placuerit, & amouendi quos viderit amouendos: Baillivos etiâ instituere valeat, castellanos, forestarios, & alios in seruitium nostrum & regni nostri ministros ponere & amouere: dignitates etiam & beneficia ecclesiastica vacantia conferre, fidelitates Episcoporum & Abbatum recipere, & eis regalia restituere, & eligendi licentiam dare capitulis & conuentibus vice nostra. Ex contrario tamen pugnat primùm ratio disputandi vsitata, vt cui per se Reginam esse ius non est, eidem regendi ius ac potestas non sit. Per se autem Reginam esse mulierem nō posse, neque Regni hereditatem ei ex eáve prognatis deferri: sed si Reginæ appellantur, per accidens, & propter Reges maritos id fieri: superiùs ex antiquis m c c. annorum monimentis demonstratum est. Eo accedit, quod superius docuimus, quemadmodum omnis & creadorum & abdicandorum regum potestas penes publicum concilium erat: ita curatoris Reip. siue moderatoris diligédi ius summum penes idem Concilium fuisse. Quinetiam creatis regibus, tamen summam imperij administrandi potestatem ab eodem Concilio retentam fuisse: neque centesimum adhuc exisse annum cùm regnante Ludouico x i. quamtumuis astuto & callido, xxxvi, Reipub. curatores, tanquam Ephori, ab eodem Concilio constituti sunt. Quòd si maiorum nostrorum auctoritatem quærimus, extat insignis apud Aimoin. lib. 4. c. 1. vbi de Brunechilde, Regina matre Childeberti regis commemorans ita loquitur: Simul, inquit, quia Brunechildis summam regni solicitudinem sibi reseruare velle intelligebatur, & primates Franciæ tanto tempore fœmineo dominatui dedignabatur subiici, &c. Itaque Franc. Connanus Senator Parisiensis lib. 1.cap.8. Quod Panormitanus putat (inquit) Reginis more nostro ius esse in Gallos, multum sallitur. nulla enim gens minus passa est fœminarum imperium, cum lex Saliorum, id est Gallorum, eas regni successione excludat. Itaque videmus Reginas viro mortuo redigi fere in ordinem: sic ut ne vmbram quidem Regiæ dignitatis retineant. Hæc Connanus. Et profecto ita est, ut si quando regni procurationem apud maiores nostros mulieres adeptæ sunt, semper ea res miras in Rep. nostra tragœdias, summa denique miseriarum incendia excitarit. Cuius rei non alienum videtur exempla quædam proponere. Dominata est quondam Chrotildis, Regina, mater Childeberti & Clotarij regum, quæ cùm alterius filij nomine Chlodomeris demortui filios insano quodam amore prosequeretur, summam contentionem abhibuit, ut nepotes remotis filiis in regiam dignitatem perducerentur. Itaque capillitium eorum, pro eo instituto de quo superius diximus, summa cum cura & diligentia nutriebat. Cuius rei Reges fratres certiores facti, confestim Arcadium quendam ad eam miserunt, qui nudum gladium simulque forcipem ei ostentans, optionem illi faceret, utrum illorum nepotum suorum capiti admoueri mallet. At illa, inquit Gregorius Turon. nimium felle commota, præcipuè cum gladium cerneret euaginatum ac forcipem, amaritudine præuenta, respondit: Satius mihi est, si ad regnum non eriguntur, mortuos eos videre, quàm tonsos. Ita nepos vterque in ipsius conspectu interfectus est. Auctore eodem Gregor.lib.3.cap.18. vbi tamen subiungit, Reginam hanc liberalitatibus & donationibus in monasteria collatis plebis & vulgi benevolentiam conciliasse. Dato frenos (inquibat Cato) impotenti naturæ, & indomito animali, & sperare ipsas modum licentiæ facturas. Quid? quàm effrenatū illud fuit animal, illa, inquam, Theodorici Regis filia, natione Itala, quæ ferui sui amore insana, vbi matris iussu illū interfectum cognouit, per speciem reconciliatæ cum matre gratiæ sacramentum se dominicæ cœnæ cum illa communicare velle ostendit, venenóq; in calicem infuso impietate simul & crudelitate nefaria matrem sustulit. Verba Gregorij Turonensis lib.3.c.33. hæc sunt: Erant sub Ariana secta viuentes: & quia consuetudo eorum est, vt ad altarium veniêtes de alio calice Reges communicent, & de alio populus minor (notanda cõsuetudo calicis cum plebe communicati) venenum in calice illo posuit, de quo mater communicatura erat: quo illa hausto protinus mortua est. Age, reliquas videamus. Dominata est quondam Fredegunda, Regina mater, Chilperici primi vidua. Hæc marito superstite cū Landerio quodam adulterij consuetudinem habuerat. Vbi Chilpericum id'sensisse animaduertit, interficiendum eum curauit: cõsestimque Regni procurationem filij sui Regis Clotharij nomine, tanquam Regina mater suscepit: eamque annos xiii. fuftinuit. Primùm Childebertum filij fui patruum, eiufque vxorem veneno fuftulit: tum Hunnos aduerfus ipfius filios concitauit: bellumque ciuile in Remp. immifit. fax denique illorum incendiorum fuit, quibus Francogallia multos annos exarfit. auctore Aimoino lib.3.c.36.& lib. 8.cap. 29. & fcriptore Chronici Befnenfis. Dominata eft Regina mater Childeberti, Brunechildis, Sigeberti Regis vidua. Hæc Italum quendam nomine Protadium in delitiis habebat, eumq; omnibus honoribus amplificabat. eademque filios fuos Theodebertum & Theodoricum adolefcentes in eam vitæ flagitiofæ confuetudinem adduxit, vt tandem capitales inter fe inimicitias gererent, belloque diuturno conflictati prælium atrociffimum committerent. Merouueum nepotem fuum Theodeberti filium fua manu interfecit. Theodoricum veneno fuftulit. Quid amplius? Date frenos (inquibat Cato) impotenti naturæ, & indomito animali: & fperate ipfas modum licentiæ facturas. Decem principibus Regiis necis caufiam attulit. Cúmque ab Episcopo quodam obiurgata effet, rogataque vt fe ad frugem converteret, illum in profluentem præcipitari iuffit. Ad extremum concilio Francorum indicto, in iudicium vocata, damnata, & ab equo currente diftracta, membratimque dilaniata eft. Auctoribus Greg. Turon. lib. 5. cap. 39. & lib. 8. cap. 29. & Adone Ætat. vi. Ottone Frifingef. Chron. parte 16. & Aimoino lib. 4. cap. 1. iremque Appendice Gregor. Turon. lib. ii. cuius hæc verba sunt: Reputantes ei quòd v. Reges Francorum per eam interfecti fuissent: id est, Sigebertus, Meroveus, & genitor suus Chilpericus, Theobertus & filius suus Clotharius, item Meroveus filius Clotharij, Theodoricus, eiusdémque tres qui ad præsens extincti fuerant: per triduum eam diuersis tormentis afflictam iubet prius camelo per omnem exercitum sedentem perducere: posthæc comam capitis vno pede & brachio ad ferocissimi equi caudam ligare: à quo calcibus & velocitate cursus membratim disrumpitur. quam eandem historiam reperio in Chronico Monasterij Besnensis manuscripto his verbis: Nam camelo superpositam girari fecit per exercitum: quam cùm omnes inclamando horruissent, velut sub carnis vel animæ zabulú iterú iussit reduci: & inter equos quatuor indomitos ligari, ad quorum primam erumpétium fugam partibus rupta, postea igne cōbusta cum satellitio peccatorū ab ipsis inferioribus est immersa. Itē alio loco, Tanta mala & effusiones sanguinum Brunechildis consilio in Francia facta sunt: vt prophetia Sibyllæ impleretur, dicétis, Veniens Bruna de partibus Hispaniæ, ante cuius cōspectum gentes peribunt: hac verò equitum calcibus disrumpetur. Age, de ceteris videamus. Dominata est Plectrudis non Regis, sed Regij præfecti Pipini vidua, qui tum regium imperiū obtinebat, dum inane regium nomē Dagobertus secundus sustineret. Hæc Plectrudis propter adulterij & flagitiosæ vitæ turpitudinem à Pipino repudiata, marito mortuo multarum in Gallia seditionum auctor fuit. Carolum Martellū Palatij magistrum, fortissimū virum abire Magistratu coegit, aliumq; Theobaldum impurum & nefarium hominem in ipsius locum suffecit. tandem funestum ciuile bellum inter Francos ipsos excitauit. qui variis prælijs, & vt (ait Aimoinus) durissimis cædibus sese mutuo prostrauerunt. lib.4. cap. 50. & cap. seq. Quinetiam auctor libelli cui titulus est, Status regni Franciæ, sub Dagoberto II. his vtitur verbis: Cùm Franci Plectrudis furores atque insanias ferre nō possent, neq; in Dagoberto rege spem vllam reliquam viderent, Danielem quendam sibi regem delegerūt, qui antea monachus fuerat, eumque Chilpericum nominarunt. quam historiam superiùs quodā loco perstrinximus. Sed reliquas videamus. Dominata est Regina mater Caroli Calui, nomine Iuditha, Ludovici cognomento Pij coniux: qui non modò Francogalliæ Rex, verumetiam Italiæ & Germaniæ Imperator fuit. Hęc miserum fatalęque bellum inter Ludouicum & ipsius filios priuignos suos excitauit: vnde nata horum aduersus parentem tanta coniuratio, vt illum imperio se abdicare, suámque illis dignitatem cedere magno totius propè Europæ incommodo coegerēt. Quorum incommodorum culpam Historici omnes magna ex parte in illam Reginam matrem Iuditham conferunt: Abbas Vrspergₑ Michael Ritius & Otto Frising. Chron. 5. capite 34. Ludouicus, inquit, propter mala opera vxoris suæ Iudith regno pulsus est. Itemque Regino in Chro. anni DCCCXXXVIII. vbi sic scribit: Ludouicus à suis imperio priuatur, & priuatus custodiæ traditur, Regnique monarchia Lothario filio eius per electionem Francorum datur. Fuit autem hæc deiectio pro maxima parte facta propter multimodam fornicationem Iudithæ vxoris eius. Aliquot post seculis dominata est Blanca Regina, mater Ludouici cognomento Diui, natione Hispana. Vt primùm gubernaculum arripuit, concurrere ad arma Galliæ proceres cœperunt, Duce Philippo, Comite Bolonico, Regis patruo: qui (vt summus auctor scribit Ioan. Ionuillæus capite histor. 4.) serendum non esse clamitabant, tantum Regnum à muliere, eaque peregrina, administrari. Itaque Comitem Philippum proceres illi, repudiata Blanca, Regni procuratorem delegerunt. At Blanca nihilominus in instituto perseuerare, & auxilia vndique accersere: Ferdinandum denique Hispaniæ Regem fœdere sibi atque amicitia adiugere instituit. Cùm Duci Philippo Dux Britanniæ & Comes Eboracensis ipsius frater sese coniunxissent, de improuiso oppida aliquot interceperunt, eaque præsidiis firmarunt, quod Ionuillæus capite quinto commemorat: atque ita grauissimum in Gallia bellum, propter occupatâ à Regina matre Regni procurationem, exarsit. Forte tum accidit, vt Rex Stampas à matre armorum causa missus, proficisceretur. Eò confestim multis ex partibus Proceres aduolarunt, Regémq; obsidere cœperunt: non lædendi (inquit Ionuillæus) aut violandi illius consilio: sed (vt idem testatur) vt eum à matris potestate abducerent. Qua re ad illam perlata, quæ tum Lutetiæ permanserat, celeriter armari Parisienses, & Stampas proficisci iubet. Vix eæ copiæ Montlerium peruenerant, cùm Rex obsidione liberatus, ad eos accedit: Lutetiámque vnà cum ipsis reuertitur. Vbi se Philippus domesticis copiis minus instructum animaduertit, Reginam Cypri, quæ in regno controuersiam quandam habebat, subsidio accersit. Hæc magnis copiis in Campaniam ingressa, latè regionem illâ populatur. Blanca nihilominus in sententia permanet. Itaque Anglorum auxilium Proceres ad extremum in Regni fines introducunt. Hi magnis incommodis Aquitaniam, ceterasque maritimas regiones afficiunt: quæ incommoda omnia ex Reginæ illius matris impotentia atque ambitione nata fuisse, Ionuillæus multis verbis commemorat: c.6,7,8,9,&10. Et quoniâ longe alia de Blancæ ingenio & moribus noftrorû hominum opinio est, propter eorum (vt credi par est) qui per ea tempora scripserunt, assentationes (nam Reginis matribus Scriptores ferè vel supplicij metu, vel propter Regum filiorum existimationem parcunt) non prætermittendû videtur, quod idem Ionuillæus ca. 76. commemorat, illam vsq; eò filium in potestate sua habuisse, vsque adeò illum timidum abiectúmque redegisse, vt cùm ipsius vxorem, nurum suam, Margaretam odio haberet, raro admodum Regem cum illa versari pateretur. Itaque cùm rex iter faceret, Blanca metatorib. imperabat, vt hospitium Reginæ separatim à rege assignaret. quinetiam si quando rex noctu furtim ad coniugem accedebat, tum hostiarios in speculis collocabat: & si forte Blancam aduentare intelligerent, tum fuste canes ab illis cædi imperabat: quorum clamore de sese occultando commoneretur. Quid amplius? Die quodam (inquit Ionuillæus) cùm Regina Margareta è puerperio ægrotaret, Rexque pro amicitia ad illam venisset, repente Blanca interuenit. Rex clamore canum admonitus, sese in lectuli angulum abdidit, cortinisque inuoluit. Illa nihilominus inuétum Regem manu, inspectantibus omnibus, prehendit, ac simul è cubiculo eduxit: Tu hîc, inquiens, nihil agis. Egredere. At puerpera cùm tantam contumeliam acerbius tulisset, dolore exanimata est: coactíque sunt cubicularij Regem reuocare, cuius aduentu puerpera recreata est, animumque recepit. Atque hæc quidem Ionuillæus, capite hist.76. totidem propè verbis commemorat. Rursus aliquot intermissis annis dominata est Isabella Caroli v i. dementis vidua. Prius enim quàm Concilij auctoritate Regni procuratio certis ac delectis viris mandari posset, multæ ab hominibus ambitiosis contentiones exortæ sunt. Sexies deniq; controuerfiæ renouatę, sexies interpositis pactionibus sedatæ sunt. Tandem Ifabella Parisiis exacta, Carnutum se recepit. Ibi Philippum Moruillerium veteratorem nacta, Senatum sibi, & Prætorem, & Cancellarium Moruilleiium illum instituit eiusdémque consilio Typum regium (quod Cancellariæ Sigillum vulgò appellant) insculpi iussit, suámque in eo imaginem demissis brachiis imprimi: cùm in diplomatibus hac præfatione vteretur: Ifabella Dei gratia Regina Franciæ: quæ propter incommodam Regis valetudinem Regni procurationem obtinet. Verum vbi Respub. multis affecta incommodis, ac prope iam ad interitum adducta videretur, publico consilio Turones amandata est: quatuorque illi tutores attributi: qui belluam illam indomitam domi continerent: viderentque ne quam rem agere, ac ne literam quidem vllam sine ipsorum permissu scribere posset. Cuius rei extat apud Monstrelletum copiosa historia cap. 161. & cap. 168. Multóque vetustius eiusdem seueritatis exemplum extat in Placidina Childeberti Regis matre, quam propter impietatem, & nimiam in episcopo Quintiano vexando & ecclesiæ pace conturbanda insaniam, in oppido Cadurco comprehensam, & rebus omnibus spoliatam ac nudatam Franci exilio damnarunt, vt testatur Gregor. Turon. libro tertio capite duodecimo.
units.tr: But since the discussion concerns the administration of the kingdom and the highest office of governing the state, the question seems not to be passed over: whether women are excluded from the administration of the kingdom, just as they are excluded from its inheritance. First, however, we want it clearly stated that we are treating only the institutions of our own France, not the law of the Romans or of other peoples. For, as is known to everyone, under Roman institutions women, because of their weakness of judgement, were in perpetual guardianship and were excluded not only from public but also from private affairs. Among some other peoples, by ancient custom, women hold supreme power. Tacitus, in the Life of Agricola, says that the Britons make no distinction of sex in their commands. Having settled this point, and having stated our position plainly and clearly, let us now come to the question. The examples of some earlier times seem to have given occasion for it. It is established that the kingdom of France was administered by queens, especially widows, and by the mothers of kings who were either children or absent. I do not know whether any instance of female audacity can be recorded more striking than that of Queen Blanche, mother of Louis Transmarinus, of whom we shall speak later. When her son the king had gone to Africa to wage war, she claimed for herself the supreme power not only in the government of the state but also in the administration of the Churches and bishoprics, as can be learned from certain old documents lately brought to light: We have granted to our most dear lady and mother the Queen, and we will that she, in this our absence on pilgrimage, shall have full power to receive and draw into the affairs of our kingdom whomever she pleases, and to remove whomever she sees fit to be removed. She may also appoint bailiffs, castellans, foresters, and place and remove others as servants of ours and ministers of our kingdom; she may also confer vacant dignities and ecclesiastical benefices, receive the fealties of bishops and abbots, restore to them their regalian rights, and grant licence to chapters and convents to elect, in our place. On the other side, however, first comes the usual method of argument: that the right to rule is not held by one who has no right to be queen in her own right. That a woman cannot be queen in her own right, nor can the inheritance of the kingdom pass to her or to those born of her, but that if women are called queens, this happens by accident and on account of their husbands the kings, has been shown above from monuments more than 1,200 years old. To this we add what we taught above: just as the whole power of creating and deposing kings lay with the public council, so the supreme right of appointing the guardians or governors of the state lay with the same council. Moreover, even after kings were created, the same council kept for itself the supreme power of administering the realm. Not yet a hundred years had passed since, under Louis XI, however crafty and cunning, the guardians of the state were appointed by the same council, like ephors, in the thirty-sixth year of his reign. If we seek the authority of our forefathers, there is a notable passage in Aimoinus, book 4, chapter 1, where, speaking of Brunhilda, mother of King Childebert, he says: "At the same time," he says, "because Brunhilda was understood to wish to keep the whole care of the kingdom for herself, and the chief men of France disdained to be subjected for so long to a woman's rule, etc." Accordingly, Franciscus Connanus, a senator of Paris, in book 1, chapter 8, writes: "What Panormitanus thinks (he says), that by our custom queens have right over the Gauls, is greatly mistaken. For no nation has less tolerated the rule of women, since the Salic law, that is, the law of the Gauls, excludes them from the succession to the kingdom. Thus we see queens, when their husbands are dead, reduced almost to the rank of private persons, so that they do not even keep the shadow of royal dignity." Thus Connanus. And indeed it is so: whenever women have obtained the administration of the kingdom among our forefathers, that business has always stirred up strange tragedies in our state and, in the end, the greatest fires of misery. It does not seem out of place to set out some examples of this. Once ruled Queen Chrotildis, mother of the kings Childebert and Clotaire, who, when she was pursuing with an insane love the sons of her other son Chlodomer, who had died, exerted the greatest effort so that her grandsons, with their uncles removed, might be raised to the royal dignity. Accordingly, she nursed their hair, following the custom of which we spoke above, with great care and diligence. When the kings, her sons, were informed of this, they at once sent to her a certain Arcadius, who, showing her a naked sword and at the same time a pair of shears, offered her the choice of which of her grandsons she preferred to have brought to the shears or to the sword. But she, says Gregory of Tours, greatly moved by bile, and especially when she saw the drawn sword and the shears, answered in her bitterness: "It is better for me to see them dead than shorn, if they are not raised to the kingdom." So both grandsons were killed in her sight. The same Gregory, book 3, chapter 18, is the authority, where, however, he adds that this queen had won the goodwill of the common people and of the crowd by her generosity and gifts to monasteries. "Put a bridle (Cato used to say) on unbridled nature and an untamed animal, and hope that they will set some limit to their licence." What of it? How unbridled was that animal, I mean that daughter of King Theodoric, of Italian birth, who, mad with love for her lover, when she learned that he had been killed by her mother's order, showed, under the appearance of a reconciliation with her mother, that she wished to share the sacrament of the Lord's Supper with her, and, pouring poison into the cup, with impiety and cruelty together, destroyed her mother by a wicked deed. The words of Gregory of Tours, book 3, chapter 33, are these: "They lived under the Arian sect; and because it is their custom that kings, coming to the altar, communicate from one cup, and the lesser people from another (a custom worth noting: communicating from the cup with the common people), she put poison in that cup from which her mother was about to communicate; and when she had drunk from it, she died at once." Come, let us look at the others. Once ruled Fredegund, the queen mother, widow of Chilperic I. While her husband was still alive, she had a habit of adultery with a certain Landeric. When she noticed that Chilperic had become aware of this, she took care that he should be killed; and at once she took up the administration of the kingdom in the name of her son, King Clotharius, as queen mother, and held it for thirteen years. First she destroyed by poison Childebert, her husband's brother, and his wife; then she stirred up the Huns against her own sons; and she brought civil war into the state. Lastly, she was the torch of those fires by which France burned for many years. Authorities: Aimoinus, book 3, chapter 36, and book 8, chapter 29, and the writer of the Chronicle of Besançon. Queen Brunhilda, mother of Childebert, widow of King Sigebert, ruled. She kept as her favourite a certain Italian named Protadius, and loaded him with every honour. She also led her sons, the young men Theodebert and Theodoric, into such a habit of shameful living that at last they waged mortal enmities against each other, and, worn out by a long war, joined in a most savage battle. She killed with her own hand her grandson Merovech, son of Theodebert. She destroyed Theodoric with poison. What more? "Put a bridle (Cato used to say) on unbridled nature and an untamed animal, and hope that they will set some limit to their licence." She gave the cause of death to ten royal chiefs. When she was rebuked by a certain bishop and asked to mend her ways, she ordered him to be thrown into a river. At last a council of the Franks was called; she was summoned to judgement, condemned, and, bound to a galloping horse, torn apart and mangled limb from limb. Authorities: Gregory of Tours, book 5, chapter 39, and book 8, chapter 29, and Adon in the Sixth Age, Otto of Freising, Chronicle, part 16, and Aimoinus, book 4, chapter 1; and also the Appendix to Gregory of Tours, book 2, whose words are these: "Considering that five kings of the Franks had been killed through her, namely Sigebert, Merovech, and his father Chilperic, Theodebert and his son Clotharius, also Merovech son of Clotharius, Theodoric, and three of her own sons who had been put to death at that time: for three days he had her afflicted with various tortures, and first ordered her to be led on a camel through the whole army, sitting; afterwards he ordered her hair to be tied to the tail of a most fierce horse by one foot and one arm; and she was torn limb from limb by its kicks and the speed of its running." I find the same story in the manuscript Chronicle of the monastery of Besançon, in these words: "For he had her, set upon a camel, led round through the army; when all had shuddered at her, crying out, he ordered her to be brought back as if under the stroke of the flesh and soul, and to be tied between four untamed horses, at whose first bolt she was torn apart by parts, afterwards burned with fire, and cast down by the lower ones, together with the band of sinners." Again in another place: "So many evils and effusions of blood were done in France by the counsel of Brunhilda that the prophecy of the Sibyl was fulfilled, which says: 'The Bruna coming from the parts of Spain, before whose sight nations will perish; she herself will be torn apart by the kicks of horsemen.'" Come, let us look at the rest. Once ruled Plectrudis, widow not of a king but of Pippin, the royal prefect, who then held the royal power while Dagobert II bore the empty royal name. This Plectrudis, repudiated by Pippin because of her adultery and the foulness of her shameful life, after her husband's death was the author of many seditions in Gaul. She forced Charles Martel, the fortunate man, master of the palace, to give up his office, and put in his place another, Theobald, an impure and wicked man. At last she stirred up a deadly civil war among the Franks themselves, who, in various battles and, as Aimoinus says, in most cruel slaughters, laid each other low. Book 4, chapter 50, and the following chapter. Moreover, the author of the little book entitled The State of the Kingdom of France, under Dagobert II, uses these words: "When the Franks could no longer bear the frenzies and madness of Plectrudis, and saw no hope left in King Dagobert, they chose for themselves a certain Daniel as king, who had previously been a monk, and named him Chilperic." We touched on this history in another place above. But let us look at the rest. Once ruled the mother of Charles the Bald, named Judith, wife of Louis, surnamed the Pious, who was king not only of France but also emperor of Italy and Germany. She stirred up the miserable and fatal war between Louis and his stepsons, from which such a conspiracy arose among their sons against their father that they forced him to abdicate the empire and yield his dignity to them, to the great harm of almost all Europe. All the historians largely lay the blame for these harms on that queen mother Judith: Abbot Ursperg, Michael Ritius, and Otto of Freising, Chronicle, book 5, chapter 34. "Louis," he says, "was driven from the kingdom because of the evil deeds of his wife Judith." Likewise Regino, in the Chronicle for the year 838, where he writes thus: "Louis is deprived of power by his own people, and being deprived is handed over to custody, and the monarchy of the kingdom is given by election of the Franks to his son Lothair. This deposition was, however, for the most part brought about by the many-sided fornication of his wife Judith." Some centuries later ruled Queen Blanche, mother of Louis, surnamed the Saint, a Spaniard by birth. As soon as she seized the helm, the nobles of Gaul began to take up arms, with Duke Philip, Count of Boulogne, the king's uncle, as leader; they cried out that so great a kingdom should not be endured to be administered by a woman, and a foreigner at that. Accordingly those nobles, rejecting Blanche, chose Count Philip as guardian of the kingdom. But Blanche nevertheless persevered in her purpose, and sent for help from everywhere; at last she resolved to bind Ferdinand, King of Spain, to herself by treaty and friendship. When the Duke of Brittany and the Earl of York, brother of Philip, had joined the Duke Philip, they suddenly seized several towns and strengthened them with garrisons; Joinville records this in chapter 5. Thus a most grievous war broke out in Gaul, because the administration of the kingdom had been seized by the queen mother. It happened at that time that the king, sent by his mother to take up arms, set out for Étampes. Immediately, from many parts, nobles flew there and began to besiege the king, not, says Joinville, with intent to harm or violate him, but, as the same writer testifies, in order to take him away from his mother's power. When this was reported to her, who then remained at Paris, she quickly ordered the Parisians to arm and to set out for Étampes. Hardly had those forces reached Montlhéry when the king, freed from the siege, came to them, and returned with them to Paris. When Philip saw that he was less well provided with his own forces, he sent for help from the Queen of Cyprus, who had a certain dispute in the kingdom. She entered Champagne with great forces and laid waste that region far and wide. Blanche nevertheless remained of the same mind. So at last the nobles brought in the help of the English to the borders of the kingdom. These caused great harm to Aquitaine and the other maritime regions. Joinville relates at length that all these harms arose from the impotence and ambition of that queen mother: chapters 6, 7, 8, 9, and 10. And since the opinion about Blanche's character and morals is quite different, on account of the flattery (as is fair to believe) of those who wrote in those times (for writers spare queen mothers almost always, either from fear of punishment or out of regard for the reputation of the king's sons), it seems not to be passed over what the same Joinville records in chapter 76: that she kept her son so much in her power, and had reduced him to such timidity and dejection, that, since she hated his wife, his daughter-in-law Margaret, she hardly ever allowed the king to be with her. So when the king was travelling, Blanche ordered the quartermasters to assign the queen's lodging separately from the king's. Moreover, if at any time the king went secretly by night to his wife, then she placed doorkeepers on watch, and if they happened to perceive that Blanche was coming, then she ordered the dogs to be beaten with clubs by them, so that the king might be warned by their barking to hide himself. What more? "One day," says Joinville, "when Queen Margaret was sick after childbirth, and the king had come to her out of affection, Blanche suddenly came in. The king, warned by the barking of the dogs, hid himself in a corner of the bed and wrapped himself in the curtains. Nevertheless she seized the king, who had been found, by the hand, while everyone looked on, and at once led him out of the bedroom, saying: 'You have no business here. Get out.' But the woman in childbed, taking so great an insult more bitterly, was overcome with grief, and the chamberlains were forced to call the king back; by his coming the woman in childbed was restored and took heart again." Thus Joinville, chapter 76, relates almost in these very words. Again, after some years had intervened, ruled Isabella, widow of the mad Charles VI. For before the administration of the kingdom could be entrusted, by authority of the Council, to certain chosen men, many quarrels arose from ambitious men. Six times the disputes were renewed, and six times they were calmed by intervening agreements. At last Isabella was driven out of Paris and withdrew to Chartres. There, having found the crafty Philip de Morvilliers, she set up for herself a senate, a praetor, and Morvilliers as chancellor, and by his advice ordered the royal seal (which they commonly call the chancery seal) to be engraved, and her own image with lowered arms to be impressed on it; she used in her documents this preface: "Isabella, by the grace of God Queen of France, who, because of the king's unfitting ill health, holds the administration of the kingdom." But when the state, afflicted with many harms and seemingly brought almost to ruin, was sent to Tours by public counsel, four guardians were assigned to her, who should keep that untamed beast at home and see that she could do nothing, nor write even a single letter, without their permission. A full account of this is found in Monstrelet, chapters 161 and 168. And a much older example of the same severity is found in Placidina, mother of King Childebert, whom the Franks condemned to exile for her impiety and her excessive madness in harassing Bishop Quintianus and disturbing the peace of the Church; she was seized in the town of Cahors, stripped of all her possessions and left naked, as Gregory of Tours attests in book 3, chapter 12.

units.la: SVb eadem Capeuingiorū familia exortum est in Francogallia Regnum Rabularium, de quo nobis propter incredibilem artificum industriam, & inauditam seculis omnibus solertiam dicendum videtur. Dominatur hoc tempore passim in Gallia genus hominum, qui Iuridici à nonnullis, Pragmatici ab aliis, itémq; Rabulæ appellantur. Horum tanta trecentis ferè abhinc annis fuit solertia, vt non modò publici concilij auctoritatem (de qua superiùs diximus) propè iam oppresserint, verùm etiam omnes Regni Principes, atq; adeò Maiestatem regiam amplitudini suæ parere coegerint. Itaque quibus in oppidis illius Regni sedes positæ sunt, in iis tertia ferè ciuium & incolarum pars tantis excitata præmiis ad illius se artis Rabulariæ studium ac disciplinam applicauit. quod vel Lutetiæ, quæ ceterarum ciuitatum omniū princeps numeratur, cuiuis licet animaduertere. Quis enim vel triduum in illa vrbe versatus, non animaduertit, tertiam ciuium partem, artem istam rabulariam & litigatoriam factitare? Itaq; summus in ea Pragmaticorum conuentus (qui Purpuratus Senatus dicitur) tātarum opum, tantæque dignitatis est, vt quemadmodum de Senatu Romano quondam dictum est, non iam cōsiliariorum, sed regum ac satraparum confessus videatur. quippe, cùm plerique in illum alle-ai, {ti}, quantumuis abiecto loco nati, tamen paucorum annorum spatio regales prope opes sibi concilient. Qua de causa ciuitates aliae complures omni contentione pugnarunt, ut eiusdem modi confessus iuridiciales apud se haberent: iamque celeberrima haec Parlamenta numerantur: Parisiense, Tholosanum, Rhotomagense, Gratianopolitanum, Burdegalense, Aquense, Diuionense: quae omnia stataria & sedentaria sunt. Octauum vero mobile & ambulatorium, quod Grande Consilium appellatur. Fuit & nonum Armoricis attributum, edicto Henrici regis anno MDLIII. In horum regnorum finibus sunt & aliae, ut sic dicam, Satrapiae, quae superiorum illorum amplitudinem, quoad possunt, imitantur: & vulgo Sedes praesidiales nominantur: tantaque huius morbi vis, atque contagio est, ut quemadmodum olim Aegyptiorum bona pars Tyrannorum suorum imperio in pyramidibus, & eiusmodi molibus extruendis occupata erat, sic maximus gentis Gallicae numerus in litibus & calumniis exercendis, & forensibus scriptitationibus operam consumat. Extat Claudij Seyssellij Archiepiscopi Massiliensis libellus Gallice scriptus, cui titulus est, De Monarchia Franciae: cuius in capit. 15. verba haec sunt: Opinione mea, plures sunt in una Francia scribae, procuratores, aduocati, & similes circumforanei, quam in vniuerso orbe Christiano: si alij omnes vnum in locum conferatur. Neque dissimilis illa est Philippi Comineni querimonia lib. 6.cap.6. vbi de rege Ludouico xi. scribens: Habebat, inquit, in animo leges de publico & privato iure, Gallico sermone scriptas, vnum in volumen conferre: quò facilius captiones & præstigiæ aduocatorum vitari possent: quorum numerus tantus est in hoc Franciæ regno, vt par in mundo non reperiatur; id Nobilitas Francica iampridem sensit, atque experta est. Hæc ad verbum Cominæus. Nomen autem Parlamenti (antiqua nostrorum hominum lingua) collocutionem significat, multorum variis ex locis certum aliquem in locum conuenientium, vt de communibus rebus inter se conferant, ac fermocinentur. Itaque in Chronicis veteribus, siquando principes legatiue principum de pace, aut bellicis pactionibus conuenerunt, semper condictum illud colloquium, Parlamenti nomine appellatur. Eademque ratione publicum ordinum Concilium vetusta lingua nostra Parlamentum dicebatur, quod nomen adhuc in Anglia retinetur. Thom. Walsingamius in hist. Angl. sub anno 1287. Hoc anno Rex Angliæ in Gallias transiens, Ambianos peruenit: & fecit homagium Regi Franciæ, pro terris quas de eo in regno Fraciæ tenebat Parisius: & interfuit parliamento, quod Rex Francorum tenuit.
