Itaque Philipp. Cominæus lib. 4. c. 1. Rex Angliæ, inquit, tributa suæ genti imperandi ius non habet, sine consensu atque auctoritate sui Parlamenti, quod apud nos Trium statuum Concilium appellatur. Eodémque nomine conuentus ordinum Britanniæ Armoricæ, quandiu gês illa regem proprium habuit, semper appellatus est: quemadmodum ex illius Annalib. cognosci licet: multis quidem locis, sed præsertim lib.3. vbi Ducis Malicklerici, hoc est indocti indoctæ cum Franciæ rege pactio profertur: ex anno MCCXXX. Itē Dux in signum subiectionis prædictæ, voluit quòd à suo parlamento de cetero appellaretur ad parlamentum Franciæ, in duobus tantum casibus. Et mox: A falso & prauo iudicio sui parlamenti Britanniæ appellabitur de cetero ad Franciæ parlamentum. Dicebatur etiam Curia parlamenti trium statuum: vt Stephanus Aufrerius Burdegalensis Prætor, nobilis pragmaticus, testatur in Commentario styli curiæ Parlamenti. Quinetiam videō Bartolum aliosque Doctores Italos hac eadem voce passim pro publico regionis alicuius concilio, siue comitiis, vsurpare. Nam Bartolus in l.2. C. de legation. lib.10. Præses prouinciæ, inquit, conuocat parlamentum in prouincia, & in eo proponit quod respicit vtilitatem publicam. Ex mox: Nota, quòd præsides prouinciarum coadunant vniuersale parlamentum prouinciæ: quod intellige, non quòd omnes de prouincia debeant ad illud ire, sed de omnibus ciuitatibus deputantur ambasiatores, qui ciuitatem repræsentant. Et in eandem l.Ioā.de Platea: Vbi super aliquo, inquit, prouidendum est pro vtilitate totius prouinciæ, debet congregari generale concilium seu parlamentum: non quod omnes de prouincia vadant: sed de qualibet ciuitate aliqui ambasiatores vel syndici, qui totam ciuitatem repræsentent. in quo concilio seu parlamento petitur proponi sanum & vtile consilium. Itē Lucas de Penna: Modus proponendi in cōsilio generali, seu parlamento est, vt petatur proponi sanum & vtile consilium. Budæus autem in Pandect. Nihilosecius (inquit) curiæ Parisiensis originem à conuentibus iuridicis manasse, haud dubia cōiectura crediderim: quibus olim Principes interesse, præesseque solebant: quoniam indictiui erant, nec loco, nec tempore stati. Vagam enim Parlamenti rationem fuisse constat, quasiq; prætorianum Principis concilium. Cùm autem in Gallia nostra summam illam Publici concilij auctoritatem imminuere Capeuingij molirentur, & certorum Senatorū numerum in eius concilij locum substituere, augustum illud parlamenti nomen in illum pragmaticorū & iudicum concessum transtulerunt: eique hæc auctoritatem tribuerunt: primùm vt nulla regia Lex, nulla constitutio rata esset, nisi cuius illi consiliarij auctores comprobatoresque suissent: deinde vt nullus tota Gallia Magistratus, non modò vrbanus, verumetiam militaris esset, quem non ab illo consessu inaugurari, & apud eundem in leges iurare oporteret: tum vt ab eorum iudiciis appellandi ius non esset: sed vt eorum decreta rata & fixa essent. Is qui Princeps est senatus (inquit Connanus libro 1.) cùm ius dicit, nemini, præterquam Regi ipsi, honore sere sedendi cedit. quo tamen loco Connanus Cancellarij oblitus est,cui Princeps ille senatus loco cedit,quasi (vt Budæus scribit) magiftratuū omnium antistiti. Postremò quicquid potestatis imperij, auctoritatis penes publicum Concilium & Statuum parlamentum per tot annos fuisse docuimus, id totum Senatus ille subdititius sibi vsurpauit:in quem reges cooptandos curabant,quos ad suas rationes accommodatos fore iudicabant, eaque tum Curia Parlamenti vocata est:vt in Anglico libello,cui titulus estAlearned commendatum: cap. 52.sunt quippe in regno Franciæ, in curia ibidem suprema, quæ Curia Parlamenti vocitatur,processus quidam, qui in ea plus quam triginta annis pependerűt. Et noui ego appellationis causam vnam quæ in curia illa agitata fuit iam per decem annos, & adhuc verisimile non est, eam infra annos decē alios posse decidi. Item cap.48.Omnes aduocati in Francia etiam in curia parlamenti solét placitare caussas suas in lingua Gallica. Quare quibus initiis ac radicibus in tātam amplitudinem excreuerit,paulilper considerādū est. Primum igitur Basilica regia Lutetiæ opere magnifico extructa est,imperio,vt plerique affirmant, regis Ludouici Hutini, quo nomine prisca lingua nostra Turbulentus significatur: vel, vt nonulli disputant,regis Philippi Pulchri, circiter annū MCCXCIIII. studio certè atque opera Enguerrantij Marignij, comitis Longueuillij, qui aliquot interiectis annis in patibulo Parisiēsi proter peculatus crimen recte suspensus est. Vtcūque fit, quod Ægyptij reges fecisse narrantur, vt imperio suo subiectos in pyramidibus extruendis occuparent, in quibus rex Chemnis præcipuè memoratur, qui hominum trecenta sexaginta millia ad pyramidem extruendam conduxit: idem tum Francogalliæ reges in arte rabularia tradenda fecisse dici possunt. Guaguini autem Historici in Hutini regis vita, verba hæc sunt: Hic Ludouicus instituit Parlamenti Curiam Parisiis stabilem esse, & loco non moueri, ne litigatores crebris circuitionibus vexarentur. Hæc ille. Nam quòd nonnulli ad Pipinum vel Carolum Magnum institutum illud referunt, quàm absurdum id sit, facilè ex iis quę mox docebimus, constabit. Quinetiam eiusdem Caroli Magni leges & constitutiones complures extant, quarū in nulla neq; parlamenti, neq; maioris illius Senatus mentio interponitur: sed tantum sancitur, vt certis locis forum à Iuridicis agatur, & conuentus habeatur, quæ ille vsitata consuetudine Placitum, & Mallam appellat, veluti legis Francicæ lib. 4. c. 35. Vt in anno tria solummodo generalia placita obseruare compellat: nisi forte quilibet aut accusatus fuerit, aut alium occupauerit, aut ad testimonium perhibendum vocatus fuerit. Multæque aliæ in eandem sententiam eiusdem regis leges extāt, ex quibus de litium paucitate existimare licet. Ac plane verissimū arbitror, quod video à nonnullis hominibus nostris traditum, tātam litiū, calumniarum, & sycophantiarum sementem factam primùm à Papa Clemente v. qui Philippi illius Pulchri tempore Papatus sedem Avenionem transtulit. cúmque magna ipsius aulici & pragmatici cõsuetudine cum hominibus nostris implicarentur, semina Romanę artis rabulariæ in mores nostros sparsisse. Nam Eguinarthus in vita Caroli Magni sic scribit: Cum calcia retur, aut amiciretur, nõ tantùm amicos admittebat: verumetiã si comes palatij lite esse aliquâ diceret, quæ sine eius iussu definiri non poterat, statim litigantes introduci iussit, & velut pro tribunali sederet, lite cognita, sententiam dixit. Itaque eiusdem Caroli Magni in Capitulari hæc lex extat: Hoc missi nostri notum faciant comitibus & populo, quòd nos in omni septimana vnũ diem ad causas audiendas sedere volumus. Age, ceteros videamus. Regnauit circiter annũ MCCXXX. Ludouicus cognomento Diuus: cuius vitam Ioan. Ionuillæus de quo superiùs aliquoties meminimus, conscripsit. At ex huius commentario quanta per id tempus litium & calumniarum esset raritas, vel hinc licet intelligatur; quòd Rex ipse Ludouicus vel controversias disceptabat, vel disceptandi negotium nonnullis è suo Comitatu mandabat. Itaque capit. 94. ita scribit: Solebat, inquit, imperare Domino Nellio, Domino Suessionensi, & mihi, vt iudiciis quæ ad portam appellantur, operam darem us. Tum mittebat qui nos ad se accerseret: quærebatque ex nobis, quo statu res esset, ecquod esset iudicium, quod sine ipso exerceri nó posset. ac saepe accidit, vt re per nos ad ipsum delata, litigatores ipsos accersiri ad se imperaret, causamq; ex bono & æquo disceptaret. Sæpenumerò in saltum Vicennam animi causa exibat, viridíque in cespite ad quercus alicuius radicem confidens, sibi nos assidere, &, si quis negotij quid habebat, eum ad se vocari iubebat. Quinetiam ipse clarè pronuntiabat, si quis litem & aduersarium haberet, vt accederet, & iusta sua exponeret. Tum si quis accedebat, Rex attentè ipsum audiebat, ac re cognita, sententiam ex bono & æquo pronuntiabat. Interdum negotium dabat Petro Fotanio, & Godefrido Vilettio, vt litigatoribus operam darent, & causas disceptarent. Vidi etiam aliquoties, cum bonus ille Rex Lutetię in hortum suburbanum exiret, tunica mediocri indutus: ibíque mensam tapeto insterni imperabat. Tum silētio facto introduci ad se litigatores iubebat, causasque suas agere: iúsq; ex tempore reddebat. Hæc Iouillæus.
units.tr: Under the same Capetian family there arose in France the kingdom of the pettifoggers, which deserves mention here because of the incredible industry of these men and a cunning unheard of in all ages. At present a class of men is spread throughout France who are called Juridici by some, Pragmatici by others, and also Rabulae. Within roughly the last three hundred years their skill has been so great that they have almost overpowered the authority of the public council (which I discussed above), and have forced all the princes of the realm, and even the royal majesty itself, to submit to their greatness. Accordingly, in whatever towns of that kingdom their seats are set, about a third of the citizens and inhabitants, drawn on by such rewards, have devoted themselves to the study and practice of this pettifogging art. This can be observed everywhere, but especially at Paris, which is reckoned the chief of all the cities. For who that has spent even three days in that city has not noticed that a third of its citizens practise this pettifogging and litigious art? Thus the highest assembly of these pragmatics there (called the Purple Senate) is of such wealth and dignity that, as was once said of the Roman Senate, it seems to be composed not of counsellors but of kings and satraps. Indeed, since most of those who enter it, however lowly their birth, win for themselves almost royal wealth within a few years. For this reason several other cities have fought with all their might to have similar judicial assemblies among themselves; and already these most famous Parliaments are counted: the Parisian, the Toulousan, the Rouen, the Grenoble, the Bordeaux, the Aix, and the Dijon, all of which are stationary and sedentary. The eighth, indeed, is mobile and travelling, and is called the Grand Council. A ninth was also assigned to Brittany by the edict of King Henry in the year 1553. Within the borders of these realms there are also other, so to speak, satrapies, which imitate, as far as they can, the greatness of those superior bodies, and are commonly called presidial seats. So great is the power and contagion of this disease that, just as once a large part of the Egyptians' resources was spent under the rule of their tyrants on building the pyramids and such massive works, so a very great number of the French people spend their effort on stirring up lawsuits and quarrels and on the wordy scribbling of the courts. There is a little book written in French by Claude Seyssel, Archbishop of Marseilles, entitled On the Monarchy of France, and in chapter 15 its words are these: "In my opinion, there are more clerks, procurators, advocates and similar hangers-about in France alone than in the whole Christian world, if all the others were brought together in one place." Philippe de Commynes' complaint in book 6, chapter 6, is not unlike this, where, writing of King Louis XI, he says: "He had in mind," he says, "to collect the laws on public and private right, written in the French tongue, into one volume, so that the snares and tricks of advocates could be more easily avoided; their number is so great in this kingdom of France that no equal is to be found in the world. The French nobility has long felt this and has experienced it." Thus Commynes, word for word. Now the name Parlement (in the ancient language of our people) signifies a conference, a meeting of many men from various places coming together at a certain place to confer and talk over common affairs. Accordingly, in the old chronicles, whenever princes or the envoys of princes met to agree on peace or on terms of war, that agreed conversation was always called by the name of Parlement. And by the same reasoning, in our old language the public council of the estates was called a Parlement, a name which is still kept in England. Thomas Walsingham, in his History of England, under the year 1287: "In this year the King of England, crossing into Gaul, came to Amiens and did homage to the King of France for the lands which he held of him in the kingdom of France at Paris; and he was present at the Parlement which the King of the French held." Accordingly Philippe de Commynes, book 4, chapter 1: "The King of England," he says, "has no right to impose tributes on his people without the consent and authority of his Parlement, which among us is called the Council of the Three Estates." And by the same name the assembly of the estates of Armorican Brittany was always called, for as long as that people had its own duke; as can be learned from its Annals, in many places, but especially in book 3, where the agreement of the Duke of Malestroit (that is, of the unlearned) with the King of France is set out, from the year 1230. Likewise the Duke, as a sign of the aforesaid subjection, wished that from then on appeal should be made from his Parlement to the Parlement of France in two cases only. And soon after: "From the false and wicked judgement of its Parlement, Brittany shall henceforth appeal to the Parlement of France." The court was also called the Parlement of the three estates, as Étienne Aufrère, provost of Bordeaux and a noted pragmatic, attests in his Commentary on the practice of the Court of Parlement. Indeed I see that Bartolus and other Italian doctors everywhere use this same word for the public council or assembly of some region. For Bartolus, on law 2, C. de legationibus, book 10: "The governor of a province," he says, "calls a parlement in the province, and in it lays before them what regards the public advantage." And afterwards: "Note that the governors of provinces convene a general parlement of the province; understand this not to mean that all of the province must go to it, but that envoys or syndics are chosen from every city to represent the city." And on the same law, John of Platea: "Where something must be provided for the advantage of the whole province, a general council or parlement ought to be gathered; not that all of the province should go, but that from each city some envoys or syndics should come, who represent the whole city; in this council or parlement it is requested that a sound and useful counsel be put forward." Likewise Lucas de Penna: "The method of proposing in a general council or parlement is that it be asked that a sound and useful counsel be proposed." Budé, however, in his Pandects, says: "Nevertheless," he says, "I should believe, by a not doubtful conjecture, that the origin of the Parisian court flowed from judicial assemblies at which princes were formerly accustomed to attend and preside, since they were summoned at will, fixed neither in place nor in time. For it is established that the Parlement was in the nature of a wandering thing, and was, as it were, the praetorian council of the prince." When, however, the Capetians in our France strove to diminish that supreme authority of the public council, and to put in its place a fixed number of senators, they transferred that venerable name of Parlement to the body of pragmatics and judges, and gave it these powers: first, that no royal law and no constitution should be valid unless it had been approved and confirmed by those councillors; then, that no magistrate in all France, not only civil but even military, should be installed except by that assembly, and should take an oath to the laws before it; next, that there should be no right of appeal from their judgements, but that their decrees should be final and fixed. "He who is the first of the senate," says Connanus in book 1, "when he pronounces law, yields the honour of sitting to no one except the king himself." Yet in this passage Connanus forgot the Chancellor, to whom that first senator yields his place, as (Budé writes) to the head of all the magistrates. Lastly, whatever power, command and authority we have shown to have belonged for so many years to the public council and the parliament of the Estates, all of that the spurious Senate has usurped for itself; into it the kings took care to co-opt those whom they judged suited to their purposes; and this body was then called the Court of Parlement, as is recommended in the English booklet entitled Alearned, chapter 52: "Indeed in the kingdom of France, in the supreme court there, which is called the Court of Parlement, there are certain suits which have hung on in it for more than thirty years. And I know of one case of appeal which has been pursued in that court for ten years already, and it is still not likely that it can be decided within another ten years." Likewise chapter 48: "All advocates in France, even in the Court of Parlement, are accustomed to plead their causes in the French language." Wherefore we must consider for a little while by what beginnings and roots it has grown to such greatness. First, then, the royal basilica at Paris was built with a magnificent work, by the command, as many affirm, of King Louis the Quarrelsome (which name in our old language signifies "Turbulent"), or, as some argue, of King Philip the Fair, about the year 1294, but certainly by the zeal and labour of Enguerrand de Marigny, Count of Longueville, who some years later was rightly hanged on the gallows at Paris for the crime of embezzlement. However it came about, what the Egyptian kings are said to have done, occupying their subjects in building the pyramids, in which King Cheops is especially recorded as having employed three hundred and sixty thousand men to build a pyramid, the same may be said to have been done by the kings of France in handing down the pettifogging art. But the historian Gaguin, in the life of King Louis the Quarrelsome, has these words: "This Louis established that the Court of Parlement should be fixed at Paris and not be moved from place, so that litigants should not be harassed by frequent journeys." So he. As for those who refer that institution to Pepin or Charlemagne, it will be easily clear from what we shall teach presently how absurd that is. Moreover, many laws and constitutions of this same Charlemagne survive, in none of which is any mention made of a parlement or of that greater senate; but it is only enacted that at certain places the court should be held by judicial men and assemblies held, which by his customary usage he calls the placitum and the mallus, as in the Law of the Franks, book 4, chapter 35: that he should compel them to observe in the year only three general placita, unless perhaps someone had been accused, or had seized another, or had been summoned to give testimony. And many other laws of the same king to the same effect survive, from which one may judge of the scarcity of lawsuits. And I think it quite true, what I see has been handed down by some of our countrymen, that so great a seed of lawsuits, calumnies and sycophancy was first sown by Pope Clement V, who in the time of that Philip the Fair transferred the seat of the papacy to Avignon; and since, by the great familiarity of his courtiers and pragmatics, they became entangled with our people, they scattered among our manners the seeds of the Roman art of pettifoggery. For Eginhard, in his life of Charlemagne, writes thus: "When he was putting on his shoes, or being dressed, he did not admit only friends; even if the count of the palace said that some lawsuit, which could not be settled without his order, was pending, he at once ordered the litigants to be brought in, and as if he were sitting before a tribunal, having heard the case, he gave sentence." Accordingly this law of Charlemagne himself survives in a capitulary: "Let our envoys make known to the counts and the people that we wish to sit one day in every week to hear causes." Come, let us see the others. King Louis, surnamed the Pious, reigned about the year 1230; his life was written by John de Joinville, whom we have mentioned several times above. But from his commentary one may understand how rare lawsuits and calumnies were at that time, if only from this: that King Louis himself either settled disputes or entrusted the business of settling them to some of his retinue. Accordingly in chapter 94 he writes thus: "He used," he says, "to order Lord Nesle, Lord de Soissons and me to attend to the judgements which are called at the gate. Then he sent for us, and asked us what state the matter was in, and whether there was any judgement which could not be carried out without him. And it often happened that when the matter had been referred by us to him, he ordered the litigants themselves to be summoned to him, and settled the cause according to what was good and equitable. Very often he went out to the wood at Vincennes for recreation, and sitting on the green turf at the root of some oak, he had us sit beside him, and if anyone had any business he ordered him to be called to him. Moreover he himself plainly proclaimed that if anyone had a suit and an adversary, he should come forward and set out his just claim. Then if anyone came forward, the King listened to him attentively, and when the matter was understood, he pronounced sentence according to what was good and equitable. Sometimes he gave the business to Peter de Fontaines and Geoffrey de Villette, to attend to the litigants and settle the causes. I have also seen several times, when that good King went out to a garden in the suburbs of Paris, dressed in a plain tunic, that he ordered a table to be spread with a carpet there. Then, silence being made, he ordered the litigants to be brought before him and to plead their causes, and gave judgement on the spot." So Joinville.

units.la: Ex quibus existimari potest, quanta litium & litigatorum illis temporibus esset paucitas: quantáque Regum illorum in auertedis litium moleftiis folicitudo. Quin ne illud quidem praetermittendum est, quod scribit Speculator sub tit. de Feriis, cùm suo tempore, hoc est circiter annum MCCLXX. grauiores causæ ac lites in Cōcilio publico, (quod, vt iam antè dictum est, Parlamentum appellabatur) agi solerent, atq; illuc omnibus ex regni partibus in ius adiretur, moris fuisse, propter eos qui longinquis ex regionibus venerant, vt etiam festis diebus iudicia exercerentur : Potest, inquit, excusari consuetudo Curiæ Regis Franciæ, quæ tempore Parlamentorum omni die ius reddit: vt venientes de longinquis partibus citius expediantur. At successu temporis, arte rabularia, sensim, gangrenæ modo, serpente, institutum est, vt & laepius & pluribus locis iurisdictio exerceretur. Itaque Philippi III. cognomento Pulchri constitutio hæc extat, ex anno MCCCII. Præterea propter subiectorum nostrorum comodum, & causarum expeditione proponimus ordinare, quòd duo Parlamenta Parisiis, & duo Scacaria Rhotomagi, Diésque Trecenfes bis tenebuntur in anno: & quòd Parlamentum apud Tholosam tenebitur, sicut teneri folebat temporibus retroactis, fi gentes terræ consentiant. Item, quia multæ caussæ magnæ in nostro Parlamento inter magnas & notabiles personas aguntur, ordinamus & volumus, quòd duo Prælati & duæ aliæ perfonæ sufficientes, Laicæ, de nostro consilio, vel saltem vnus prælatus, & vna persona Laica, caufas prædictas audiendi, deliberandíque gratia continuè in nostris Parlamentis existant, Quibus ex verbis intelligi potest, primùm quàm raro per ea tempora iudicia exercerentur. deinde quàm pauci iudices in illo Parlamento sederet. Nam quantum ad ceteras præfecturas Regnique prouincias, extat eiusdem Philippi Pulchri constitutio, in eodem libello his verbis edita, anno M CC CII. Præcipimus insuper, quòd Senefchalli & Balliui nostri teneant suas affisias in circuitu Senefchalliarum & Balliuiarū summariè, de duobus mensibus in duobus ad minus. Quinetiam Budæus eodem quem superiùs notaurimus loco scribit, anno M CCXCIIII. ab eodem Rege Philippo constitutum fuisse, vt in Parlamento trifarij generis sederent Prælati, Barones, & mixti Clerici cum Laicis. Cùm laici, inquit, partim ex equitibus, partim ex promiscuo genere hominum deligerentur. Item, vt Prælati & Barones ex illo tertio genere statuerent, qui ad quanq; iurisdictionem exercendam idonei videretur. simul vt tres viros deligerent, qui in eas regiones mitterentur, quæ iure scripto vtebantur: vt in iisius dicerent, & si qua capitalis quæstio habenda esset, literatissimos quosque adhiberent. Quo loco Budæus horum temporum corruptelam deplorans, simulque vilissima rabularum capita forensia, togatósq; vulturios (vt Apuleius loquitur) detestans, ex Iuuenalis versu sic exclamat: Quondam hoc indigenæ viuebant more: simúlque ita subscribit: Ita enim nobis exclamare in mētem venit: Antiquioribus illis seculis, florente tamen hoc Regno (quod ex numismatis apparet, auro obryzo percussis) simplicem & facilem ius reddendi rationem, raráque lites, nec diuturnas, vt nunc, aut etiam seculares fuisse: cùm nōdum ista turba interpretum Iuris Remp. inuasisset: nec dum scientia iuris latissime, atque etiam in infinituma tum patere crederetur. Sed æquum bonúmque & iudex prudens integritate atq; innocentia præditus, instar sexcentorum voluminū essent. Nunc vero quò res reciderit, nemo quidem nō videt. Sed omnes dicere mussant. Hactenus Budæus grauissimus vbiq; & acerrimus artis rabularię aduersarius. Nunc vt ad nostrā historiam redeamus, doceamúsq; quibus initiis ac fundamentis Regnum istud litigatorium excitatum fuerit: quemadmodum Cicero scribit Pontifices veteres propter sacrificiorum multitudinem, tres viros Epulones instituisse, quamuis essent ipsi à Numa, vt etiam illud ludorum epulare sacrificium facerér, instituti: eodem modo ex illo perexiguo ludicum Parlamentariorū numero, crescente litium multitudine, incredibilis ludicum & Conciliariorum soboles propagata est. Ac primum Basilica ingēs, sumptuosa, magnifica, Regis, vt superiùs diximus, Ludovici Hutini, vel Philippi Pulcri imperio ædificata est: tum ex mediocri iudicum numero tres decuriæ factæ, Magnæ Cameræ, Inquisitionū, & Postulatorum. quam partitionem Budæus eodem illo loco: sed copiosius Gaguinus in Regis Hutini vita commemorat. Video tamen, qui ad Stilum curiæ parlamenti, vbi Stephanus Auffrerius eundem numerum seruat, hanc notam ascripserit: Imo initio duæ tantùm cameræ fuerunt. quia Camera Requestarum est tribunal inferius. postea addita est tertia: quæ parua Camera Inquestarũ appellatur. Sed anno M D X X II. rex Frácifcus, vt corraderet sexaginta millia aureorum quartam Cameram è viginti nouis consiliariis creauit: à singulis capiēs ter mille aureos. vnde curia valde deturpata fuit. postea præsidentiū quoque numerus pretio auctus est. Rursus idem Rex ann. M D X L I I I. alios x x. quæstus caussa creauit. Quin neillud quidem prætermittendum videtur, quod & Guaguinus &Budæus eodē loco memorię prodiderunt, atque insigne est ad omnem memoriam documentum, illum iudicum conuentum non perpetuum & perennem (vt hoc tempore) sed indictiuũ fuisse, nec nisi certo Principis mādato exerceri solitum: quod quotannis ineunte mēse Nouembri edictum Regis proponi oportet, vt eum renouari liceat. Atque vt huius, inquit eodem loco Guaguinus, coitionisRegē auctorem esse certum sit, regia singulis quibusque annis rescripta eduntur, quibus ad D. Martini diem festum, id est, 11. Id. Nouem. Parlamētum inchoādi iudicibus à Rege auctoritas datur. De mirabili autem & celeri huius regni incremēto etiam illud argumento esse potest, quòd circiter centū pòst annis, hoc est, ann. M C C C C L I I I. regnante Carolo v I I. hæc ab illo constitutiō promulgata est: A festo Paschæ, vsque ad finem Parlamenti, Præsidētes & Consiliarij hora sexta de mane debent in suis cameris esse congregati, à festo S. Martini, post horam prædictam, Et aliquantò post: Pernecessarium est, vt Præsidentes & Consiliarij Curiæ post prandium veniant ad Parlamentum iudicandi & expediendi causâ. Hæc Carolus VII. At Caroli Magni tempore, qui regnū triplo maius obtinebat, quam dissimilis iudiciorum ratio fuerit, vel ex hac ipsius lege facile intellectu est: Legis Francicæ lib. 4. c. 74. Vt comes placitum non habeat, nisi ieiunus. Iam de voce Parlamenti ac nominis etiam auctoritate illud argumetum extat, quod cum in ea parte Allobrogum quæ Delphinatus dicitur antiquitus Senatus institutus fuisset, cū summa auctoritate, quod concilium Delphinale dicebatur: tam Ludouicus VI. qui bene de se meritis Delphinatibus benignè facere studebat, nomen concilij in Parlamentum mutauit: quamuis nihil ad ius atq; auctoritatem adderet: cuius rei Guidopapius testis est, q. Gratianop. 43. & rursus q. 554. Cum autem in his iuridicialibus parlamentis, regnísque rabulariis permulta sint, quæ boni & cordati viri grauiter & acerbè ferunt, tum verò quatuor hæc in primis numerantur, quòd publica iurisdictionis nundinatio exerceatur, quòd magistratus publico periurio ineantur, quòd parlamenta litium seminaria sint, postremò quod tertia propè Galliæ pars rabulariam artem exerceat. Nam quod ad primum attinet, quotusquisq; hodie numerari potest, qui iudicandi munus non & præsenti pecunia sit mercatus, & præsenti pecunia vēditet? vt verissimè Alexander Cæsar dixisse videatur, necesse esse vt qui magistratum emit, vendat, nec sine rubore puniri posse, qui quod emit, vendit. Et nummarium tribunal (inquit Seneca lib. de benefic. 1.) audita utrinque licitatione alteri addici, non mirum, quando quae emeris, vendere gentium ius est. Hanc boni viri Gallicae iurisdictionis nundinationem, hoc commercium, hoc forense latrocinium appellant: quod res quae humanarum rerum sanctissima esse debuit promercalis facta sit, pretioque & vendatur, & ematur: neque quicquam aeque Galliae existimationem apud exteras nationes onerat, quam quod, sicuti lanij bovem opimum uno pretio emptum, post in macello per partes venditant: ita magistratus uno pretio comparatur, cuius administratio singulis postea ius postulantibus diuendatur. De quo Deum immortalem, Solemque, & caelum, & genus hominum qui hodie viuunt, quique posthac victuri sunt, contestor, si non optimo iure ac meritissimo tam foedam patriae labem, infamiam, dedecus, ac turpitudinem deploro: neque me Matharelli, aut Massoni, aut nescio cuius eiusmodi rabulae scabiosi ac sycophantae meretricia impudentia, aut cuiusquam palpatoris aulici pretio conducta calumnia de hoc iuuandae patriae studio, (si Dei voluntas ferat), dimouebit.
units.tr: From these things it can be inferred how few lawsuits and litigants there were in those times, and how greatly those kings took care to spare their subjects the troubles of litigation. Nor should I pass over what the author of the Speculum writes under the title De Feriis: that in his own time, that is, around the year 1270, the more serious cases and lawsuits were customarily heard in the public council, which, as was said above, was called the Parliament, and that people came to it for justice from all parts of the kingdom. Because of those who had come from distant regions, it was the custom that judgments were held even on feast days. "The custom of the Court of the King of France," he says, "which during the sessions of Parliament renders justice every day, can be excused, so that those coming from distant parts may be dispatched more quickly." But in the course of time, by lawyers' trickery, it was gradually introduced, like a creeping gangrene, that justice was administered both more often and in more places. Hence there survives the ordinance of Philip III, surnamed the Fair, from the year 1302: "Moreover, for the convenience of our subjects and the speedier despatch of cases, we propose to order that the two Parliaments at Paris and the two Exchequers at Rouen, and the sessions at Troyes, shall be held twice a year; and that the Parliament shall be held at Toulouse, as it was accustomed to be held in past times, if the peoples of the land agree. Likewise, since many great causes between great and notable persons are heard in our Parliament, we ordain and will that two prelates and two other suitable lay persons of our council, or at least one prelate and one lay person, shall be continually present in our Parliaments to hear and deliberate on the aforesaid causes." From these words it can be understood, first, how rarely judgments were held in those times, and then how few judges sat in that Parliament. As for the other prefectures and provinces of the kingdom, there is an ordinance of the same Philip the Fair, issued in the same little book in these words, in the year 1302: "We further command that our seneschals and bailiffs hold their assizes summarily within the circuits of their seneschalships and bailiwicks, at least twice in two months." Budaeus, too, writes in the same passage I noted above that in the year 1294 the same King Philip ordained that the Parliament should consist of three kinds of men: prelates, barons, and clerics mixed with laymen. "Since the laymen," he says, "were chosen partly from the knights and partly from the common sort of men. Likewise, that the prelates and barons should choose from that third kind those who seemed fit to exercise jurisdiction in each case; and at the same time that they should choose three men who were to be sent to those regions which used the written law, to hear cases there; and if any capital question was to be tried, they should call in the most learned men." At this point Budaeus, lamenting the corruption of these times and at the same time denouncing the most worthless heads of the lawyers and the robed vultures (as Apuleius calls them), exclaims with the line of Juvenal: "Once upon a time the natives lived by this custom." And he adds thus: "For this is how it comes into my mind to exclaim: in those more ancient ages, while this kingdom nevertheless flourished (as is evident from its coins, struck in pure gold), the method of rendering justice was simple and easy, and lawsuits were rare, nor long-drawn-out as now, nor even perpetual; for that crowd of interpreters of the law had not yet invaded the Commonwealth, nor was the knowledge of law then believed to extend very widely, even to infinite lengths. Rather, a fair and good judge, endowed with integrity and innocence, was worth as much as six hundred volumes. But now, where things have fallen, no one fails to see. Yet all are afraid to say so." Thus far Budaeus, most serious everywhere and most bitter opponent of the lawyers' art. Now, to return to our history and to teach on what beginnings and foundations this litigious kingdom was roused: just as Cicero writes that the ancient Pontiffs, because of the multitude of sacrifices, instituted three men as Epulones, though these had themselves been instituted by Numa to perform the sacrificial feast of the games, so in the same way, from that very small number of Parliamentary judges, as the multitude of lawsuits grew, an incredible progeny of judges and councillors was propagated. And first a huge, costly and magnificent Basilica was built by the command of the king, as we said above, Louis Hutin or Philip the Fair. Then from the moderate number of judges three chambers were made: the Grand Chamber, of Inquests, and of Requests. Budaeus mentions this division in the same passage, but Gaguin more fully in the life of King Louis Hutin. I observe, however, that someone who annotated the Stilus of the Parliament of Paris, where Stephen Aufrerius keeps the same number, has added this note: "Indeed, at the beginning there were only two chambers, because the Chamber of Requests is a lower tribunal; afterwards a third was added, which is called the little Chamber of Inquests." But in the year 1522 King Francis, in order to raise sixty thousand gold crowns, created a fourth chamber from twenty new councillors, taking three thousand gold crowns from each; by this the court was greatly disfigured. Afterwards the number of presidents also was increased for a price. Again the same king, in the year 1543, created twenty others for the sake of profit. Nor does it seem right to pass over what both Gaguin and Budaeus have recorded in the same place, and what is a remarkable lesson for all memory: that that assembly of judges was not perpetual and permanent (as it is in this age), but was held only on notice, and was customarily convened only by the express command of the prince; that is, the king's edict had to be published each year at the beginning of November, so that it might be renewed. "And so that it may be certain that the king is the author of this assembly," says Gaguin in the same place, "royal rescripts are issued each year, by which authority is given to the judges by the king to begin Parliament on the feast of St Martin, that is, on the 11th day before the Ides of November." Concerning the wonderful and rapid growth of this kingdom, this too can serve as proof: that about a hundred years later, that is, in the year 1454, in the reign of Charles VII, this ordinance was promulgated by him: "From the feast of Easter until the end of Parliament, the Presidents and Councillors must be assembled in their chambers at six o'clock in the morning; from the feast of St Martin, after the aforesaid hour, and a little later. It is most necessary that the Presidents and Councillors of the Court come to Parliament after dinner, for the sake of judging and dispatching cases." Thus Charles VII. But how different the manner of judging was in the time of Charles the Great, who held a kingdom three times larger, can easily be understood from his own law: Lex Francica, book 4, chapter 74: "A count shall not hold a court except fasting." Now there is also this argument from the very word Parlamentum and the authority of the name: when a Senate had been established in antiquity in that part of the Allobroges which is called Dauphiné, with the highest authority, and was called the Dauphinese Council, King Louis VI, who wished to show kindness to the Dauphinese, who had deserved well of him, changed the name of the council into Parliament, although he added nothing to its law or authority. Guido Papa bears witness to this matter, in question 43 and again in question 554 at Grenoble. But since in these judicial parliaments and lawyers' kingdoms there are very many things which good and sensible men bear gravely and bitterly, four of these are especially counted: that the public trade in justice is carried on; that magistrates are obtained by public perjury; that the Parliaments are nurseries of lawsuits; and lastly, that nearly a third part of France practises the lawyer's art. For as to the first, how few today can be counted who have not bought the office of judging for ready money, and do not sell it for ready money? So truly did Alexander Caesar seem to say that it was necessary that he who buys a magistracy must sell it, and that he could not be punished without shame who sells what he has bought. And Seneca in his book On Benefits (book 1) says: "A court of money, with bidding heard on both sides, being awarded to another, is no wonder, since to sell what you have bought is the law of nations." This trade in Gallic jurisdiction, this commerce, this forensic robbery, good men call it: that a thing which ought to be the most sacred of human affairs has been made a matter of merchandise, and is both sold and bought for a price. Nothing burdens France's reputation among foreign nations more than this: just as a butcher buys a fat ox for one price and afterwards sells it piece by piece in the market, so a magistracy is bought for one price, and its administration is then sold off in parts to each person who seeks justice. Concerning this I call to witness the immortal God, the Sun, the heavens, and the human race that lives today and that will live hereafter: if I do not, with the best and most deserved right, lament so foul a stain, infamy, disgrace and shame upon my country; and let no one, by the shameless impudence of Matharellus, or of Masson, or of some scabby lawyer and sycophant of that kind, or by the calumny of some courtly flatterer bought for a price, turn me aside, if God wills, from this zeal for helping my country.

units.la: Quid? an quisquam est, qui cogitare illud sine lachrymis possit, quod non modo clientes & beneficiarij Romani Pontificis, & clerici iureiurando ei deuincti, & opimis sacerdotiis praediti, magnam illorum magistratuum partem obtinent: verum etiam ij, qui se Laicos appellari volunt, istiusmodi beneficiis in suos liberos conferendis eiusdem Pontificis tyrannidi se, suamque fidem ac religionē venditant? Iam vero, de periurio passim toto Gallia visitato, quid dicemus? Vetus Imp. Theodosij lex est, gentium, vt opinor, omnium vsu ac moribus comprobata, vt qui magistratum ineunt, publicè iusiurandum dent, se nihil eo nomine neque per se, neque per alium dedisse, aut promisisse. l. vlt. C. de repetund. Hoc quidem iusiurandum, in Gallia quoque, omnibus magistratuum mercatoribus in Parisiensi aliôve Parlamento defertur. at quid dixi defertur? Imò vero confidenter accipitur, conceptisque verbis praestatur, cum tamen admodum pauci ac prope dicam nulli, tota Gallia numerari possint, qui non praesenti numerata ad manum quaestoris pecunia suum Ossicium, ac iurisdictionem sit mercatus. atque is primus sacris istis initiatibus aditus in Gallia patet. Age, reliqua videamus. Nam complures istiusmodi iudicium conuentus qui ad diuimendas lites, ad ciues iudicialibus molestiis liberandos instituti sunt, meras esse litium officinas & ergastula, quis ignorat? aut cui tandem notum in Gallia non est, lite semel institutam hominum istorum artificiis non modò immortalem reddi, sed etiam in alias complures propagari? units.tr: What then? Is there anyone who can think of this without tears: that not only the clients and beneficiaries of the Roman Pontiff, the clergy bound to him by oath and endowed with rich benefices, hold a large part of those magistracies, but that even those who want to be called laymen offer themselves, their loyalty and their religion, to the tyranny of the same Pontiff, by bestowing such benefices on their own children? And as for perjury, practised everywhere throughout the whole of Gaul, what shall we say? There is an old law of the Emperor Theodosius, approved, I think, by the custom and practice of all nations, that those who enter upon a magistracy shall publicly swear that they have given or promised nothing for that office, either by themselves or through another (Cod. last law, de repetundis). This oath is indeed administered in Gaul also to all who buy magistracies in the Parlement of Paris or elsewhere. But why do I say "administered"? Rather, it is taken lightly and sworn in set words, although there are very few, I may almost say none, throughout the whole of Gaul who have not bought their office and jurisdiction by ready money paid into the hand of the treasurer. And this is the first entrance opened to those sacred initiations in Gaul. Come, let us look at the rest. For who does not know that the several courts of this kind, established to settle disputes and to free citizens from legal troubles, are mere workshops and prisons of lawsuits? Or who in Gaul does not know that a suit once begun, by the tricks of these men, is not only made immortal but is also spread into many others? And what comes last: who would not think it miserable and unworthy that the Gallic nation,

Atque huius ego morbi Rabularij (quam verissime scabiem Gallicam appellare possumus) quo magis magisque origi- nem inuestigo: eo magis in illa quam superius protuli, opinione confirmor, vt superstitionum lues, vt alia complura, ex Romanorum Pontificum officina profluxerunt, sic rabulariæ artis disciplinam ex eorundem curia & iurisdictione ad nos defluxisse quod peradmodū paucis post Decretalici iuris promulgationem annis contigisse constat. Nam in Gratiani Decretum (c. vides. 10. dist.) relata est Epistola Leonis Papæ (quem illi in Deorum suorum numerum retulerunt) ad Ludouicum II. vtriusque Franciæ Regem & Imperatorem scripta, qua testatur, se Imperatorum legibus, & constitutionibus, & iuri ab illis constituto parere. & in c. vlt. ab eodem Imp. pro sua clementia petit, vt iuris Ro. leges vbiq; obseruari velit. quinetiam exstat Papæ Honorij III. Decretalis in c.1.Ext.de Iuram. cal.vbi dilucide ostendit, Papales clericos vsq; ad illud tempus Ro. iuris legibus & Christianorum Imp-p. constitutionibus, quæ in Codice Iustiniani exstant, parui sse: íísque etiam in iurifiurandi controuersiis vsos esse. Ecquódnam igitur (dicet aliquis, tantis malis remedium afferemus? Caussam quidem illorum omnium constat esse partim impietatem, partim incredibilem gentis nostræ superstitionem, quæ per eadem illa tempora ex eodem illo fonte ad nos fl axit, quibus immensa caligo vniuersum orbē Christianum obtexerat, & vnico Christianæ religionis lumine extincto, sacris scilicet Bibliis obrutis ac sepultis, omnia densissimis superstitionum tenebris oppressa tenebantur. Quare si per nostros Alastoras, si per furias ciuilium bellorum incentrices licebit, vel (vt verius loquamur) per singularem Dei benignitatem dabitur, vt sacrorum Bibliorum auctoritas in Gallia valeat, & iuuentus in iis se studiis exerceat, non dubium est, quin, vt exorto sole tenebræ fugantur, sic artes rabulariæ vnà cum superstitionibus ex eodem fonte deductis, depellantur. quod vt Deus optimus maximus propter Christi filij sui & Emanuelis nostri gloriam nostræ huic ætati concedat, toto pectore ab eo precor, quæsoque.
units.tr: the most suited of all the nations the sun sees to good arts, and especially to the study of letters and, I add, of piety, should spend its life in stirring up lawsuits, in practising calumnies and sycophancy, and finally in the filth of pettifoggery, as if emptying sewers and privies? This nation, which some three hundred years ago was almost free of lawsuits and, as they then put it, managed the affairs of the commonwealth and the public good in its yearly assemblies, now lets the whole care of the commonwealth, occupied with these muddy filths, be entrusted to a few courtiers and royal flatterers. And the more closely I investigate the origin of this disease of pettifoggery (which we may most truly call the Gallic itch), the more I am confirmed in that opinion I put forward above: just as the plague of superstitions and many other things flowed from the workshop of the Roman Pontiffs, so the discipline of the pettifogging art has flowed down to us from their court and jurisdiction. It is established that this came about within a very few years after the publication of the canon law. For in Gratian's Decretum (c. Vides, dist. 10) is cited a letter of Pope Leo (whom they have placed among their gods) written to Louis II, King and Emperor of both France, in which he testifies that he obeys the laws and constitutions of the Emperors and the law established by them. And in c. last, he asks of the same Emperor, for his clemency, that he wish the laws of Roman law to be observed everywhere. Moreover there is extant a decretal of Pope Honorius III (c. 1, Ext. de iurand. cal.), where he clearly shows that the Papal clergy, up to that time, obeyed the laws of Roman law and the constitutions of the Christian Emperors which are in the Code of Justinian, and that they also used them in controversies over oaths. What remedy, then, will someone say, shall we bring to such great evils? The cause of all of these is clearly partly impiety and partly the incredible superstition of our nation, which flowed to us from that same source in those times when an immense darkness had covered the whole Christian world, and with the single light of the Christian religion extinguished, namely the holy Bibles buried and entombed, everything was held oppressed by the thickest darkness of superstitions. Therefore, if through our Alastors, through the Furies who stir up civil wars, it shall be allowed, or (to speak more truly) through the singular kindness of God it shall be granted, that the authority of the holy Bibles prevails in Gaul and the youth exercise themselves in those studies, there is no doubt that, just as darkness is put to flight when the sun rises, so the arts of pettifoggery, together with the superstitions derived from the same source, will be driven away. That God, best and greatest, may grant this to our age for the glory of his Son Christ and our Emmanuel, I pray and beseech him with my whole heart.
